lineages.title: The Man in the High Castle
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick

divergence.label: Zangara kills President-elect Roosevelt
divergence.delta: Real: Giuseppe Zangara fires at Franklin D. Roosevelt in Miami on 15 February 1933 and misses; Chicago mayor Anton Cermak takes the fatal bullet and dies on 6 March, and Zangara is executed on 20 March. Fiction: the same shots kill Roosevelt, the New Deal never happens, the United States stays isolationist, and the Axis wins the Second World War in 1947.
divergence.note: Dick states the assassination and its consequences directly in the novel's background chapters. The attempt itself is historical; the fork is who it killed.

ending.why: The Reich stands but its succession is breaking open; Dick leaves the world mid-crisis, with a novel-within-the-novel hinting it is not the real one.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real collapse of the American stock market opens the Great Depression, the economic catastrophe that in our history Roosevelt's New Deal is built to fight; in the novel that answer never comes, and the slump is still running in the 1960s.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and load-bearing for the fiction, which states that the Depression simply continued for want of a Roosevelt. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929. Sits in T3 because the tier cutoffs are absolute calendar dates, and carries phase prehistory because it is before this branch forks.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: Miami, 15 February 1933: the shot that misses in our history
events.description: In the real world Zangara's five shots mortally wound Mayor Anton Cermak while Roosevelt is untouched; here the same afternoon kills the president-elect, and Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America under German and Japanese rule.
events.note: One real-world year, one event: this entry carries both the historical attempt and the fictional outcome, because the fork and the contrast are the same afternoon. Dated at the divergence, so it is T3 by the taxonomy rather than T4. Real Cermak died on 6 March 1933 and Zangara was executed on 20 March.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: president-elect alive → killed before taking office

events.title: The Axis wins the Second World War
events.description: Germany takes continental Europe and the European Soviet Union, Japan takes the Pacific and lands on the American west coast, and the Allies surrender in 1947; the United States is partitioned into the Pacific States, the Rocky Mountain buffer, the Nazi-ruled South and a northeastern puppet state.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Allies won in 1945. The novel dates the Allied surrender to 1947 and sets its present day fifteen years later. Two background facts share this year with no dates of their own - the Reich's rockets have already carried colonisation missions to the Moon and to Venus and Mars, and the Mediterranean has been drained for farmland - so they are folded in here rather than given entries.
events.binWhy: The Allies surrender and the country is partitioned.

facets.change: world war → Allied surrender and partition

events.title: The Grasshopper Lies Heavy is published
events.description: Hawthorne Abendsen publishes a counterfactual novel in which the Allies beat the Axis in 1945; the Reich bans it, Japan permits it, and within the novel's own world it is exactly the kind of alternate history this dataset describes.
events.note: The book is in wide circulation by 1962 but the novel never fixes its publication year; 1955 is an approximation chosen to sit between the 1947 peace and the 1962 narrative.
events.binWhy: A banned book tells the population the other history.

facets.change: official history → banned counter-history circulates

events.title: Bormann dies and the Reich's succession crisis breaks open
events.description: Hitler is already incapacitated by tertiary syphilis and Martin Bormann has been running the Reich as acting chancellor; his death of a short illness opens the contest to succeed, Goebbels is named chancellor and plans a surprise nuclear strike on Japan under the code name Operation Dandelion, and Heydrich launches a putsch to stop him.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Hitler died in a Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945 and Bormann disappeared days later, his remains identified only in 1972. In the novel both are alive into the 1960s. Three linked succession facts share the novel's undifferentiated present year, so they are merged into one entry rather than split across invented dates.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: acting ruler dies → contest for succession

lineages.groupingNote: Textbook alternate past: one bullet in Miami in 1933 removes Roosevelt, and Philip K. Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America in 1962. The novel is the source of truth here. Where the 2015 Amazon series diverges: it keeps the 1933 assassination but stretches the war to an Axis victory in 1945-46, renames the neutral buffer the Neutral Zone, makes Juliana and Joe's road trip the spine of the story, keeps Abendsen alive and central, and replaces the novel's ambiguous I Ching mysticism with an explicit multiverse in which films of the Allies winning are literally windows into our world; it also rotates Nazi leadership figures the novel leaves alive. Confidence on the novel's core divergence is high; series-only dates are excluded rather than blended. On coverage: this lineage spans 1929 to 1962, so it has T3 events and one T4, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the fiction never goes past 1962, and its furthest reach is the Reich's off-world colonisation mentioned in the same year as the story. No future events were invented to fill those tiers. For franchiseStatus, the novel is concluded but was adapted into a 2015-2019 series, so read this as the lineage of the 1962 book, not of the Amazon show.

lineages.title: Watchmen
lineages.creator: Alan Moore & Dave Gibbons

divergence.label: Hooded Justice puts on a mask and is not a comic-book character
divergence.delta: Real: the costumed hero of 1938 is a newsstand invention called Superman, and masked vigilantism stays fiction. Fiction: a real hooded man starts operating in New York in 1938, masked adventurers become an American institution, and by 1959 one of them is a god who wins Vietnam and keeps Nixon in the White House.
divergence.note: The comic's own backmatter dates the start of the Minutemen era to the late 1930s and names Hooded Justice as the first; the sharper break is 1959 and Doctor Manhattan, who is what actually rewrites global history.

ending.why: Peace is bought with a staged massacre and a lie, and Rorschach's journal sits in a slush pile waiting to unmake it.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real stock market collapse of October 1929 opens the Depression that the 1930s costumed adventurers emerge out of, and it is unchanged in this timeline: Watchmen's history is identical to ours until a man puts on a hood in 1938.
events.note: Real-history anchor, genuinely before this lineage's fork and consistent with everything the comic shows about the period it borrows. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: The real Miami attempt and the rest of our century
events.description: Zangara's shots kill Mayor Cermak and miss Roosevelt, and from that afternoon the real twentieth century runs its course - New Deal, world war, Cold War, Vietnam lost in 1975 - which is the history Watchmen quietly replaces with its own.
events.note: Genuinely before this lineage's 1938 fork, so its phase is prehistory and it is unchanged in this fiction: Watchmen does not fork on this afternoon the way The Man in the High Castle does, and that contrast is the point of this group. Its tier is still T3, because tier is an absolute calendar bucket and 1933 is the twentieth century. The rest of the real century is not enumerated as separate entries; the events below mark where the fiction leaves it.
events.binWhy: The attempt on Roosevelt fails; real history keeps its leader and its century.

facets.change: attempt on the president-elect fails → the century runs its course

events.title: Hooded Justice starts the costumed era
events.description: A masked man in a hood and noose begins operating in New York, the first of a real tradition of costumed adventurers; the following year eight of them are assembled into a public team called the Minutemen, turning masked vigilantism from a curiosity into an institution that will define the century.
events.note: Real history for contrast: in 1938 the costumed hero is Superman, published in Action Comics #1 and entirely fictional. The comic names Hooded Justice as the first real masked adventurer and dates the Minutemen's formation a year later; the two founding beats share this short window and are merged rather than given invented months. Both are phase fork.
events.binWhy: Masked adventurers are assembled into a public team.

facets.change: no masks → costumed vigilantes organise

events.title: Jon Osterman becomes Doctor Manhattan
events.description: A physicist disintegrated in an intrinsic-field test chamber reassembles himself as a being who perceives all time at once and can transmute matter at will; from this year the United States has a superpower that is a person, and the Cold War becomes a one-sided contest.
events.note: The accident is firmly in the late 1950s but the comic does not print a single unambiguous year on the page; 1959 is the standard reading and matches the in-universe chronologies. Real history for contrast: 1959 is the year DARPA is founded, not the year a man becomes a god.
events.binWhy: A person, or humanity, passes beyond the human.

facets.change: a physicist → a being who remakes matter

events.title: Vietnam is won in weeks
events.description: Doctor Manhattan is deployed to Indochina and the war ends in a decisive American victory; Nixon becomes a national hero, the anti-war movement never happens, and the United States is free to press the Soviet Union everywhere else.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Saigon fell in 1975 and the last American combat troops left in 1973. Two years later, in the real 1972, the Watergate break-in destroyed a president; in this timeline it is never uncovered and Nixon serves on into the 1980s. Both facts share this stretch of the fiction's history and are noted together rather than split across a contested year.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: quagmire → decisive victory by one superweapon

events.title: The Keene Act outlaws masked vigilantes
events.description: After years of police strikes and public hostility to costumed crime-fighters, Congress bans freelance vigilantism; only government employees keep their masks, and the rest of the heroes either retire, sell out or go underground.
events.note: Dated directly in the comic's backmatter; this is the legal event that creates the story's central condition of retired heroes.
events.binWhy: The state bans, disarms or attacks a group.

facets.change: vigilantes tolerated → outlawed

events.title: November 1985: the Comedian's murder and the psychic squid
events.description: Edward Blake is thrown from his apartment window on 12 October, pulling the surviving heroes back into each other's lives; three weeks later Adrian Veidt teleports a manufactured alien into lower Manhattan, where its dying psychic scream kills millions, the world reads it as an extraterrestrial attack, and the United States and the Soviet Union step back from war over the largest lie in human history.
events.note: Both landmark beats fall in the story's single present year, so they are merged into one entry with the psychically loudest date. The comic ends with Rorschach's journal sitting in a newspaper slush pile, so whether the lie holds is deliberately unresolved; the HBO continuation answers it in 2019 and continues the same continuity rather than forking a new one.
events.binWhy: A manufactured monster kills half of Manhattan to force a peace.

facets.change: brink of nuclear war → staged attack forces a peace

lineages.groupingNote: Alternate past with the fork in the 1930s-50s: real masked adventurers, then a real atomic superman, and every subsequent historical event downstream - Vietnam won in 1971, Watergate buried, Nixon in the White House into the 1980s, and a 1985 that ends with millions dead in Manhattan to avert Armageddon. The comic is the source of truth. The 2009 film keeps the same historical spine, and the 2019 HBO series is a continuation set in 2019 rather than a divergence, so there is no adaptation conflict of the kind The Man in the High Castle has. The one place confidence drops is Doctor Manhattan's transformation year, which the comic never states outright. On coverage: the branch runs 1938 to 1985, so every event sits in the twentieth century and this lineage is T3 with a couple of T4 anchors, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the comic's furthest reach is 1985 and the sequel material stops in 2019. This is the archetype's purest case of a branch that stays inside living memory, and nothing was invented to give it a future tier.

lineages.title: SS-GB
lineages.creator: Len Deighton

divergence.label: The Luftwaffe wins the Battle of Britain and the invasion comes
divergence.delta: Real: in 1940 the RAF holds off the Luftwaffe through the summer and autumn, and on 17 September Hitler postpones Operation Sea Lion indefinitely. Fiction: the RAF loses, German troops land near Ashford and take London, the King and Churchill are captured, and in February 1941 Britain's forces surrender.
divergence.inUniverse: The invasion of 1940; the instrument of surrender of February 1941; the story in November 1941
divergence.note: The novel keeps real history to the summer of 1940 and changes the outcome of the air battle. It gives the surrender as February 1941 in its opening document and sets the story nine months later, in November 1941; the landings themselves are dated only to 1940 in the summaries consulted. Its 1941 also lacks the German invasion of the Soviet Union, a consequence of the fork rather than a second one.

sources.title: Wikipedia: SS-GB
Speesh Reads: Review of SS-GB - 'In February 1941 British Command surrendered'
Wikipedia: Operation Sea Lion

ending.why: Britain is still occupied and the King is dead, but the Americans have taken Germany's atomic research and the King's death beside US Marines is meant to bring them into the war; the novel ends before either consequence arrives.

events.title: Hitler becomes chancellor
events.description: President Hindenburg appoints Adolf Hitler chancellor of Germany after weeks of backroom negotiation, and within months the Reichstag fire gives him the pretext for dictatorship. The regime that occupies Britain in the novel is this one, eight years on.
events.note: Real history, before the fork.
events.binWhy: A leader wins office by appointment and legal manoeuvre and uses it to rule alone.

facets.change: a weak republic → a dictatorship by decree

sources.title: Wikipedia: Adolf Hitler's rise to power

events.title: The Night of the Long Knives
events.description: Hitler has the SS and Gestapo murder the SA leadership under Ernst Röhm and other rivals, confirming his supremacy and binding the army to him. The SS that comes out of it is the organisation of the novel's title, and its feud with the army and the Abwehr drives the plot.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The official toll was 85; estimates run to a thousand. In the novel the SS runs the police of occupied Britain and is at odds with the German Army, which conspires with the British Resistance to embarrass it.
events.binWhy: Rivals inside the ruling movement are killed in a planned purge.

facets.change: a rival private army → the SS supreme

events.title: The Luftwaffe is revealed
events.description: Germany officially establishes an air force that the Versailles Treaty forbade, weeks before announcing rearmament and conscription. It is the force that, in the novel, wins the air battle over England that it lost in ours.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia dates the Luftwaffe's official establishment to 26 February 1935 and the announcement of rearmament to 16 March.
events.binWhy: A new military body is founded that will decide the war over Britain.

facets.change: a banned air arm → an open air force

sources.title: Wikipedia: Luftwaffe

events.title: Edward VIII abdicates
events.description: Edward VIII gives up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson, and his brother becomes George VI. In the novel George VI is the king held in the Tower of London, and the Duke of Windsor has escaped to the Bahamas.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Edward signed the instrument of abdication on 10 December and broadcast from Windsor on 11 December. In our history he was made Governor of the Bahamas in July 1940; the novel keeps him there.
events.binWhy: A ruler steps down and his brother succeeds.

facets.change: Edward VIII → George VI

sources.title: Wikipedia: Abdication of Edward VIII

events.title: Nuclear fission is discovered
events.description: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin find barium in bombarded uranium, and Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explain it as the splitting of the nucleus. The novel's plot turns on where that knowledge leads: a German atomic research station at Bringle Sands in Devon, and an American wish to have it.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Hahn wrote to Meitner on 19 December and the results were submitted on 22 December 1938. The novel's German programme is code-named 'Apocalypse'.
events.binWhy: A discovery about matter arrives that makes an atomic bomb possible.

facets.change: radiochemistry → the splitting of the atom

sources.title: Wikipedia: Discovery of nuclear fission

events.title: The Nazi-Soviet Pact
events.description: Germany and the Soviet Union sign a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe, and on 1 September Germany invades Poland; Britain declares war two days later. In the novel the pact is still in force in 1941: the Soviet Navy has bases at Rosyth, Scapa Flow and Invergordon, and Karl Marx's body is to be moved from Highgate to Moscow.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The pact was signed on 24 August and dated 23 August; Germany invaded Poland on 1 September. In our history it ended with the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, which the novel's 1941 does not have.
events.binWhy: Two enemies sign a pact that frees one of them to make war in the west.

facets.change: ideological enemies → partners in conquest

sources.title: Wikipedia: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact

events.title: The RAF loses, and the Germans land in Kent
events.description: The Luftwaffe wins the air battle over southern England and the invasion goes ahead: German troops land near Ashford, Canterbury is declared an open city and London falls, while a rearguard at Colchester holds long enough for the Royal Navy to escape from Harwich. The King and Churchill are taken prisoner, and Britain's gold is shipped to Canada.
events.inUniverse: Landings near Ashford; Canterbury an open city; the Colchester rearguard
events.note: In our history the RAF held the Luftwaffe off between July and October 1940 and Hitler postponed Operation Sea Lion indefinitely on 17 September. Wikipedia's summary of the novel places the landings in 1940; the reviews count the novel's 'nine months' from the surrender of February 1941, so the fighting in England may run on into that winter. No month is given for the landings.
events.binWhy: Britain is defeated and its capital and territory occupied.

facets.change: an island at war → an occupied country

events.title: The King dies at Bringle Sands
events.description: Britain's forces sign an instrument of surrender in February and Churchill is court-martialled in Berlin and shot. In November, while Superintendent Douglas Archer of Scotland Yard investigates the murder of an atomic scientist, the Resistance and the German Army free the comatose George VI from SS custody and try to get him to an American landing party; he is killed in an SS ambush, and the rescue turns out to be cover for a larger US raid that carries off the Bringle Sands research.
events.inUniverse: November 1941, 'nine months' after the surrender
events.note: The surrender is dated February 1941 by the novel's opening document and by reviews; one search summary gives 19 February, which could not be confirmed. The story is set in November 1941 and the raid comes at its end; the day is not given. Archer concludes that the Resistance leader Mayhew arranged a martyr's death beside American Marines to bring the United States into the war, and that Princess Elizabeth, fifteen, will be crowned in exile.
events.binWhy: An imprisoned monarch is killed in a fight between the occupiers and those trying to free him.

facets.change: a captive king → a dead one and a queen in exile

events.description: Jonathan Cape publishes Len Deighton's novel, subtitled in some editions 'Nazi-Occupied Britain 1941'.
events.note: The BBC adapted it as a five-part series broadcast on BBC One from 19 February to 19 March 2017, which changes several details; this lineage follows the novel.
events.binWhy: A publication date, not a moment in the story's history; it carries no bin.

The fiction covers two years, the invasion and the occupation's first November, so it has two fictional events; the six before it are the real history it builds on, from Hitler's appointment to the Nazi-Soviet Pact. All events are T3: nothing before 1933 bears on it and the novel ends in 1941.

lineages.title: The Plot Against America
lineages.creator: Philip Roth

divergence.label: Lindbergh takes the nomination and the White House
divergence.delta: Real: 1940 - the Republicans nominate Wendell Willkie and Roosevelt wins a third term. Fiction: Charles Lindbergh makes a surprise appearance on the convention's last night, is nominated, and beats Roosevelt in a landslide in November.
divergence.note: Roth keeps every real person and every real date up to the Republican convention of June 1940 and changes only the nominee; his closing 'True Chronology' documents the real history. The novel then rejoins our history in late 1942, a year late, when Roosevelt is back and Pearl Harbor brings America into the war.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Plot Against America
Wikipedia: 1940 United States presidential election
LitCharts: The Plot Against America plot summary

ending.why: Lindbergh is gone, Wheeler's coup collapses in days, Roosevelt is re-elected and America enters the war against Hitler, though Seldon Wishnow has lost his mother in the riots and the Roths' street is not the same.

events.title: Lindbergh flies to Paris
events.description: Charles Lindbergh, a twenty-five-year-old airmail pilot, flies alone and nonstop from New York to Paris in the Spirit of St. Louis in about thirty-three hours, and becomes the most famous man in the world. The fame is what makes him a candidate thirteen years later.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Charles Lindbergh (1927 flight; 1932 kidnapping)

events.note: Real history, which Roth's novel and its closing 'True Chronology' rely on: the flight of 20-21 May 1927.
events.binWhy: A first flight into untried distance makes an aviator a national hero.

facets.change: an unknown airmail pilot → the first solo nonstop Atlantic crossing

events.title: The Lindbergh baby is kidnapped
events.description: The Lindberghs' twenty-month-old son, Charles Jr., is taken from his cot and murdered, in what the press calls the crime of the century. In the novel the kidnapping returns in 1942, when rumour and the regime's own propaganda claim the child is still alive.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Charles Lindbergh (1927 flight; 1932 kidnapping)
LitCharts: Chapter 8 'Bad Days' (the newsreel chronology, 6-16 October 1942)

events.note: Real history: 1 March 1932. In the novel's October 1942 the newspapers run the headline 'AGAIN!' over the child's photograph, and Aunt Evelyn repeats Rabbi Bengelsdorf's claim that the Nazis took the boy and used him to control his father.
events.binWhy: A targeted crime against a public figure's family becomes the lever for later conspiracy theories.

facets.change: a hero's family → a murdered child and a national obsession

events.title: War in Europe; Lindbergh speaks against intervention
events.description: Germany invades Poland and Britain and France declare war. On 15 September Lindbergh makes his first national radio address against American involvement, and becomes the leading voice of the movement to keep the United States out.

sources.title: Wikipedia: America First Committee (Lindbergh's first radio address, 15 September 1939)

events.note: Real history before the fork. The America First Committee was founded on 4 September 1940; in reality Lindbergh joined its national committee in April 1941 and gave his Des Moines speech blaming Jews for pushing America to war on 11 September 1941, a speech the novel's Lindbergh never needs to give.
events.binWhy: The Second World War begins, and with it the American argument over whether to join it.

facets.change: an uneasy peace → war in Europe and an isolationist movement at home

events.title: Lindbergh beats Roosevelt
events.description: Lindbergh makes a surprise appearance on the last night of the Republican convention in June and is nominated. On the slogan 'Vote for Lindbergh, or vote for war' he beats Franklin Roosevelt in a landslide in November, with the isolationist Senator Burton K. Wheeler as his running mate.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Plot Against America
LitCharts: The Plot Against America plot summary
Wikipedia: 1940 United States presidential election

events.note: Real 1940: the Republicans nominated Wendell Willkie on the sixth ballot at Philadelphia, and Roosevelt won a third term on 5 November with 449 electoral votes to 82. The novel's narrator, Philip, is seven that autumn.
events.binWhy: A national hero with Nazi sympathies takes the presidency at the ballot box on a platform of staying out of the war.

facets.change: Roosevelt's third term → President Lindbergh

events.title: The Iceland Understanding
events.description: Weeks after his inauguration Lindbergh meets Hitler in Iceland and signs an agreement that the United States will not interfere in Europe; a matching Hawaii Understanding with Japan leaves Asia to Tokyo. At home a new Office of American Absorption begins sending Jewish boys to live with farm families in the heartland, and Philip's cousin Alvin goes to Canada to fight for Britain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Plot Against America
Smithsonian: The true history behind The Plot Against America
LitCharts: The Plot Against America plot summary

events.note: The novel dates the Understanding to the weeks after the January 1941 inauguration; the Just Folks summer programme and Alvin's departure (June 1941) fall in the same year. In real 1941 Lend-Lease passed in March, and in December Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
events.binWhy: The United States signs non-aggression understandings with Germany and Japan.

facets.change: an unaligned neutral → America at peace with Hitler and Japan

events.title: Lindbergh vanishes, and the country turns back
events.description: Homestead 42 relocates Jewish families from the cities to the interior. Walter Winchell runs for president against Lindbergh; his tour is met by anti-Jewish riots in Boston and Detroit that spread through the Midwest, and he is assassinated in Louisville on 5 October. On 7 October Lindbergh's plane disappears; Acting President Wheeler declares martial law, riots on 12 October kill 122, and prominent Jews are arrested, until Anne Morrow Lindbergh's broadcast on 16 October brings Wheeler down. Roosevelt wins an emergency election in November, and the next month Japan attacks Pearl Harbor.
events.inUniverse: the newsreel chronology of 6-16 October 1942

sources.title: LitCharts: Chapter 8 'Bad Days' (the newsreel chronology, 6-16 October 1942)
Wikipedia: The Plot Against America
LitCharts: The Plot Against America plot summary

events.note: Every date comes from the novel's own day-by-day chronology in chapter 8; the election falls 'two and a half weeks' after 16 October and Pearl Harbor 'the next month', i.e. December 1942 instead of December 1941. The whole climax falls in one year, so it is one entry; Lindbergh is never found.
events.binWhy: The president vanishes, his deputy's coup under martial law fails within days, and the old president returns; the crackdown and the pogroms are this year's other moments.

facets.change: President Lindbergh → vanished, Wheeler deposed, Roosevelt back

events.title: The Plot Against America is published
events.description: Roth's novel is published with a postscript, 'A True Chronology of the Major Figures', that separates the history from the invention.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Plot Against America
ReadingGroupGuides: The Plot Against America discussion guide (the postscript 'A True Chronology of the Major Figures')

events.note: Publication in October 2004, per Wikipedia. HBO's six-part adaptation by David Simon and Ed Burns followed in 2020.
events.binWhy: A publication, not an event in the story, so it has no bin or facets.

lineages.groupingNote: Alternate Past in its plainest form: one American election in 1940 goes the other way, and the story is how close the country came to fascism before history snapped back two years later. It follows Roth's 2004 novel; the 2020 HBO series is not used for dates. The pre-fork events (1927, 1932, 1939) are real history that Roth recounts in his 'True Chronology'. The novel spans only June 1940 to late 1942, so after the fork there are just three entries, one per year, and the whole 1942 climax is a single entry. Every story event is T3 (1927-1942); T4, T2 and T1 are empty because the history is Lindbergh's life and the novel ends in 1942.

lineages.title: Fatherland
lineages.creator: Robert Harris

divergence.label: Heydrich survives Operation Anthropoid
divergence.delta: Real: Czech agents mortally wound Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in May 1942 and he dies on 4 June; the SS loses the man who would have run the Final Solution's machinery from the top. Fiction: Heydrich lives, succeeds Himmler as Reichsführer-SS, and the Eastern Front goes the other way until Britain starves into surrender in 1944.
divergence.note: Harris's author's note says the historical figures are accurate up to 1942 and fictional afterwards, which pins the fork to this year; the novel never spells the survival out in one sentence, but the whole backstory depends on it.

ending.why: The Reich endures, the detective dies at the camp, and only the faint chance that the evidence reaches America is left.

events.title: Hitler's dictatorship is made legal
events.description: The Reichstag fire of 27 February is followed by the Enabling Act on 23 March, giving Hitler the power to legislate without parliament; the novel states that both the fire decree and the Enabling Act remain in force in 1964, so this is the constitutional machinery the whole alternate Reich still runs on.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and singled out by Harris himself as still-operative law in the fiction. Real dates: Reichstag fire 27 February 1933, Enabling Act 23 March 1933. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: Emergency decree makes the dictatorship legal.

facets.change: democracy → dictatorship by emergency law

events.title: Wannsee's paper trail, and the fork at Prague
events.description: In January Heydrich chairs fifteen officials at a villa on the Wannsee to coordinate the extermination of Europe's Jews, and the minutes he circulates are the paper trail Xavier March spends the novel reassembling. In May Czech agents ambush Heydrich's car in Prague; in the real world he dies of the wounds on 4 June and the SS loses the man who ran the Final Solution's machinery, while here he survives to succeed Himmler as Reichsführer-SS and to redirect the Eastern Front.
events.note: Both halves of the hinge fall in this one real-world year, so they share an entry: the conference that created the document trail every murder victim in the plot attended, and the assassination that in our history removed the man who ordered it. Both are real history - Wannsee 20 January 1942, the attack 27 May 1942, Heydrich's death 4 June 1942 - and the fiction changes only the second. The month is used rather than a day because Harris does not dramatise the attack. Phase fork.
events.binWhy: The assassination that succeeds in our history fails here; the architect of Wannsee lives.

facets.change: assassination attempt → fails; the architect lives

events.title: Case Blue takes the Caucasus
events.description: The German summer offensive succeeds where it failed in our history, cutting the Red Army off from its oil and pushing the Soviets east of the Urals; the Eastern Front becomes a German colonial war rather than a German defeat.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Sixth Army was destroyed at Stalingrad in early 1943 and the Caucasus offensive collapsed. Fatherland has the Caucasus secured by 1943.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: stalled front → offensive takes the oil

events.title: Britain starves into surrender
events.description: With the German discovery that Enigma has been broken the U-boat campaign strangles Britain, D-Day never happens, and London makes peace with the Reich; Churchill, George VI and the royal family flee to Canada while Edward VIII is reinstated on the throne.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Normandy landings took place on 6 June 1944 and Britain fought on to 1945. The novel dates the British surrender to 1944.
events.binWhy: Strangled by blockade, the island makes peace and its government flees.

facets.change: blockaded island → surrender, government in exile

events.title: The European war ends with Germany in the Urals
events.description: Germany tests an atomic bomb and fires a non-nuclear V-3 over New York to prove it can strike the American mainland; the United States beats Japan alone in 1945, and the two surviving powers settle into a Cold War with the Reich's frontier on the Ural Mountains.
events.note: The novel puts the end of the war and the German bomb test around 1946 without a month; the V-3 demonstration over New York is given as the reason the United States never tried to liberate Europe.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: war → atomic stalemate between two powers

events.title: The Urals guerrilla war grinds on
events.description: Rump Russia, kept alive by American money and weapons, bleeds the Reich in Siberia and the Urals; the novel cites at least a hundred thousand German casualties since 1960, and the colonisation of the east is quietly failing.
events.note: The novel gives the 1960 casualty figure rather than a start date for the insurgency; used as the earliest year the text explicitly quantifies.
events.binWhy: An occupation bleeds for years along a frontier.

facets.change: conquest → endless insurgency on the frontier

events.title: Himmler dies in a plane crash
events.description: The Reichsführer-SS is killed in an air crash and Heydrich succeeds him, putting the architect of the Wannsee machinery in charge of the SS and making him the likely next Führer.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Himmler was captured and killed himself in May 1945. The novel states the 1962 crash as an accomplished fact two years before its narrative present.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: security chief → dies; the architect succeeds him

events.title: Hitler withdraws from government
events.description: The Führer becomes reclusive and increasingly invisible, governing through subordinates and appearing only for set pieces; the succession question becomes the real politics of the Reich and every faction starts positioning.
events.note: The novel presents Hitler as already withdrawn when the story opens and does not date the withdrawal; 1963 is the last full year before the narrative and is used as the best-supported reading.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: visible ruler → recluse governing through others

events.title: Hitler's 75th birthday, the Kennedy visit, and the unmarked camp
events.description: Berlin stages the Führer's birthday as the centrepiece of a detente with Washington, with President Joseph P. Kennedy arriving to negotiate an end to American support for the Russian guerrillas - which is why the last Wannsee survivors, Josef Bühler fished out of the Havel among them, must be dead before the cameras arrive. March, having sent Charlotte Maguire over the Swiss border with the documents, leads the Gestapo to the razed site near Auschwitz, finds bricks under the undergrowth, and walks into the birch woods with his pistol drawn.
events.note: The novel's action runs from 14 to 20 April 1964 and all of its major beats fall in that one week, so they are merged here rather than split across invented days. Real history for contrast: Hitler died in 1945 and Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. was never president - his son John was, and was assassinated in 1963. The novel deliberately leaves March's death off the page.
events.binWhy: Those who know keep it from those who do not.

facets.change: evidence exists → erased to buy a detente

lineages.groupingNote: A single historical death inverted - Heydrich not dying in Prague in 1942 - produces a German victory in the East, a British surrender in 1944, and a 1964 in which a Berlin detective solves a murder he cannot survive. Harris's author's note dates the accuracy cutoff to 1942, so the fork is the May 1942 ambush and the real Wannsee Conference four months earlier shares its entry, because both halves of the hinge fall in the same real-world year. The pre-divergence anchor is the 1933 Reichstag fire and Enabling Act, which Harris explicitly keeps in force in his 1964. On coverage: the branch spans 1933 to 1964, so it is T3 throughout with one T4 prehistory entry, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - Fatherland ends in April 1964 and there is no sequel or continuation material, so nothing was invented to reach forward. The one device Harris reaches for - a German Cold War, a space programme at Peenemünde, nuclear submarines at Trondheim - is all contemporary with the story, not deep time. A 1994 HBO television film adapts the same plot with the same internal dates, so there is no adaptation conflict here.

lineages.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
lineages.creator: George Orwell

divergence.label: The atomic war of the 1950s
divergence.delta: Real: 1954 - the hydrogen bomb is tested at Bikini but never used, and Britain is a parliamentary democracy with a welfare state. Fiction: hundreds of atomic bombs fall on the industrial centres of Europe, Russia and North America, one on Colchester, and Britain goes through civil war to one-party rule.
divergence.inUniverse: 'the atomic war of the nineteen-fifties'; a bomb fell 'thirty years earlier' than 1984
divergence.note: Orwell dates almost nothing: the Party has rewritten the past and Winston is not even sure the year is 1984. What the book does say is that the carving of the world into blocs was 'foreseen before the middle of the twentieth century', so its 1940s are ours; the first thing it describes that our history lacks is the atomic war. The atomic war is placed at 1954 from two anchors that agree (bombs used on a large scale 'about ten years' after the 1940s; a bomb 'thirty years earlier' than 1984). Any year from about 1950 to 1956 fits the text.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text
Wikipedia: Nineteen Eighty-Four

ending.why: Winston is broken and loves Big Brother, the Party is intact, and the permanent war goes on.

events.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four is published
events.description: Secker & Warburg publish Orwell's ninth and last completed book in London. It is set thirty-five years ahead, in a Britain renamed Airstrip One.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nineteen Eighty-Four

events.note: Publication date from Wikipedia. The novel was written in 1947-48, so everything up to the late 1940s in its background is the world its first readers knew.
events.binWhy: A publication, not an event in the story, so it has no bin or facets.

events.title: The atomic war
events.description: Some hundreds of atomic bombs are dropped on industrial centres, chiefly in European Russia, Western Europe and North America; one of them falls on Colchester. The ruling groups of every country conclude that a few more would end organised society and their own power with it, and although nothing is ever agreed, no more bombs are dropped.
events.inUniverse: 'the atomic war of the nineteen-fifties' (Goldstein's book)

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: Orwell never gives the year. Goldstein's book says the bombs 'first appeared as early as the nineteen-forties, and were first used on a large scale about ten years later', which puts the war around 1955; Julia's hiding place is a belfry in country 'where an atomic bomb had fallen thirty years earlier', which from 1984 is about 1954. Winston remembers a surprise air raid, perhaps the Colchester bomb, as one of his early memories, which could push it a few years earlier. 1954 is where the two numerical anchors meet. The real 1954 had H-bomb tests but no nuclear war.
events.binWhy: An atomic war is fought on the world's industrial centres; the stalemate that follows is its result, not its start.

facets.change: a nuclear-armed peace → hundreds of atomic bombs on the industrial centres

events.title: Civil war, and the Party takes Britain
events.description: In the hunger and fighting after the bombs Britain goes through a civil war, and the Party that calls its doctrine English Socialism comes out of it in power. Winston's mother and baby sister vanish in these years, when he is ten or eleven; the Party later rewrites the period so thoroughly that no one can say when it took over.
events.inUniverse: 'the Revolution'; 'the civil war of the 1950s'

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text
Wikipedia: Nineteen Eighty-Four

events.note: Derived, not stated. Winston believes he is thirty-nine in 1984, so he was born about 1944-45; his mother disappeared when he was 'ten or eleven', 'nearly thirty years ago', which gives about 1955, and Wikipedia's summary places it in the civil war of the 1950s. Winston cannot remember when the Party came into existence and had not heard the word Ingsoc before 1960, and Goldstein's book speaks of 'the revolutionary period of the fifties and sixties', so the seizure is best read as a process through the later 1950s with 1955 as its first datable point.
events.binWhy: A faction comes out of a civil war holding the state and turns it into a one-party regime.

facets.change: parliamentary Britain in ruins → rule by the Party

events.title: Three superstates settle into permanent war
events.description: With the British Empire absorbed by the United States and Europe by Russia, Oceania and Eurasia already exist; Eastasia emerges from another decade of confused fighting. From then on the three are always at war in one combination or another, over the quadrilateral from Tangier to Brazzaville, Darwin and Hong Kong, in a war none of them means to win.
events.inUniverse: 'permanently at war, and have been so for the past twenty-five years' (Goldstein's book, read in 1984)

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: Twenty-five years back from 1984 is 1959. The absorptions are said to have been 'foreseen before the middle of the twentieth century' and are not dated; Eastasia's emergence 'after another decade of confused fighting' fits the same end of the 1950s. In our 1959 the Cold War had two blocs, not three, and no hot war between them.
events.binWhy: Open war becomes a permanent, limited war that keeps three regimes in power.

facets.change: confused fighting → a permanent war between three blocs

events.title: The past is pulped
events.description: Books, papers and records from before the Revolution are hunted down and destroyed, in the prole quarters as thoroughly as anywhere. By 1984 a book printed before 1960 is almost unobtainable, and anything written before about then can be put into Newspeak only by changing what it says; the Ministry of Truth rectifies the record daily.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: 1960 is not the date of a stated event but the horizon the novel keeps returning to: it is 'very unlikely that there existed anywhere in Oceania a copy of a book printed earlier than 1960', 'no book written before approximately 1960 could be translated as a whole', and Winston had not heard the word Ingsoc before 1960. The destruction itself is undated; this entry marks where the surviving record begins.
events.binWhy: The ruling party destroys the written past and replaces it with its own.

facets.change: a written past → a past the Party writes

events.title: Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford are arrested
events.description: The great purges of the middle sixties wipe out the original leaders of the Revolution; by 1970 none is left except Big Brother. Among the last, Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford vanish for a year, confess at show trials to treason with the enemy, are released, rearrested, confess again and are executed.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: 'It must have been in 1965 that these three had been arrested', and 'By 1970 none of them was left, except Big Brother himself'. The purges are modelled on the Moscow trials of 1936-38.
events.binWhy: The state destroys its own founding generation by arrest, confession and execution.

facets.change: revolutionary old guard → confessions and executions

events.title: The photograph that disproves the confessions
events.description: A torn half-page of The Times reaches Winston's desk by accident: a photograph of Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford at a Party function in New York on the very day they confessed to being on Eurasian soil. Frightened, he drops it into the memory hole within minutes. It is the only concrete proof of falsification he ever holds, and O'Brien destroys another copy in front of him eleven years later.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: 'In 1973, it must have been'; O'Brien later calls it the photograph Winston 'had chanced upon eleven years ago'. The date on the page is about ten years earlier, i.e. the trial years of the mid-1960s.
events.binWhy: Proof of the lie surfaces and goes back down the memory hole unseen.

facets.change: proof of a fabricated trial → ash in the memory hole

events.title: Oceania changes partners
events.description: Oceania, at war with Eastasia and allied with Eurasia, changes sides: now it fights Eurasia alongside Eastasia. Officially the change never happened, the records are altered, and by 1984 Winston is one of the few who remembers that it was only four years before.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text

events.note: 'It was only four years since Oceania had been at war with Eastasia and in alliance with Eurasia', read in April 1984. The partners change again during Hate Week later that year.
events.binWhy: Enemies become allies overnight, and the record is changed to say they always were.

facets.change: war with Eastasia → alliance with Eastasia, war with Eurasia

events.title: Winston's diary, and the Ministry of Love
events.description: On 4 April Winston Smith, a thirty-nine-year-old clerk in the Records Department, starts a diary; he takes a lover, Julia, and goes to O'Brien, who gives him Goldstein's book and turns out to be Thought Police; the lovers are arrested in their room above the junk shop. During Hate Week the enemy switches from Eurasia to Eastasia in mid-speech. In the Ministry of Love Winston is tortured until he betrays Julia and loves Big Brother.
events.inUniverse: 'April 4th, 1984' (Winston's first diary entry; he is not sure it is 1984)

sources.title: Project Gutenberg Australia: Nineteen Eighty-Four, full text
Wikipedia: Nineteen Eighty-Four

events.note: The date is the first line of the diary, though Winston himself is only 'fairly sure' of the year. The arrest comes later that year, after Hate Week; the imprisonment lasts an unstated time and the final café scene may fall in 1985. The Newspeak appendix, written in the past tense, is read by some critics as a sign that the Party later fell, but the novel never shows it.
events.binWhy: The secret police entrap and break a dissenter; the story ends in his submission.

facets.change: a clerk's private rebellion → a man who loves Big Brother

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Alternate Past because Orwell's future is now our past: the fork is an atomic war in the 1950s that did not happen, and the story is set in a 1984 we lived through differently. It follows the novel alone (not the 1954 BBC play or the 1984 film). Tiers: every event is T3 (1949-1984); there is no T4 because nothing is dated before the novel's own time, and no T2 or T1 because the only later date, 2050 in the Newspeak appendix, is a Party target, not an event.

lineages.creator: Stephen King

divergence.label: Jake Epping steps out of the rabbit hole into 9 September 1958
divergence.delta: Real: 9 September 1958 is an ordinary Tuesday in Lisbon Falls, Maine, five years before Lee Harvey Oswald shoots President Kennedy from the Texas School Book Depository. Fiction: a schoolteacher from 2011 walks out of a diner's pantry into that morning, carrying a dying friend's notes on Oswald and a plan to live in the past until November 1963.
divergence.inUniverse: The portal always opens at 11.58 a.m. on 9 September 1958; every return trip lasts two minutes in 2011 and a new trip resets the last one's changes
divergence.note: The arrival date is stated in the novel. The first change Jake makes, killing Frank Dunning before his Halloween murders in the fictional town of Derry, falls in the same autumn; the change the title refers to comes five years later. Jake's earlier trial run, in which he half-saves the Dunnings and the boy he saved dies in Vietnam, is reset by his second trip and is not charted.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 11/22/63 (plot: the portal leads to Lisbon Falls on 9 September 1958)
11.22.63 Wiki: 11/22/63 (Novel) - every journey lands at 11:58 a.m. on 9 September 1958

ending.why: In the history where Kennedy lives, Jake's June 2011 is a radioactive, earthquake-torn United States under martial law whose scientists expect the Earth to come apart around 2080, and the only way out Jake finds is to go back and erase it.

events.title: A man from 2011 in 1958, and the Dunning murders that never happen
events.description: Jake Epping, calling himself George Amberson, arrives on 9 September with money and a list of sports results. In Derry, Maine, he kills Frank Dunning before the Halloween night on which Dunning would have murdered his wife and three children with a hammer, then heads south to wait for Oswald.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 11/22/63

events.note: Both dates are stated. Derry and the Dunnings are King's inventions, so the first change sits in local history that never had a real counterpart; it is Jake's test of whether the past can be changed, and it can, although the past pushes back in proportion to the size of the change.
events.binWhy: A traveller from the future arrives and changes the present.

facets.change: a family murdered on Halloween → a family that lives

events.title: Oswald is stopped in the Book Depository
events.description: Jake, half-crippled from a beating, and Sadie Dunhill reach the sixth floor of the Texas School Book Depository as the motorcade passes. Jake spoils Oswald's aim; Oswald's shot kills Sadie, police fire through the window and kill Oswald, and Kennedy drives on unhurt.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 11/22/63
11.22.63 Wiki: 11/22/63 (Novel) - Oswald shot by police through the window; Sadie dies

events.note: Real: at 12.30 p.m. on 22 November 1963 Oswald's shots kill Kennedy in Dealey Plaza, Lyndon Johnson is sworn in that afternoon, and Oswald is himself shot by Jack Ruby two days later. Jake had waited until 10 April 1963, when Oswald fired at General Edwin Walker as in real history, to be sure Oswald was the man. The Kennedys telephone Jake to thank him; the FBI tells him to disappear.
events.binWhy: A targeted attack on the president fails, and what follows turns on its failure.

facets.change: a president shot dead → a president unhurt and an assassin killed

events.title: Saigon is lost
events.description: Re-elected narrowly over Barry Goldwater in 1964, Kennedy faces a Congress that blocks civil-rights legislation, and in Vietnam he tries to hold only the Saigon region, West Berlin style. It falls to the communists in 1967, and his presidency never recovers.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - Kennedy re-elected against Goldwater; Saigon taken by the communists in 1967
Wikipedia: 11/22/63 (the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was never passed)

events.note: The account is Harry Dunning's, told to Jake in the ruined 2011; the dates here follow the French Wikipedia's detailed summary of chapter 31, which the English page does not break down by year. Real: Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in July 1964, and Saigon fell in April 1975.
events.binWhy: An American-held city is lost and South Vietnam is occupied eight years early.

facets.change: a defended enclave → Saigon in communist hands

events.title: The cities burn and Wallace is elected
events.description: Race riots break out in about a dozen American cities after a clumsy statement by Kennedy, and Martin Luther King is assassinated by an FBI agent on J. Edgar Hoover's orders. In November the segregationist George Wallace is elected president.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - riots in 1968, King killed on Hoover's orders, Wallace elected in November 1968
Wikipedia: 11/22/63 (Wallace elected president in 1968; King assassinated by the FBI)

events.note: The English page confirms Wallace's 1968 election and the FBI killing King; the French summary adds the riots and names the agent, a character borrowed from James Ellroy. Real: King was killed by James Earl Ray on 4 April 1968; riots followed in more than a hundred cities; Nixon won the election, and Wallace, running third with Curtis LeMay, carried five Southern states.
events.binWhy: A subjugated people rises in the cities after its leader is murdered by the state.

facets.change: a stalled civil-rights movement → burning cities and a segregationist president

events.title: Wallace drops the bomb on Hanoi
events.description: President Wallace, who has put down the riots with firebombs, tells North Vietnam to make Saigon a free city or see Hanoi destroyed, and on the twenty-fourth anniversary of Nagasaki drops an atomic bomb on Hanoi. The taboo is gone: over the next decades some thirty nuclear weapons are used, including in an India-Pakistan war that destroys Bombay and Karachi.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - atomic bomb on Hanoi on 9 August 1969
Wikipedia (German): Der Anschlag (Roman) - some thirty atomic bombs since 1969; Bombay and Hanoi destroyed
Lancaster University: The Survival of a President (Wallace orders the Hanoi bomb on the Nagasaki anniversary)

events.note: The novel dates the strike by the Nagasaki anniversary, which gives 9 August 1969; the Lancaster article prints '1960', an obvious slip for 1969. Real: no nuclear weapon has been used in war since 9 August 1945, and in August 1969 Nixon was starting to withdraw troops from Vietnam.
events.binWhy: A nuclear strike on a capital kills on a scale that changes the world that follows.

facets.change: a conventional war → an atomic strike on a capital

events.title: Wallace is shot dead
events.description: Arthur Bremer assassinates President Wallace, and the vice-president takes over. The presidency passes through Curtis LeMay and Hubert Humphrey before Ronald Reagan beats Humphrey in 1976.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - Wallace assassinated by Arthur Bremer in May 1972
Wikipedia: 11/22/63 (Wallace assassinated by Bremer and succeeded by LeMay; Reagan defeats Humphrey in 1976)

events.note: The month is from the French summary. The two summaries disagree on the successor: the English page says LeMay, the French says Humphrey as vice-president; the English order (LeMay, then Humphrey) is used. Real: Bremer shot Wallace, then a presidential candidate, on 15 May 1972 in Laurel, Maryland; Wallace was paralysed and lived until 1998.
events.binWhy: A president is killed and the succession is opened.

facets.change: a segregationist president → a dead one and a string of successors

events.title: Hostages executed on television in Tehran
events.description: Iranian Revolutionary Guards seize about two hundred Americans in Tehran and execute some on live television. The American response gives rise to al-Qaeda, attacks multiply, one of them on a peace concert by a reunited Beatles, and the Middle East goes up in flames while the Soviet Union collapses.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - November 1979, two hundred Americans taken hostage in Tehran and executed on television

events.note: Only the French summary lists this; the English sources say only that the US and the world fractured. Real: on 4 November 1979 students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days; none was executed, and all were released in January 1981.
events.binWhy: A televised massacre of hostages starts the cycle of terrorism that follows.

facets.change: an embassy siege → executions on live television

events.title: Atomic bombs in the Middle East, and the oil runs short
events.description: With Russian gangsters selling atomic weapons from the ruins of the Soviet Union, bombs explode across the Middle East. Oil becomes scarce, and the shortage runs on into the ruined America of 2011.

sources.title: Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - in 1994 atomic bombs explode in the Middle East, causing a severe oil shortage

events.note: Only the French summary gives the year. Real: the Soviet Union dissolved peacefully in 1991, oil in 1994 sold at under twenty dollars a barrel, and no nuclear weapon has been used since 1945.
events.binWhy: An oil shock from destroyed producers throws the economy into lasting crisis.

facets.change: cheap oil → a region of producers bombed and a lasting shortage

events.title: An earthquake breaks a reactor in New England
events.description: Among the earthquakes that grow more frequent every year, one wrecks a nuclear plant in Vermont and contaminates New England and Quebec for decades; other nuclear accidents make Florida and New Mexico uninhabitable.

sources.title: Wikipedia (German): Der Anschlag (Roman) - an earthquake on 19 June 1999 causes a reactor accident that contaminates New England and Quebec
Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - catastrophic nuclear accident in Vermont in 1999

events.note: The German summary gives the day; the French gives the year and the state. In the novel's logic the earthquakes are the damage time does when it is changed: Jake hears of the first, in California, as he leaves Dallas. Real: Vermont Yankee ran without a major accident until it closed in 2014.
events.binWhy: A disaster poisons a whole region and changes the society left in it.

facets.change: an inhabited Northeast → a contaminated one

events.title: Maine leaves for Canada
events.description: The United States has fractured, and Maine votes to become a Canadian province. Hillary Clinton, elected in 2004 after her husband died suddenly as the favourite, governs what is left under martial law and can do nothing about the earthquakes.

sources.title: Wikipedia (German): Der Anschlag (Roman) - in 2005 Maine joined Canada
Wikipedia (French): 22/11/63 - Clinton elected in 2004 after Bill Clinton's death; Maine votes to join Canada

events.note: The year is from the German summary; the English and French summaries give the secession without a date. Real: Maine has been a US state since 1820, and George W. Bush was re-elected in 2004.
events.binWhy: A state leaves the union and joins its neighbour without being conquered.

facets.change: the fifty United States → a union losing its northeast

events.title: 11/22/63 is published
events.description: Scribner publishes Stephen King's novel, an idea he first tried in the early 1970s and abandoned; it becomes a number-one bestseller and wins the Los Angeles Times Book Prize for mystery and thriller.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 11/22/63

events.note: Published 8 November 2011. The novel's present is June 2011, the month in which Jake finds the ruined world; that state is recorded in the ending rather than as a separate entry, since the lineage allows one entry per year.
events.binWhy: The original release; not a moment in the story.

lineages.groupingNote: A pure alternate past: one prevented assassination on 22 November 1963, and a history that runs forward from it to 2011. The novel is the source of truth; its alternate history after 1963 is told compactly by Harry Dunning in chapter 31, so the dates come from the most detailed published summaries (English, French and German Wikipedia), and where only one gives a year the entry is marked medium. The fork is Jake's arrival in 1958, the first moment the story's history differs from ours; the reset Jake makes at the end, which returns history to our own, is recorded in the ending and not as an event, because it restores the real record rather than changing it. The 2016 Hulu series 11.22.63 is a separate continuity with a different ruined present and is not charted. Tiers: T3 holds 1958 to 1999 and T2 2005 and 2011; T4 and T1 are empty, since the story begins in 1958 and its furthest reach is the scientists' forecast that the Earth will come apart around 2080.

lineages.title: On the Beach
lineages.creator: Nevil Shute

divergence.label: Albania bombs Naples, and a short war ends the north
divergence.delta: Real: in 1961 the Berlin Wall goes up and the Soviet Union tests a 50-megaton bomb, but no nuclear weapon is used in war and no small state has one. Fiction: cheap bombs have spread to countries like Albania and Egypt; a bomb on Naples sets off a chain of mistaken retaliation and a Russian-Chinese cobalt war that kills the Northern Hemisphere in thirty-seven days.
divergence.inUniverse: The war is 'a year previously' as of Thursday 27 December 1962; Holmes married 'in 1961 six months before the war'
divergence.note: Shute, writing in 1957, prints only one year, 1961, for a wedding six months before the war. The opening chapter's 'Thursday the 27th' of December and 'Tuesday, New Year's Day' fit 1956-57, 1962-63 and 1973-74; with a 1961 wedding before the war only 1962-63 works, which fixes the story in 1963 and the war about a year earlier. The 1959 film states 1964 instead; this lineage follows the novel.

Wikipedia: On the Beach (novel)

ending.why: The radiation reaches Melbourne, the characters take their pills or go down with the submarine, and the novel leaves the last human society dying with only New Zealand and the far south a few weeks behind.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.description: The United States destroys two Japanese cities with single bombs. In the novel the scientist Osborne says the original uranium bomb came to cost only about fifty thousand pounds, cheap enough for a country like Albania to hold a stockpile.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Nagasaki was bombed on 9 August. Osborne's cost figure is Shute's, spoken in the Scorpion's wardroom.
events.binWhy: A nuclear weapon kills a city's population for the first time.

facets.change: cities bombed by fleets → a city destroyed by one bomb

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

events.title: Szilard describes the cobalt bomb
events.description: On a radio programme Leo Szilard describes a hydrogen bomb jacketed in cobalt whose fallout could end human life, as a warning of where the weapons were heading. In the novel Russia and China both use cobalt bombs, and their fallout is what reaches Australia.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia dates Szilard's description to 26 February 1950 and notes that no cobalt bomb is known to have been built. The 1959 film also names the cobalt bomb as the reason the fallout is so heavy.
events.binWhy: A physicist works out that a weapon able to end human life is possible; the novel's war uses it.

facets.change: big bombs → a bomb that could end the species

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cobalt bomb

events.title: Castle Bravo, and fallout that travels
events.description: The largest American hydrogen bomb test, at Bikini Atoll, yields 15 megatons, two and a half times the prediction, and drops fallout on inhabited islands and on the Japanese fishing boat Lucky Dragon No. 5, whose radioman dies months later. It shows the world that fallout from one explosion can sicken people far downwind.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia records that traces of Bravo's fallout spread around the world and that the test caused strong international reaction; Shute's novel extends the idea to a hemisphere's worth of bombs carried south by the winds.
events.binWhy: A thermonuclear weapon is tested whose fallout alone could poison a region, and the fear of such weapons becomes public.

facets.change: a test at sea → fallout on people downwind

sources.title: Wikipedia: Castle Bravo

events.title: Nautilus sails under nuclear power
events.description: The first nuclear-powered submarine leaves her pier and signals that she is 'underway on nuclear power'. The novel's USS Scorpion is one of her successors, and because she needs no oil she is the only warship left in Australian waters that can sail north.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Real history, before the fork. The novel's Scorpion is a fictional ship of the same kind; the novel says her nuclear fuel had to be prepared in Australia after she arrived.
events.binWhy: A new kind of vessel that can cross oceans submerged without refuelling goes into service.

facets.change: submarines tied to fuel → submarines that can stay down

sources.title: Wikipedia: USS Nautilus (SSN-571)

events.title: The Suez Crisis
events.description: Israel invades Egypt and Britain and France join two days later to retake the canal Nasser has nationalised, before American and Soviet pressure forces them out. The novel's war begins in the same corner of the world: a bomb on Tel Aviv, an Anglo-American show of force over Cairo, and Egyptian crews flying Soviet-built bombers to Washington and London.
events.note: Real history, before the fork and the year before the novel appeared. In the book the Russians had been supplying Egypt with aircraft for years, and the Egyptian bombers carried Russian markings, which is why NATO commanders struck Russia by mistake.
events.binWhy: Two powers and a neighbour attack Egypt; the regional war the novel's world war grows out of.

facets.change: a nationalised canal → an invasion and a forced withdrawal

sources.title: Wikipedia: Suez Crisis

events.title: On the Beach is published
events.description: Heinemann publishes Nevil Shute's novel, expanded from a four-part story, 'The Last Days on Earth', that the Sunday Graphic printed in April 1957.
events.note: Shute wrote it after emigrating to Australia. The title page quotes T. S. Eliot's The Hollow Men.
events.binWhy: A publication date, not a moment in the story's history; it carries no bin.

sources.title: Wikipedia: On the Beach (novel)

events.title: Stanley Kramer's film opens on seven continents
events.description: On the Beach, with Gregory Peck, Ava Gardner and Fred Astaire, opens the same day in 18 cinemas on every continent.
events.note: The film moves the story to 1964 and changes the ending; this lineage follows the novel's dates.
events.binWhy: A publication date, not a moment in the story's history; it carries no bin.

sources.title: Wikipedia: On the Beach (1959 film)

events.title: The thirty-seven-day war
events.description: Albania drops a bomb on Naples, someone bombs Tel Aviv, and Egyptian-crewed Soviet-built bombers hit Washington and London; NATO commanders with no government left strike Russia, and Russia and China blanket each other with cobalt bombs. About 4,700 explosions are recorded, the last on the thirty-seventh day, and the Northern Hemisphere is dead or dying.
events.inUniverse: 'The short, bewildering war ... died away with the last seismic record of explosion on the thirty-seventh day'
events.note: The novel gives no date for the war itself. Chapter one, which is Thursday 27 December 1962, says the short war 'had ended a year previously' and that Peter Holmes married Mary 'in 1961 six months before the war', so the war falls in the second half of 1961 and may run into the first weeks of 1962. The seismic count and the thirty-seven days are both stated in the text.
events.binWhy: A war between the great powers breaks out and is fought with thermonuclear and cobalt weapons.

facets.change: small states with bombs → every northern power at war

events.title: The fallout crosses the equator
events.description: A year after the war the winds have carried the fallout south: Cairns, Port Moresby and Darwin have gone silent, the oil is gone, and the scientists' estimate gives Melbourne until about September. On Thursday 27 December Lieutenant-Commander Peter Holmes is posted as liaison officer to the American nuclear submarine Scorpion.
events.inUniverse: 'this must be Thursday the 27th'; 'You'll report in Scorpion on Tuesday, New Year's Day'
events.note: The date is fixed by the text: 'this must be Thursday the 27th', just after Christmas, and Holmes is to report aboard on 'Tuesday, New Year's Day'. After a 1961 wedding, the only fit is 1962-63 (the next is 1973-74), which gives the year the novel never prints.
events.binWhy: Radiation from a war fought elsewhere is killing its way south through the last inhabited regions.

facets.change: a war in the north → a death line moving south

events.title: Seattle, and the end in Melbourne
events.description: Scorpion sails to the dead cities of the American Pacific coast to trace a Morse signal from near Seattle and finds only a window frame knocking against a telegraph key; the hope that radiation would thin out is disproved. Radiation sickness reaches Adelaide and Sydney on 1 August and Melbourne within weeks, and the people who are left take the government's suicide pills while Towers takes Scorpion out to sea to scuttle her.
events.inUniverse: 'the first day of August, the day the radio announced ... cases of radiation sickness in Adelaide and Sydney'
events.note: The year follows from the opening's calendar. Months are given in the text: Scorpion's second cruise leaves once the crew is clear of measles, which Towers expects by 10 March; the first narcissi and the Adelaide and Sydney cases are 'the first day of August'; the Grand Prix is brought forward to 17 August; the Melbourne cases begin shortly after. The last deaths are late August or early September.
events.binWhy: The last organised human society dies of radiation and does not come back.

facets.change: the last cities → no one left

lineages.title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
lineages.creator: Stanley Kubrick (director, co-writer); Peter George and Terry Southern (co-writers), from George's novel Red Alert

divergence.label: A SAC general launches his wing, and the Soviets have a Doomsday Machine
divergence.delta: Real: in 1963 the superpowers are backing away from the Cuban brink; they agree a hot line in June and sign the Partial Test Ban Treaty in August, and no doomsday machine exists outside Herman Kahn's book. Fiction: a paranoid wing commander sends 34 airborne B-52s against the Soviet Union under a retaliation plan, and the Soviets turn out to have built the machine Kahn warned about.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is stated; the film is set in its own present, the day Ripper issues Wing Attack Plan R
divergence.note: The film never prints a year. It was shot at Shepperton from 29 January 1963, was due out in December 1963 until the Kennedy assassination delayed it, and carries a 1963 copyright; so the one day it covers is filed in 1963. A reader who takes it as happening on release in January 1964 should add a year. Peter George's novel Red Alert (1958), on which the film is loosely based, has the same Plan R, the same recall-code doodles and the same one damaged bomber, but no doomsday machine, and there the bomber is shot down before it can bomb.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dr. Strangelove

ending.why: The last bomber hits its target, the Doomsday Machine fires, and the film ends on a montage of explosions with the surface of the Earth to be uninhabitable for ninety-three years and a few hundred thousand chosen people planned for the mineshafts.

events.title: The first nuclear explosion
events.description: The United States detonates a plutonium bomb at Trinity in the New Mexico desert. Its footage is among the real test explosions Kubrick cuts together for the film's last minutes, when the Doomsday Machine goes off to Vera Lynn singing 'We'll Meet Again'.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia's account of the ending names Trinity, Crossroads Baker, Sandstone, Ivy and Redwing as the sources of the closing montage.
events.binWhy: The weapon that can end a civilisation is tested for the first time, and the balance of terror the film mocks is built around it.

facets.change: conventional explosives → the atomic bomb
