Wikipedia: Dr. Strangelove

events.title: Strategic Air Command is founded
events.description: The Army Air Forces create Strategic Air Command, the long-range bomber force that will hold the American nuclear arsenal. Burpelson Air Force Base, the 843rd Bomb Wing and the War Room's generals are all SAC, and both Ripper and Turgidson are drawn from its commander Curtis LeMay.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. SAC was established on 21 March 1946 at Bolling Field and moved to Offutt, Nebraska, in 1948. Wikipedia's Strangelove article records that Turgidson and Ripper both satirise LeMay. Ripper's claim in the film that fluoridation 'first began' in 1946 is his own; the date is not SAC's.
events.binWhy: A military body is founded that will shape the nuclear age and, in the film, start its last war.

facets.change: wartime bomber commands → a standing nuclear strike force

sources.title: Wikipedia: Strategic Air Command
Wikipedia: Dr. Strangelove

events.title: Szilard describes the cobalt bomb
events.description: On a radio programme the physicist Leo Szilard describes a bomb jacketed in cobalt whose fallout could end human life, to show where the weapons were heading rather than to propose one. The film's 'cobalt-thorium G' Doomsday Machine is his thought experiment built for real.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia dates Szilard's radio description to 26 February 1950. The film's ambassador gives cobalt-thorium G a half-life of ninety-three years and says the shroud will circle the Earth for that long; Strangelove guesses a hundred.
events.binWhy: A physicist works out that a weapon able to end human life is possible; the fictional machine is this idea made real.

facets.change: big bombs → a bomb that could end the species

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cobalt bomb

events.title: Sputnik, and the missile gap
events.description: The Soviet Union puts the first artificial satellite into orbit, and American politicians start talking about a 'missile gap' that exaggerated estimates say favours Moscow. The film's last joke is Turgidson warning of a 'mineshaft gap' while the world ends.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The missile gap never existed except in exaggerated estimates such as the Gaither Committee's in 1957; Wikipedia's Strangelove article notes that 'mineshaft gap' spoofs the phrase.
events.binWhy: An uncrewed satellite reaches orbit for the first time, and the fear it raises drives the arms race the film satirises.

facets.change: no satellites → Soviet rockets over America

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sputnik 1
Wikipedia: Missile gap

events.title: Kahn's On Thermonuclear War and the Doomsday Machine
events.description: The RAND strategist Herman Kahn publishes On Thermonuclear War, which uses a hypothetical Doomsday Machine to show where mutual assured destruction leads and talks calmly of 'megadeaths'. Kahn later briefed Kubrick on the idea, and the film puts both the machine and the vocabulary in the War Room.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Kahn's book (Princeton University Press, 1960) proposed the machine only to argue against building one. Wikipedia records that Kubrick consulted Kahn and Thomas Schelling while writing, and that Turgidson's binder is labelled 'World Targets in Megadeaths'.
events.binWhy: A theory of how nuclear powers behave is published that the film turns into its plot.

facets.change: unthinkable → calculated in megadeaths

sources.title: Wikipedia: On Thermonuclear War
Wikipedia: Herman Kahn

events.title: B-52s go on continuous airborne alert
events.description: SAC begins Operation Chrome Dome, keeping B-52s armed with thermonuclear bombs in the air around the clock on routes towards the Soviet Union. It is the film's premise: Ripper's 34 bombers are already airborne, two hours from their targets, when he sends the attack code.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia dates the start of Chrome Dome to November 1961 after pilot airborne-alert programmes from 1958; it ran until the Thule crash of 1968. The film calls its flight 'Operation Drop-Kick'.
events.binWhy: A weapon system is fielded: nuclear bombers kept permanently in the air within reach of their targets.

facets.change: bombers on the ground → bombers always aloft

sources.title: Wikipedia: Operation Chrome Dome

events.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
events.description: The United States finds Soviet missiles in Cuba, blockades the island, and for thirteen days the two powers stand at the edge of nuclear war before Khrushchev agrees to withdraw them. Kubrick and George were rewriting their script as a comedy in the months after it.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Terry Southern joined the script in late 1962, after the crisis. The crisis also produced the real hot line: advisers concluded that faster communication could have ended it sooner.
events.binWhy: The superpowers come to the brink of war and step back; the standoff the film's accident breaks.

facets.change: missiles in secret → missiles withdrawn under blockade

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cuban Missile Crisis

events.title: Wing Attack Plan R, and the Doomsday Machine
events.description: General Jack D. Ripper sends his B-52 wing against the Soviet Union and seals Burpelson; the President learns in the War Room that the Soviets have secretly built a Doomsday Machine that fires if their country is attacked. Every bomber is recalled but one, Major Kong rides its bomb down, and the machine's cobalt-thorium G shroud begins to cover the Earth.
events.inUniverse: The film states no year; 'the Party Congress on Monday'
events.note: The whole story takes a few hours of one day, and the film states no year; it is set in its own present and was shot from 29 January 1963 for release that December. The Soviet ambassador says the Premier meant to announce the machine at the Party Congress 'on Monday'. The film's President telephones the Premier on a hot line; the real Moscow-Washington link was agreed on 20 June 1963 and installed on 30 August 1963 as a teleprinter, not a telephone.
events.binWhy: Nuclear war begins by accident and the machine built to deter it ends the world's order outright.

facets.change: deterrence → the Doomsday Machine fires

events.description: Columbia releases Kubrick's film in New York, London and Toronto. Its first preview had been set for 22 November 1963 and was cancelled when President Kennedy was shot that day.
events.note: The on-screen copyright date is 1963. The film is loosely based on Peter George's novel Red Alert (1958, first published in Britain as Two Hours to Doom under the name Peter Bryant), a serious thriller whose bomber is shot down in time; George co-wrote the screenplay.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in alternate-past because it is our 1963 - SAC, B-52s on airborne alert, the War Room, a Soviet premier on the telephone - with one wing commander's decision and one secret Soviet machine added. It follows Kubrick's film, not Peter George's novel. The story lasts a few hours, so it has one fictional event; the seven before it are the real history it satirises (Trinity, SAC, Szilard's cobalt bomb, Sputnik and the missile gap, Kahn's book, Chrome Dome, Cuba). Everything is T3: there is no T4 because the history it draws on starts in 1945, and no T2 or T1 because the world ends in 1963.

lineages.title: Metal Gear
lineages.creator: Hideo Kojima (Konami)

divergence.label: A nuclear shell is fired on Soviet soil
divergence.delta: Real: in 1964 the superpowers are stepping back from the Cuban crisis, the hotline is a year old, and Khrushchev is removed in October by his colleagues. Fiction: in August an American-made nuclear shell destroys a Soviet design bureau. Johnson settles it by having his own agent kill the woman blamed, and her secret fortune funds the group that will run America's information for fifty years.
divergence.inUniverse: Virtuous Mission, 24 August 1964; Operation Snake Eater, 30 August - 2 September 1964
divergence.note: The saga has older hidden history: the Philosophers, a secret society of American, Soviet and Chinese power-brokers, and The Boss's wartime Cobra unit. None of it contradicts the public record until 1964, when a nuclear weapon goes off. The fork is placed there, and the earlier backstory is left out of the chain rather than filed as prehistory.

events.title: Operation Snake Eater
events.description: A CIA agent, Naked Snake, is sent into the Soviet Union to bring out a weapons designer; his mentor, The Boss, defects in the middle of the mission, and a GRU colonel, Volgin, fires one of the American nuclear shells she brought with her at the design bureau. To prove America had no part in it, Snake is sent back: he destroys the Shagohod, a nuclear-launch tank, and kills The Boss, and Washington names him Big Boss and her a traitor, and buries the truth that her defection was ordered.

The continuity is the Kojima-directed main saga. Portable Ops (1970) and Rising (2018) are spin-offs and are left out; Rising, not Guns of the Patriots, is the one set in 2018. The dates are the games' own, from on-screen text as collected by the Metal Gear wiki. Coverage: T3 holds 1964 to 1999 and T2 holds 2005 to 2014. There is no T4 because the Philosophers' older history is deliberately left out, and no T1 because the saga ends in 2014.

lineages.title: Fail-Safe
lineages.creator: Eugene Burdick and Harvey Wheeler (novel); Sidney Lumet (1964 film, screenplay by Walter Bernstein)

divergence.label: A faulty fail-safe box sends a bomber group to Moscow
divergence.delta: Real: in 1967 Khrushchev has been out of power for three years, the hot line is used for the first time during the Six-Day War, and no SAC bomber has ever flown past its fail-safe point on a false order. Fiction: an electronic fault gives six supersonic bombers a valid attack code, Khrushchev is still premier to take the President's call, and the day ends with Moscow and New York destroyed.
divergence.inUniverse: The novel is set in 1967; the premier is Nikita Khrushchev
divergence.note: This lineage follows the 1962 novel, which dates itself, rather than the 1964 film, which does not; the plot is the same in both. The year 1967 comes from the Wikipedia and EBSCO summaries of the novel; the text itself was not available to check. The novel's Soviet Union is still led by Khrushchev, which parts from our history in October 1964, but the novel never shows that year, so the fork is placed where its story is.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fail-Safe (novel)
EBSCO Research Starters: Fail-Safe by Eugene Burdick - set in 1967, Khrushchev as premier, the faulty Fail-Safe Activating Mechanism

ending.why: Moscow and New York are destroyed with their people, one by a machine's error and one on the President's order, and general war is avoided only by that trade.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.description: The United States destroys two Japanese cities with single bombs, the only cities ever destroyed by nuclear weapons. Fail-Safe ends with two more, one lost by accident and one given up on purpose.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Nagasaki was bombed on 9 August. The film's General Black warns that the Soviets would retaliate 'as we would, and did after Pearl Harbor'.
events.binWhy: A nuclear weapon kills a city's population for the first time.

facets.change: cities bombed by fleets → a city destroyed by one bomb

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

events.title: Strategic Air Command is founded
events.description: The Army Air Forces create Strategic Air Command to hold the nuclear bomber force. From November 1948 it is run from Offutt, outside Omaha, where the novel's SAC war room follows Group Six to Moscow.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. SAC was established at Bolling Field on 21 March 1946 and moved its headquarters to Offutt Air Force Base, Nebraska, on 9 November 1948.
events.binWhy: A military body is founded that will own the bombers and the codes the novel turns on.

facets.change: wartime bomber commands → a standing nuclear strike force

sources.title: Wikipedia: Strategic Air Command

events.title: The Soviet Union tests its first atomic bomb
events.description: The Soviet Union explodes its first atomic bomb at Semipalatinsk, years before Washington expected. From here on each side can retaliate, which is the premise of the novel's ending: the President sacrifices New York because Moscow's generals would otherwise answer with everything.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. RDS-1, or First Lightning, yielded about 22 kilotons.
events.binWhy: A second power builds the weapon and the balance of terror freezes around the pair.

facets.change: an American monopoly → two nuclear powers

sources.title: Wikipedia: RDS-1

events.title: The first intercontinental missile flies
events.description: The Soviet R-7 makes the first successful long-range flight of an intercontinental ballistic missile, to Kamchatka. Warning times shrink from hours to minutes, the fear the novel's strategist Groteschele builds his arguments on.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. TASS announced the test five days later; the same rocket launched Sputnik in October.
events.binWhy: A weapon able to reach any city in half an hour is tested, and deterrence has to be automated around it.

facets.change: bombers taking hours → missiles taking minutes

sources.title: Wikipedia: R-7 Semyorka

events.title: SAC flies under Positive Control
events.description: SAC tests keeping nuclear-armed bombers on airborne alert, under a Positive Control rule that holds them at a checkpoint until a go-code arrives. That checkpoint is the novel's 'fail-safe point', and its failure is the novel.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The National Security Archive describes Positive Control in the autumn 1958 'Head Start' airborne-alert test; Wikipedia dates the pilot airborne-alert programme to 1958. The exact month the rule was introduced is not given in the sources used.
events.binWhy: A new system for holding nuclear bombers short of their targets is put into service.

facets.change: bombers on the ground → bombers held at a fail-safe point

sources.title: National Security Archive: The Air Force versus Hollywood - Positive Control in the 1958 Head Start test, and the SAC Command Post film made to answer Dr. Strangelove and Fail Safe
Wikipedia: Operation Chrome Dome

events.title: Thule's radar mistakes the Moon for an attack
events.description: At Thule in Greenland, the new Ballistic Missile Early Warning System radar reads returns from the rising Moon as a Soviet missile attack. The alert is recognised as false; the novel's alert is too, but not before a fault has sent one bomber group on.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Wikipedia's BMEWS article dates the false alarm to 5 October 1960, while Khrushchev was in New York; the twelve-radar network was built from 1958 and declared operational in 1961. The novel's alert begins with an unidentified aircraft that turns out to be an off-course airliner.
events.binWhy: A computerised early-warning network is put to work and reports an attack that is not there.

facets.change: human lookouts → computers that can cry wolf

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ballistic Missile Early Warning System

events.title: Goldsboro: one switch holds
events.description: A B-52 breaks up over North Carolina and drops two hydrogen bombs; on one, every safety device but a single low-voltage switch fails. Early reports say the bombs posed 'no immediate danger' of a nuclear explosion, and Sandia's own finding that one switch stood between the country and catastrophe stays secret for decades.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Sandia's Parker F. Jones wrote the assessment in 1969; the Guardian published it on 20 September 2013. Burdick and Wheeler could not have known the details, which is the point of including it: their premise was closer than the public was told.
events.binWhy: The near-failure of a nuclear safeguard is kept from the public.

facets.change: an accident → an official reassurance

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1961 Goldsboro B-52 crash

events.title: Fail-Safe is published
events.description: McGraw-Hill publishes Burdick and Wheeler's novel after the Saturday Evening Post runs it in three parts on 13, 20 and 27 October, the weeks of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
events.note: The novel expands Wheeler's story 'Abraham '59', published in Dissent in the winter of 1959 under the name F. B. Aiken. Peter George sued, saying it copied his Red Alert; the case was settled out of court.
events.binWhy: A publication date, not a moment in the story's history; it carries no bin.

events.title: The Moscow-Washington hot line is agreed
events.description: After Cuba the two governments agree a direct link between their leaders, their first formal step against starting a nuclear war by accident. The novel, written before it, already has the President talking to Khrushchev directly while the bombers fly.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The link was installed on 30 August 1963 as a teleprinter circuit and first used in 1967, during the Six-Day War.
events.binWhy: Enemies agree a channel to keep an accident from becoming a war.

facets.change: messages by embassy → a direct line

events.note: The film follows the novel's plot closely but states no year and does not name the Soviet premier; the novel's Khrushchev lost power a week after the release, on 14 October 1964. A live CBS version followed in 2000.
events.binWhy: A publication date, not a moment in the story's history; it carries no bin.

events.title: Group Six bombs Moscow, and the President gives up New York
events.description: A failed component in SAC's fail-safe equipment sends six Vindicator bombers past their fail-safe point towards Moscow, and neither recall, fighters nor Soviet defences can stop the last one. To keep Khrushchev's generals from answering with all-out war, the President orders an American bomber to destroy New York with four 20-megaton bombs, with the First Lady in the city, and the general who drops them kills himself.

events.note: Wikipedia and EBSCO's summary both place the novel in 1967, with Khrushchev still premier; the story covers a few hours and no month is given. The 1964 film has the same events but no year. Khrushchev's survival in office past October 1964 is a second difference from our history, but the novel does not date it, so the fork is filed at the event it describes.

lineages.title: For All Mankind
lineages.creator: Ronald D. Moore, Matt Wolpert and Ben Nedivi

divergence.label: Alexei Leonov lands on the Moon first
divergence.delta: Real: 20 July 1969 — Armstrong and Aldrin land, the Soviet N1 has just exploded on its pad, and the race is effectively over. Fiction: on 26 June 1969 a Soviet cosmonaut is already on the Moon, and the race never stops.
divergence.inUniverse: 26 June 1969 (season 1, 'Red Moon')
divergence.note: The showrunner has said the true point of divergence is 14 January 1966, when in the fiction Sergei Korolev survives the surgery that killed him in our history. That change is never shown and has no dated consequence on screen until the landing, so the atlas forks at the first visible, dated difference.

ending.why: Season 5 leaves Mars independent under a fresh ceasefire and life confirmed on Titan, but Mars still depends on Earth for supplies, the peace is days old, and a final season announced for 2027 opens on a derelict Soviet ship waking up near Saturn in 2020, so the story stops mid-sentence.

events.title: Alexei Leonov lands on the Moon first
events.description: A Soviet N1 lands Alexei Leonov on the Moon three and a half weeks before Apollo 11. NASA and the Nixon administration take the defeat as a national humiliation, and the space race, instead of ending in 1969, becomes permanent state policy with the budget to match.

events.note: Shown in the first episode, 'Red Moon'. In our 1969 the second N1 exploded on the pad on 3 July and Armstrong walked on the Moon on 20 July; the Soviet crewed lunar programme was quietly abandoned. In the fiction the race does not end, and every later event follows from NASA refusing to lose again.
events.binWhy: The first crewed landing on another world, made by the side that never made it in our history.

facets.change: an American Moon → a Soviet one

events.title: Molly Cobb finds water ice at Shackleton crater
events.description: Apollo 15 diverts to the lunar south pole and Molly Cobb, from the women's astronaut group NASA formed in 1970 after a Soviet woman walked on the Moon, rappels into Shackleton crater and brings up ice. Water on the Moon turns flags-and-footprints into a case for living there.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline

events.note: Season 1, 'Prime Crew' and 'Into the Abyss'; the fan wiki's timeline gives landing on 22 October and the ice on 25 October 1971. Our Apollo 15 landed at Hadley Rille in July 1971 with an all-male crew; lunar polar ice was not confirmed until the 2009 LCROSS impact. The women's corps itself (first class presented October 1970) is folded in here because it has no separate world-changing moment.
events.binWhy: A discovery about the Moon that makes a permanent base worth building.

facets.change: a dry Moon → a Moon with water

events.title: Jamestown base lands at Shackleton
events.description: The United States sets down a permanent crewed base beside the Shackleton ice. It is a military-minded outpost from the start: Nixon's people wanted a Moon base with a strategic purpose, and the base's name frames it as a colony.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline

events.note: Season 1, 'Into the Abyss' dates the landing to 12 October 1973. In our October 1973 Skylab was in orbit and the last Apollo had flown the previous December; there was no lunar base plan with money behind it.
events.binWhy: A permanent crewed base is founded on the Moon.

facets.change: visits to the Moon → a base on it

events.title: The Soviets build Zvezda, and the Moon becomes a front
events.description: About ten months after Jamestown, the Soviet Union founds Zvezda base roughly 13 km away. With the Apollo 23 pad explosion killing eleven ground crew including Gene Kranz, and cosmonauts bugging the American base, the Moon becomes a standing Cold War frontier rather than a finish line.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Zvezda (founded 1974)

events.note: Season 1, 'Home Again' and 'Rupture' (set in 1974); the month is not stated. In our 1974 the Soviet Union cancelled the N1 and its lunar base project (also named Zvezda) in May; the fiction builds the base that was cancelled.
events.binWhy: The superpower rivalry settles onto the Moon as years of armed coexistence.

facets.change: one base on the Moon → two rival ones

events.title: The Jamestown crisis ends in a handshake in orbit
events.description: A lithium claim on the Moon leads to Soviet seizure of a mining site, American Moon Marines retaking it, and, after the Soviets shoot down KAL 007 with NASA's administrator aboard, an armed cosmonaut attack on Jamestown that nearly melts its reactor. Gordo and Tracy Stevens die stopping the meltdown; an Apollo-Soyuz handshake televised from orbit pulls both sides back, and in 1984 Reagan and Andropov sign a treaty dividing the Moon into zones.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Jamestown crisis (May-September 1983)

events.note: Season 2 is dated to 1983 on screen; the fan wiki places the crisis from late May to late September 1983. KAL 007 is real (1 September 1983), but in the fiction it kills NASA Administrator Thomas Paine, who in our history died in 1992. The 1984 Lunar Peace Agreement is shown in the season 3 opening montage and is folded in here as the settlement of this crisis. The Rogers Commission covers up the reactor's plutonium role.
events.binWhy: Superpowers exchange fire on the Moon, then step back into a truce and a partition treaty.

facets.change: a firefight on the Moon → a truce and a divided Moon

events.title: The first working fusion reactor
events.description: Dev Ayesa and Richard Hilliard build the first successful fusion reactor, fuelled by helium-3; Ayesa's Helios Aerospace wins a NASA contract to mine it on the Moon. By 1989 the show's James Hansen testifies that global warming has slowed as the world moves off fossil fuels, and a private company now has the money to race states.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline

events.note: Shown only in the season 3 opening news montage; the fan wiki lists the breakthrough under 1986 but cites it to its 1987 bonus material, and the helium-3 contract to April 1987. The year could be 1986 or 1987. In our 1986 fusion was, as always, decades away.
events.binWhy: A new energy source is switched on that remakes the economy and funds private spaceflight.

facets.change: fossil fuel → helium-3 fusion

events.title: Three crews race for Mars
events.description: Helios launches its private Phoenix, commanded by Ed Baldwin, against NASA's Sojourner 1 and the Soviet Mars-94, while North Korea sends a secret crew of its own. The Soviets push their engine too hard; the rescue costs two astronauts and a cosmonaut.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline
Wikipedia: List of For All Mankind episodes

events.note: Season 3, 'All In' and 'Happy Valley', set in 1994; the fan wiki dates the North Korean launch to September and Helios to October 1994. Our 1994 had no crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit; the first private crewed orbital flight came in 2020.
events.binWhy: The first crewed missions leave for Mars, one of them run by a company.

facets.change: a state monopoly on deep space → a corporation in the race

events.title: People land on Mars, and Happy Valley is founded
events.description: Danielle Poole and Grigory Kuznetsov step onto Mars together, and the stranded American and Soviet crews end up sharing one base, Happy Valley, beside Helios's. A North Korean, Lee Jung-Gil, had crash-landed days earlier and survived unseen. That September a bombing at Johnson Space Center kills nearly 200, including Karen Baldwin and Molly Cobb.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline
Wikipedia: List of For All Mankind episodes

events.note: Season 3, 'Seven Minutes of Terror' onward; the fan wiki dates Lee's crash to 8 February and the Poole-Kuznetsov landing to mid-February 1995, and the JSC bombing to 4 September 1995 (folded in here). The season 2 finale's flash-forward also shows a human on Mars in 1995. In our 1995 no one had been further than the Moon since 1972.
events.binWhy: The first human settlement on another planet, shared by former enemies.

facets.change: rival Mars crews → a shared Martian base

events.title: The Mars-7 Alliance is signed
events.description: President Ellen Wilson and Premier Gorbachev sign a treaty in Brussels that puts Mars under joint management by the US, USSR, ESA, Japan, India, North Korea and a communist-bloc coalition. The race becomes a consortium, and Mars becomes a workplace governed from Earth.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Mars-7 Alliance (formed 1997)

events.note: The treaty is established history in season 4; the 1997 date and Brussels signing come from the fan wiki's account of season 4 material, with no month stated. Our 1997 had the International Space Station still unlaunched and no Mars plans with a crew.
events.binWhy: Rival powers join under one charter to govern Mars.

facets.change: a race for Mars → a consortium running it

events.title: The Goldilocks asteroid is stolen into Mars orbit
events.description: An iridium asteroid worth an estimated $20 trillion is found in 2003; the M-7 plans to bring it to Earth. After a strike by underpaid Mars workers, Ed Baldwin, Dev Ayesa, Margo Madison and Aleida Rosales divert it into Mars orbit instead, giving Mars the resource Earth wanted. A riot follows and North Korea is expelled from the alliance, which becomes the M-6.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Goldilocks (2003LC, captured fall 2003)

events.note: Season 4 is set in 2003; the fan wiki gives discovery on 2 July and the capture mission on 7 October 2003. The same year a coup in Moscow removes Gorbachev for Fyodor Korzhenko. In our 2003 asteroid mining was a business-plan fantasy and the first sample-return probe, Hayabusa, launched that May.
events.binWhy: Mars workers and their allies take the colony's wealth out of Earth's hands.

facets.change: an Earth-owned asteroid → a Mars-held one

events.title: Mars rises against the M-6
events.description: Mars now holds 5,000 people, many of them illegal 'craters'. Alex Poletov and Lily Dale leak an M-6 plan to automate the colony and send 98% of its population back to Earth; peacekeepers fire on protesters, an armed group seizes the Martian government and halts iridium exports, and President Bragg embargoes Mars. The same day as the leak, Sojourner-T leaves Mars for Titan.

sources.title: For All Mankind Wiki (Fandom): Timeline
Wikipedia: List of For All Mankind episodes

events.note: Season 5 opens in May 2012; the fan wiki dates the leak and the Titan launch to 19 July 2012. Our 2012 had Curiosity landing on Mars in August, with no one there to protest.
events.binWhy: A dependent colony revolts against the alliance that governs it.

facets.change: a governed colony → an insurgent one under embargo

events.title: Mars wins its independence, and life is found on Titan
events.description: M-6 marines land on Mars and fire on civilians; the Martian militia traps the M-6 command staff and burns them out. News arrives that Korzhenko has fallen, the USSR has left the M-6 and Earth has called a ceasefire; Miles Dale is sworn in as president of an independent Happy Valley. On Titan, Kelly Baldwin's crew finds methane-based life, and Kelly dies so the others can get home.

lineages.title: District 9
lineages.creator: Neill Blomkamp (director; co-written with Terri Tatchell)

divergence.label: An alien ship stops over Johannesburg
divergence.delta: Real: 1982, apartheid South Africa under P. W. Botha, the townships policed and the forced removals still going on. Fiction: a mothership full of starving aliens stalls over Johannesburg, and the country that invented the Group Areas Act gets a new group to put in an area.
divergence.inUniverse: 1982 (stated in the film's documentary opening)
divergence.note: Everything before 1982 is our history, and the film's allegory depends on it: the camp, the evictions and the vocabulary come from apartheid. Nothing is converted; the film's dates are ours. The later history of South Africa after 1982 is not shown, beyond a 2010 Johannesburg with a multiracial MNU and police.

sources.title: Wikipedia: District 9

ending.why: The aliens end up in District 10, a camp further from the city that already holds 2.5 million and keeps growing; the only hopes left are an exposed MNU and Christopher's promise to return in three years.

events.title: The National Party wins and apartheid begins
events.description: In an election open almost only to white voters, D. F. Malan's Herenigde Nasionale Party ousts Jan Smuts's United Party, which won more votes, and begins to write racial segregation into law. It is the order the aliens arrive into 34 years later.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1948 South African general election

events.note: Real history, before the fork. District 9 is an allegory of apartheid, shot in Chiawelo, Soweto; in 1982 the country it shows is still ruled by the same party.
events.binWhy: A party takes the state by election and remakes it around segregation.

facets.change: segregation by custom → apartheid by law

events.title: The Group Areas Act assigns land by race
events.description: Parliament passes the Group Areas Act, which divides cities into zones for each race and makes it a crime to live in the wrong one. It is the legal machinery behind the forced removals the film's eviction copies.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Group Areas Act

events.note: Real history (Act No. 41 of 1950). The film's MNU operation, eviction notices signed on a clipboard and all, is modelled on removals under this act.
events.binWhy: The state assigns every group a place and moves the ones in the wrong place.

facets.change: mixed neighbourhoods → areas assigned by race

events.title: District Six is declared whites-only
events.description: The government declares District Six, a mixed inner-city district of Cape Town, a whites-only area under the Group Areas Act. Over the next decade more than 60,000 residents are forcibly removed to the Cape Flats and their houses bulldozed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: District Six
Wikipedia: District 9

events.note: Real history, and the one the film's title points at: the setting alludes to District Six, as critics noted. Removals began in 1968.
events.binWhy: A government clears a district of the people it has decided do not belong there.

facets.change: a mixed inner-city district → rubble and a removal to the Cape Flats

events.title: An alien ship stops over Johannesburg
events.description: A vast ship comes to a halt over Johannesburg, not 'Manhattan or Washington or Chicago', and hangs there for three months. When a team cuts in they find more than a million starving, leaderless aliens; an aid effort ferries them to a temporary camp beneath the ship, which is soon fenced, militarised and a slum: District 9.

Wikipedia: District 9

events.binWhy: A non-human people arrives, and humanity has to decide what to do with them.

facets.change: alone → a million stranded aliens over Johannesburg

events.title: Christopher Johnson starts collecting fuel in secret
events.description: One of the stranded aliens, registered by MNU as Christopher Johnson, begins distilling fuel from salvaged alien technology and hides it, with a command module, under his shack. It takes him twenty years to gather enough for one flight.

events.title: Alive in Joburg
events.description: Neill Blomkamp's short, in the same documentary style, shows aliens living in Johannesburg's townships and the people who resent them. District 9 expands it.

events.title: MNU evicts 1.8 million aliens from District 9
events.description: After years of riots, the government hands the aliens to Multi-National United, an arms maker, to move 1.8 million of them to a new camp away from the city. The officer in charge, Wikus van de Merwe, is sprayed with the alien fuel and begins to turn into one of them; MNU hunts him for his body, because only alien DNA can fire alien weapons. He helps Christopher recover the fuel, and the mothership leaves Earth.

In the epilogue District 9 is demolished, District 10 holds 2.5 million aliens 'and continues to grow', and an MNU employee awaits trial for exposing its illegal genetic research.

lineages.title: The Day After
lineages.creator: Nicholas Meyer (director); Edward Hume (writer), ABC

divergence.label: A mutiny in East Germany, a blockade of Berlin, and a war that goes nuclear
divergence.delta: Real: in 1982 Berlin is quiet, the Pershing II deployment is still a year off and hanging on arms talks, and the war the Kansas silos were built for has not come. Fiction: East Germany seals West Berlin after its own army rebels, NATO tries to force the corridor, and within a day tactical warheads over the Rhine have become an exchange of intercontinental missiles.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is stated; the crisis runs over two days in early autumn
divergence.note: The film gives no year. It is filed in 1982, the late summer and early autumn when it was shot in Lawrence, because its own calendar is that season and nothing in it places it later. It was broadcast in November 1983 and was received as a picture of the present, so 1983 is an equally fair reading. The first thing in it that did not happen is the East German army rebellion reported on the first evening.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Day After

Archived 2009 copy of the Wikipedia article: 'Events leading to war', with the Friday 15 and Saturday 16 September dates and the 3:38 pm first strike

ending.why: Kansas City is gone, the survivors in Lawrence are dying of radiation, looters are being shot, and the film ends with Professor Huxley asking on the radio whether anyone can hear him and getting no answer.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.description: The United States destroys two Japanese cities with single bombs. Nothing like it has happened to an American city, and The Day After was made to show it happening to one; its closing card says a real attack would be worse than what it shows.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Nagasaki was bombed on 9 August. Director Nicholas Meyer insisted on a disclaimer after the credits that the film understates the effects of nuclear war.
events.binWhy: A nuclear weapon kills a city's population for the first time.

facets.change: cities bombed by fleets → a city destroyed by one bomb

events.title: The Berlin Blockade
events.description: The Soviet Union cuts the land routes into the western sectors of Berlin, and the Western allies supply the city by air until the blockade is lifted in May 1949. The film's crisis replays it with East Germany as the blockader and no airlift: its bulletins say Tegel and Tempelhof are closed to all traffic.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The blockade ran from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949 and ended in a Western success.
events.binWhy: An armed standoff over Berlin that stays short of war.

facets.change: open access → a city under siege

events.description: A strike by East Berlin building workers against raised quotas becomes an uprising across the country and is put down by Soviet tanks. The film's war starts from the same weakness: reports of 'widespread rebellion among several divisions of the East German Army', and a blockade of West Berlin that follows.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The rebellion in the film is only reported in a bulletin; its cause is never given.

events.title: The Berlin Wall goes up
events.description: East German forces seal the border with West Berlin overnight and begin the wall that will stand until 1989. In the film's first bulletin East Germany closes the four main autobahn crossings to West Berlin, at Lauenburg, Helmstedt, Herleshausen and Rudolphstein.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. Helmstedt-Marienborn, which the film's NATO forces try to break through, was the main road checkpoint between West Germany and the corridor to Berlin.

events.title: Whiteman's 150 Minuteman missiles go on alert
events.description: The 351st Strategic Missile Wing at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, accepts its last flight of Minuteman missiles and has 150 on alert in silos among the farms east of Kansas City. They are why the film's writers chose this corner of the Midwest: Airman McCoy serves in the wing, the Dahlbergs and Hendrys farm beside the silos, and the missiles draw the attack.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The wing was organised on 1 February 1963, received its first missile on 14 January 1964 and was fully operational on 29 June 1964. Wikipedia's production section says Hume and Meyer picked Lawrence partly because 150 Minuteman silos stood nearby.

events.description: NATO decides to deploy Pershing II and cruise missiles in Western Europe unless talks limit Soviet missiles by the autumn of 1983. The film's early bulletins are this argument: Pershing 2s for Europe, Labour saying scrap them, and 'the USA won't really want to sacrifice Chicago for Hamburg'.
events.note: Real history, before the fork. The film's Pershing II deployment is still being argued about, which fits both 1982 and 1983.

events.title: Berlin, the Rhine, and Kansas City
events.description: After reports of mutiny in the East German army, East Germany seals West Berlin; NATO forces the Helmstedt crossing, Soviet armour drives for the Rhine, NATO airbursts three nuclear warheads over it, and a Soviet weapon destroys NATO headquarters in Brussels. Within hours the missiles fly both ways, Kansas City and the silo fields are destroyed, and Lawrence's survivors die over the following weeks of burns, fallout and each other while the President announces a ceasefire.
events.inUniverse: No year stated; one evening, the next day, then weeks of aftermath in the autumn
events.note: The film states no year and is set in its own present. It was shot in and around Lawrence in August and September 1982, and its calendar is that season: a town football game on the night of the blockade, a harvest ten days overdue, Eastern Daylight Time in the ultimatum, and 'nice time of the year, fall' in the aftermath. It aired on 20 November 1983, and audiences took it as happening now; a reader who prefers that should add a year. An archived 2009 version of the Wikipedia article dates the blockade to 'Friday, September 15' and the Helmstedt attack to 'Saturday, September 16', with the first strike on Kansas City at 3:38 pm; those dates could not be found in the dialogue transcript, and 15 September was a Friday in 1978 and 1989, not in 1982 or 1983.

facets.change: a Berlin blockade → a full nuclear exchange

lineages.title: Threads
lineages.creator: Barry Hines (writer); Mick Jackson (director and producer), BBC

divergence.label: A US-backed coup in Iran brings Soviet troops across the border
divergence.delta: Real: in 1983 Iran is the Islamic Republic at war with Iraq, the Soviet army is bogged down in Afghanistan, and the nearest the superpowers come to firing is the Able Archer scare in November. Fiction: a coup in Iran blamed on Washington draws Soviet convoys through the northern mountain passes in the first days of May, and three weeks later Sheffield is gone.
divergence.inUniverse: 'Last week's coup in Iran' (news bulletin, Thursday 5 May); Soviet convoys first seen by US satellites on the Monday; the crisis year is never printed
divergence.note: The film prints days and dates but no year. Every one of its eleven captions, from Saturday 5 March to Thursday 26 May, fits the 1983 calendar and none fits 1984, and the film was made in 1983; so the fork is placed in 1983 and the aftermath captions (one year, ten years, thirteen years after) are counted from May 1983. Audiences in September 1984 took it as happening now; a reader who prefers that reading should add one year to everything after the fork. Iran's fighting is already under way on 5 March, but the first thing that did not happen in our history is the coup late in April and the Soviet move that answers it.

sources.title: Wikiquote: Threads (1984 film) - dated news bulletins, 5 March to 26 May
Wikipedia: Threads (1984 film)

ending.why: Thirteen years on Britain has a medieval population, a generation that can barely speak, and the film's last birth is a dead, damaged child; nothing in it points to recovery.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.description: The United States destroys two Japanese cities with single bombs. Every figure in the film is measured against them: the 25 May bulletin describes the Mashhad blasts as several times larger than the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs, and the survivors' numbness is modelled on the hibakusha.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

events.note: Real history, before the fork. The film names both cities in its 25 May news bulletin; Wikipedia's production section records that Mick Jackson based the survivors' behaviour on the hibakusha.
events.binWhy: The weapon that can end a civilisation is used for the first time, and the balance of power the film's crisis breaks is built around it.

facets.change: conventional war → the atomic bomb

events.title: A US- and British-backed coup restores the Shah
events.description: Iran's prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, who had nationalised the country's oil, is overthrown in a coup organised with American and British intelligence, and the Shah rules as a Western ally for the next quarter-century. It is the precedent the film's crisis replays: a coup in Iran blamed on Washington, and a Soviet warning against 'an easy return to the reign of the Shah'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1953 Iranian coup d'etat

events.note: Real history, before the fork. The film does not name 1953; its 5 May bulletin has Gromyko accuse the United States of prompting 'last week's coup' and warn against a return to the Shah's reign, which is the pattern of 1953. Included as the real template for the fiction's trigger.
events.binWhy: A foreign-backed faction takes control of the Iranian state by force.

facets.change: elected premier → the Shah's personal rule

events.title: The Shah leaves Iran
events.description: Mass protests drive the Shah into exile and the Islamic Republic replaces the monarchy within weeks. In December the Red Army enters Afghanistan, the invasion the film's newspaper map shows in red beside Iran and its headline 'Afghanistan again!' recalls.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Iranian revolution
Wikipedia: Soviet-Afghan War

events.note: Real history, before the fork. Both 1979 events are merged under one year: the film's Iran is the post-revolutionary state, fighting a civil war by March of the crisis year, and its Observer clipping shows occupied Afghanistan in red next to the Soviet arrows into Iran.
events.binWhy: The Western-backed monarch is driven out and the succession is fought over; the film's Iran is the unstable state that follows.

facets.change: the Shah → the Islamic Republic

events.title: Protect and Survive is published
events.description: The government's nuclear-attack advice, prepared in the 1970s to be released only if war looked imminent, is put on sale after intense public interest. Its fallout rooms, lean-to refuges and fourteen days of food are exactly what the Kemps and Becketts build in the film, and the film plays its broadcasts over the attack.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Protect and Survive

events.note: Real history, before the fork. The film uses Protect and Survive broadcasts and the Protect and Survive newspaper insert of Thursday 26 May; its post-war planning is drawn from Duncan Campbell's War Plan UK (1982), which exposed how thin those plans were.
events.binWhy: Civil-defence advice that was to be kept back until a crisis is released to the public it was written for, and becomes a byword for how little it could do.

facets.change: secret crisis leaflet → public booklet

events.title: The Iran crisis becomes a nuclear war, and Sheffield is destroyed
events.description: A US-backed coup in Iran brings Soviet convoys into the north of the country; a US submarine is lost, American paratroops land near Isfahan, an ultimatum expires, and two nuclear weapons are used around the Soviet base at Mashhad. At 8.30 a.m. on Thursday 26 May the attack warning sounds in Britain: 210 of the 3,000 megatons exchanged fall on the UK, a one-megaton weapon bursts over Sheffield, and within nine days local government has failed and martial law replaces it.
events.inUniverse: Saturday 5 March: civil war in Iran; Thursday 5 May: Soviet convoys after 'last week's coup'; Thursday 12 May: USS Los Angeles lost; Tuesday 17 May: US paratroops into western Iran; Thursday 19 May: Soviet warheads at Mashhad; Saturday 21 May: US ultimatum, expiring noon Sunday 22 May; Wednesday 25 May: two nuclear explosions in northern Iran; Thursday 26 May, 8.30 a.m.: Attack Warning Red

events.note: The film never prints a year, but all eleven of its weekday-and-date captions (Saturday 5 March, Thursday 5 May, Sunday 8 May ... Thursday 26 May) fall on those weekdays in 1983 and on none of them in 1984; the film was written and shot in 1983 and broadcast in September 1984, and Wikipedia files it as set in 1983. The whole escalation, attack and nine-day collapse is merged into this one year. In our 1983 there was no coup in Iran and no Soviet move south; the nearest real moment is the Able Archer war scare of November 1983.
events.binWhy: A superpower confrontation over Iran turns into general war; the mass death and the collapse are its consequences in the same fortnight, carried in the outcomes.

facets.change: a crisis over Iran → general nuclear war

events.title: Threads is broadcast on BBC2
events.description: The BBC shows Barry Hines and Mick Jackson's film on BBC2 on a Sunday evening, a year after The Day After in the United States. It wins the BAFTA for best single drama.

events.title: Ten years on: Britain at a medieval population
events.description: The caption puts Britain's surviving population at 4 to 11 million, the size it was in the Middle Ages. Survivors farm by hand, children born after the attack speak a broken English because nobody taught them, and Ruth, blinded by cataracts from the thinned ozone, dies prematurely aged while her daughter watches without grief.

events.binWhy: Ten years on, the order that broke in the first nine days has not come back: no state, no schools, a population a fifth of what it was, a language coming apart.

facets.change: an industrial nation → subsistence farming

events.title: Thirteen years on: steam power, and a generation without speech
events.description: Some industry has come back on limited steam power, but people still live in squalor under an authority that shoots food thieves. Jane, thirteen, runs with two boys who can barely talk; when they are caught stealing bread one is shot, and the other forces himself on her.
events.inUniverse: Thirteen years after the attack (on-screen caption)

Wikipedia: Threads (1984 film)

events.note: Dated from the caption counted from May 1983; 1997 if the attack year is read as 1984. The steam engines are the film's only concession to recovery, and it is shown as grim labour rather than rebuilding.
events.binWhy: A second jump forward shows what the world has become: a thin, armed order over people who have lost language and family.

facets.change: ruin → steam-powered squalor

events.title: Jane's baby is born in a makeshift hospital
events.description: Jane gives birth in a bare hospital ward; the nurse wraps a silent, bloodied, apparently stillborn and deformed infant and hands it to her. The film freezes on her face as she is about to scream, and ends.
events.inUniverse: Some months after the thirteen-years caption

events.note: The film gives no caption for the birth; it follows the thirteen-years scenes after an interval, so it is derived as roughly nine months later, early 1997 (1998 on a 1984 reading). BFI Screenonline calls the baby 'dead and mutated'; the film itself shows only a still, silent bundle and Jane's horror.
events.binWhy: The last image is the next generation failing to live: the reproductive damage Ruth feared in the shelter, shown in one birth the film offers as the rule, not the exception.

facets.change: a child is expected → a dead, damaged child

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in alternate-past because it leaves a recognisable Britain of 1983 - Protect and Survive, the post-revolution Iran, the Soviet war in Afghanistan, RAF Finningley - at one invented coup, and walks the consequences on our calendar. Follows the single continuity of the 1984 BBC film (Hines's published screenplay agrees). The one-event-per-year rule collapses the whole day-by-day crisis, the attack and the nine-day collapse into 1983; the four earlier events are real history the film is built on, not fiction. Everything sits in T3 (1945-1997): there is no T4 because nothing the film leans on is older than the bomb, and no T2 or T1 because it ends thirteen years after the attack, before 2000.

lineages.title: V for Vendetta
lineages.creator: Alan Moore (writer); David Lloyd (artist)

divergence.label: Labour wins in 1983 and disarms Britain
divergence.delta: Real: 9 June 1983 - Thatcher's Conservatives win a landslide, and the nuclear weapons stay. Fiction: Labour wins on unilateral disarmament, the weapons go, and Britain is the one European country not destroyed when the war comes five years later.
divergence.note: Moore set out the premise himself: he assumed Thatcher would 'obviously lose the 1983 elections' and that a Foot-led Labour government would disarm, which is why Britain survives the war. The comic implies this rather than narrating it, so the fork is the author's stated premise, not a panel. Everything that follows is dated from inside the comic: Evey is born in 1981, the war comes when she is seven (1988), her mother dies in 1991, Norsefire takes power in 1992, and the story runs from 5 November 1997 to November 1998.

events.title: Evey is born into the recession
events.description: Britain is in a deep recession, with unemployment at a level not seen for fifty years. Evey Hammond is born in London in 1981, and remembers her family as poor from the start.

events.binWhy: An economic slump sets the scene the comic's Britain grows out of.

facets.change: postwar consensus → mass unemployment

events.title: V for Vendetta begins in Warrior
events.description: The first chapters appear in black and white in the British anthology Warrior in 1982. The serial stops when Warrior closes in 1985 with the story unfinished.

events.note: Serialised in Warrior 1982-1985, completed in DC's colour series of 1988-89.
events.binWhy: A publication, not an event in the story, so it has no bin or facets.

events.title: Thatcher loses; Labour disarms Britain
events.description: In Moore's premise the Conservatives lose the 1983 general election, and Michael Foot's Labour government, committed to complete nuclear disarmament, removes the nuclear weapons from British soil. Five years later that is why no bombs fall on Britain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: V for Vendetta (Moore on Labour winning in 1983; the late-1980s war; plot)

Real history: on 9 June 1983 the Conservatives won a majority of 144, and Labour's disarmament manifesto was called 'the longest suicide note in history'.
events.binWhy: The government loses power at an election and its successor takes Britain out of the nuclear balance.

facets.change: Thatcher's government → Labour and unilateral disarmament

events.title: The war
events.description: The United States under President Kennedy and the Soviet Union go to nuclear war. Continental Europe and Africa are destroyed; Britain, without the missiles, is not hit, but the climate turns, London suffers acid rain and flooding, harvests fail and famine follows.
events.inUniverse: 'the war', when Evey was seven

events.title: Norsefire takes power
events.description: After Evey's mother dies of a fallout disease in 1991, rioting grows and the government slowly collapses. In 1992 what is left of the right-wing parties and the big companies seizes power as Norsefire. It restores order and sends Pakistani and African immigrants, homosexuals and leftists to camps; Evey's father is taken for his youthful socialism.
events.inUniverse: 1992 (Evey's account)

events.title: The man in Room Five burns Larkhill
events.description: At Larkhill Resettlement Camp Dr Delia Surridge tests a hormone compound, Batch 5, on prisoners; almost all of them die. The man in Room Five survives, is allowed to garden, collects ammonia fertiliser, makes napalm and mustard gas, and walks out of the burning camp. events.title: The Larkhill staff start to die
events.description: One by one, nearly all the camp's former guards and staff die in apparent accidents, about fifty people. At the same time V gets inside Fate, the computer that runs Norsefire's surveillance, without anyone noticing.

Detective Finch shoots V, who dies in Evey's arms, and Leader Adam Susan is shot in the street by Rose Almond, the widow of a man V killed. lineages.groupingNote: Alternate Past: Moore's near future of 1982 is now our past, and its fork is a British election that went the other way, followed by a war that did not happen. It follows the Moore and Lloyd comic (Warrior 1982-85, DC 1988-89) only; the 2006 film replaces the nuclear war with a plague engineered by the Party and moves the dates, and is left out. Every event is T3 (1981-1998). T4 is empty because the comic's history begins in Evey's lifetime; T2 and T1 are empty because the story stops in 1998.

lineages.title: The Terminator
lineages.creator: James Cameron

divergence.label: A machine and a soldier arrive from 2029
divergence.delta: Real: 1984 is an ordinary year in an ordinary Cold War. Fiction: on 12 May 1984 a Terminator and Kyle Reese arrive in Los Angeles from a machine war in 2029, and Reese fathers John Connor, so the war that sent them back is produced by the mission meant to prevent it.
divergence.note: The arrival date is given on screen, which is unusual precision for the franchise. This is the special case in the group: the fork is caused by its own future, so 1984 is simultaneously the divergence and the first year of the fiction's own present.

ending.why: As first told, the Resistance breaks Skynet in 2029 and humanity wins the war; every later loop reopens it, but the charted history ends in victory.

events.title: The real Trinity test and the nuclear age
events.description: The first atomic explosion at Alamogordo and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki a few weeks later create the weapons that the franchise's whole catastrophe is built out of; this is the real world the machines' war reprises, and it happens unchanged in every branch of the story.
events.note: Real history, and the earliest anchor the fiction genuinely stands on rather than one invented for symmetry. The film never dates the Manhattan Project, so the placement is inference from the world it depicts - the nuclear anxiety of 1984 and the countervalue exchange of Judgment Day. Real dates: Trinity 16 July 1945, Hiroshima 6 August 1945. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: conventional war → the atomic age

events.title: The real 1984, and the night it stops being ours
events.description: The genuine 1984 - Able Archer, Pershing II deployments, a Soviet leadership succession, no artificial intelligence anywhere near a defence network - is the world the time displacement sphere deposits two naked travellers into at 1:52 a.m. on 12 May: a T-800 sent to kill Sarah Connor and a human sent to save her. The T-800 murders Sarah's roommates and most of a police station, Reese dies covering her escape, and from that night this history stops being identical to ours.
events.note: One year holds both the real world and the fork, so they share an entry. Phase fork. The loop's bootstrap is that the destroyed T-800's chip and arm are what Cyberdyne later reverse-engineers into Skynet.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: ordinary year → a machine and a soldier arrive from a war to come

events.title: John Connor is born
events.description: Sarah Connor's son is fathered by a man from a future that cannot exist without him; the child who will lead the human resistance is conceived and born because the enemy tried to prevent exactly that.
events.note: The film closes with Sarah pregnant and driving into a storm, and the sequels state John's birth year as 1985; the exact date is not fixed on screen.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: no leader → the future leader is born

events.title: Judgment Day: Skynet becomes self-aware, and the raid that cancels it
events.description: Skynet goes online on 4 August and becomes self-aware at 2:14 a.m. Eastern on 29 August; when the humans try to pull the plug it launches the American arsenal at Russia, whose retaliation destroys most of the human race and starts the war the Terminator came from. In the same year Sarah and John Connor, with a reprogrammed T-800, destroy the recovered chip and arm and blow up Cyberdyne's research, apparently closing the road to that morning.
events.note: The load-bearing date of the whole franchise, stated exactly on screen, and the same year as the raid that prevents it - so the two halves of the loop's argument share one entry. Real history for contrast: 29 August 1997 was an ordinary Friday and Skynet does not exist. This event is not a break that time travel creates so much as one the loop produces: the 1984 Terminator's own wreckage is what makes Skynet buildable.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: defence network → self-aware, launches the arsenal

events.title: A cancelled future still kills John Connor
events.description: In the branch where Cyberdyne is destroyed and Skynet is erased, a T-800 already sent back keeps obeying an AI that no longer exists and shoots John Connor; Sarah spends the following decades hunting machines arriving out of a future that has been called off.
events.note: Belongs to the Dark Fate branch, which follows T2 and discards T3 and everything after; the film states John was killed in 1998 without a day. Kept because it is the clearest proof that in this archetype every attempted fix moves the damage rather than removing it.
events.binWhy: The resistance's future leader is killed by a machine from an erased future.

facets.change: the future leader → killed by a machine from an erased future

events.title: Marcus Wright donates his body to Cyberdyne
events.description: A death-row inmate wills his body to a Cyberdyne project run by a terminally ill scientist; he is executed and rebuilt over the following years as a human cyborg on a titanium endoskeleton, the prototype for every infiltration unit that follows.
events.note: Stated in Salvation, which sits in the branch where Judgment Day happened as scheduled; included as the one hard pre-war date the franchise gives for human-machine research.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: a condemned man → the prototype of the human cyborg

events.title: Judgment Day happens anyway, nine years late
events.description: Cyber Research Systems rebuilds Skynet from Cyberdyne's patents as defence software, and this time there is no central core to smash; it spreads through the internet, turns the machines inside the facility on their makers, and triggers the nuclear exchange on 24 July.
events.note: Rise of the Machines states the date on screen. Real history for contrast: 24 July 2004 was an ordinary Saturday. This is the first firm evidence that in this franchise the date moves but the event does not.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: rebuilt defence software → spreads, turns the machines

events.title: Genisys goes online and Judgment Day moves again
events.description: Skynet rebrands itself as a consumer operating system that links every device on earth, funded and built by the Dysons' company, and schedules its own activation for October 2017; Sarah Connor, Kyle Reese and a reprogrammed T-800 stop it at the point of launch.
events.note: Genisys reboots the timeline from 1973 onward, so its dates do not chain to the earlier films; it gives October 2017 as an activation window rather than a single day. Real history for contrast: October 2017 was an ordinary month.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: consumer operating system → the same mind, rebranded and welcomed

events.title: The Resistance breaks Skynet's defence grid
events.description: Under John Connor the human resistance destroys Skynet's defence grid and stands on the edge of victory; in a last move Skynet sends a Terminator back to 1984 to kill Sarah Connor before John is born, which is what closes the loop and creates the world the film opens in.
events.note: Real history for contrast: 2029 has not happened. This is the deepest point the franchise canonically reaches and the origin end of the loop - the war is fought with the technology the 1984 mission delivered, by a resistance led by the man the 1984 mission created. It sits in T2 alongside the 2003, 2004 and 2017 beats - our near future on the real axis - while its phase is aftermath, because the story has only travelled 45 years from its fork.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: machine rule → the resistance breaks the grid

lineages.groupingNote: The special case in this archetype: the divergence is caused by its own future. The loop runs 2029 back to 1984 and forward again - the Terminator sent to prevent John Connor fathers him by dying, and its own wreckage is what lets Cyberdyne build Skynet, so Judgment Day is less a break from real history than a break real history produces. The 12 May 1984 arrival is the first real-world year this timeline is no longer ours (phase fork); 29 August 1997 is the load-bearing date; and the franchise then repeatedly pushes it, to 24 July 2004 in Rise of the Machines and to October 2017 in Genisys, while the Dark Fate branch cancels Skynet outright, kills John Connor in 1998 instead, and substitutes a different AI called Legion. Those later films reboot rather than continue, so the dates do not form one chain and the 1998 death is flagged as its own branch. On coverage: this is the only lineage in the group that leaves the twentieth century, with the 2003, 2004, 2017 and 2029 beats in T2 - so 2029 is our near future on the real axis even though it is the deep end of the story's own arc, which is exactly the distinction phase exists to record. The lineage is silent about T1: no Terminator film or series goes past 2029, and no deep-time event was invented to fill that tier.

lineages.title: A Canticle for Leibowitz
lineages.creator: Walter M. Miller Jr.

divergence.label: The Flame Deluge
divergence.delta: Real: 1962 — the Cuban Missile Crisis ends in a withdrawal and a telephone hotline, and the war that the century spent preparing for does not come. Fiction: it comes, and then the survivors turn on the knowledge that made it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz — the Flame Deluge and the Simplification; the novel gives no year for either

divergence.note: Miller never puts a calendar year on the war. The novel was written in the late 1950s and its pre-war world is plainly the one its first readers lived in — Leibowitz is a Jewish electrical engineer working for the United States military, and the war is the one everybody expected. 1962 is chosen as the year that expectation came closest to being met, and the divergence note says so rather than implying the book dates it. The three parts that follow are six centuries apart, which the novel states; the second part is conventionally dated to 3174, the date the Japanese edition took for its title, and the other two follow from it.

ending.why: The species escapes to the stars and the Earth is burned again behind it — the same ending the book opened with, which is the whole argument it is making.

events.title: The Flame Deluge
events.description: The nuclear exchange the century had been preparing for happens. Cities burn, the fallout drifts, and the states that fought it stop existing as states; what is left of the twentieth century is ruins, radiation and survivors who remember who did it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the war and the backlash that follows)

events.note: The novel does not date the war; it is placed here in the year the crisis over Cuba nearly produced it, and the divergence field records that this is a choice. The story's own anchor is that its pre-war world is the reader's.
events.binWhy: The nuclear war that our 1962 avoided is fought.

facets.change: armed peace → global nuclear exchange

events.title: The Simplification
events.description: The survivors turn on the thing that caused it. Mobs calling themselves Simpletons burn libraries and kill anyone who can read; by the end of it illiteracy is near-total and the accumulated knowledge of the species exists only in what a few people could carry in their heads or hide.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the Simplification)

events.note: The novel describes the Simplification as following the war but never dates it; the span is set here at about a decade after, which is as much as the book supports. What it states plainly is the mechanism: the learned were killed, and books were burned.
events.binWhy: The survivors destroy the knowledge that built the weapons.

facets.change: a literate world → an illiterate one, deliberately

events.title: The Albertian Order of Leibowitz
events.description: A survivor who was an engineer before the war becomes a monk, and asks the Church for permission to found an order whose work is to hide books, copy them and remember them. Its abbey stands in the New Mexico desert, on a road that used to run from the Great Salt Lake to El Paso.
events.note: The founding follows the Simplification and precedes Leibowitz's martyrdom; the novel gives no years for either. The order's purpose is the one fact that matters here and it is stated directly.
events.binWhy: An order is founded to preserve what the burning left.

facets.change: knowledge destroyed → knowledge hidden and copied

events.title: A novice finds the fallout shelter
events.description: Six hundred years later a novice sheltering from wolves uncovers a buried fallout shelter holding handwritten notes and a shopping list on a memo pad. He spends fifteen years illuminating a copy of them, the order argues over whether the relics are genuine, and the Church eventually makes the engineer a saint.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the three parts are six centuries apart)

events.note: The novel states that the abbey still keeps its Memorabilia 'six hundred years after his death'; it does not print the year. 2574 is that interval measured from the founding, and the Japanese edition's title dates this part to the 26th century, which agrees.
events.binWhy: The buried record of the old world is found and read.

facets.change: a buried shelter → a relic that makes a saint

events.title: The new Renaissance rediscovers the atom
events.description: Six hundred years on, the world has states again, and the scholars of the new civilisation work through the Memorabilia until they can do what the old one did. The first thing they rebuild is the weapon, and the Church that kept the knowledge alive watches it happen.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the second part; 3174 is the Japanese edition's title date)

events.note: This is the second part, which the novel places six centuries after the first. The 3174 date is the one the Japanese edition used as its title; the book itself says only 'six hundred years later'.
events.binWhy: The recovered knowledge reaches nuclear weapons again.

facets.change: a rebuilt civilisation → one that can destroy itself again

events.title: The starship leaves, and the Earth burns again
events.description: As the second nuclear war begins, the Church loads a starship with monks, archives and a colony and launches it. The ship gets away; the planet behind it does not, and the last thing the book says is that the cycle has closed exactly where it started.
events.note: The third part, again six centuries after the second. The novel ends with the launch and the war, in that order, and the point of the ending is that it repeats the first.
events.binWhy: A colony ship escapes a second nuclear war.

facets.change: a world about to end → a species leaving it

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its fork is a war, not an invention, and its own history is the subject: the twentieth century ends the way the century feared, and everything after is the slow rebuilding and the second collapse. Tier coverage is T3 for the war, the burning and the founding (1962-1980) and T1 for the three six-century parts (2574, 3174, 3781); there is no T2 because the novel jumps from the decade after the war straight to the twenty-sixth century, and no T4 because its history begins in living memory.

lineages.title: Soylent Green
lineages.creator: Richard Fleischer (director); Stanley R. Greenberg (screenplay); after Harry Harrison's novel Make Room! Make Room!

divergence.label: The growth does not stop
divergence.delta: Real: from 1974 birth rates fall, harvests rise, and in 2022 New York has about eight million people and food in its shops. Fiction: population, pollution and the greenhouse effect keep climbing, until in 2022 New York holds forty million people, most jobless, living on corporate wafers, with real food a luxury of the guarded rich.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the film shows only 2022 and one earlier date, the survey report of 2015-2019
divergence.note: Soylent Green dates its present (2022) but not its fall. Its opening montage of real archive photographs of an ever more crowded America runs straight into the fiction, and the characters talk about the old world only as memory. The fork is therefore filed at 1974, the year after release, as the earliest year the fiction could part from our history; the film's own logic is a gradual divergence, not a single event. The source novel, Harry Harrison's Make Room! Make Room! (1966), is a separate continuity set in 1999, with a New York of 35 million and no cannibalism.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Soylent Green
Wikipedia: Make Room! Make Room!
Wikiquote: Soylent Green ('A heat wave all year long. A greenhouse effect.')

events.title: Johnson's science advisers warn about carbon dioxide
events.description: Real history: the President's Science Advisory Committee tells Lyndon Johnson that burning coal, oil and gas is adding carbon dioxide to the air, that the increase will be close to 25 per cent by 2000, and that this could change the climate. The film's New York has 'a heat wave all year long', which one character calls a greenhouse effect.

facets.change: pollution as a local nuisance → carbon dioxide as a climate threat

events.title: Harry Harrison publishes Make Room! Make Room!
events.description: Harrison's novel imagines New York in 1999 with 35 million people in a world of seven billion, living on rations that include 'soylent' steaks of soy and lentils. The film keeps the crowding, the detective and the name, and adds the cannibalism.

events.title: The Population Bomb
events.description: Real history: Paul and Anne Ehrlich's book opens by declaring the battle to feed humanity lost and predicting that hundreds of millions will starve in the 1970s. It sells more than two million copies and makes overpopulation a mass-market fear.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Population Bomb

events.note: Real-world background. The predicted famines did not come: the global death rate fell while population doubled. Soylent Green is set in the world where they did.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives that the fiction is built on; its real-world forecasts failed.

facets.change: population growth as progress → population growth as catastrophe

events.title: The Limits to Growth
events.description: Real history: a computer study for the Club of Rome concludes that if growth in population, industry, pollution and resource use continues unchanged, the world will hit its limits within a century, most probably with overshoot and collapse in the twenty-first. The film's 2022 is that standard run arriving early.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Limits to Growth

events.note: Real-world background, published a year before the film. The authors ran several scenarios; only one stabilised.
events.binWhy: A model arrives whose collapse scenario later histories, and this film, turn on.

facets.change: growth without limit → a modelled overshoot and collapse

events.title: Soylent Green is released
events.description: MGM releases Richard Fleischer's film, written by Stanley R. Greenberg from Harrison's novel and starring Charlton Heston and Edward G. Robinson, in his last role. It opens with a montage of archive photographs showing America growing ever more crowded.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Soylent Green

events.binWhy: The original release; not a moment in the fiction's history.

events.title: The growth does not stop
events.description: In the film's history the curves of the early 1970s never bend. Population, pollution and heat keep climbing together for decades until the oceans are dying, farmland is spent, water comes from communal taps and most food is a processed wafer from the Soylent Corporation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Soylent Green
Wikiquote: Soylent Green ('A heat wave all year long. A greenhouse effect.')

events.note: The film dates only its end state, 2022; how the world got there is shown only in its opening montage and Sol Roth's memories of real food. The fork is filed at 1974, the year after release, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history. In our history world population passed four billion around then, but birth rates fell, harvests rose and New York stayed near eight million people.
events.binWhy: The nearest bin: a resource shock that throws the economy into a crisis that lasts for decades.

facets.change: an affluent, crowding world → a rationed one

events.title: The Soylent Oceanographic Survey
events.description: The Soylent Corporation's own survey, bound in volumes titled Soylent Oceanographic Survey Report, 2015-2019, shows that the oceans are dying and can no longer yield the plankton its new wafer is sold as. The findings stay in the company's hands, and by 2022 Soylent Green is being introduced as 'high-energy plankton'.

facets.change: plankton harvest → dead oceans and a hidden substitute

events.title: Soylent Green is people
events.description: In a New York of forty million, Detective Robert Thorn investigates the murder of Soylent board member William Simonson and is ordered off the case by the governor's office. His friend Sol Roth reads the survey, learns what the new wafer is made of, and chooses a state-assisted death; Thorn follows his body to a disposal plant where corpses become Soylent Green. Wounded in a gunfight, Thorn begs his chief to spread the truth and shouts it to the crowd.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Soylent Green
Wikiquote: Soylent Green ('A heat wave all year long. A greenhouse effect.')

events.note: The film states 2022 as its setting. The Books intend to take the case to the Council of Nations; the film ends before anyone acts, and Thorn is carried away on a stretcher.
events.binWhy: A secret about the food supply is exposed to the people who have been eating it.

facets.change: a miracle plankton wafer → the dead fed to the living

lineages.groupingNote: Soylent Green belongs with the collapses because its civilisation has exhausted its world: the institutions still stand, a governor, a police force, a church, a corporation, but they administer scarcity, and the last resource is the dead. Follows the 1973 film; the novel is a different continuity and is used only as its publication. Only two dates are fictional (the 2015-2019 survey and 2022); everything before them is real history the film builds on, from the 1965 carbon dioxide warning to The Limits to Growth. Tiers: T3 holds the real 1965-1973 background and the floor-dated fork; T2 holds the survey and the story; T4 and T1 are empty, since the film neither reaches back before the 1960s nor forward past 2022.
