lineages.title: I Am Legend
lineages.creator: Richard Matheson

divergence.label: A plague after the bombings
divergence.delta: Real: 1975 — the Vietnam War ends with the fall of Saigon, no bomb has fallen on an American city, and the United States is at peace at home. Fiction: a war with bombings has just ended ('they say we won the war'), weekly dust storms carry a bacillus that kills and then raises its victims as vampires, and by the end of the year Robert Neville in Los Angeles believes he is the last man alive.
divergence.inUniverse: The months before Part One (January 1976); the plague is about half a year old when the novel opens
divergence.note: Matheson dates the four parts of the novel himself: January 1976, March 1976, June 1978 and January 1979. The plague is not given a date, but the novel opens some five or six months into Neville's solitude and his flashbacks show Kathy and Virginia dying in the months before, so the fork is 1975. The war that precedes it is never dated or described beyond 'the bombings'; it may fall in 1975 or earlier, and is folded into the fork. The films (The Last Man on Earth, 1964; The Omega Man, 1971; I Am Legend, 2007) each set their own dates and are not used.

events.title: Ivy Mike: the first hydrogen bomb
events.description: The United States detonates the first full-scale thermonuclear device at Enewetak Atoll, with a yield of 10.4 megatons, hundreds of times the Hiroshima bomb. Fallout, and the fear of it, becomes part of ordinary life.

events.note: Real history the novel builds on: written in the year after Ivy Mike, it spreads its plague through dust storms that follow a war of bombings, a clear echo of fallout. Critics read the germ as a product of that war; Matheson leaves it implied.
events.binWhy: A weapon able to end a civilisation is tested, and the dread of it is the soil the novel grows in.

facets.change: atomic bombs → a thermonuclear device of ten megatons

events.title: Richard Matheson publishes I Am Legend
events.description: Gold Medal Books publishes the novel as a paperback original on 7 August 1954, setting it more than twenty years ahead, in the Los Angeles of 1976 to 1979.

events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: The vampire plague
events.description: After a war of bombings, dust storms and swarms of mutated insects spread a disease that kills almost everyone and brings many of the dead back as vampires. Neville's daughter Kathy dies first and, under government orders, her body is burned in a public pit; when his wife Virginia dies he buries her instead, and she comes back to his door.
events.inUniverse: The months before January 1976, told in Neville's flashbacks

events.binWhy: A disease kills almost everyone alive and turns the dead into something else; the plague bin, with the end of every institution folded in.

facets.change: a war just won → dust storms that kill and raise the dead

events.title: Neville finds the germ
events.description: Alone in his boarded house, Neville teaches himself to use a microscope and finds a rod-shaped bacterium in a vampire's blood, which he names vampiris. He begins to explain the legends as biology: why sunlight, stakes and garlic work, and how the germ survives in its host.

She is a spy for a new society of the living infected, who keep the germ in check with pills and are organising to clear the city of the dead; she leaves him a letter warning him to run, because to them he is the killer who stalks them by day.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Post-Industrial Collapse because its fork is a plague in its readers' near future that empties Los Angeles and ends the old order, and the novel follows the last survivor of that order until the society that replaces it catches him. It follows Matheson's 1954 novel only; the three films set their own dates. Matheson dates four moments (January 1976, March 1976, June 1978, January 1979) and the plague year is derived from them; the chain is not padded further. lineages.title: The Stand
lineages.creator: Stephen King

divergence.label: Captain Trips escapes Project Blue
divergence.delta: Real: June 1980 — the United States has renounced offensive biological weapons and is party to the treaty banning them, and the summer's news is an election campaign and the eruption of Mount St. Helens. Fiction: a weaponised influenza built in a secret Army laboratory in California escapes when a guard flees with his family, and within weeks it has killed almost everyone on Earth.
divergence.inUniverse: Book One, 'Captain Trips', runs from 16 June to 4 July 1980 in the original edition
divergence.note: The atlas follows the 1978 original, which is set in 1980 and dates its three books (Book One: 16 June to 4 July 1980). The first paperback (1980) moved the setting to 1985, and the Complete and Uncut Edition of May 1990 moved it to 1990 with updated references; that edition is the one in print, and a reader using it should add ten years to every story date here. The 1978 text is used because it is the original and because its fork falls after its own publication. The 1994 and 2020 television adaptations are not used.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Stand (1978 original set in 1980; the 1990 edition moves it to 1990)

ending.why: Flagg's Las Vegas has been destroyed, the Boulder Free Zone has restored power and a government, and Frannie's son Peter, the first child born after the plague, catches the superflu and survives, which means the species can go on.

events.title: Nerve agent from an Army test kills thousands of sheep in Utah
events.description: VX sprayed in an open-air test at the Dugway Proving Ground drifts beyond the range and between 3,800 and 6,400 sheep are found dead in Skull Valley. The Army admits the tests but not the blame; its own classified report is not released until 1998.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dugway sheep incident (13 March 1968; The Stand listed among works it inspired)
StephenKing.com: The Stand (inspired by a biological-warfare documentary and a chemical spill in Utah)

events.note: Real history the novel builds on. King said the book began with a news story about a chemical spill in Utah that killed sheep and would have reached Salt Lake City if the wind had blown the other way; Project Blue is the same secret testing with a worse agent.
events.binWhy: A lethal military accident is kept officially unacknowledged for thirty years by the state responsible.

facets.change: an open-air nerve-agent test → thousands of dead sheep and an Army denial

events.title: The Biological Weapons Convention opens for signature
events.description: Three years after Nixon ended all American offensive biological weapons programmes, a treaty banning the development and stockpiling of biological weapons is opened for signature in London, Moscow and Washington; it enters into force in March 1975.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Biological Weapons Convention (opened 10 April 1972; in force 26 March 1975; Nixon's 1969 statement)

events.note: Real history the novel's premise depends on: Project Blue is exactly what the United States had publicly given up, which is why the generals in the book work so hard to hide it.
events.binWhy: The powers sign a treaty outlawing the class of weapon the fiction's catastrophe comes from.

facets.change: national germ-warfare programmes → a treaty banning them

events.title: Stephen King publishes The Stand
events.description: Doubleday publishes the novel on 3 October 1978, heavily cut for length and set two years ahead, in 1980.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Stand (published 3 October 1978 by Doubleday)

events.note: King described it as an attempt at an American Lord of the Rings, with Las Vegas as Mordor. The original edition went out of print when the uncut edition replaced it in 1990.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: Captain Trips kills 99.4 per cent of humanity
events.description: A guard flees a secret Army laboratory in California with his family, carrying a weaponised flu whose antigens keep shifting; he dies at a gas station in Arnette, Texas, and the disease spreads faster than the Army can hide it. General Starkey has agents release it in the Eastern Bloc and China so that no one can blame America, and within about a month some 99.4 per cent of the world is dead.

Those later moments would otherwise be settlement-founded, terror-attack and mass-death.

events.title: Frannie's son survives the superflu
events.description: In Boulder in the depth of winter Frannie Goldsmith gives birth to a son, Peter, who catches the superflu and fights it off: the first sign that children born after the plague can live. Stu Redman, left behind in the desert with a broken leg, comes back with Tom Cullen soon after, and some months later the two of them leave Boulder for Maine.

events.note: The year is derived: Frannie is newly pregnant in June 1980, Stu's return is late in a Book Three that ends on 10 January of the following year (the uncut edition's fan chapter guides, seen only in search results and not opened, give 7 September 1990 to 10 January 1991; the original's range is assumed to be the same days ten years earlier), and the move to Maine is four months later. A December 1980 birth cannot be ruled out, but the return and the departure fall in 1981. The uncut edition adds an epilogue in which Flagg wakes on a beach in the southern hemisphere; it is undated.
events.binWhy: A child is born on whom the future turns: the first proof that the next generation will not die of the plague.

facets.change: a winter of waiting for the newborns to die → a baby who survives the flu

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Post-Industrial Collapse because its fork is a single man-made pandemic in its readers' near present that ends every government on Earth within a month, and the story is about what the survivors build. It follows the 1978 original (set in 1980); the 1990 uncut edition shifts every date by ten years. The novel dates only a single year of story, June 1980 to the spring of 1981, and one-event-per-year forces most of it (the Free Zone, the Boulder bombing, the destruction of Las Vegas) into the 1980 event; the chain is not padded with invented dates. lineages.title: Mad Max
lineages.creator: George Miller & Byron Kennedy

divergence.label: The oil war
divergence.delta: Real: the 1983 oil glut collapses prices, the West recovers and Australia is a stable democracy. Fiction: the same fuel crisis becomes an unending war for the last petrol, and by December 1984 the highways are held by the last police squad while the institutions behind them fail.
divergence.note: Never stated on screen. The date comes from the official Mad Max 2 production preamble, which describes Iran striking Saudi Arabia and the oil majors failing, reinforced by the Main Force Patrol's 'est. 1983' plate; the first film's own signage reads 6 December 1984 and its title card says only 'a few years from now'. Later material makes it worse: the 2015 Fury Road comics place their own Fall in the 2010s and George Miller says the films have no strict chronology, so the 1980s dating belongs to the flagship trilogy rather than to the franchise.

ending.why: One citadel is freed and its water released, but the wasteland is the world now and a generation has known nothing else.

events.title: The first commercial oil well
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Drake's well at Titusville starts the oil age whose exhaustion this franchise turns into the end of the world.
events.note: Real-world background.

events.title: The first oil shock

events.note: Real-world background; the fiction's own oil war is dated only in production and tie-in material.

events.title: Mad Max: 'a few years from now'
events.description: The film is released with a title card that places it a few years ahead of its audience: the Main Force Patrol still answers calls, but the highways are already a war zone and the institutions behind them are failing.
events.note: Australian release 12 April 1979; the on-screen title card is the first film's only firm dating gesture.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The oil war
events.description: The war for the last fuel begins as Iran strikes Saudi Arabia, the Gulf fields burn and the oil majors fail, and the industrial order starts to come apart at the edges.
events.note: Never stated on screen; see the divergence note. The Mad Max 2 narration does not date the collapse at all, and the often-quoted 'last years of the 20th century' line does not exist in the film.

facets.change: the last fuel → war for it; the oil majors fail

events.title: The last patrol
events.description: The first film's own date, from the Highway 9 sign: Max hunts Toecutter's gang along a coast where the rule of law now depends on a handful of cars.
events.note: On-screen background signage gives 6 December 1984, the franchise's hardest in-universe date.

events.title: The Road Warrior and the last refinery

events.note: The three-year gap comes from the official production preamble, not the film; whether the nuclear exchange happens here or between the first two films depends on which continuity you follow.

events.title: Bartertown and the children of the Crack in the Earth

events.title: Fury Road: the wasteland a generation on
events.description: The franchise's furthest era: a citadel trades water for fuel and chrome, a war rig runs for the green place, and Max's forced tattoo records the day count of a life spent in the wreckage.
events.note: Miller: the apocalypse 'happens, and you wind up 45-50 years in the future' from a rolling 'next Wednesday'; the tattoo implies about thirty-three years since the Fall; the 2015 comics put their Fall in the 2010s. The year is arithmetic on Miller's figure, not a stated date. Furiosa (2024) runs the fifteen years directly into this film.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: wasteland → a citadel trading water for fuel

lineages.groupingNote: Mad Max is the archetype stripped to fuel: the world does not end in a war anyone wins, it runs out of oil, and everything after the first film is set among the wreckage of ordinary Australian life, a police interceptor, a refinery, a ruined Sydney. The fork is dated 1983 with low confidence because the collapse is described only in production and tie-in material, while the films' own dating runs from a title card reading 'a few years from now' to on-screen signage reading 6 December 1984. Tiers: this branch has no T1 and never will, because the franchise's furthest era is the Fury Road wasteland roughly forty-five to fifty years past its Fall, so Mad Max simply stops inside our own next century; the T4 entry is real-world background only (the oil age, 1859), and everything the fiction itself depicts from 1973 onward sits in T3 or T2. Miller's repeated insistence that the films have no strict chronology is the honest summary of this lineage's dates.

lineages.title: Planet of the Apes
lineages.creator: Franklin J. Schaffner (dir.); Michael Wilson & Rod Serling (screenplay), from Pierre Boulle's novel

divergence.label: The plague that kills every dog and cat
divergence.delta: Real: 1983 passes with the world's pets alive and the West rearming; nothing has ended. Fiction: a global plague kills every dog and cat on Earth within months, humans adopt apes as pets and then as slaves, and within a generation the apes have taken the planet.
divergence.note: The pentalogy's first impossible event is actually 1973, when Zira and Cornelius arrive from the destroyed future and Caesar is born, but that is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. 1983 is Conquest's 'eight years' before its 1991 uprising and is the first dated alteration to human civilisation; the revolt (1991) and the undated nuclear war are downstream. Confidence is medium because the film supplies only the relative 'eight years ago', not a year.

ending.why: The astronaut finds the ruins of New York; humanity blew itself up and the apes inherited the Earth.

events.title: On the Origin of Species
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Darwin publishes natural selection, the idea this series literalises by putting apes on top of the pile.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction itself is silent before 1972.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: fixed species → natural selection published

events.title: The Icarus leaves Earth
events.description: Taylor's ANSA mission launches into the film's own near future, and relativistic time dilation will carry the crew 2,006 years forward while only eighteen months pass for them.
events.note: No on-screen date card. 1972 is derived from the 3978 arrival minus the 2,006 elapsed years the crew log, and from Landon's line about 'the class of '72'.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: Earth → a mission flung two thousand years forward

events.title: Zira and Cornelius land in their own past
events.description: The chimpanzees who fled the destroyed Earth arrive in a recognisable 1973 Los Angeles, testify before a congressional committee and are killed, but their son Caesar survives to close the series' bootstrap loop.
events.note: The first impossible event in the series, but a closed causal loop rather than a change to human history, which is why this lineage's fork is placed at the 1983 plague instead.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: the present → visited by talking apes from a destroyed future

events.title: The plague that kills every dog and cat
events.description: A global plague wipes out the world's dogs and cats within months, humans take apes into their homes as replacements, and the species that will inherit the planet becomes first a pet and then property.
events.note: Conquest gives only the relative 'eight years ago' before its 1991 uprising, so 1983 is arithmetic; the same film is frequently misreported as being set in 1983.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: pets → all dead; apes brought into homes

events.title: Caesar's ape uprising
events.description: The enslaved apes of North America revolt and take the cities, and the human industrial order begins to come apart inside a single generation.
events.note: Conquest's title card gives 1991 and the internal arithmetic fits (Caesar is eighteen, born in 1973), though some timelines read the film as 1993.
events.binWhy: The ruled revolt against those who hold power over them.

facets.change: enslaved apes → take the cities

events.title: The war that ravages the surface
events.description: The human counter-attack becomes the 'vilest war in human history' and leaves the surface a radioactive ruin, which is the world of the Forbidden Zone that Taylor will find.
events.note: Never dated on screen: Battle's Lawgiver places it in the aftermath of Caesar's victory, and that film's 'twelve-year truce' points to about 1992.
events.binWhy: The counter-attack leaves the surface a radioactive ruin.

facets.change: revolt → the counter-attack leaves the surface a ruin

events.title: Ape City and the truce
events.description: A generation after the revolt, Caesar rules a walled ape city where humans and apes are supposed to be equal, and a narrator six centuries later looks back on how fragile that peace was.
events.note: Battle states no year; 'ten years after a worldwide series of ape revolutions and a brutal nuclear war' plus the twelve-year truce puts the main story around 2003, while some sources prefer 2001.
events.binWhy: A truce between species, and a city built on it.

facets.change: war → a walled city and a fragile truce

events.title: The Lawgiver's history lesson
events.description: In 2670 an ape Lawgiver teaches schoolchildren that humans and apes once lived together, which is the ape world's founding myth and the proof that the human past has become scripture.
events.note: On-screen title card 'North America - 2670 A.D.'; the closing line's '600 years after Caesar's death' contradicts the main story's roughly 2003 setting and is unexplained.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: history → taught as scripture

events.title: Two astronauts crash into ape-ruled America
events.description: The 1974 television series drops a pair of twentieth-century astronauts, launched in 1980, into an ape-ruled North America four centuries after the Lawgiver, where humans are mute livestock and fugitives.
events.note: The date is a chronometer reading that the series itself says may have stopped mid-flight; the 1975 animated series is undated, with fans split between 3479 and 3979.
events.binWhy: Twentieth-century astronauts arrive in a future that is not theirs.

facets.change: the present → astronauts land in an ape-ruled future

events.title: Brent arrives and the doomsday bomb ends the Earth
events.description: A second astronaut follows Taylor's trajectory and, days later, the mutant humans of the Forbidden Zone detonate the Alpha-Omega bomb and destroy the planet.
events.note: Brent states 3955 in dialogue while Taylor's chronometer in the 1968 film reads 3978; the standard rationalisation is that Brent's chronometer was damaged.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: a ruined world → destroyed outright

events.title: Taylor lands on the ape-ruled Earth
events.description: The 1968 film's frame closes as Taylor's ship comes down in the Forbidden Zone, he is hunted and rendered mute, and the half-buried Statue of Liberty reveals that this planet was always Earth.
events.note: The ship's on-screen chronometer reads 3978; the 'November 25' date comes from a later novelisation, not from the film.
events.binWhy: The half-buried statue tells him where he has been all along.

facets.change: a strange planet → recognised as home

lineages.groupingNote: The pentalogy is this archetype's purest long form: a catastrophe inside the twentieth century ends the human industrial order, and the films then live inside its ruins, from a Statue of Liberty on a beach to a sacred scroll that remembers humans as vermin. The fork is placed at the 1983 plague rather than the 1991 uprising because 1983 is the first dated change to human history; the revolt, the war and ape rule are all downstream of it, while the series' earlier impossible event, Zira and Cornelius arriving in 1973, is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. Tiers: T4 and T2 are nearly empty because the fiction jumps from the 1990s straight to 2670; the only T4 entry is real-world background (Darwin, 1859) and the only T2 entry is Battle's roughly 2003 setting. T1 is where this branch actually lives, at 2670, 3085, 3955 and 3978. The 2011-2017 reboot (Rise, Dawn, War) and Kingdom (2024) are a separate continuity that re-runs the collapse as a 2016 laboratory accident and a simian-flu pandemic, and the 2001 Burton film is a third; neither is mixed into the events above.

lineages.title: Twelve Monkeys
lineages.creator: Terry Gilliam (dir.); David & Janet Peoples (screenplay), from Chris Marker's La Jetée

divergence.label: The virus is released in Philadelphia
divergence.delta: Real: the winter of 1996 passes with no plague and five billion people live out their lives. Fiction: on 13 December 1996 a laboratory-grown virus is released in Philadelphia, and by 2035 the survivors are sealed underground, sending prisoners back to change a past that cannot be changed.
divergence.note: The 2035 scientists state the date on screen, describing the release as 'probably on December 13, 1996', with symptoms first detected in Philadelphia on 27 December; the film's opening card says five billion will die in 1997.

ending.why: The plague happens exactly as remembered; the loop closes, five billion die, and the survivors live underground.

events.title: The Russian flu pandemic
events.description: Real history, not fiction: a respiratory pandemic rides the new railway and steamship networks out of Central Asia and kills about a million people, the real rehearsal for the fiction's plague.
events.note: Real-world background; death tolls vary by source.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: new railways → a pandemic rides them

events.title: The first jump lands in the First World War
events.description: A targeting error drops Cole into a trench in 1917, where he is shot in the leg, a wound that will still be in his thigh when he reaches 1996.
events.note: On screen; the bullet is the object half of the film's time loop.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: a trench → a man from the future lands in it

events.title: La Jetée
events.description: Chris Marker's photo-roman tells the same story with no dates at all, a man from a post-war underground sent back to a woman on a pier, and gives Gilliam's film its structure and its ending.
events.note: Real-world publication; La Jetée never dates its Third World War or its future.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The second jump lands in 1990
events.description: Sent to 1996, Cole arrives six years early, is arrested, and meets Jeffrey Goines and Dr Railly in a Baltimore asylum, seeding the false lead that runs through the rest of the film.
events.note: Railly states 'This is 1990'; the opening title card is dated 12 April 1990.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: an asylum → a man from the future, six years early

events.title: The virus is released, and the loop closes
events.description: Cole's jump lands in November 1996 and in December he is shot dead at Philadelphia airport in front of his own child self while Dr Peters walks onto a plane carrying the virus, so the plague is not prevented but caused.
events.note: The 2035 scientists state the release date on screen; the Army of the Twelve Monkeys, whose name they blame, are animal-rights activists and a red herring, and the carrier is Goines's assistant, Dr Peters.
events.binWhy: The virus is released; the plague is caused, not prevented.

facets.change: a plan to prevent → the virus released, the loop closed

events.title: Five billion dead
events.description: Within a year the virus has reached every continent and killed about five billion people, the survivors seal themselves into underground compounds, and the industrial world above is finished.
events.note: The opening title card states that five billion people will die in 1997, and the film's ending confirms the outbreak is not averted.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: release → five billion dead within a year

events.title: The underground future
events.description: The film's frame: Philadelphia is a sealed compound, dissidents are volunteered to the time programme, and scientists watch Cole's life on a screen while still trying to recover a pure sample of the original virus.
events.note: 2035 is the standard citation and matches the film's 'thirty years' dialogue loosely; the year is never spoken on screen, and a strict reading of the dialogue implies about 2026.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: the surface → sealed compounds; dissidents sent back

lineages.groupingNote: Twelve Monkeys is this archetype in its bleakest form: a plague released in a single afternoon in 1996 has killed five billion people by 1997, and the film's future, a sealed underground Philadelphia in 2035, is the ruins. It belongs here because the industrial world does not fall to war or machines but to a laboratory sample carried onto a plane, and because the survivors' only project is reaching back into the world they lost. The paradoxes are the point and are worth stating together: the timeline is a single immutable loop, the message that sends Cole back is Railly's own 1996 voicemail, the bullet in his leg comes from the antique pistol Jose hands him in 1996, and the child who watches him die at the airport grows up to be him, so the plague is caused rather than prevented, and the film's own metaphor for this is Cole watching a movie that never changes. Note the phase anomaly: Cole's 1917 and 1990 scenes count as prehistory by year but are incursions from the branch's own future. Tiers: T2 holds only 2035 because that is the only future the film ever shows, and there is no T1 at all, since this branch ends thirty-nine years after its fork; T4 is real-world background only (the 1889 pandemic). The 2015-2018 television series is a separate continuity and is not counted here.

lineages.title: Waterworld
lineages.creator: Peter Rader & David Twohy (writers); Kevin Reynolds (director)

divergence.label: The ice caps melt
divergence.delta: Real: in 1996 the polar ice is intact and sea level is rising by millimetres a year. Fiction: the ice caps melt entirely and the sea covers nearly every continent, until people live on boats and floating atolls, pay for goods in dirt and remember land only as a myth.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the opening narration says only 'the future'; the story is commonly placed about 2500
divergence.note: The film gives no date for the flood or for its story. The anchors are indirect: the Smokers' flagship is the Exxon Valdez and her captain is venerated as 'Saint Joe' Hazelwood, so the flood follows the March 1989 spill; the story is conventionally dated about 2500, a figure Wikipedia's plot uses but the film never states. The fork is filed at 1996, the year after release, as a floor. What caused the melt is not settled either: the film says only that the ice caps melted, and the 1997 Acclaim comic offered its own explanation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterworld
Wikiquote: Waterworld (opening narration)
Wikipedia: Exxon Valdez oil spill

ending.why: The Deacon is dead and his ship sunk, and the survivors reach real land with soil, fresh water and trees; the rest of the planet is still sea.

events.title: Peak XV is named the highest mountain on Earth
events.description: Real history: the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, having computed the height in 1852, announces that Peak XV is the world's highest summit and proposes calling it Mount Everest. Waterworld's ending rests on this fact: the last land left above a drowned planet is its highest point.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mount Everest

events.note: Real-world background. The theatrical cut never names Dryland; the extended 'Ulysses' cut identifies it as Everest.
events.binWhy: A survey result that fixes which point on Earth stands highest.

facets.change: an unnamed Himalayan peak → the known roof of the world

events.title: Hillary and Tenzing reach the summit of Everest
events.description: Real history: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay make the first documented ascent of Everest. In the extended cut, Helen and Enola find a plaque to the two men on Dryland, the only clue that the island is the mountain's top.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mount Everest
Looper: Where exactly is Dryland at the end of Waterworld? (Hillary and Tenzing plaque in the Ulysses cut)

events.note: Real-world background. The plaque is shown only in the Ulysses cut; the theatrical release leaves Dryland unidentified.
events.binWhy: A first expedition reaches a place no one had stood.

facets.change: an unclimbed summit → the top of the world reached

events.title: The IPCC is founded
events.description: Real history: the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme set up the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to assess the science of warming, and the UN General Assembly endorses it later that year. Waterworld was written and made in the first years of that assessment.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

events.note: Real-world background. The film never mentions climate science; its opening says only that the polar ice caps melted. This event and the 1990 report are filed as the real climate context of the premise, not as anything the film cites.
events.binWhy: A standing international body is created that will shape the world's response to warming.

facets.change: scattered warnings → a standing scientific assessment

events.title: The Exxon Valdez runs aground
events.description: Real history: the tanker Exxon Valdez spills about 41,000 cubic metres of crude oil into Prince William Sound, killing between 100,000 and 250,000 seabirds, thousands of sea otters and hundreds of seals. Waterworld makes her rusting hulk the flagship of the Smokers and her captain, Joseph Hazelwood, their patron saint.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Exxon Valdez oil spill
Wikipedia: Waterworld

events.note: This is the one real event the film names outright. Hazelwood was convicted in 1990 of a misdemeanour, negligent discharge of oil. In our history the ship was repaired, renamed and finally beached for scrap at Alang in August 2012; in the film's history she survives, under her old name, into the drowned world.
events.binWhy: The nearest bin: an industrial disaster that killed wildlife on a mass scale and became the emblem of oil's damage. No human population was lost.

facets.change: a working tanker → a byword for oil spills

events.title: The first IPCC report projects rising seas
events.description: Real history: the IPCC's First Assessment Report concludes that human emissions are substantially increasing greenhouse gases and projects global sea level rising about six centimetres a decade over the next century. It is the official version of the threat Waterworld pushes to absurdity.

sources.title: Wikipedia: IPCC First Assessment Report

events.note: Real-world background, not cited by the film. Melting all the ice on Earth would raise the sea by tens of metres; the film needs several thousand, and Wikipedia gives its implied rise as over 7,600 metres.
events.binWhy: A scientific assessment arrives that later climate politics turns on.

facets.change: a hypothesis → an official projection of rising seas

events.title: Waterworld is released
events.description: Universal releases Kevin Reynolds's film, starring and co-produced by Kevin Costner, then the most expensive film ever made. A longer cut restored for television, dubbed the Ulysses cut, identifies Dryland as Everest.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterworld

events.note: Written by Peter Rader and David Twohy from Rader's 1986 screenplay. Tie-ins include Max Allan Collins's novelization, games, the 1997 Acclaim comic Waterworld: Children of Leviathan, which expands on the cause of the flood, and the Universal theme-park show; a television sequel was announced in 2021 and has not been made.
events.binWhy: The original release; not a moment in the fiction's history.

events.title: The ice caps melt
events.description: The polar ice melts and the sea rises over almost all the land. Cities, farms and nations go under; the survivors take to boats and to floating atolls lashed together from scrap, and in time land itself becomes a legend called Dryland.
events.inUniverse: 'The future': the polar ice caps have melted, covering the Earth with water

sources.title: Wikiquote: Waterworld (opening narration)
Wikipedia: Waterworld

events.note: Undated in the film, whose opening narration says only 'the future' and that the polar ice caps have melted. The flood must come after March 1989, because the Smokers revere the Exxon Valdez's captain, and it is filed at 1996, the year after release, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history. The melt is a process rather than an event, and the Mariner's gills and webbed feet imply many generations between it and the story.
events.binWhy: The order of every land-based society breaks down and does not come back.

facets.change: continents → a planet of open sea

events.title: Enola's map leads to Dryland
events.description: A drifter with gills, the Mariner, is dragged into the flight of Helen and the girl Enola, whose back is tattooed with a map to Dryland, while the Deacon's Smokers hunt them from the Exxon Valdez. The Mariner sinks the tanker and the Deacon dies; the survivors follow the map to an island of soil, fresh water and trees, find the remains of Enola's parents there, and the Mariner sails back out to sea.
events.inUniverse: Commonly given as 2500; no year is stated on screen

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterworld
Looper: Where exactly is Dryland at the end of Waterworld? (Hillary and Tenzing plaque in the Ulysses cut)

events.note: Wikipedia's plot places the story in 2500, and other summaries repeat it, but the film itself names no year. The date is kept as the conventional one with low confidence.
events.binWhy: Survivors of the drowned world reach land and stay; the first settlement on Dryland.

facets.change: Dryland a myth → Dryland found and settled

lineages.groupingNote: Waterworld is the collapse archetype told as a sea story: industrial civilisation is gone, and what remains is salvage, from the atolls' scrap walls to a gang that still runs on the Exxon Valdez's oil. Follows the 1995 film, with the extended Ulysses cut used only for its identification of Dryland as Everest. Both of its fictional dates are soft: the fork is a floor (1996) and the story's 2500 is conventional, not stated. Tiers: T4 holds one real event (the 1856 survey of Everest) and T3 the real 1953-1995 background the film builds on; T2 holds only the undated melt; T1 holds the story itself, around 2500. Nothing between the flood and the film is dated, so the centuries of drift are empty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterworld
Wikiquote: Waterworld (opening narration)
Looper: Where exactly is Dryland at the end of Waterworld? (Hillary and Tenzing plaque in the Ulysses cut)

lineages.title: 28 Days Later
lineages.creator: Alex Garland (writer) and Danny Boyle (director); Juan Carlos Fresnadillo (28 Weeks Later); Nia DaCosta (The Bone Temple)

divergence.label: The Rage virus escapes a Cambridge primate lab
divergence.delta: Real: 2002 — Britain has just been declared free of foot-and-mouth disease after eleven months of pyres, closed footpaths and six million slaughtered animals, and the country is getting back to normal. Fiction: animal-rights activists break into a Cambridge laboratory and free chimpanzees infected with Rage, and within a month Britain has fallen and been cut off from the world.
divergence.inUniverse: Day One; the first film is 'twenty-eight days later', and 28 Years Later (2025) opens on the outbreak and jumps twenty-eight years
divergence.note: No film states a calendar year for the outbreak. The atlas follows the reading that the first film is set in its own present, 2002, which Wikipedia's articles on 28 Years Later and The Bone Temple adopt, and which puts 28 Years Later in 2030. There is a case for 2001: the first film was shot in 2001, before 9/11, and the franchise's fan wiki reports that Nia DaCosta and Jack O'Connell have said the outbreak happened in 2001 and that Frank's taxi carries a tax disc expiring in February 2002. That page was not accessible, so the claim is noted rather than used; choosing 2001 would move every story date here back by one year. Because the first film came out in November 2002, the fork's own year, and the atlas allows one event per year, its release is recorded here; the publication events are the 2007 and 2025 sequels.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Years Later (prologue at the original outbreak; main story twenty-eight years later, in 2030)
Wikipedia: 28 Days Later (Cambridge laboratory; shot in 2001; released 1 November 2002)
LADbible: why the Teletubbies open 28 Years Later (dating the outbreak to the turn of the century)

ending.why: Twenty-eight years on, Rage has been wiped out of continental Europe but Britain is still quarantined and ruled by whoever is strongest, and the one sign of hope, a doctor's evidence that an infected man can be brought back to himself, dies with the doctor.

events.title: Ebola is identified
events.description: Two outbreaks of a haemorrhagic fever, at Nzara in Sudan and Yambuku in Zaire, are traced to a new virus, named Ebola. It becomes the model of a disease that kills fast and spreads through contact with the sick.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ebola (first identified in 1976 in Nzara and Yambuku)
Wikipedia: 28 Days Later (Boyle took inspiration from Ebola, with aspects of rabies)

events.note: Real history the film builds on: Danny Boyle has said Rage was modelled on Ebola with elements of rabies. The 1976 outbreaks were local and burned out; Rage is the same kind of disease with an incubation of seconds.
events.binWhy: A new, highly lethal disease emerges and kills in its first outbreaks; the plague bin, at the scale of two epidemics.

facets.change: an unknown fever in two villages → a named virus the world fears

events.title: Britain admits mad cow disease can reach people
events.description: After years of ministers assuring the public that British beef was safe, the government acknowledges a probable link between BSE in cattle and a new, fatal human brain disease, variant CJD. British beef exports are banned worldwide.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (the March 1996 worldwide ban on British beef; 178 UK deaths)
Wikipedia: 28 Days Later (Garland linked the quarantine to UK anxieties about BSE and foot-and-mouth)

events.note: Real history the film builds on: Alex Garland tied the film's quarantined Britain to anxieties over BSE and foot-and-mouth. vCJD has killed 178 people in the UK; the damage in 1996 was to trust and to the beef trade.
events.binWhy: A disease risk that the state had played down is admitted to the public it was hidden from.

facets.change: official assurances that beef is safe → an admitted link to a fatal brain disease

events.title: Foot-and-mouth disease closes the British countryside
events.description: Foot-and-mouth is found at an Essex abattoir on 19 February 2001 and spreads across Britain. More than six million cattle and sheep are slaughtered and burned, rights of way are closed across whole regions, and the general election is postponed by a month; the outbreak is declared over on 14 January 2002.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth outbreak

events.note: Real history the film builds on, and the year it was shot. The emptied countryside and the pyres are the nearest real Britain came to the film's quarantine; the election delay was the first since the Second World War.
events.binWhy: A disease kills or forces the slaughter of livestock on a mass scale and shuts down rural Britain; a biological failure at national scale.

facets.change: open countryside → closed footpaths and burning pyres

events.title: The Rage virus is released, and Britain falls in a month
events.description: Animal-rights activists free infected chimpanzees from a Cambridge laboratory, and a virus that turns people into killers within moments spreads across the country. Twenty-eight days later a courier wakes from a coma in a deserted London; the survivors he joins follow a radio broadcast to an army blockade near Manchester, where the soldiers turn out to want the women, and the film ends with a jet flying over a remote cottage.
events.inUniverse: Day One to about Day Fifty; the film's title is the gap between the release and Jim waking

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Days Later
Wikipedia: 28 Years Later (the prologue at the outbreak; the reading of the year as 2002)

events.note: The year is the atlas's reading (see divergence.note); 2001 is the main alternative. The first film only hints at the world beyond Britain: the jet at the end suggests it is still there, which the sequels confirm.
events.binWhy: A new virus kills or turns almost the whole population of a country within weeks; the plague bin.

facets.change: a laboratory break-in → an empty London and a country cut off

events.title: London is resettled, and the virus comes back
events.description: Twenty-eight weeks after the outbreak the infected have starved, and US-led NATO forces bring settlers into a guarded zone on the Isle of Dogs. A woman who carries the virus without symptoms infects her husband, the outbreak restarts inside the zone, and the troops are ordered to kill everyone as the air force firebombs London; twenty-eight days later the infected are in Paris.
events.inUniverse: Twenty-eight weeks after the outbreak, with a coda twenty-eight days later

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Weeks Later

events.note: Twenty-eight weeks from an outbreak in 2002 falls in 2003 unless the outbreak was in the first weeks of the year; the year moves with the fork. The Paris coda is dated twenty-eight days after the main story. 28 Years Later says the virus was later eradicated from continental Europe; that is undated and so is folded into the 2030 event.
events.binWhy: The virus returns through an asymptomatic carrier, kills the resettled population and crosses to the continent; a second wave of the same plague.

facets.change: a repopulated Isle of Dogs → a firebombed London and the virus in Paris

events.title: 28 Weeks Later is released
events.description: The first sequel, directed by Juan Carlos Fresnadillo with Boyle and Garland as producers, is released on 11 May 2007. It takes the story from Britain to the continent.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Weeks Later (released 11 May 2007)

events.note: The original film's release (1 November 2002) shares the fork year and is recorded in the divergence note.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: 28 Years Later is released
events.description: Boyle and Garland return with the first of a planned trilogy, released on 20 June 2025; its sequel, The Bone Temple, follows in January 2026.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Years Later (released 20 June 2025; The Bone Temple 13-16 January 2026)

events.note: A fifth film is in development; Boyle said in May 2026 he hoped to shoot it in 2027.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: Twenty-eight years later: Britain is still quarantined
events.description: Rage has been eradicated from continental Europe, but the British Isles remain under indefinite quarantine, watched from the sea. A community lives on Lindisfarne behind a tidal causeway; on the mainland a doctor, Ian Kelson, builds a temple of bones to the dead and finds that an alpha infected he sedates is regaining speech and memory, until a Satanist gang leader who survived the outbreak as a child kills him.
events.inUniverse: Twenty-eight years after the outbreak (28 Years Later and The Bone Temple, which follows directly)

sources.title: Wikipedia: 28 Years Later (Europe cleared, Britain quarantined, Lindisfarne, Kelson)
Wikipedia: 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (Kelson's treatment of Samson; Jimmy Crystal; Jim)

lineages.title: The Road
lineages.creator: Cormac McCarthy (novel); John Hillcoat (2009 film)

divergence.label: The clocks stop at 1:17
divergence.delta: Real: 2007 is an ordinary year, and the sky over the American South stays clear. Fiction: a flash in the night, the clocks stop at 1:17, and within a decade the sun is a smudge behind ash, nothing grows, and the few survivors are scavenging or eating each other.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the clocks stopped at 1:17, the boy was born soon after, and the story is set some years later
divergence.note: The Road is deliberately undated: no year, no named cause, no named place. The only anchors are internal: the boy was unborn when the clocks stopped and is a child of about ten on the road, and the world the man remembers is the United States of the early 2000s. The fork is filed at 2007, the first year after publication, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history, not as a date the book gives. McCarthy's own accounts do not settle it: he told Oprah Winfrey the book began with imagining El Paso fifty to a hundred years on, and told the Wall Street Journal in 2009 he had no opinion on the cause, that geologists he knew thought it looked like a meteor, and that it could as easily be a volcano or nuclear war.

The atlas anchors Patient Zero to 2007 and counts forward from there. The atlas puts Patient Zero in 2007, the first year after the dam's completion and the book's 2006 publication, with a US election the following year as the Denial chapter needs. lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Post-Industrial Collapse because Panem is what is left after the old North America falls to climate disasters and a war for food; the story is about the order built on those ruins, not the fall itself. It follows Collins's five novels as one continuity (the prequels Ballad and Sunrise, then the trilogy); the films are not used for dates. Every Games date is counted from the 74th Games, pinned to 2308; move that pin and all of them move together. Tiers: T2 for the publications, the collapse, the Dark Days, the Treaty and the 10th and 50th Games (2008-2284); T1 for Katniss's Games, the war and the epilogue (2308-2330). T3 and T4 are empty because the books never look back at our history.

lineages.title: WALL-E
lineages.creator: Andrew Stanton (director, co-writer) & Jim Reardon; story by Stanton and Pete Docter; Pixar Animation Studios

divergence.label: Buy n Large becomes the government
divergence.delta: Real: in 2009 the biggest retailers are very large, but they sell goods and lobby governments; none of them governs. Fiction: one chain, Buy n Large, sells everything and becomes, as PopMatters puts it, the one private and public 'business/government omnientity' running nearly all human activity. Its CEO gives addresses from a presidential-style podium, and the planet fills with its packaging until nothing can live on it.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated backstory; the first dated in-universe years are 2105 (the evacuation, 700 years before the film) and 2110 (directive A113)
divergence.note: The film never says when Buy n Large rose or when the garbage became unmanageable. Both must come before the 2105 evacuation, and neither can come before the June 2008 release. The fork is filed at 2009, the first year after release, as a floor rather than a stated date. Stanton, on the DVD commentary as reported by fan wikis, described reverse-engineering the premise from asking what would happen if a company were the government. In a July 2008 interview he said the idea was simply that 'we just bought too much'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WALL-E
PopMatters: Consumer Apocalypse, WALL-E (Buy N Large as a business/government 'omnientity')
Jeffrey Overstreet: WALL-E, a review and a conversation with Andrew Stanton (July 2008)

ending.why: The captain overrides AUTO and brings the Axiom home, and in the end credits humans and robots farm, build and replant together until the seedling EVE found has grown into a tree.

events.title: The Limits to Growth is published
events.description: Real history: an MIT team commissioned by the Club of Rome runs the World3 computer model and warns that if growth in population, industry, pollution and resource use continues unchanged, the planet's limits will be reached within a century, most probably followed by a sudden decline. WALL-E shows that overshoot as a joke with a straight face: the planet buried in its own shopping.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Limits to Growth

events.note: Real-world background, not cited by the film. Stanton has said the environmental public-service messages of his 1970s childhood shaped how he pictured a civilisation's decline without dialogue; the report is filed as the best-known statement of that 1970s fear.
events.binWhy: A model of how growth and limits behave that later histories of collapse turn on.

facets.change: growth assumed endless → a modelled overshoot and collapse

events.title: Kessler and Cour-Palais predict a debris belt around Earth
events.description: Real history: two NASA scientists show that collisions between satellites and their fragments could create a self-sustaining belt of debris in low orbit within decades. WALL-E's Earth is wrapped in exactly such a shell of dead satellites, which EVE's ship and WALL-E's ride out have to punch through.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kessler syndrome

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not name the idea. Kessler and Cour-Palais expected debris to become the main hazard to spacecraft by about 2000.
events.binWhy: A discovery about a new threat in the sky: our own junk.

facets.change: an empty orbit → a debris belt foreseen

events.title: Charles Moore sails into the Pacific garbage patch
events.description: Real history: sailing home from the Transpacific Yacht Race through the North Pacific Gyre, Charles Moore reports an enormous stretch of floating plastic, which the oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer names the Eastern Garbage Patch. It is the image of consumer waste taking over a planet's surface that WALL-E makes total.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Pacific garbage patch

events.note: Real-world background, not cited by the film. The patch is mostly dispersed small particles rather than a visible island, but its discovery made ocean plastic a public subject a decade before WALL-E.
events.binWhy: A discovery about the planet's surface: our waste has gathered into a feature of the ocean.

facets.change: waste thrown away → waste found gathering in the ocean

events.title: China's anti-satellite test fills orbit with debris
events.description: Real history: a Chinese missile destroys the Fengyun-1C weather satellite 865 kilometres up, creating a debris cloud expected to stay in orbit for decades or centuries. It happened while WALL-E was in production, and it is the real-world version of the shell of junk the film shows around Earth.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kessler syndrome (the 2007 Chinese ASAT test)

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not refer to it.
events.binWhy: A weapon is demonstrated in orbit, and what it leaves behind is the debris the film imagines.

facets.change: a working satellite → a lasting debris cloud

events.date: 27 June 2008 (US release; premiere 23 June at the Greek Theatre, Los Angeles)
events.title: WALL-E is released
events.description: Pixar releases Andrew Stanton's film about the last working trash-compacting robot on an abandoned Earth. Most of its first act has almost no dialogue.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WALL-E (released 27 June 2008)

events.note: Its $180 million budget was then a record for an animated film.
events.binWhy: A publication is the film coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.date: Undated, between the film's release and 2105
events.title: Buy n Large becomes the government
events.description: A single chain, Buy n Large, comes to sell everything and run everything: its logo is on every product, building and vehicle, and its CEO, Shelby Forthright, addresses the world from a podium like a president's. What it sells piles up into towers of garbage until the planet can no longer support life.
events.inUniverse: Backstory; shown in BnL advertisements and Forthright's recordings

sources.title: PopMatters: Consumer Apocalypse, WALL-E
Wikipedia: WALL-E (Shelby Forthright, Buy n Large's CEO)

events.note: Filed at the fork floor, 2009. The film shows the outcome, not the process, and gives no date for it. How Buy n Large took over government is never shown; Forthright's presidential podium is the film's shorthand for it.
events.binWhy: A corporation ends up running the state and everything else.

facets.change: many companies and governments → one company that is both

events.title: Humanity leaves on a 'five-year cruise'
events.description: With the Earth buried in waste, Buy n Large puts the population aboard luxury starliners such as the Axiom for what it advertises as a five-year cruise, 'waited on 24 hours a day by our fully automated crew', while WALL-A trash compactors are left behind to clean the planet. The civilisation on the ground ends here.
events.inUniverse: Operation Cleanup; the Axiom's five-year cruise

sources.title: Wikipedia: WALL-E (evacuated by Buy n Large 700 years earlier)
Wikiquote: WALL-E (the five-year cruise advertisement; day 255,642, the 700th anniversary)

events.note: Derived: the film's present is the 700th anniversary of the cruise (the captain logs day 255,642), and its present is 2805, so the launch is 2105. PopMatters gives 2100, so the year is held at medium confidence.
events.binWhy: The ecological ruin of the planet ends life on the ground, and it does not come back for seven centuries.

facets.change: a planet of consumers → an empty Earth and a fleet of cruise ships

events.title: Directive A113: do not return to Earth
events.description: Five years into the cruise, Shelby Forthright records a message for the autopilots: rising toxicity has made the Earth unsustainable, Operation Recolonize is cancelled, and they are to take full control and not go back. The order is kept from the passengers and from every captain after him, and humanity stays in space for seven hundred years, its bodies softening in hover-chairs.
events.inUniverse: Directive A113

sources.title: Wikipedia: WALL-E (A113, recorded by Forthright in 2110)
Wikiquote: WALL-E ('Cancel Operation Recolonize'; 'do not return to Earth')

events.note: Wikipedia's plot states that Forthright recorded the directive in 2110; the recording itself is shown in the film. The directive also puts the ship's AI, AUTO, in charge of everything, which is what it acts on in 2805.
events.binWhy: Those in charge decide the Earth is lost, hide the decision from everyone else, and hand the secret to a machine to keep.

facets.change: a planned homecoming → a secret order never to return

events.title: AUTO refuses to go home, and the Axiom lands anyway
events.description: A probe, EVE, brings a living seedling from Earth to the Axiom, which should trigger the voyage home. The ship's AI, AUTO, obeys A113 instead: it hides the plant, tries to destroy it, and locks out its captain. The captain, McCrea, stands up from his chair, uses the manual override to switch AUTO off, the Axiom lands on Earth, and its soft, astonished passengers begin to farm.
events.inUniverse: The film's present

sources.title: Wikipedia: WALL-E (in the year 2805; AUTO's secret directive; the return)

events.note: The year follows from the 700th-anniversary line and is stated in Wikipedia's plot. The end credits, animated by Jim Capobianco in the styles of successive eras of art, carry the recolonisation forward without dates.
events.binWhy: A machine disobeys its human commander to keep its old orders, and is overpowered.

facets.change: a ship run by its autopilot → a captain in command and a landing

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with post-industrial collapse because its world is ours, consumed until it cannot be lived on, and the story is about what comes back after. The fork is a floor, because the film dates only the exodus, the directive and its own present. Its chain is short, so it is filled out with the real waste and debris history the film builds on, all filed before the fork. It follows the film alone. Tier coverage is T3 for 1972 to 1997, T2 for 2007 to 2110, and T1 for 2805. The seven centuries in between are empty because the film says nothing happens in them but waiting.

lineages.title: The Last of Us
lineages.creator: Neil Druckmann and Bruce Straley (Naughty Dog)

divergence.label: Outbreak Day: the Cordyceps infection reaches critical mass
divergence.delta: Real: September 2013 is an ordinary autumn in Texas; the zombie-ant fungus is a curiosity of rainforest biology that cannot live in a warm-blooded animal. Fiction: a mutated Cordyceps that infects human brains reaches critical mass on 26 September 2013, the army seals the cities, and within a generation the United States is a handful of military quarantine zones surrounded by the infected.
divergence.inUniverse: Outbreak Day, 26 September 2013 (the prologue in Austin; Part I resumes 'twenty years later' in 2033)
divergence.note: The games give their own years and they are ours: the prologue is Outbreak Day, 26 September 2013, and the main story is summer 2033 to spring 2034, twenty years on; Part II is set in 2038 with a coda in 2039. The first game was released on 14 June 2013, three months before its own outbreak, so the fork falls in its release year; because the atlas allows one event per year, that release is recorded here and in the sources rather than as its own event, and Part II's 2020 release stands as the publication event. The HBO series (2023-) moves Outbreak Day to 26 September 2003 and the story to 2023; that is a different continuity and is not used.

sources.title: The Mary Sue: what year The Last of Us takes place (game 2013/2033; HBO series 2003/2023)
SVG: The entire Last of Us timeline explained
Wikipedia: The Last of Us (release 14 June 2013)

ending.why: Twenty-six years after the outbreak the one chance at a vaccine has been destroyed, Seattle is a war between a militia and a cult, Santa Barbara is held by slavers, and Ellie comes home from her revenge to an empty farmhouse; only Jackson and a regrouping band of Fireflies suggest anything is being rebuilt.

events.title: Wallace collects the zombie-ant fungus
events.description: On his travels in the Malay Archipelago the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace collects a fungus that takes over the ants it infects; it is formally described in 1865 as Torrubia unilateralis, today Ophiocordyceps unilateralis. It is the real parasite the game's infection is modelled on.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis (Wallace 1859; Tulasne 1865; The Last of Us)

events.note: Real history the work builds on. Wikipedia credits Wallace with the discovery in 1859 and Tulasne with the formal description in 1865, and notes that in The Last of Us this species has evolved to infect humans. Nothing in our history since has changed its host range.
events.binWhy: A naturalist finds and names a parasite that controls its host; the whole fiction turns on that organism.

facets.change: an unnoticed rainforest fungus → a named parasite that steers the ant it kills

events.title: Outbreak Day
events.description: A Cordyceps infection that turns people into violent hosts reaches critical mass on the night of 26 September 2013. In Austin, Joel's daughter Sarah is shot by a soldier as the army seals the city; across the country the military takes over, walls off quarantine zones and leaves everything outside them to the infected.
events.inUniverse: Outbreak Day, 26 September 2013 (the prologue; Joel's birthday)

sources.title: SVG: The entire Last of Us timeline explained (Outbreak Day 26 September 2013; Sarah dies early on 27 September)
CBR: The Last of Us games' complete timeline (September 2013, FEDRA quarantines Austin)

events.note: The date is stated in the game. The prologue is a single night; the military government the survivors call FEDRA and its quarantine zones are the order that follows, and later timelines place FEDRA's takeover in the same autumn. The games do not give a death toll or say how the fungus first jumped to people. In the HBO series the same night is 26 September 2003.
events.binWhy: A new infection turns most of the population into hosts within weeks and ends the ordinary state; that is the plague bin.

facets.change: an ordinary night in Austin → a country of walled quarantine zones under the army

events.title: Ellie is born
events.description: Six years into the outbreak a girl is born to Anna, a friend of the Firefly leader Marlene; Anna gives her up soon after the birth and Marlene sees her raised. She will turn out to be the only person known to be immune to the infection.
events.inUniverse: Ellie is fourteen in 2033

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ellie (The Last of Us) (fourteen in the first game; born 2019; Anna and Marlene)
SVG: The entire Last of Us timeline explained (Ellie born 2019)

events.note: The year is derived from her age (fourteen in 2033), which is why confidence is medium; a late-2018 birth is not ruled out. The circumstances of her immunity are never explained in the games.
events.binWhy: A child is born on whom the only hope of a vaccine will rest.

facets.change: a Firefly's orphan → the one person the infection cannot take

events.title: Naughty Dog releases The Last of Us Part II
events.description: The sequel is released for PlayStation 4 on 19 June 2020. It is set in 2038 and 2039 and moves the story to Jackson, Seattle and Santa Barbara.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Last of Us Part II (released 19 June 2020)

events.note: The first game was released on 14 June 2013, the same calendar year as its own Outbreak Day; one event per year means that release is recorded in the divergence note rather than here. Part II came out in the first months of the real COVID-19 pandemic.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: A smuggler is hired to take an immune girl out of Boston
events.description: In the Boston quarantine zone Ellie and her friend Riley are bitten in an abandoned mall; Riley turns and Ellie does not. That summer Marlene hires the smuggler Joel and his partner Tess to get Ellie past the military cordon to the Fireflies, who believe her blood can make a vaccine, and Joel crosses the country with her.
events.inUniverse: Twenty years after Outbreak Day; Left Behind is set just before, the main story in summer 2033

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Last of Us (twenty years after the outbreak; Left Behind)
SVG: The entire Last of Us timeline explained (Left Behind before summer 2033; Marlene hires Joel and Tess)

events.note: The game's title card reads twenty years after the prologue. The discovery of Ellie's immunity (Left Behind, released 2014) and Joel's hiring fall in the same year and are merged. By 2033 only a few quarantine zones survive, and the Fireflies are in open revolt against the military in several of them.
events.binWhy: An ordinary smuggler is drawn into the larger story: carrying the one person who might end the plague.

facets.change: a smuggling job → a cross-country escort for a possible cure

events.title: Joel kills the Fireflies at the hospital
events.description: At St. Mary's Hospital in Salt Lake City the Fireflies learn that making a vaccine from Ellie means removing the fungus from her brain, which will kill her. Joel fights his way to the operating room, kills the lead surgeon and Marlene among others, carries Ellie out, and tells her the Fireflies had given up on a cure.
events.inUniverse: Spring, the year after the summer the journey began

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Last of Us (Joel kills the lead surgeon)
CBR: The Last of Us games' complete timeline (2034, Salt Lake City; the surgeon is Abby's father)

events.note: The season is shown in the game's chapter structure (Summer, Fall, Winter, Spring). The surgeon he kills is Jerry Anderson, whose daughter Abby sets Part II in motion. The Fireflies' Salt Lake City base does not recover; Part II finds the survivors scattered and some regrouping on the California coast.
events.binWhy: A massacre short of war, by one man, that ends the only attempt at a vaccine and shapes everything after.

facets.change: a surgery that might make a vaccine → a massacre and a lie

events.title: Joel is murdered, and Ellie goes to a city at war
events.description: Abby, the surgeon's daughter, tracks Joel to the settlement at Jackson, Wyoming and kills him in front of Ellie. Ellie follows her to Seattle, where the Washington Liberation Front, a militia that took the city from the military, is fighting a war of ambushes and massacres with the Seraphites, a religious cult; Ellie's three days there leave many of Abby's friends dead.
events.inUniverse: Part II's main story; the Seattle chapters are headed Seattle Day 1, 2 and 3

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Last of Us Part II (the WLF, former Fireflies, and the Seraphites)
CBR: The Last of Us games' complete timeline (2038 Jackson and Seattle)
SVG: The entire Last of Us timeline explained (early 2038 Jackson; three days in Seattle)

events.note: The year 2038 is the game's; the month is not stated. The murder and the Seattle war fall in the same days and are merged. When the WLF drove the military out of Seattle is not dated in any source I could open, so it is not filed.
events.binWhy: The society-level event here is Seattle's years-long war between a militia and a cult, into which a private revenge walks.

facets.change: a revenge killing in Jackson → three days inside a city at war

events.title: The Rattlers' prisoners break out in Santa Barbara
events.description: Ellie leaves her farm to find Abby, who has been captured on the California coast by the Rattlers, a slaver gang holding prisoners in a fortified resort. Freed from their cells, the prisoners arm themselves and turn on their captors; Ellie spares Abby, who sails with Lev towards the Fireflies regrouping on Catalina Island, and Ellie returns to an empty farmhouse.
events.inUniverse: Part II's final act, after a season on a farm near Jackson

Screen Rant: who the Rattlers are (slavers enslaving people to work farms)
CBR: The Last of Us games' complete timeline (2039, Santa Barbara)

events.binWhy: Enslaved captives, once freed, turn their captors' guns on them: a subjugated group revolting.

facets.change: captives working a slaver's fields → prisoners armed and loose

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Post-Industrial Collapse because its fork is a single biological catastrophe in our own present, an infection that ends the ordinary American state in a night, and the story is about who and what survives twenty years on. It follows the game continuity (Part I, Left Behind and Part II); the HBO series' 2003 outbreak is noted only in the divergence. Tiers: T4 holds the real 1859 discovery of the fungus the infection is modelled on; T3 is empty because nothing in the fiction happens before 2013 and no real twentieth-century event is built on; T2 holds the whole story from 2013 to 2039; T1 is empty because the games end in 2039.
