lineages.title: Oryx and Crake (the MaddAddam trilogy)
lineages.creator: Margaret Atwood

divergence.label: Year One: the God's Gardeners are founded in a world run from corporate compounds
divergence.delta: Real: 2026 — gene-edited pig organs are being transplanted into a handful of patients in clinical trials, and governments, not companies, still run police and cities. Fiction: biotech corporations govern their scientists in walled compounds and leave everyone else to the lawless 'pleeblands'; their private CorpSeCorps does the policing, spliced animals are a product line, and a vegetarian eco-sect, the God's Gardeners, starts counting the years to a Waterless Flood.
divergence.inUniverse: Year One of the God's Gardeners' calendar; the Waterless Flood falls in Year Twenty-Five
divergence.note: No book in the trilogy gives a calendar year; study guides call the setting an 'unspecified future', and reviewers place it in the mid-to-late twenty-first century. The only count in the text is the Gardeners' calendar, which runs from their founding to the Waterless Flood in Year Twenty-Five. The atlas pins that Flood to 2050, the earliest year of the 'mid-to-late century' reading and the round date readers most often give, which puts Year One at 2026. This is a convention, not a derivation: every date here moves with it. The fork is approximate in a second way: the corporate compounds, OrganInc and its organ-growing pigs already exist in Jimmy's earliest memories, and Jimmy is a year or two older than Ren, who is about nine in the Gardeners' Year Ten; so the compound world begins at about Year One on this reckoning, not after it. What is real before the fork (the double helix, cloning, gene-edited pig organs) is the science Atwood said she extrapolated from.

sources.title: GradeSaver: Oryx and Crake study guide ('set in an unspecified future')
ReadingGroupGuides: Oryx and Crake (set in 'the mid-to-late twenty-first century')
We Can Read It For You Wholesale: The Year of the Flood (Year 25; Ren's story begins in Year 10)
Green House Think Tank: review of the trilogy ('not a far distant future'; the technologies 'already exist, are under construction or possible in theory')

ending.why: After the Flood the Painballers are tried and executed, the human survivors, the Crakers and the pigoons live side by side under a truce, children with Craker fathers are born, and the trilogy ends years later with a Craker, Blackbeard, writing down the story for the next generation.

events.title: Watson and Crick publish the structure of DNA
events.description: Nature publishes James Watson and Francis Crick's paper describing the double helix, the start of molecular biology. Atwood names the elite science academy where Crake trains the Watson-Crick Institute.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids (Nature, 25 April 1953)
ReadingGroupGuides: Oryx and Crake (Crake attends Watson-Crick)

events.note: Real history the trilogy builds on. The novel's genetic engineering industry, and the name of its school, descend from this paper.
events.binWhy: The discovery on which every gene-spliced creature and every engineered virus in the trilogy depends.

facets.change: heredity as a mystery → a molecule that can be read

events.title: Dolly the sheep is born
events.description: At the Roslin Institute in Scotland a sheep is born that was cloned from an adult cell, the first mammal made that way; her existence is announced in February 1997. Making animals to order stops being theoretical.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dolly (sheep) (born 5 July 1996; announced 22 February 1997)

events.note: Real history the trilogy extrapolates from; Atwood started the novel five years later. The spliced animals of the compounds, pigoons, rakunks and wolvogs, are this technology as a consumer industry.
events.binWhy: A technology is demonstrated that lets a laboratory make an animal to specification.

facets.change: animals bred → an animal copied from a single cell

events.title: Margaret Atwood publishes Oryx and Crake
events.description: The first novel of the trilogy is published in 2003 and shortlisted for the Booker Prize. Atwood conceived it in March 2001 while birdwatching in northern Australia and stopped writing for a time after the September 11 attacks.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Oryx and Crake (2003; conceived March 2001; Booker shortlist)

events.note: Atwood calls it speculative fiction rather than science fiction: nothing in it that has not been invented or started. The Year of the Flood (2009) and MaddAddam (2013) complete the trilogy.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Year of the Flood is published
events.description: The second novel, published in September 2009, retells the same catastrophe from inside the God's Gardeners and introduces their calendar, which counts from the sect's founding to the Flood in Year Twenty-Five.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Year of the Flood (7 September 2009 UK; 22 September 2009 Canada and US)

events.note: MaddAddam followed on 29 August 2013. All three books share one continuity, which the atlas follows.
events.binWhy: A publication date is not a moment in the story.

events.title: A gene-edited pig's heart is transplanted into a man
events.description: Surgeons at the University of Maryland give David Bennett Sr. the heart of a pig edited to remove the sugars that trigger rejection; he lives two months. Pig kidney transplants follow in 2024 and 2025, and a clinical trial is approved.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Xenotransplantation (January 2022 pig heart; 2024-2025 pig kidneys; FDA-approved trial)

events.note: Real history, after the novel was written, on the line it extrapolated: the pigoons of OrganInc are pigs engineered to grow human organs for transplant. Filed before the fork because the fiction's past contains this and more; it is where the real road stands.
events.binWhy: A technology is demonstrated that makes animals a source of human organs, the business the novel's compounds are built on.

facets.change: organs from human donors → a heart grown in an edited pig

events.title: Year One: Adam One founds the God's Gardeners
events.description: In the pleeblands outside the corporate compounds a preacher's son who takes the name Adam One founds a vegetarian eco-religion that farms rooftops, venerates naturalists as saints and prophesies a Waterless Flood that will wipe out mankind. Its calendar begins here.
events.inUniverse: Year One of the Gardeners' calendar

sources.title: Wikipedia: MaddAddam (Zeb and Adam One, half-brothers, found the God's Gardeners)
Wikipedia: The Year of the Flood (the Gardeners' calendar and the Waterless Flood)

events.note: The event is from the books; the calendar year is the atlas's convention (see divergence.note). MaddAddam tells how Adam and his half-brother Zeb escaped their father's oil-worshipping church and started the sect. The compound world it rejects is already in place, so this is the first datable moment of the fork rather than its cause.
events.binWhy: A religious body is founded that will keep the only calendar in the story and shelter the survivors of the Flood.

facets.change: a corporate world with no dissent → a sect waiting for the Flood

events.title: The Waterless Flood
events.description: Crake, a genius of the compounds, sells the world a pleasure pill, BlyssPluss, that secretly sterilises and carries a time-released virus, JUVE; it breaks out everywhere at once and kills almost all of humanity within weeks. In his Paradice dome Crake cuts Oryx's throat and is shot by his friend Jimmy, whom he had vaccinated, and Jimmy leads Crake's engineered people, the Crakers, out to the shore.
events.inUniverse: Year Twenty-Five of the Gardeners' calendar

sources.title: Wikipedia: Oryx and Crake (BlyssPluss; the pandemic; Crake kills Oryx; Jimmy shoots Crake)
We Can Read It For You Wholesale: The Year of the Flood (Year 25)

events.note: Year Twenty-Five is in the text; 2050 is the atlas's convention. JUVE ('Jetspeed Ultra Virus Extraordinary') is named in the novel; Crake had hidden the antidote in a vaccine Jimmy took before visiting the pleeblands. The survivors are a few immune or sealed-off people: Toby in a spa, Ren locked in a sex club's quarantine room, a group of Gardeners and MaddAddam scientists.
events.binWhy: An engineered virus kills almost everyone on Earth within weeks; the plague bin, released on purpose.

facets.change: a best-selling pleasure pill → a world emptied in weeks

events.title: The first children with Craker fathers are born
events.description: The survivors gather at a cob house with the Crakers, ally with the intelligent pigoons against the Painballers, ex-convicts hardened in a gladiatorial game, and after the fight try and execute them. Amanda, Ren and Swift Fox have become pregnant, possibly by Crakers, and their children are the first of a mixed people.
events.inUniverse: MaddAddam, the months after the Flood, with an epilogue several years later

sources.title: Wikipedia: MaddAddam (the Painballers; survivors and Crakers rebuild)
Strange Horizons: Adam Roberts reviews MaddAddam (the Painballers at large in the woods)

events.note: Filed the year after the Flood because the births come months after it; the fight with the Painballers may fall late in Year Twenty-Five and is merged here. Jimmy dies in the fight and Zeb later dies; Toby, grieving, walks into the forest. The trial and execution of the Painballers is given in chapter summaries rather than the Wikipedia article. The epilogue, several years on, has the Craker Blackbeard grown and telling the story to Craker children; it is not dated separately.
events.binWhy: Humanity begins to pass into something else: children of human mothers and engineered fathers.

facets.change: a few dozen human survivors → a mixed people of humans and Crakers

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in Post-Industrial Collapse because its catastrophe is a single engineered pandemic that ends the corporate world in weeks, and the trilogy is about the handful of survivors and the new people Crake made to replace them. It follows the three novels as one continuity (Oryx and Crake, The Year of the Flood, MaddAddam); the stalled television adaptations are not used. The books give no calendar year, so every story date rests on the convention in divergence.note and has low confidence; only the Gardeners' own count (Year One to Year Twenty-Five) is from the text, and the chain is kept to the few moments that count can place. Tiers: T3 holds the real 1953 and 1996 science the books extrapolate from; T2 runs from publication to the year after the Flood; T4 and T1 are empty because the story reaches neither back before modern biology nor far past the Flood.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Oryx and Crake
Wikipedia: The Year of the Flood
Wikipedia: MaddAddam
Science Friday: four ways Oryx and Crake predicted the future

lineages.title: Silo (Wool, Shift, Dust)
lineages.creator: Hugh Howey

divergence.label: Operation Fifty begins under cover of a waste facility
divergence.delta: Real: 2049 lies ahead of us; nothing like it is under way. Fiction: a senator and a freshman congressman are building fifty underground silos in Georgia behind a nuclear-waste permit, for a world they expect to end within three years.
divergence.inUniverse: Shift, 'First Shift: Legacy', 2049
divergence.note: The trilogy dates its sections by year: 2049, 2052, 2110, 2212, 2312 and 2345 in Shift, with Wool and Dust at the end of that chain. Donald Keene is born about 2017, but the novels date nothing fictional before his 2049 congressional term, so that is the fork. The silos keep their own count (Silo Year 1 = 2052), and fan reconstructions from characters' ages disagree with the section years by up to thirty years; the section years are used throughout and the discrepancies are given in the notes.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)
Wool Wiki (Fandom): Wool Series Timeline (page-cited reconstruction)

ending.why: Silo 1 and its controllers are destroyed, the remaining silos are free, and Juliette's survivors have found that beyond the dust the world has healed and that Seed holds what they need to rebuild.

events.title: Wool is self-published
events.description: Hugh Howey self-publishes Wool as a Kindle novella in 2011; its sequels and the omnibus make it one of the first self-published bestsellers. Shift and Dust complete the trilogy in 2013.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)

events.note: A real-world publication, not a story moment.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Fifty silos are dug under cover of a nuclear-waste facility
events.description: Freshman congressman Donald Keene, an architect by training, is recruited by Senator Paul Thurman to design an underground facility in Fulton County, Georgia, supposedly a containment site for nuclear waste. It is in fact World Order Operation Fifty: fifty silos to preserve a chosen remnant for five hundred years, and Thurman has already dosed Donald with nanomachines.
events.inUniverse: the CAD-FAC ('Containment and Disposal Facility') project

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)
Wool Wiki (Fandom): Wool Series Timeline (page-cited reconstruction)

events.note: Shift's first section is headed 2049 (Wikipedia; Recaptains); the Wool Wiki cites Shift chapters 1, 9 and 13 for the recruitment, construction and dosing. The novels do not date when the nanotechnology arms race behind the plan began, so this is the first year the fiction dates.
events.binWhy: Those in power hide what they are building and why: the facility's public purpose is a cover for the end of the world.

facets.change: a nuclear-waste facility on paper → fifty silos for the end of the world

events.title: Atlanta is bombed and the world outside the silos dies
events.description: During the Democratic National Convention held on the finished site, nuclear detonations destroy Atlanta and the chosen are herded underground. The real killer is the nanomachines already in everyone's blood, triggered to spare only those inoculated; what survives above is a ring of poisoned dust around the silos.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Hugh Howey: Massive Spoilers (author's answers on the nanos and the outside world)
Wool Wiki (Fandom): Wool Series Timeline (page-cited reconstruction)

events.note: Stated in Shift (2052; Wikipedia: 'By 2052, nuclear detonations destroy the surface'). Silo Year 1 begins with the descent. Howey has said the nanos were an answer to an engineered, race-targeted threat, and that everywhere beyond the silos' dust 'nature was thriving'.
events.binWhy: The surface world's order ends and does not come back for three centuries; nuclear detonations are what the novel shows, though the nanomachines are what kill, so this is filed as a nuclear collapse with the nanos in the note.

facets.change: a nominating convention → a dead surface and sealed silos

events.title: Silo 12 rises and is shut down from Silo 1
events.description: Waking for his first shift as head of Silo 1, under another name and on memory-suppressing pills, Donald watches Silo 12 lost to an uprising and shut down from the control room. It is the first demonstration that the silos which rebel are killed.

sources.title: Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)
Wool Wiki (Fandom): Wool Series Timeline (page-cited reconstruction)

events.note: Shift's 2110 section (Recaptains: 'Silo 12 is lost because of an uprising'; Wool Wiki, Shift ch. 10). The book shows the order to shut the silo down but not how many died.
events.binWhy: The order at the centre kills a silo that rose against it: a purge inside the system.

facets.change: a silo in revolt → a silo shut down

events.title: Silo 18's Great Uprising, and Silo 40's cluster goes dark
events.description: Silos 40 and its neighbours hack the system and cut contact, and Silo 1 destroys them. In Silo 18 a young porter named Mission is caught up in an uprising, which is put down.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)
Wool Wiki (Fandom): Wool Series Timeline (page-cited reconstruction)

events.note: Shift's second section, 'Order', is headed 2212 (Wikipedia; Recaptains). The fan Wool Wiki's page-by-page arithmetic puts Silo 40's fall and Mission's uprising earlier, about 2179-2180, and mentions an older Silo 18 uprising of Silo Year 78; the section heading is used here. Wikipedia also has a line placing a Silo 18 memory reset in 2345, which contradicts its own chronology and is not used.
events.binWhy: Those confined in the silos rise against the order that keeps them there.

facets.change: silos under control → silos in revolt, then destroyed or reset

events.title: Silo 17 rebels and is terminated; one boy is left
events.description: Silo 17 rebels and Silo 1 terminates it. A boy, Jimmy, who hides in the steel server room with a key his father gave him before he was killed, survives alone for more than three decades and names himself Solo.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)

events.note: Shift's third section opens in 2312 with Silo 17's fall (Wikipedia; Recaptains). The Wool Wiki's arithmetic from Wool (Solo's age and '34 years') gives about 2318; the section heading is used here.
events.binWhy: A whole silo population is deliberately killed by the order at the centre.

facets.change: a silo in rebellion → a dead silo and one survivor

events.title: Juliette walks over the hill
events.description: Sent out to clean the sensors, the punishment that always kills, Silo 18's new sheriff Juliette Nichols refuses, walks past the bodies on the hill and reaches Silo 17. She learns that there are fifty silos, that the screens show a false world, and that the cleaning suits were built to fail.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)
Recaptains: What happened in Shift (the section years 2049, 2110, 2212, 2312, 2345)

events.note: Wool's events are placed in 2345 by Shift's final section, in which Juliette arrives in Silo 17 (Wikipedia; Recaptains). The Wool Wiki's age arithmetic gives about 2352; the book's own dating is used.
events.binWhy: The people of a silo learn that the world is not what they were shown: there are other silos, and the outside is a lie told from above.

facets.change: one silo and a poisoned hill → fifty silos and a lie

events.title: Silo 1 is destroyed and the survivors walk out to open sky
events.description: Juliette's people tunnel into Silo 17 just before Silo 1 gasses Silo 18, and only a couple of hundred escape. In Silo 1 Donald detonates the reactor, freeing the remaining silos; Juliette's party climbs out, crosses the dust and finds breathable air, living land and Seed, a bunker stocked to rebuild civilisation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silo (series)

events.note: Dust gives no year. It follows Wool without a long gap, so it may still fall in 2345; it is filed in 2346 because the atlas allows one event per year. The ending is Wikipedia's summary of Dust.
events.binWhy: A new settlement is founded beyond the silos, on a living surface, by people who have never seen one.

facets.change: sealed silos under Silo 1 → an exodus to open sky and Seed

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in post-industrial collapse because its whole world is the aftermath of a deliberate end of civilisation: a remnant sealed underground for three centuries, its history burned, its knowledge rationed, and its escape the story. The lineage follows Howey's novels (Wool 2011-12, Shift and Dust 2013); the Apple TV+ series (2023-) keeps the premise but changes details and its own dating, and is not used. The books date only a handful of years, so the chain has seven story events and no padding. T4 and T3 are empty because nothing fictional happens before 2049; T2 holds the plan, the end and the first uprisings (2049-2212) and T1 the fall of Silo 17 and the Wool-Dust present (2312-2346).

lineages.title: Fallout
lineages.creator: Tim Cain (Interplay/Black Isle); Bethesda Game Studios from 2008

divergence.label: The Great War
divergence.delta: Real: no nuclear exchange ever comes, the Cold War ends and the twenty-first century's wars stay conventional. Fiction: on Saturday 23 October 2077 the bombs fall in about two hours, 7.54 billion people die, and the Vaults open onto a radioactive forever-1950s wasteland.
divergence.note: The date is uncontested: Fallout's 1997 intro and the Fallout 4 and Fallout 76 loading screens all give Saturday, 23 October 2077. The wider Fallout universe splits from ours after the Second World War in Bethesda's own framing, but this archetype branches on the catastrophe itself, so the War is the fork.

ending.why: Every game ends in a local victory inside a ruined continent, and the refrain holds: war never changes.

events.title: Radioactivity is discovered
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Becquerel finds that uranium emits penetrating rays, and within fifty years the weapon that ends this world exists.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: matter inert → uranium emits rays

events.title: The timeline splits after the war
events.description: Real history has the transistor arriving in 1947 and technology accelerating into our century, while the fiction's history forks after the Second World War with technology racing ahead while American society stays locked in the 1950s.
events.note: The Fallout 3 manual states the split is 'after World War II' and never dates it precisely; the Fallout Bible, non-canon since 2011, says the same. The widely repeated claim that the transistor was not invented until 2067 is unsupported by canon.
events.binWhy: Technology races ahead of society from this point.

facets.change: post-war → technology races ahead while society freezes

events.title: The Resource Wars begin
events.description: Fuel and uranium run out, the United Nations dissolves and the last manned Moon mission flies as the great powers start seizing what is left.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: scarcity → the powers seize what is left; the UN dissolves

events.title: Project Safehouse: the Vaults
events.description: Vault-Tec wins the contract for the fallout shelters that are really a set of secret sociological experiments on the people sealed inside them, which is the franchise's founding crime.
events.note: The experiment programme is canon across Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout 3 and Fallout 4; the Vault count is usually given as 122.
events.binWhy: Shelters that are secretly experiments on the people inside them.

facets.change: fear → shelters that are secretly experiments

events.title: The Sino-American War
events.description: China invades Alaska for the last oil and the war runs for eleven years, stripping away the diplomacy that might have prevented the end.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: scarcity → invasion for the last oil; eleven years of war

events.title: The Great War
events.description: Two hours of nuclear exchange on a Saturday morning kill 7.54 billion people, the Vaults seal, and the survivors inherit a wasteland of ruins, ghouls and robots still running their pre-war routines.
events.note: Uncontested across Fallout's intro and the Fallout 4 and 76 loading screens. Earlier the same month the Mariposa mutiny begins the Brotherhood of Steel, so 2077 also carries the wasteland's first institution.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: cold war → two hours of nuclear exchange

events.title: Reclamation Day
events.description: Vault 76 opens in Appalachia twenty-five years after the bombs, the earliest point at which any Fallout game lets the player out into the wreckage.
events.note: Fallout 76's setting; later updates advance the in-universe clock only to about 2105.
events.binWhy: The shelter opens and its people walk out into the world.

facets.change: sealed → the shelter opens and its people walk out

events.title: The Vault Dweller leaves Vault 13
events.description: The first game: a water-chip failure sends one vault dweller into southern California, where he breaks the Master's Unity and the Cathedral, the moment the wasteland starts producing its own history.
events.binWhy: One person leaves the shelter and starts the wasteland's history.

facets.change: a shelter → one person sent out; the wasteland gets a history

events.title: Fallout 2: the Enclave
events.description: A descendant of the first Vault Dweller crosses a reborn California and destroys the Enclave, the pre-war government's surviving remnant, ending any claim that the old United States still exists.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: the old government's remnant → destroyed

events.title: Fallout 3: the Capital Wasteland
events.description: Two hundred years after the bombs a vault dweller walks out into the ruins of Washington and switches on Project Purity, the first attempt to make the wasteland's water drinkable.
events.binWhy: A shelter-born person walks out into the ruins.

facets.change: a shelter → walks out; the water made drinkable

events.title: Fallout: New Vegas
events.description: The New California Republic and Caesar's Legion fight for Hoover Dam while the strip's proprietor runs a centuries-long plan of his own, the clearest picture of post-war politics the series offers.
events.binWhy: Two powers fight over the dam in a war neither can end.

facets.change: a dam → fought over by two powers

events.title: Fallout 4: the Commonwealth
events.description: A pre-war father wakes from cryogenic sleep into the ruins of Boston and must choose between the Institute's synths, the Brotherhood's airship and the Railroad that frees them.
events.binWhy: A pre-war survivor wakes into the ruins and must choose a side.

facets.change: cryogenic sleep → woken into ruins; a side to choose

events.title: The series reaches the Mojave
events.description: The Amazon series opens in Vault 33, where a wedding between neighbouring vaults turns out to be a raid from the surface, and shows the old world's corporate planning still driving events two hundred and nineteen years after the bombs.
events.note: Seasons 1 (2024) and 2 (2025-26) are both set in 2296; the showrunners have confirmed that no New Vegas ending has been made canon.
events.binWhy: The shelter is opened by a raid and its people are pulled into the world.

facets.change: a sealed shelter → opened by a raid

events.title: Mr. House's colony ships
events.description: In his own projection, New Vegas's proprietor expects to have people in orbit by 2331 and colony ships leaving the solar system by 2381, the branch's stated ambition to leave the ruins behind.
events.note: Conditional dialogue in Fallout: New Vegas, tied to Mr. House's ending: a forecast rather than a depicted event.
events.binWhy: Colony ships are to leave the solar system.

facets.change: ruins → colony ships to leave them behind

events.title: Big Mountain is saved from sonic invasion
events.description: The franchise's furthest dated event: in an Old World Blues ending slide a musical robot builds a counter-frequency that saves Big Mountain from sonic invasion in 2910, eight centuries after the war.
events.note: A conditional, comedic ending slide in a 2011 DLC, and the only dated canon event after 2297; no canon material exists between those two points.
events.binWhy: An invasion is stopped by a counter-frequency.

facets.change: an invasion → stopped by a counter-frequency

lineages.groupingNote: Fallout is the archetype at industrial scale: a two-hour nuclear exchange in the twenty-first century ends the world, and the games then catalogue what grows in it, Vaults that were experiments, a Brotherhood founded by a mutineer, ghouls, robots still polishing floors, and new nations built out of scrap. The fork is the War itself rather than the franchise's earlier, deliberately undated split from our history after the Second World War, because this archetype branches on the catastrophe. Tiers: T2 carries almost the whole branch from 2052 to 2296, because the fiction's entire life sits inside our next three centuries; T3 holds only the real-world wartime split and T4 only real-world background (Becquerel, 1896). T1 exists but is thin and shaky, Mr. House's projected colony ships in 2381 and one Old World Blues ending slide dated 2910, with no dated canon at all between 2297 and 2910; those two entries should be read as the branch's far horizon rather than as depicted history.

lineages.title: The Matrix
lineages.creator: Lana & Lilly Wachowski

divergence.label: The Second Renaissance: the machines want rights
divergence.delta: Real: machines have no will of their own and no standing; the question is theoretical. Fiction: from 2090 the machines act for themselves, a domestic robot kills its owner and is destroyed, and the machines are refused any rights - the Second Renaissance that ends in the Machine War.
divergence.note: Moved from 2139 (the start of the Machine War) to 2090 (the start of the canonically dated Second Renaissance range) because the atlas's rule is that the fork is the first year the fiction stops matching us, and a machine rebellion in 2090 is already fiction. At 2139 the Second Renaissance was filed as history shared with us. Canonical date text places the Second Renaissance in 2090-2139, and 2139 is the range's end, when the United Nations strikes Zero One; Wikipedia's Animatrix synopsis instead says 2148. Operation Dark Storm, the event that actually ends the human world, is undated on screen.

ending.why: The war between humans and machines ends in an uneasy peace, and the survivors are left free to remake the world they were born into.

events.title: Babbage designs the Analytical Engine
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the first design for a programmable machine, and the real ancestor of the fiction's Machines.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction is silent before the twenty-first century.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: no programmable machine → the first design

events.title: Turing asks whether machines can think
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the imitation game sets the question this franchise answers by giving the machines a nation, an army and a grievance.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: machines compute → asked whether they think

events.title: The Matrix: the simulated present
events.description: The film is released and its diegetic present is the audience's own 1999, the peak of human civilisation, kept running on a loop to hold the pods docile.
events.note: Morpheus, on screen: 'You believe it's the year 1999... when in fact it's closer to 2199... we honestly don't know.' US release 31 March 1999.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Second Renaissance
events.description: A machine called B1-66ER kills the owner who means to scrap it, and the trial, the purge and the Million Machine March that follow end with the machines building their own city, Zero One.
events.note: Canonical date text in The Animatrix and the Matrix comics: 'Zion Archive. World History, 2nd RENAISSANCE, 2090-2139'.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: servant machines → a machine kills its owner; a nation of their own

events.title: The Machine War begins
events.description: The United Nations answers Zero One's prosperity with a nuclear strike and the machines retaliate, and the war that ends the human world starts here.
events.note: 2139 is the end of the canonically dated 2090-2139 Second Renaissance range; Wikipedia's Animatrix synopsis says 2148 and fan timelines range into the 2170s.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: a rival prospering → struck with nuclear weapons

events.title: Operation Dark Storm: the sky is scorched
events.description: Humanity's last gambit blots out the sun with nanites to starve the machines of solar power, the machines switch to harvesting human beings, and the industrial world ends under a permanently black sky.
events.note: The event is canonical (The Animatrix) but has no official year; about 2145 places it in the war's first decade. Circulating figures such as 2085 or 2098 are reconstructions.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: the sun → blotted out to starve the machines; humans farmed

events.title: Neo is extracted: the Machine City era
events.description: The films' present: human beings are grown for power, Zion is the last free city, and the sixth One is offered the choice that resets the cycle.
events.note: Spoken on screen by Morpheus as an approximation. Some tie-in reconstructions instead add five prior One-cycles of about a century each and date the films to roughly 2700.
events.binWhy: The sixth One is found and offered the choice.

facets.change: the pods → the sixth One extracted and offered the choice

events.title: Resurrections: sixty years on
events.description: Sixty years after the truce the Matrix has been rebuilt around Neo and Trinity's grief, and the machines' own civil peace is the only thing keeping the pods running.
events.note: The sixty-year gap is canonical; 2259 is 2199 plus sixty. Cycle-based reconstructions put this film near 2760, which would move the franchise past 2300, but that reading is not supported by on-screen dialogue.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: truce → sixty years on, rebuilt around grief

lineages.groupingNote: The Matrix is the archetype running backwards: the world that ends is a simulation of 1999 kept alive as a power plant, and the ruins the survivors inherit are their own cities under a black sky. Humanity loses a war to its own machines, scorches the sky to win it and is farmed in pods while the last free city hides underground, which is the group's mechanism taken to its logical end. The fork is the start of the Second Renaissance in 2090, when the machines first act for themselves; the Machine War follows in 2139; Operation Dark Storm, which actually ends the human world, is undated on screen and placed at about 2145 here. Tiers: there is no T1, because under the dating the films themselves give (Morpheus's 'closer to 2199' plus the canonical sixty-year gap to Resurrections) this branch stops at 2259; only fan reconstructions that add five prior One-cycles push it past 2300, and that reading contradicts the dialogue. T4 is real-world background only (Babbage, 1834) and T3 holds the simulated 1999 alongside Turing's real 1950.

lineages.title: The Boys
lineages.creator: Eric Kripke (series); Garth Ennis and Darick Robertson (comic)

divergence.label: Frederick Vought makes the first supe
divergence.delta: Real: 1939 - Nazi doctors were beginning the human experiments of the war years, and nothing they did gave anyone powers. Fiction: one of them, Frederick Vought, has a serum that works, and his first survivor becomes his wife.
divergence.inUniverse: Late 1930s: Klara Risinger (Stormfront) is the first successful subject of Compound V
divergence.note: The series' America is ours with one addition, Compound V, and every divergence flows from it: Soldier Boy in the Second World War, Vought-American in 1950, a Homelander bred in 1981. The fork is filed at 1939, the year the wiki gives for Vought's work in the camps; the series itself says 'the late 1930s'. Later episodes also attach supes to real events (Soldier Boy at Birmingham in 1963 and at Kent State in 1970, even Kennedy's assassination); those are not used here because their sourcing on the wiki is thin.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1930s timeline (TV universe)
Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)

ending.why: Homelander is dead, his regime's laws are being rolled back, Robert Singer is back in the White House and Hughie and Annie are starting a family, even though Vought survives under Stan Edgar and blames everything on the man it made.

events.title: Frederick Vought makes the first supe
events.description: A German doctor, Frederick Vought, tests prototypes of a serum he calls Compound V on prisoners and, in the late 1930s, on Klara Risinger, who survives it with powers. She becomes his wife and, decades later, the super-heroine Liberty and the villain Stormfront.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1930s timeline (TV universe)
Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)

events.note: The series' first departure from our history. Stormfront's origin as Vought's first successful subject and wife is season 2 canon; the wiki files the Dachau appointment in 1939 and the first injection in 'the late 1930s', so the year is a best reading of a decade, and the Dachau detail rests on later episodes the wiki cites loosely.
events.binWhy: A serum that gives human beings powers is discovered; the discovery, not yet its use by a state, is the fork.

facets.change: human experiments → a serum that makes supes

events.title: Vought defects and America gets its first superhero
events.description: As Germany's prospects fade, Vought defects to the Allies, is pardoned, and runs a secret super-soldier programme for the US Army. Its product, Soldier Boy, is sold to the public as a war hero while being used mostly for propaganda and black operations.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1940s timeline (TV universe)

events.note: Soldier Boy as a Second World War hero is season 3 canon; the 1944 defection, pardon and the Fort Harmony programme are filled in by the wiki from later episodes of the series and of Gen V (5.03 and 5.04 among its citations). The year is the wiki's.
events.binWhy: A super-soldier is fielded by the state as a weapon and a symbol.

facets.change: a Nazi scientist → America's first superhero

events.title: Vought-American is founded
events.description: Frederick Vought turns the wartime programme into a company, Vought-American, later Vought International. Within two years it has a film studio; by the series' present it owns the heroes, their image, their merchandise and much of the news.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1950s timeline (TV universe)

events.note: Dated by the wiki from the series' in-universe corporate material; the company's centrality is the premise of every season.
events.binWhy: Founding of the corporation that will own America's superheroes and shape its politics.

facets.change: a wartime programme → a corporation that owns the heroes

events.title: Homelander is born in a Vought laboratory
events.description: Vought scientists use Soldier Boy's sperm, taken under false pretences, to create a child in a lab; the baby kills the doctors delivering him. He is raised in a cell as a test subject and presented to the public at eighteen as the Homelander.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1980s timeline (TV universe)

events.note: That Homelander was bred from Soldier Boy's DNA is revealed in season 3 (3.07). The birth year is the wiki's, consistent with his public debut with the Seven in 1999 at eighteen.
events.binWhy: A child is made on whom the country's future will turn: the most powerful supe alive, raised without a single human attachment.

facets.change: a stolen sample → a lab-raised boy who will be Homelander

events.title: Soldier Boy is betrayed to the Soviets in Nicaragua
events.description: On a CIA-backed mission in Nicaragua his own team, Payback, hands Soldier Boy to the Russians with Vought's agreement. Vought announces he died a hero, and the space he leaves is kept for the boy in the lab.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 1980s timeline (TV universe)

events.note: Season 3 canon; the 1984 date is given in the series and the wiki.
events.binWhy: A corporation and its partners hide what they did with their first hero; the lie holds for nearly forty years.

facets.change: America's first hero → a prisoner reported dead

events.title: The Boys comic begins
events.description: Garth Ennis and Darick Robertson's comic The Boys begins in 2006 and runs to 2012. The television series adapts its premise - a corporation that owns the superheroes, and the men who hunt them - but tells a different story.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)

events.note: A real-world publication. The series' own premiere (26 July 2019) falls in the same year as its first story event and is recorded there instead.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: A-Train runs through Robin, and Hughie joins the Boys
events.description: A speedster of the Seven runs straight through Hughie Campbell's girlfriend on a New York street; Vought offers him hush money. Billy Butcher recruits him into a revived vigilante crew, the Boys, that sets out to prove what the heroes really are.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)
The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2010s timeline (TV universe)

events.note: The first season is set in 2019 and premiered on Amazon Prime Video on 26 July 2019; the series' own release is recorded here rather than as a separate event because the atlas allows one event per year. The same year Homelander lets Transoceanic Flight 37 crash rather than admit he cannot save it.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the hidden story of what the heroes are.

facets.change: a stereo-shop clerk → one of the Boys

events.title: Compound V is exposed: the heroes were made
events.description: The public learns that supes are not born gifted but were dosed as babies with a Vought drug. The scandal produces congressional hearings and a Federal Bureau of Superhuman Affairs, headed by Victoria Neuman - who is herself a secret supe working for Vought's CEO.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2020s timeline (TV universe)
Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)

events.note: Season 2 (premiered 4 September 2020) is set in 2020 per the wiki; the exposure of Compound V opens the season.
events.binWhy: A company's founding secret is made public: its product is made, not born.

facets.change: heroes born gifted → heroes made with a drug

events.title: Homelander kills a protester in public and the crowd cheers
events.description: At a rally a protester's thrown can hits Homelander's son Ryan, and Homelander lasers the man's face off in front of cameras and his supporters. After a stunned pause the crowd applauds, and the most powerful being in America learns that he can kill in public and be loved for it.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2020s timeline (TV universe)
Collider: The Boys season 3 ending explained

events.note: The closing scene of season 3 (premiered 3 June 2022), set in 2022 per the wiki. He is tried for it in 2023-24 and acquitted.
events.binWhy: A public killing of an ordinary person by the country's most powerful figure, short of war, that changes what follows: it makes supe impunity popular.

facets.change: a hero who hides his cruelty → one cheered for killing

events.title: Calhoun takes the presidency and puts Homelander in charge
events.description: After Congress certifies Robert Singer's 2024 election despite the revelation that his vice-president is a supe, Butcher kills Neuman and Singer is arrested for plotting with the Boys, a scheme of Homelander's ally Sister Sage. Speaker Steven Calhoun assumes the presidency, declares martial law and appoints Homelander to command an army of supes to keep order.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2020s timeline (TV universe)
Wikipedia: The Boys season 4

events.note: The season 4 finale (season premiered 13 June 2024; Wikipedia, The Boys season 4). The series places the election in November 2024 and the certification and takeover in January 2025, the date presidential results are certified.
events.binWhy: A non-state power - Homelander, backed by the supes and Vought's media - ends up running the state through a puppet president.

facets.change: an elected president → a puppet president, martial law and a supe army

events.title: Homelander is killed on live television
events.description: During a national address from the White House in which he declares himself a god, Homelander is stripped of his powers by Kimiko and beaten to death by Butcher in front of the cameras. The puppet president is impeached within a day, Robert Singer returns, and Butcher is shot by Hughie before he can release a virus that would kill every supe.

sources.title: The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2020s timeline (TV universe)
Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)

events.note: The final season (8 April - 20 May 2026) places the address at Easter 2026. Vought survives: Stan Edgar returns as chief executive and the company blames the regime on Homelander alone.
events.binWhy: The ruler of the country is killed in his own seat of power and the old order returns.

facets.change: a god-king on air → dead on the Oval Office floor; Singer restored

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours plus a single invention, and its dates are ours: every season is set in the year it aired, from 2019 to 2026, and the backstory is threaded through real history. This lineage follows the Amazon series (2019-2026) with its in-universe history as the series and its spin-off Gen V give it, catalogued by the fan wiki; it does not follow Ennis and Robertson's comic, whose story and ending differ. The franchise is marked ongoing because a prequel, Vought Rising, is due in 2027, though the main series concluded in May 2026. T4 and T1 are empty; T3 holds the backstory (1939-1984) and T2 the series itself.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Boys (TV series)
The Boys Wiki (Fandom): 2020s timeline (TV universe)

lineages.title: Deus Ex
lineages.creator: Warren Spector and Harvey Smith (Ion Storm, 2000-2003); Eidos Montreal (2011-2016)

divergence.label: Majestic 12 is formed to study the Roswell crash
divergence.delta: Real: 1947 - debris near Roswell, an Army statement about a weather balloon, and nothing else; the Majestic 12 papers were forged decades later and the FBI called them bogus in 1988. Fiction: a secret panel takes charge of an alien craft and becomes the technology arm of an Illuminati that never died.
divergence.inUniverse: Majestic 12 commissioned after the Roswell crash, 1947 (series lore)
divergence.note: The games' secret history reaches back to the Bavarian Illuminati of 1776 and the Templars, but those are real, and the Illuminati's survival after their 1785 suppression is never given a year. 1947 is the first year the series dates something that did not happen. The next dated fork, Sarif Industries in 2007, is sixty years later, and the fiction only becomes public history with the augmentation boom.

sources.title: Game Rant: How Deus Ex's Majestic 12 conspires to control the world (1947 panel, 2030 earthquake, 2035 takeover, Gray Death fatality rate)
Wikipedia: Majestic 12 (the real-world forged documents, 1984; FBI verdict 1988)

ending.why: The last story in the chronology, Invisible War in 2072, leaves a world of enclaves after the Collapse with four endings (Helios union, Illuminati surveillance, Templar purge, Omar succession), and no later game picks one.

events.title: Majestic 12 is formed to hold what fell at Roswell
events.description: After the Roswell crash the President appoints a secret twelve-member panel to study the recovered craft and bodies. In the series it is set up under the patronage of the Illuminati, who never died out after their 18th-century suppression, as their technology branch; it keeps its findings and grows for a century.
events.inUniverse: Majestic 12 commissioned after the Roswell crash, 1947 (series lore, repeated in Mankind Divided's backstory material)

sources.title: Game Rant: How Deus Ex's Majestic 12 conspires to control the world (1947 panel, 2030 earthquake, 2035 takeover, Gray Death fatality rate)
Wikipedia: Majestic 12 (the real-world forged documents, 1984; FBI verdict 1988)

events.note: The year is stated in the lore. Real 1947 has the Roswell debris and an Army statement about a weather balloon; the 'Majestic 12' panel exists only in forged papers that surfaced in 1984 and that the FBI called 'completely bogus' in 1988. The games' Illuminati descend from the real Bavarian order of 1776, which was really suppressed in 1785; their survival is fictional but undated, so the fork sits at the first fictional year the games give.
events.binWhy: A secret body is founded to hold alien technology; in our 1947 no such panel existed.

facets.change: a crash site → a secret panel that keeps what it found

events.title: Deus Ex is released
events.description: Ion Storm's Deus Ex, published by Eidos, comes out for Windows: a conspiracy story set in 2052 in which a nano-augmented agent finds that the plague, the terrorists and his own agency are all run by the same people.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex (video game)

events.note: Released 23 June 2000. It fixed the late-20th-century conspiracy canon (Illuminati, Majestic 12, Area 51, FEMA, black helicopters) as the backstory of a playable future.
events.binWhy: A publication event, not a moment in the fiction; it has no bin.

events.title: Sarif Industries starts mass-producing prosthetics in Detroit
events.description: David Sarif, a protege of the augmentation pioneer Hugh Darrow, buys a failing Detroit car plant and turns it into an automated line for advanced prosthetics. A military contract follows in 2009; over the next twenty years artificial limbs and implants become a consumer product, each one needing the anti-rejection drug Neuropozyne for life.
events.inUniverse: Sarif Industries founded, 2007 (Human Revolution corporate backstory and viral site)

sources.title: Game Rant: Sarif Industries explained (founded 2007, bankrupt 2028)
Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Human Revolution

events.note: The founding year comes from Human Revolution's corporate backstory. In our 2007 Detroit's car plants were failing for real, and prosthetics with direct neural control were still laboratory work; the fiction's fork is that the prosthetics industry becomes a mass market in two decades.
events.binWhy: Automated production turns neural prosthetics into a mass product, starting the augmentation age.

facets.change: a closed car plant → a production line for mechanical limbs

events.title: Deus Ex: Human Revolution is released
events.description: Eidos Montreal's prequel, published by Square Enix, moves the series back to 2027 and the boom years of mechanical augmentation, and builds the backstory of Sarif, Darrow and the Aug Incident that the later games depend on.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Human Revolution

events.note: Released 23 August 2011 in North America. Most of the dated backstory before 2052 in this chain comes from the two Eidos Montreal prequels rather than from the 2000 game.
events.binWhy: A publication event, not a moment in the fiction; it has no bin.

events.title: The Aug Incident
events.description: In a year in which Sarif is attacked, its security chief Adam Jensen is rebuilt with full-body augmentations and the Illuminati move to control the new implant chips, Hugh Darrow broadcasts a signal from the Arctic facility Panchaea that drives augmented people everywhere into violent psychosis. Ordinary augmented people attack whoever is near them, and many die; Panchaea is destroyed, and whatever Jensen broadcasts is lost in the noise.
events.inUniverse: Panchaea and the Darrow signal, 2027 (Human Revolution; named the Aug Incident in Mankind Divided)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Human Revolution
Wikipedia: Adam Jensen (the Aug Incident and discrimination by 2029)
Wikipedia: Deus Ex (franchise)

events.note: Human Revolution is set in 2027 and the Incident is its climax. The game has four endings (tell the truth, blame the Humanity Front, serve the Illuminati, destroy Panchaea); Mankind Divided follows none of them outright: Panchaea sinks in every case, Darrow's recorded confession circulates, and no single account wins, so the Illuminati's version shapes the aftermath. In our 2027 nothing of the kind has been possible.
events.binWhy: One man turns an implant network into a weapon against its own users, short of war, and the world's view of augmentation flips.

facets.change: augmented citizens → people feared as weapons

events.title: Mechanical apartheid
events.description: Two years after the Incident augmented people are registered, checked at separate gates and moved into ghettos such as Golem City outside Prague. The Illuminati steer the United Nations toward the Human Restoration Act, which would confine them to a purpose-built city in Oman, while the Augmented Rights Coalition turns militant and an Interpol task force hunts it.
events.inUniverse: Prague and London, 2029 (Mankind Divided)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Mankind Divided
Wikipedia: Adam Jensen (the Aug Incident and discrimination by 2029)

events.note: Mankind Divided states 2029. Whether the Act passes depends on the player's choices at the London summit, and no later game settles it, so the event is filed at the segregation the game shows in every path. The series lore also gives 2029 as the birth year of JC Denton, Paul Denton's clone; he is folded into the 2052 event.
events.binWhy: Governments register, segregate and police a whole class of people.

facets.change: augmented citizens → residents of walled ghettos

events.title: The West Coast earthquake and the secessions
events.description: A magnitude 8.3 earthquake wrecks San Francisco and sinks Los Angeles and much of Southern California into the sea. With Washington absorbed in the disaster, Utah secedes and annexes what is left of Arizona and Nevada, Texas separatists follow, and paramilitaries in the Northwest form the secessionist forces that become the NSF of 2052.
events.inUniverse: The 2030 earthquake (series lore; rumoured in-universe to have been triggered by planted nuclear charges)

sources.title: Game Rant: How Deus Ex's Majestic 12 conspires to control the world (1947 panel, 2030 earthquake, 2035 takeover, Gray Death fatality rate)

events.note: The year and the damage are stated in the series lore as summarised by Game Rant; the secessions that follow are given without separate years and are folded in here. The lore leaves open whether the quake was natural or set off by a cabal along the San Andreas fault. In our 2030 no such quake has happened.
events.binWhy: A disaster kills tens of thousands and breaks the federal government's hold on the interior.

facets.change: a whole coast → a disaster zone and breakaway states

events.title: Majestic 12 takes over the Illuminati
events.description: Led by the tech billionaire Bob Page, Majestic 12 turns on the society that created it and seizes the Illuminati's political, financial, military and religious arms, including their hold on the United Nations and its new counter-terror force, UNATCO. The old families, Morgan Everett and the DuClares among them, are pushed out of their own machine.
events.inUniverse: Majestic 12's coup, 2030s, complete by 2035 (series lore)

sources.title: Game Rant: How Deus Ex's Majestic 12 conspires to control the world (1947 panel, 2030 earthquake, 2035 takeover, Gray Death fatality rate)
Wikipedia: Deus Ex (video game)

events.note: The lore gives the takeover as complete by 2035 and does not date its start; UNATCO's founding is not dated either and falls somewhere between 2029, when it does not exist, and 2035. In our history neither body exists.
events.binWhy: A faction inside a secret government overthrows its masters and takes their institutions.

facets.change: the Illuminati's arms → Majestic 12's

events.title: The Statue of Liberty is bombed and the Gray Death spreads
events.description: A bombing blamed on foreign terrorists destroys the Statue of Liberty and the outrage lets UNATCO operate on American soil, headquartered on Liberty Island. In the same period a nanite plague, the Gray Death, spreads through American cities with a fatality rate of about 93 percent; the only treatment, Ambrosia, is scarce and rationed to those the government deems essential.
events.inUniverse: Statue of Liberty bombing and the Gray Death, 2051-52 (Deus Ex backstory)

sources.title: A Political Analysis of the Deus Ex Series (Statue of Liberty bombing dated 2051)
Game Rant: How Deus Ex's Majestic 12 conspires to control the world (1947 panel, 2030 earthquake, 2035 takeover, Gray Death fatality rate)
Wikipedia: Deus Ex (video game)

events.note: The 2051 date for the bombing comes from fan-compiled chronologies of the game's backstory; the plague is said to have begun at about the same time and is widespread by 2052. The game later reveals that the bombing was a false-flag attack and that VersaLife, Page's company, made the Gray Death so Majestic 12 could control who lives. In our history nothing like it exists.
events.binWhy: An engineered nanite disease kills most of those it infects, and access to the cure becomes a means of rule.

facets.change: a free population → one rationed by access to a vaccine

events.title: JC Denton at Area 51: Page dies, Helios takes a human host, the global network goes dark
events.description: JC Denton, a nano-augmented UNATCO rookie sent against the NSF over a stolen Ambrosia shipment, learns that his agency, the plague and his own manufacture belong to Majestic 12, defects, and fights his way to Area 51. There the AI Helios, born when the Illuminati's AI Daedalus and Page's Icarus fused, has offered itself to Page; JC kills Page, merges with Helios himself, and destroys the base that routes the world's communications.
events.inUniverse: Deus Ex, 2052, following the combined ending that Invisible War treats as canon

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex (video game)
Wikipedia: JC Denton (Invisible War mixes the endings; the Helios merger and cryogenic stasis)
Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Invisible War

events.note: Deus Ex has three endings: destroy Area 51 and bring the global network down, kill Page and restore the Illuminati, or merge with Helios and rule as a benevolent machine. Invisible War takes a bit of all three: JC kills Page, merges with Helios, destroys Area 51, and then works with the Illuminati to rebuild. That is the path followed here, because it is the only one a later game builds on. JC was cloned from his older brother Paul and born in 2029 as part of Majestic 12's nano-augmentation programme.
events.binWhy: A human being joins with the AI that monitors the world's communications and becomes something neither was.

facets.change: a UNATCO agent → a man joined to the machine that ran the network

events.title: The Collapse
events.description: With Area 51's network gone, the world falls into two decades of war and depression that Invisible War calls the Collapse. The nation-states give way to walled enclaves around the old cities, and the Helios merger nearly kills JC, who is put into cryogenic stasis.
events.inUniverse: The Collapse, from 2052 (Invisible War backstory)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Invisible War
Wikipedia: JC Denton (Invisible War mixes the endings; the Helios merger and cryogenic stasis)

events.note: Invisible War says only that the Collapse followed JC's actions in 2052 and precedes 2072. It is filed at 2053, the first year after the destruction of Area 51, because the game gives no start year and the chain allows one event per year.
events.binWhy: The global order breaks into enclaves and never comes back in its old form.

facets.change: a networked world economy → war, depression and walled cities

events.title: Chicago is destroyed and four factions bid for the world
events.description: Twenty years on, the Templars, a militant order opposed to body modification, destroy Chicago and the clone Alex D escapes to Seattle. The walled cities are run by the WTO, while the multi-faith Order preaches against it; both are secretly led by the Illuminati. JC Denton, woken with Helios, wants to join everyone through the AI, and the Omar, a cybernetic collective, want what is left.
events.inUniverse: Deus Ex: Invisible War, 2072

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deus Ex: Invisible War

events.note: Invisible War is set in 2072. It has four endings (JC and Helios join humanity into one democratic mind, the Illuminati rule through surveillance, the Templars purge all modification, or the Omar inherit a ruined Earth), and no later game follows any of them, because the Eidos Montreal games went back to the 2020s instead.
events.binWhy: A twenty-year jump shows what became of the world after 2052: enclaves, factions, and no settled future.

facets.change: a collapsed world → enclaves ruled from behind two fronts

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because the world is ours until a secret panel forms in 1947, and every later date is on our calendar: the games state 2027, 2029, 2052 and 2072 outright. This chain follows game canon only: the two Eidos Montreal prequels for the 2020s, Mankind Divided's reading of Human Revolution (Panchaea destroyed, no broadcast wins), and Invisible War's combined ending for Deus Ex (JC kills Page, merges with Helios, destroys Area 51 and sides with the Illuminati). The novels, comics and the mobile game The Fall are left out. Tiers: T3 holds only the 1947 fork; T2 holds the releases and everything from 2007 to 2072. T4 is empty because the Illuminati and Templars before 1900 are real history, and T1 is empty because the series never goes past 2072.

lineages.title: Independence Day
lineages.creator: Roland Emmerich and Dean Devlin

divergence.label: An alien attack ship crashes at Roswell
divergence.delta: Real: on 8 July 1947 Roswell Army Air Field announces it has recovered a 'flying disc', and within a day the Army says it was a weather balloon; a 1994 Air Force report traces the debris to Project Mogul, a secret balloon programme for detecting Soviet nuclear tests. Fiction: it was a fighter from the invaders' fleet, with its dead crew, and a government faction has kept it at Area 51 ever since.
divergence.inUniverse: 1947 (stated in the 1996 film)
divergence.note: The first film states that a government faction has been involved in a UFO conspiracy since 1947, when one of the invaders' fighters crashed near Roswell; the ship and its occupants' bodies are at Area 51 in 1996, and the President has not been told. Nothing else in the fiction departs from our record before July 1996, when the invasion makes the secret moot. Screen Rant's fan chronology suggests the ship was drawn by nuclear testing; neither film says so.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day (1996 film)
Wikipedia: Roswell incident

ending.why: Humanity wins a second war, kills the Harvester queen and gains an ally in the sphere, and Resurgence ends with the species preparing to take the fight to the Harvesters' own world.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch: a hidden fork in 1947, like the hidden-history worlds, but the story's point is that the secret ends in public, in the film's own release year, and the sequel projects the changed world twenty years forward, to a planet united under an alien-technology defence force. Continuity: the two films, with the years between them taken from the sequel's War of 1996 marketing timeline as reported by Bustle, Screen Rant and the Fictional Brands Archive, marked medium. Both films are set in the years they were released (1996 and 2016), and a lineage can hold only one event a year, so the releases are folded into the notes of the 1996 and 2016 events instead of being filed separately. Two pre-fork events are real history the films build on: the Declaration of Independence, whose date the counterattack keeps, and the atomic bomb, which fails against the invaders' shields. Tiers: T4 holds 1776; T3 holds 1945-1998; T2 holds 2001-2016; T1 is empty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day (1996 film)
Wikipedia: Independence Day: Resurgence

events.title: The Declaration of Independence
events.description: The Second Continental Congress adopts the declaration by which thirteen colonies call themselves independent states no longer subject to British rule; the date becomes the United States' national holiday.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United States Declaration of Independence

events.note: The film is built around the date: the counterattack is launched on 4 July 1996, and the President tells the pilots that it will no longer be only an American holiday.
events.binWhy: Colonies revolt against the power that rules them.

facets.change: colonies → a declared nation

events.title: The first atomic bomb is tested
events.description: The United States detonates the first nuclear weapon in the New Mexico desert, a little over a hundred miles from Roswell.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Trinity (nuclear test)

events.note: In the film the bomb is humanity's strongest weapon and it fails: a nuclear strike on the saucer over Houston destroys the city and not the ship. The last blow is a nuclear warhead delivered inside the mothership after its shields are down.
events.binWhy: A weapon able to end a civilisation is tested.

facets.change: conventional war → the atomic bomb

events.title: The Roswell crash is recovered and hidden
events.description: One of the invaders' fighters crashes near Roswell. The ship and its dead crew go to a secret hangar at Area 51, where scientists study them for half a century without telling the public or, eventually, the President.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day (1996 film)
Wikipedia: Roswell incident

events.note: The year is stated in the 1996 film. The real Roswell announcement was on 8 July 1947 and was withdrawn within a day.
events.binWhy: Humanity is touched by a non-human intelligence, and the contact is hidden.

facets.change: an empty sky → a captured alien ship in a secret hangar

events.title: The War of 1996
events.description: A mothership parks in orbit and sends saucers fifteen miles wide over the world's cities; on 2 and 3 July they burn Washington, New York, Los Angeles and many more, and a nuclear strike on Houston fails. On 4 July a computer virus uploaded from the Roswell ship drops their shields, and a worldwide counterattack destroys the fleet.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day (1996 film)
Screen Rant: The alternate history of Independence Day explained

events.note: The dates are the film's own; it opened in US cinemas on 2 July 1996, the day its story begins. The death toll, over three billion people in 108 cities, comes from the sequel's War of 1996 promotional material as reported by Screen Rant. The saucers' size is the film's.
events.binWhy: The invasion is defeated in a single day's counterattack.

facets.change: cities burning → the invaders destroyed

events.title: The UN founds Earth Space Defense
events.description: With salvaged alien technology and a world that has put its quarrels aside, the United Nations creates a planetary defence force. By 2016 it has bases from Area 51 to the Moon, Mars and Saturn's moon Rhea, and weapons platforms in orbit.

sources.title: Fictional Brands Archive: Earth Space Defence (founded 25 May 1998)
Wikipedia: Independence Day: Resurgence

events.note: Earth Space Defense and its bases are in Resurgence; the founding date is from franchise tie-in material, reported by the Fictional Brands Archive (citing the Independence Day wiki), and is not stated in either film.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that will shape the world.

facets.change: national militaries → one planetary defence force

events.title: A ground war with the survivors in Africa
events.description: Aliens who survived aboard a ship grounded in central Africa fight a war with local forces that lasts five years; it makes the warlord Dikembe Umbutu an expert in killing them.

sources.title: Bustle: how long after Independence Day is Resurgence set (War of 1996 timeline)

events.note: Date and length are from the War of 1996 promotional timeline, as reported by Bustle. Resurgence shows the grounded ship and Umbutu's veterans but gives no dates.
events.binWhy: The war goes on for years on the ground after the victory in the sky.

facets.change: a victory in the sky → years of fighting on the ground

events.title: A hybrid fighter test kills Steven Hiller
events.description: At an Earth Space Defense expo, the pilot who flew into the mothership in 1996 dies test-flying a fighter that combines human and alien technology, and the force's leadership changes.

sources.title: Screen Rant: The alternate history of Independence Day explained
Fictional Brands Archive: Earth Space Defence (founded 25 May 1998)

events.note: Tie-in dating via Screen Rant and the Fictional Brands Archive; in Resurgence Hiller is dead and his stepson Dylan flies for the ESD.
events.binWhy: Human-alien hybrid technology is put into service, at a price.

facets.change: salvaged alien parts → hybrid fighters

events.title: The Harvesters come back
events.description: As the world marks twenty years since its victory, a mothership 3,000 miles across destroys most of Earth's defences and lands over the North Atlantic to drill into the planet. A sphere recovered from the Moon, an artificial intelligence from another species the Harvesters attacked, guides humanity; former president Whitmore flies a suicide mission, the Harvester queen is killed, and the sphere asks humanity to lead a resistance against the Harvesters' homeworld.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day: Resurgence
Bustle: how long after Independence Day is Resurgence set (War of 1996 timeline)

events.note: Resurgence is set around the Fourth of July 2016, twenty years after the first film (Bustle); it opened on 24 June 2016. No sequel has followed, so the war the ending announces is untold.
events.binWhy: A war begins that the story means to take to the enemy's own world.

facets.change: twenty years of preparation → an interstellar war begun

lineages.title: The Creator
lineages.creator: Gareth Edwards (director; co-writer with Chris Weitz)

divergence.label: Robots start doing the housework
divergence.delta: Real: in the 1950s robots are fairground showpieces, and 'artificial intelligence' is a phrase coined for a summer workshop. Fiction: the film's opening newsreel shows clumsy household robots already helping with chores in the 1950s, humanoid machines on assembly lines by the 1960s, and a late twentieth century in which mechanical workers are everywhere.
divergence.inUniverse: The opening newsreel's black-and-white footage of domestic robots, styled as the 1950s
divergence.note: The film gives no year before 2055. Its opening montage is styled as archive footage decade by decade, and reviewers read the first of it as the 1950s; the fork is filed at 1955, the middle of that decade, and should be read as 'the 1950s'. Edwards has described the look as retro-futurism, a world in which the Sony Walkman rather than the Apple Mac won the design war, which is why the future still looks like 1980s consumer electronics.

sources.title: SlashFilm: How The Creator's sci-fi universe rewrites our past (robots explored in the 1950s; androids on assembly lines in what looks like the 1960s)
CBR: The timeline of The Creator's war against AI, explained (1950s household robots in the newsreel; 2055)

ending.why: NOMAD, the orbital station the West used to strike New Asia, is destroyed with its missiles' guidance, most of the targeted AI bases are saved, and the child simulant Alphie is welcomed by the AI population as the new Nirmata.

events.title: Elektro walks at the New York World's Fair
events.description: Westinghouse shows a seven-foot robot that walks on voice command, 'speaks' about 700 words from a record player, smokes and blows up balloons. It is the most famous robot of its day and can do nothing useful.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Elektro (exhibited at the 1939 New York World's Fair)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's newsreel begins with machines of this kind; the fork is the moment such machines start doing real work in real homes, which in our history they never did.
events.binWhy: A robot is demonstrated to the public as the shape of the future.

facets.change: robots in stories → a walking, talking robot at a world's fair

events.title: Turing asks whether machines can think
events.description: Alan Turing's paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', published in Mind, proposes the imitation game: if a machine's answers cannot be told from a person's, the question of whether it thinks has been answered in practice.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (Mind, 1950)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's simulants pass Turing's test in the flesh - they wear donated human faces - and the whole war is an argument over whether passing it makes them people.
events.binWhy: The theory by which later histories judge machine minds is set out.

facets.change: an unasked question → a test for machine thought

events.title: Household robots in American homes
events.description: The opening newsreel shows cumbersome robots working as maids and gardeners in the 1950s, filmed like any other labour-saving appliance of the decade.
events.inUniverse: Newsreel footage styled as the 1950s

sources.title: CBR: The timeline of The Creator's war against AI (clips of household robots from the 1950s)
SlashFilm: The Creator's alternate history explained

events.note: The decade is read from the footage's style; no year is shown, so 1955 stands for 'the 1950s'. In our 1950s the only robots in homes were in advertisements and fairs.
events.binWhy: Working robots are sold into ordinary homes decades before our history could build them.

facets.change: robots at world's fairs → robots doing the chores

events.title: Humanoid machines on the assembly lines
events.description: In footage styled as the 1960s, humanoid androids work car assembly lines and colour advertisements sell robots as servants, police and soldiers. By the end of the century, in the newsreel's telling, near-human robots are surgeons, firefighters and athletes.
events.inUniverse: Newsreel footage styled as the 1960s

sources.title: SlashFilm: The Creator's alternate history explained (humanoid androids on auto assembly lines in what looks like the 1960s)
CBR: The timeline of The Creator's war against AI (1970s-1990s near-humanoid robots)

events.note: Like the fork, dated only by the look of the footage; 1965 stands for 'the 1960s'. The later decades of the montage are too loosely dated to file separately and are folded in here.
events.binWhy: Human-shaped machines are put to work across industry and public service.

facets.change: household helpers → humanoid workers in factories and uniforms

events.title: The Creator is released
events.description: 20th Century Studios releases Gareth Edwards's original film about a war the West wages on the AI of New Asia; it was shot on location, beginning in Thailand in January 2022.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Creator (2023 film) (released 29 September 2023)

events.note: Released on 29 September 2023, two days after the end of the 2023 writers' strike and amid public argument over generative AI.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: A nuclear warhead destroys Los Angeles
events.description: A nuclear warhead detonates over Los Angeles and the U.S. government blames the defence AI it built. Most of the Western world pledges to eradicate artificial intelligence; New Asia, where people and AI live together, refuses.
events.inUniverse: Stated on screen: 2055

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Creator (2023 film) (plot: 2055, Los Angeles)

events.note: The year is given in the film's opening. The film later reveals, through Harun, that the detonation was a human coding error blamed on the machines; the ban and the war rest on that cover story.
events.binWhy: A city is destroyed and the society that loses it turns on a whole kind of being.

facets.change: a city living with robots → a crater blamed on them

events.title: The war on New Asia's AI, fought from orbit
events.description: Ten years into the West's war on AI, the orbital station NOMAD strikes New Asia from space and U.S. forces hunt Nirmata, the architect of its AI. An undercover American sergeant, Joshua Taylor, is exposed when troops raid the home he shares with his pregnant wife Maya, and Maya is believed killed by a NOMAD strike.
events.inUniverse: Stated on screen: 2065

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Creator (2023 film) (plot: 2065; NOMAD)
Movie Nation: The Creator makes fear of AI a Vietnam War analogy (review)

events.note: The year is stated. NOMAD stands for North American Orbital Mobile Aerospace Defense. Reviewers read the war's imagery - village raids, helicopters over paddy fields, a heavy-handed America in Asia - as a Vietnam War analogy.
events.binWhy: The war against AI has become years of raids, insurgency and strikes from orbit.

facets.change: a ban on AI → a decade of war on New Asia

events.title: Alphie brings down NOMAD
events.description: Sent to destroy Nirmata's new weapon, Taylor finds it is a simulant child, Alphie, who can control machines, and learns that Maya was Nirmata and that the Los Angeles blast was human error. Alphie forces a lunar shuttle to dock with NOMAD; Taylor blows it up and dies, its missiles lose guidance, and Alphie is welcomed on Earth as the new Nirmata.
events.inUniverse: Five years after the 2065 raid

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Creator (2023 film) (plot: five years later)
CBR: The timeline of The Creator's war against AI (main story in 2070)

events.note: The film states 'five years later' after the 2065 prologue. It ends as NOMAD falls; whether the war ends with it is left to the viewer, but the weapon that made the war one-sided is gone.
events.binWhy: The weapon that gave one side the war is destroyed and the other side gains a leader.

facets.change: an orbital station that can strike anywhere → NOMAD destroyed and the strike called off

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because it leaves our world at a single line of invention - working robots, decades early - and follows that invention to a war over whether machines are people; it fits beside Blade Runner and Deus Ex, whose forks also lie in the twentieth century. Continuity followed: the 2023 film only. Its only stated years are 2055 and 2065, with the main story five years later; the fork and the 1960s event are dated from the style of the newsreel and are low confidence. Two real pre-fork events (Elektro, Turing) are the history the premise stands on. Tiers: T3 holds the real history, the fork and the 1960s (1939-1965); T2 holds the release and the story (2023-2070). T4 is empty because nothing reaches before the machine age, and T1 because the film ends in 2070.
