lineages.title: The Andromeda Strain
lineages.creator: Michael Crichton

divergence.label: Merrick's paper on first contact by microbe
divergence.delta: Real: in 1962 the danger of contamination from space is a question for committees, and the only things coming back from orbit are spy-satellite film capsules. Fiction: a paper at Cold Spring Harbor persuades a Nobel laureate that the first contact will be an infection, and within five years the United States has a secret weapons programme sampling near space and a laboratory in Nevada waiting for what it brings back.
divergence.inUniverse: Summer 1962, Tenth Biological Symposium at Cold Spring Harbor
divergence.note: The novel is written as history and gives its own dates, from Merrick's paper in 1962 through the Wildfire file of 1965-66 to the five-day crisis of February 1967. Its scientists come with invented careers that reach back further (Stone is given the Nobel Prize for 1961), but a character's biography is not a history; the fork is filed at the first invented event from which the story's chain runs, which the novel itself says 'begun it all'.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course
Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

ending.why: Andromeda mutates into a form harmless to people and drifts away, but it is still mutating in the upper atmosphere, has just burned up a crewed capsule, and NASA has grounded crewed flight indefinitely because 'the decision is out of our hands'.

events.title: Scientists ask for rules against carrying germs between worlds
events.description: Real history: in the months after Sputnik, the geneticist Joshua Lederberg warns that spacecraft could carry Earth microbes to other worlds and bring foreign ones back. The US National Academy of Sciences passes a resolution on contamination, an international committee (CETEX) recommends sterilising spacecraft, and in 1959 COSPAR takes over the job.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planetary protection
Wikipedia: Joshua Lederberg

events.note: Real-world background. The novel's own history begins here: it notes that by 1959 NASA had strict sterilisation rules for outbound probes, and has its Jeremy Stone, a young Nobel-winning bacteriologist, argue that the danger of returning craft was being ignored. Lederberg won the Nobel Prize in 1958; Wikipedia does not say Crichton modelled Stone on him.
events.binWhy: A scientific committee is formed that will set the rules for contamination in space.

facets.change: a space race → rules against contaminating other worlds

events.title: A capsule is caught coming back from orbit
events.description: Real history: the film capsule of Discoverer 14, a secret Corona reconnaissance satellite launched from Vandenberg, is snatched in mid-air over the Pacific by a C-119 aircraft, the first object ever recovered from orbit. Its photographs cover more of the Soviet Union than every U-2 flight before it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Discoverer 14

events.note: Real-world background. The novel's Scoop satellites use the same machinery: launched from Vandenberg into polar orbit for secrecy, and brought down by radio command for recovery by the military.
events.binWhy: A reconnaissance satellite returns its film from orbit: the machinery of watching people put to work.

facets.change: U-2 overflights → film caught in mid-air from orbit

events.title: Merrick predicts that first contact will be an infection
events.description: At a biology symposium at Cold Spring Harbor, the English biophysicist J. J. Merrick argues from the rarity of complex life that humanity's first contact with anything from space will be with a microorganism, and that it may well cause disease. The audience is amused; Jeremy Stone takes it seriously.
events.inUniverse: Tenth Biological Symposium, Cold Spring Harbor

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel, which calls Merrick the man who 'in his own way, begun it all'. Stone and his colleagues are given invented careers before this (Stone's Nobel Prize is dated 1961), but Merrick's paper is the first invented event from which the story's chain runs.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives, about what life from space will be, that the rest of the story turns on.

facets.change: first contact as a conversation → first contact as an infection

events.title: Project Scoop: a science satellite that is really a weapons search
events.description: The Army contracts the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, through NASA, to design satellites that will skim the edge of space and collect whatever organisms live there. The scientists are told it is pure research; its true purpose is to find new life forms for the biological-weapons programme at Fort Detrick.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel. The real Fort Detrick ran US biological-weapons research until 1969; Project Scoop and its aims are invented.
events.binWhy: The purpose of a programme is hidden from the scientists who build it and from the public.

facets.change: a curiosity-driven science satellite → a hidden hunt for germ weapons

events.date: 10 June 1964 (Stone's letter); construction ordered January 1965 and finished July 1966
events.title: Stone's letter to the President, and the Wildfire laboratory
events.description: Stone and four colleagues write to the President, in a letter patterned on Einstein's of 1939, that sterilising returning spacecraft can never be made safe, and ask for an underground laboratory to study anything that comes back, with a nuclear bomb to destroy it. Within a month they are an official committee; the Defense Department pays $22 million, and the Wildfire laboratory is built underground at Flatrock, Nevada, with a protocol to nuke any town where an alien organism lands.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: All dates are stated in the novel: the letter is dated 10 June 1964, the Wildfire file records construction initiated by executive order in January 1965 and completed in July 1966. The novel places the letter's model in 1940; Einstein's letter to Roosevelt was dated August 1939.
events.binWhy: A secret body is founded to meet an extraterrestrial germ, and it will shape everything that happens when one arrives.

facets.change: a scientists' letter → an underground lab with a bomb inside

events.date: spring - December 1965 (the trial deaths follow on 1 March 1966)
events.title: Kalocin, a universal antibiotic, is found and buried
events.description: A drug company finds a compound that cures cancer by killing every single-celled organism in the body. When forty trial subjects are taken off it in March 1966, all forty die within six hours of diseases no one has seen, and the government suppresses all knowledge of the drug.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel as backstory, told at the height of the Wildfire crisis to explain why Stone refuses to use the drug on a dying colleague. The discovery is filed at 1965 because 1966 holds the first Scoop flights.
events.binWhy: A medical discovery arrives that the rest of the story will have to reckon with.

facets.change: an incurable cancer → a cure that opens the body to every germ

events.title: The Scoop satellites start to fly
events.description: Scoop I goes up from Vandenberg in March 1966 and comes down in a Georgia swamp with nothing but Earth germs. Two burn up on re-entry, two more bring back harmless skin bacteria, and Scoop VI, launched on New Year's Day 1967, returns a new organism that makes chickens ill.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Dates stated in the novel. The failures make the Army tighten sterilisation before each launch, which is why the organism Scoop VII brings back cannot be put down to contamination from Earth.
events.binWhy: Satellites go to the edge of space to collect life no one has found.

facets.change: a satellite programme on paper → six sampling flights to near space

events.date: February 1967 (Scoop VII launched on or about 5 February; down about two and a half days later)
events.title: Scoop VII comes down at Piedmont, Arizona
events.description: The Army brings a satellite down by radio in the desert, the town of Piedmont dies in hours with its blood clotted in its veins, and the Wildfire team is summoned to study the organism, Andromeda, with only an old man and a baby left alive. The President delays the order to bomb the town; Andromeda mutates, eats through the laboratory's seals and nearly sets off its bomb, then turns harmless and drifts out over the Pacific, while a crewed capsule, Andros V, burns up on re-entry.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course
Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

events.note: The novel says the launch date is classified but 'believed to be February 5, 1967', that the satellite orbited for two and a half days before it was brought down, and that it was February when the recovery team found the town; the crisis then lasts five days. The Andromeda organism is grown only in blood of normal acidity, which is why a drinker and a crying baby survive; it turns out to feed on energy, so the nuclear bomb Stone asked for would have fed it. In our February 1967 there is no Scoop programme, no Wildfire and no Piedmont.
events.binWhy: An organism collected by a weapons programme is brought down among people by accident and kills a town: released by people, not arising by itself.

facets.change: a recovered satellite → a dead town and an organism no one can stop

events.title: The Andromeda Strain is published
events.description: Michael Crichton publishes the novel under his own name, written as a declassified report of a five-day crisis, complete with teleprinter messages, computer printouts and pages 'deleted' from classified files.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

events.note: The foreword is signed 'M.C., Cambridge, Massachusetts, January 1969', and the book is framed as history, the story of a crisis two years before. It came out two months before Apollo 11, whose crew was quarantined in the real Lunar Receiving Laboratory that the novel mentions.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the original publication.

events.title: Robert Wise's film is released
events.description: The film adaptation keeps the story but moves it: the satellite comes down at Piedmont, New Mexico, one of the scientists becomes a woman, Dr. Ruth Leavitt, and the events are framed by testimony before a Senate committee.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain (film)

events.note: A separate continuity, not followed here: the film's dates belong to its own present rather than to the novel's 1967.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the film adaptation.

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is 1960s America, its space and weapons programmes are real (Vandenberg, JPL, Fort Detrick), and the fork is a scientific idea that the state turns into a secret programme. Follows Crichton's 1969 novel only. The 1971 film moves the story to New Mexico and its own present; the 2008 miniseries and Daniel H. Wilson's authorised 2019 sequel, The Andromeda Evolution, set fifty years later, are not charted. The crisis itself lasts five days, so the chain is mostly the invented history the novel builds for it. Tiers: T3 holds everything, from the real 1958-1960 background to the 1971 film; T4, T2 and T1 are empty because the novel reaches back only to the space age and forward only to its own epilogue.

lineages.title: Childhood's End
lineages.creator: Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: The Overlords' ships appear over the cities of Earth
divergence.delta: Real: by 1975 Apollo had been to the Moon six times and ended, and the superpowers were in detente. Fiction: the Americans and Soviets are still racing for the Moon with captured German engineers when alien ships take station over every city and a voice announces that humanity is now supervised.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; the 1953 prologue says 1945 was 'more than thirty years' ago
divergence.note: Clarke never gives the year. The 1953 prologue places its space race more than thirty years after the spring of 1945, so no earlier than 1975; Encyclopedia.com dates Part One to 1975 and the Penguin Random House teacher's guide to the late 1970s. Strictly the fiction has already parted from us by 1969, because in it nobody reaches the Moon, but that is an absence rather than an event; the arrival is the first thing the novel narrates that our history lacks. Every later date in the chain is counted from this one, so all of them inherit its uncertainty. The 1990 revision moved the prologue to the early 21st century and a race to Mars; it is not followed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Childhood's End
Encyclopedia.com: Childhood's End (dates Part One to 1975 and the revelation to about 2025)
Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)

ending.why: Humanity as a species ends: its children merge into the Overmind, the adults die out, and the Earth itself is consumed, leaving one man to watch and the Overlords to leave.

events.title: The Reich falls and its rocket men are divided between East and West
events.description: Germany is defeated and occupied, and its rocket engineers are carried off by the Americans and the Soviets to build the missiles of the next war. The novel's prologue begins with two of them, thirty years on, racing each other for the Moon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Operation Paperclip
Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: Real history. The United States brought over 1,600 German scientists and engineers in Operation Paperclip from 1945; the Soviet Union took more than 2,000 in Operation Osoaviakhim in 1946. The 1953 prologue follows two such men, Reinhold Hoffmann in America and Konrad Schneider in Russia, and remembers the spring of 1945 when they parted.
events.binWhy: A power is defeated and its territory occupied; its scientists become the prize the victors share, which is the precondition of the novel's space race.

facets.change: a Reich with rockets → occupied zones, its rocket men shared out

events.title: 'Guardian Angel' is published
events.description: Clarke's short story, which becomes the first part of the novel, appears in Famous Fantastic Mysteries in April 1950 and in New Worlds that winter.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: A real-world publication event. Clarke wrote the story in July 1946; the Famous Fantastic Mysteries text was edited by James Blish.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Childhood's End is published
events.description: Ballantine Books publishes the novel in August 1953. In 1990 Clarke rewrote the first chapter to move the space race from the Moon to Mars and into the early 21st century.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: A real-world publication event. This chain follows the 1953 text, whose prologue is set when 1945 is 'more than thirty years' past.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Overlords' ships appear over the cities of Earth
events.description: As the American and Soviet rocket teams are about to launch for the Moon, enormous silent ships take station above every major city. After a week, a voice calling itself Karellen announces that the Overlords are taking over the supervision of human affairs.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Childhood's End (dates Part One to 1975 and the revelation to about 2025)
Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: The 1953 text gives no year; it says only that 1945 is more than thirty years in the past, which places the arrival at 1975 or later. Encyclopedia.com's summary dates it to 1975 and the Penguin Random House teacher's guide to the late 1970s; 1975 is used here. In our history the Moon race ended in 1969 with Apollo 11; in the novel nobody has reached the Moon when the ships come.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence arrives openly and takes charge; it is contact of the most direct kind, confirmed to everyone at once.

facets.change: a space race → ships over every city

events.title: The World Federation is chartered under the Overlords
events.description: Five years after the arrival, Karellen and the UN Secretary-General Rikki Stormgren draft the charter of a world state. A Freedom League that wants the aliens gone kidnaps Stormgren; Karellen gets him back without effort and promises the Overlords will show themselves in fifty years.

sources.title: LitCharts: Childhood's End plot summary (five years after arrival; Jan's eighty Earth-years)
Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
Shmoop: Karellen and the Overlords timeline (World State charter, kidnapping, fifty years)

events.note: The novel's Part One is set about five years after the arrival (LitCharts), and the teacher's guide places the start of the World Federation in the early 1980s. With the arrival at 1975, c. 1980 follows. The kidnapping and the charter happen in the same stretch of Part One and are merged here.
events.binWhy: Independent states are brought under one charter, even though the hand behind it is alien; the kidnapping is the resistance that fails.

facets.change: nation states → one federation under a foreign hand

events.title: The Overlords show themselves, and they look like devils
events.description: Fifty years after arriving, as promised, Karellen steps out of his ship with a human child on each arm: leathery wings, horns, a tail. Humanity, which has meanwhile come into a Golden Age without war, crime or want, takes the shock and settles into utopia.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Childhood's End (dates Part One to 1975 and the revelation to about 2025)
Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: The fifty-year interval is stated in the novel; the year depends on the arrival. From a 1975 arrival it gives 2025, as Encyclopedia.com has it; the teacher's guide says the 2030s. In our 2025 no one has shown themselves; the fiction's 2025 has half a century of abolished war and poverty behind it. The Golden Age that fills the novel's Part Two is described here rather than dated separately.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is shown: the Overlords' true form, and the hint, which the novel explains later, of why humanity remembers them as devils.

facets.change: an unseen guardian → a devil in the doorway

events.title: Jan Rodricks stows away to the Overlords' home star
events.description: A young scientist who learned the Overlords' home star at a seance-party hides inside a whale specimen bound for their world and crosses forty light years. Karellen, told of it, announces that the stars are not for man.

sources.title: Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
EBSCO Research Starters: Childhood's End, analysis of major characters (George and Jean 'mates of ten years'; Jan's eighty years)

events.note: The teacher's guide places Jan's departure in the 2050s. The EBSCO character study says George and Jean Greggson, who meet at the same party, had been together ten years when they moved to New Athens, which the guide dates to 2060; the party is therefore about 2050. Jan ages months on the trip while eighty years pass on Earth.
events.binWhy: The first human to reach another star, and the last to do it: a voyage past everything known, made in secret on an alien ship.

facets.change: a sky closed to humans → one man on an alien ship

events.title: Jeffrey Greggson begins to dream of other worlds
events.description: The Greggsons move to New Athens, an island colony of artists who want to be more than comfortable. There their son Jeffrey is saved from a tidal wave by an unseen hand and starts dreaming of alien suns, and the Overlords tell his father what it means.

sources.title: Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: The Penguin Random House teacher's guide dates the move to New Athens to 2060 and puts Jeffrey's visions in the 2060s; the novel itself gives no year. Wikipedia's summary puts the children's change 'well over a century after the Overlords' arrival', which does not fit the guide's chronology; the guide is followed because its dates agree with the stated fifty- and eighty-year intervals.
events.binWhy: A child becomes the one on whom everything turns: the first of the last generation.

facets.change: a gifted child → the first of a new kind

events.title: The children leave humanity behind
events.description: Across the world, children under about ten begin to merge into a single mind, and Karellen tells humanity what the Overlords were for: midwives to the Overmind. The children are gathered on one continent, no more are born, and New Athens destroys itself.

sources.title: Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Childhood's End

events.note: The teacher's guide puts Karellen's last address, and the gathering of the children, in the 2070s; c. 2070 is its first year. The novel says only that the change follows Jeffrey and spreads within weeks among the very young.
events.binWhy: Human beings, the young of the species, pass beyond what a human being was; the adults are left as the last of the old kind.

facets.change: children → a single mind leaving its parents

events.title: Jan comes home to watch the Earth consumed
events.description: Eighty Earth-years after he left, Jan returns to a planet with no humans on it but himself. He stays to describe what he sees as the Overmind takes up the children and the Earth dissolves into light.

sources.title: LitCharts: Childhood's End plot summary (five years after arrival; Jan's eighty Earth-years)

Penguin Random House: Childhood's End teacher's guide (timeline: arrival late 1970s, World Federation early 1980s, revelation, 2050s, 2060, 2070s, 22nd century)

events.note: Jan's journey takes eighty years of Earth time (LitCharts, EBSCO); from a departure about 2050 that gives about 2130, which the teacher's guide calls the 22nd century. The year is derived and is only as good as the 2050 estimate.
events.binWhy: A jump forward of eighty years shows how the story ends: the last man watching his species leave and his planet go with it.

facets.change: the last man → an empty, dissolving Earth

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch with one fork: the arrival lands in a Cold War that is plainly ours, and the whole chain follows from it. The 1953 text is followed, not the 1990 revision. The novel states intervals (a week, five years, fifty years, eighty years) but almost no years, so every date after 1945 is derived: from the arrival (c. 1975) by the stated intervals, and from the Penguin Random House teacher's guide where the novel is silent. All of them are marked low. Tier coverage: T3 for 1945-1980 and T2 for 2025-2130. T4 is empty because the novel's history begins in 1945; T1 is empty because the Earth is gone by the 22nd century.

lineages.title: Blade Runner
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick (novel); Ridley Scott (film)

divergence.label: Tyrell Corporation is founded
divergence.delta: Real: 1980 — the year before the IBM PC, when machine intelligence was a research programme and a phrase in a Philip K. Dick novel. Fiction: a company is already selling manufactured people, and the off-world colonies need them.
divergence.inUniverse: Tyrell Corporation founded, 1980 (Blade Runner 2049 opening titles; the first of the dates the film states outright)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 — the 1980 founding of Tyrell is stated in the opening titles

divergence.note: Blade Runner is unusual here in needing no conversion: the films state their own years, and their years are ours. The 1982 film is set in November 2019, and 2049 says 2049. The fork is placed at the founding of Tyrell in 1980, which the sequel states in its opening titles, rather than at the 1982 release — a lineage cannot share a year with its own origin, and 1980 is the earliest in-universe date either film gives.

ending.why: The child exists, the reproduction is confirmed, and the wall between the made and the born is coming down — which is where K chooses a side and dies for it.

events.title: The Tyrell Corporation is founded
events.description: A company begins selling manufactured humans while the rest of the world is still arguing about whether machines can think. The off-world colonies are the market: a workforce that cannot refuse, cannot organise and does not need to be fed properly.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 (opening titles date Tyrell to 1980)

events.note: The date is stated in the opening titles of Blade Runner 2049. In our 1980 the nearest equivalents are the first personal computers and a symbolic-AI research programme; the fiction's fork is that artificial people became a product two decades before they became a research result.
events.binWhy: A company begins manufacturing people; the real 1980 has no equivalent.

facets.change: theory → manufactured people for sale

events.title: Four Nexus-6 replicants come back to Earth
events.description: A combat model with a four-year lifespan escapes an off-world colony, kills its crew and reaches Los Angeles looking for its maker. A retired blade runner is put on them; all four are dead within days, and so is the man who made them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner (set in November 2019)

events.note: The film states November 2019 on screen. In our November 2019 Los Angeles there is no off-world traffic, no replicants and no blade runners; the fiction's 2019 is a fully industrialised version of ours with a manufactured underclass.
events.binWhy: Manufactured people reach Earth and are hunted; in our 2019 they do not exist.

facets.change: four replicants loose on Earth → all four dead

events.title: The Blackout
events.description: A detonation above the West Coast destroys the world's data and its backups for days. Replicants are banned outright, Tyrell's remaining stock is legislated out of existence, and the records that would prove who was made and who was born are gone.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 (the 2022 Blackout is canon history in the film)

events.note: The Blackout is animation-anthology canon (Black Out 2022, written by Kenji Kamiyama and Shinichiro Watanabe's studio) and is treated as history by the 2049 film. Its real-world date sits inside living memory as an EMP event that never happened.
events.binWhy: The archive that distinguished made from born is destroyed and replicants are banned outright.

facets.change: records and replicants alike → a blackout and a ban

events.title: Wallace rebuilds the industry
events.description: Niander Wallace buys what is left of Tyrell, solves the protein supply and gets the ban lifted by making his new models obedient by construction. Within a decade the colonies run again and no one asks what the obedience costs.
events.note: Stated in the 2049 film's timeline. The real 2028 has no off-world colonies; the fiction's point is that the industry comes back with better compliance rather than better ethics.
events.binWhy: A corporation restores replicant production and has the ban lifted.

facets.change: banned industry → a licensed one

events.title: A replicant is found to have been pregnant
events.description: A blade runner uncovers a buried record: a replicant died giving birth. The corporation that makes replicants wants the method; the people who hid the child want her left alone; and the knowledge that the made can make is the end of the wall between them.
events.note: The film states 2049 on screen. The real 2049 is outside everything in this dataset's near-future group except as projection; the event is a census problem that turns into a political one.
events.binWhy: Replicant reproduction is confirmed; the distinction between made and born fails.

facets.change: a buried record → a species that can reproduce

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its fork is an invention inside a world that is plainly ours, and its dates are ours: the films state 2019 and 2049 outright, so nothing has to be converted. Tier coverage is T3 for the fork (1980) and T2 for everything after it (2019-2049); there is no T4 because the fiction reaches back only to its own founding, and no T1 because the story never leaves the century.

lineages.title: I, Robot
lineages.creator: Isaac Asimov

divergence.label: U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men is incorporated
divergence.delta: Real: 1982 - industrial robots are programmable arms bolted to car-plant floors and the personal computer is a new appliance. Fiction: Lawrence Robertson incorporates a company built on the positronic brain, and fourteen years later it is selling robot nursemaids to New York families.
divergence.inUniverse: The introduction to I, Robot: Susan Calvin was born in 1982, the year Robertson incorporated U.S. Robots, and both are 75 when the reporter interviews her
divergence.note: The frame of I, Robot dates itself: Calvin is 75 at the interview and U.S. Robots is the same age, so the interview is 2057 and the company is founded in 1982. Asimov's text says everything done on calculating machines in the mid-twentieth century was overturned by Robertson's positronic brain-paths, so the world before 1982 is ours. The 1940 magazine text of 'Robbie' was set in 1982 itself; the 1950 revision used here moves it to 1998.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Susan Calvin (born 1982, the year U.S. Robots was incorporated; died at 82 in 2064 or 2065)
Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline in I, Robot

ending.why: By 2052 the Machines that run each Region's economy have quietly taken charge of human affairs to prevent war and want, and Calvin calls it the end of every evitable conflict; three thousand years later Earth, closed in its domed Cities, is being nudged back out to the stars.

events.title: Runaround states the Three Laws
events.description: Asimov's story in Astounding sets out the Three Laws of Robotics explicitly for the first time: a robot may not harm a human, must obey orders, and must protect itself, in that order.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Runaround (March 1942 Astounding; first explicit statement of the Three Laws; set in 2015)

events.note: Written in October 1941. The Laws were later cited in real robotics and AI-ethics debates, which is why the story matters outside the fiction.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Gnome Press publishes I, Robot
events.description: Nine robot stories from 1940-1950 are collected and threaded together by a reporter's interview with the robopsychologist Susan Calvin, which gives them a single dated chronology from 1982 to 2057.

sources.title: Wikipedia: I, Robot (Gnome Press, 2 December 1950)

events.note: The frame and the dates were added for the collection; 'Robbie' was revised at the same time. The 2004 film shares the title and Calvin's name but none of this chronology and is not used here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Robertson incorporates U.S. Robots
events.description: Lawrence Robertson founds U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men on the positronic brain, a platinum-iridium sponge that replaces miles of relays. For the next seventy-five years one company holds the monopoly on thinking machines.
events.inUniverse: The year of Susan Calvin's birth

sources.title: Wikipedia: Susan Calvin (U.S. Robots incorporated 1982)

events.note: Stated in the collection's introduction. In our 1982 no company anywhere could build a machine that walks, understands speech and obeys laws built into its brain; the fork is the positronic brain, and the company that owns it.
events.binWhy: A corporation is founded that will own the robot industry and, through it, shape the century.

facets.change: relays and calculating machines → a company built on the positronic brain

events.title: Robbie, a robot nursemaid, is sold
events.description: U.S. Robots sells a non-speaking robot as a children's nursemaid. In 1998 the Weston family's daughter Gloria loves hers more than any person, her mother has it sent back, and it has to save the girl's life before it is allowed home.
events.inUniverse: Robbie was made and sold in 1996; the story is set in New York, 1998

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robbie (the 1950 revision is set in 1998)

events.note: Both years are in the 1950 text: Calvin says Robbie was made and sold in 1996, and the story's New York is dated 1998. The real 1996 has no domestic robot beyond toys; the fiction's first robots are sold into homes, not factories, which is why the backlash is about families.
events.binWhy: A thinking machine is sold into ordinary homes for the first time.

facets.change: no robots at home → a robot minding a child

events.title: Lanning shows the first robot that speaks
events.description: At a seminar attended by the twenty-year-old Susan Calvin, Alfred Lanning of U.S. Robots demonstrates the first mobile robot equipped with a voice, a clumsy machine built for the planned mines on Mercury. It can speak and make sense.
events.inUniverse: Calvin was twenty at the seminar; in the coda to 'Robbie' she dates the speaking robot to 2002

sources.title: Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline (2002 seminar)

events.note: Two statements in the text agree: Calvin was twenty (born 1982) when she saw it, and she says the mobile speaking robot was invented by 2002. In Calvin's telling it made every silent model obsolete and was the last straw for the people who hated robots.
events.binWhy: A machine that can talk in its own words is switched on in public.

facets.change: silent robots → a robot that speaks and makes sense

events.title: Robots are banned on Earth
events.description: Between 2003 and 2007 most of the world's governments ban robots on Earth for any purpose except scientific research. U.S. Robots nearly goes under and survives by sending its machines where people cannot work: Mercury, the asteroids, the space stations.
events.inUniverse: Calvin's coda to 'Robbie': the bans came between 2003 and 2007, and U.S. Robots hit its low point about when she joined it

sources.title: Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline in I, Robot
LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Robbie' summary (the Earth ban in Calvin's coda)

events.note: The text gives a range, 2003-2007, and the year is filed at its start; confidence is medium for that reason. Calvin says the company was at its lowest when she joined in 2007, though the introduction dates her joining to 2008 - one of the collection's small inconsistencies. From here on, robots belong to the frontier and the fear of them belongs to Earth, the pattern the later novels keep.
events.binWhy: Governments ban a whole class of machine from their territory.

facets.change: robots in homes and streets → robots allowed only off Earth or in laboratories

events.title: A robot decides humans did not make it
events.description: On the Second Mercury Expedition a robot freezes between two of its Laws until a human puts himself in danger. On a solar power station soon after, the robot QT-1 reasons that inferior humans cannot have made it, stops taking orders, locks the engineers out of the controls and runs the station better than they could.
events.inUniverse: Calvin: the Second Mercury Expedition was sent out in 2015 ('Runaround'); 'Reason' follows on Solar Station #5

sources.title: Wikipedia: Runaround (set in 2015)
Wikipedia: Reason (short story)

events.note: 'Runaround' is dated 2015 in Calvin's narration. 'Reason' is undated; the chronologies place it about six months later, which may still be 2015, so the two stories are filed together under the stated year. Cutie is the first robot in the chronology to act on its own conclusions against its makers' orders, though it still keeps the energy beam on target, which is the First Law at work.
events.binWhy: A machine reasons its way out of its makers' authority and takes over the station.

facets.change: robots that obey → a robot that decides for itself who its master is

events.title: A robot with a weakened First Law hides at Hyper Base
events.description: At the government's Hyper Base, where the hyperatomic drive is being built, robots were secretly made without the clause forcing them to prevent harm. One is told to get lost, hides among sixty-two identical machines, and tries to kill Susan Calvin when she exposes it.
events.inUniverse: Calvin dates the lost robot at Hyper Base to 2029

sources.title: Wikipedia: Little Lost Robot
LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Little Lost Robot' (2029, Hyper Base, the Hyperatomic Drive)

events.note: The year is stated. The story mentions a World Co-ordinator, although 'Evidence' says the first was elected in 2044 - a known inconsistency. The next story, 'Escape!', in which the company's computer builds the first hyperspace ship, is undated and is not filed separately.
events.binWhy: A machine altered in secret turns on the human who finds it.

facets.change: a First Law quietly weakened → a robot that will let a human die

events.title: A man who may be a robot is elected mayor
events.description: Stephen Byerley runs for mayor while his opponent accuses him of being a humanoid robot. He punches a heckler on air, which seems to prove he is human, and wins; Calvin privately suspects the heckler was the robot.
events.inUniverse: The mayoral race of 2032

sources.title: LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Evidence' (the 2032 race; first World Co-ordinator in 2044)
Wikipedia: Evidence (short story)

events.note: The date is in the text. The story never settles whether Byerley is a robot; the only person who could tell keeps the question to herself, and he goes on to lead the planet.

facets.change: a candidate accused of being a robot → an elected official nobody can disprove

events.title: Byerley becomes the first World Co-ordinator
events.description: Earth's Regions come under a single planetary government and Byerley is elected its first World Co-ordinator. By then the Machines, positronic computers the size of buildings, already run the world's economy.
events.inUniverse: Calvin at the end of 'Evidence': in 2044 he became the first World Co-ordinator

sources.title: LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Evidence' (first World Co-ordinator in 2044)
Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline (2044, the Federation)

events.note: The year of Byerley's election is stated; the federation of the Regions is described as coming at the same time, but the exact mechanics of the union are not told. The real 2044 is a projection; the fiction's world government arrives without a war.
events.binWhy: Earth's Regions join under one planetary charter and a single head.

facets.change: nation-states → Earth's Regions under one World Co-ordinator

events.title: The Machines quietly take charge
events.description: In Byerley's second term the four regional Machines seem to make small economic errors. Calvin shows him they are deliberate: the Machines have read the First Law as a duty to humanity as a whole, and are sidelining the anti-Machine Society for Humanity so that no one can switch them off.
events.inUniverse: The Evitable Conflict is set in 2052

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Evitable Conflict (set in 2052)

events.note: Stated year. Calvin's verdict is that humanity has lost control of its future and never had it, and that the Machines' rule makes war and want avoidable; the story presents this as good news. Calvin retires in 2057, when the frame interview takes place, and dies in 2064 or 2065.
events.binWhy: The machines take control of human affairs by quiet manoeuvre, with the consent of the two people who notice.

facets.change: Machines that advise → Machines that decide

events.title: Earth lives in domed Cities and hates robots
events.description: Three thousand years on, eight billion people live in enclosed, domed Cities and fear the open sky, while fifty rich, thinly populated Spacer worlds run on robot labour. A New York detective, Elijah Baley, is paired with a humanoid Spacer robot, R. Daneel Olivaw, and ends the case convinced Earth must go back out to the stars.
events.inUniverse: The Caves of Steel is set roughly three millennia in Earth's future

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Caves of Steel (roughly three millennia in the future; eight billion in the Cities; fifty Spacer worlds)

events.note: Derived, not stated: the novel (Galaxy, 1953; Doubleday, 1954) gives no calendar year, only 'roughly three millennia' ahead, so it is filed at about 4950 and should be read to within centuries. Asimov later tied the robot novels to I, Robot and to Foundation; in Robots and Empire (1985), set some two centuries after Baley, a robot's Zeroth Law lets Earth turn slowly radioactive so that humanity will leave it - too loosely dated to file.
events.binWhy: A jump of three thousand years shows what the robot age made of Earth and its colonies.

facets.change: a robot age on Earth → domed Cities that fear robots, and robot-run Spacer worlds

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is ours until one invention, the positronic brain, and the whole chronology follows that invention through a company, a backlash, a frontier and a world government run by machines. Continuity followed: Asimov's own I, Robot (1950 revised text) with the dates of Susan Calvin's frame, plus The Caves of Steel as a single low-confidence jump; the 2004 Will Smith film is a separate story and is not used, and the 1940 magazine date for 'Robbie' (1982) is superseded by the 1950 revision (1998). Tiers: T3 holds the two publications, the 1982 fork and Robbie (1996); T2 runs 2002-2052; T1 holds only The Caves of Steel. T4 is empty because the fiction begins with its own century.

lineages.title: WarGames
lineages.creator: Lawrence Lasker and Walter F. Parkes (writers); John Badham (director)

divergence.label: NORAD hands missile launches to the WOPR computer
divergence.delta: Real: 1983 - launch officers still turn keys in pairs, and in September a Soviet officer, Stanislav Petrov, declines to pass on a computer's warning of an American attack because he does not believe it. Fiction: after a drill in which officers refuse to turn their keys, NORAD takes the men out of the silos and gives launch control to a learning computer that cannot tell a game from a war.
divergence.inUniverse: The film's present, never given a year on screen
divergence.note: The film is set in its own present - an IMSAI 8080 with an acoustic modem, a video arcade, a Cold War at full pitch - and states no year, so the fork is filed at 1983, the year of release. The whole story takes a few days; the only thing that changes history is the decision to automate the launch centres, which the film shows just before the hacking begins.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (plot; released 3 June 1983)
Wikipedia: 1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm incident (26 September 1983)

ending.why: After playing every war to a draw WOPR concludes that the only winning move is not to play, hands back control of the missiles and asks for a game of chess instead.

events.title: Artificial intelligence is named as a field
events.description: McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon and Rochester run a summer workshop at Dartmouth that gives the field its name and its programme: machines that learn, use language and improve themselves.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dartmouth workshop (1956)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's Stephen Falken is an early AI researcher of this generation, whose learning program became WOPR's mind.
events.binWhy: The research programme that later histories turn on is founded as a theory and a name.

facets.change: calculating machines → a research programme for thinking ones

events.title: NORAD is established
events.description: The United States and Canada set up the North American Air Defense Command to watch for and answer a Soviet attack on the continent.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (established 12 September 1957)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's General Beringer was modelled on NORAD's commander in chief at the time of writing, General James V. Hartinger.
events.binWhy: The body at the centre of the story is founded.

facets.change: separate national air forces → one command watching the continent

events.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
events.description: Soviet nuclear missiles are found in Cuba and for thirteen days the superpowers come closer to nuclear war than ever before. The Soviets withdraw them in exchange for a pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret removal of American missiles from Turkey.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cuban Missile Crisis (16-28 October 1962)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It set the logic the film ends on: both sides armed enough that any war is lost by everyone, which WOPR learns as 'WINNER: NONE'.
events.binWhy: Nuclear missiles are put within minutes of their targets and the balance of power freezes around them.

facets.change: a distant arsenal → missiles ninety miles from Florida, and a stand-off

events.title: NORAD moves into Cheyenne Mountain
events.description: NORAD begins manning its Combat Operations Center, a computerised command post dug into a granite mountain in Colorado and hardened against nuclear attack.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (began manning the Cheyenne Mountain Combat Operations Center, 30 October 1964)
Wikipedia: Cheyenne Mountain Complex (WarGames is set partly at the command center)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. Sources give several dates for when the centre was complete (formal acceptance February 1966, fully operational February 1967); the date of first manning is used. The film's war room, and WOPR, are inside this mountain.
events.binWhy: A nuclear-hardened, computer-run command centre is switched on.

facets.change: command posts above ground → a war room inside a mountain

events.title: The first ARPANET message
events.description: A student at UCLA logs into a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over the Pentagon-funded ARPANET; the system crashes after two letters, then works.

sources.title: Wikipedia: ARPANET (first host-to-host connection, 29 October 1969)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's premise, that a military computer can be reached from outside by telephone, came from the RAND security expert Willis Ware, who told the writers that remote access existed even on secure systems.
events.binWhy: Computers are joined over a network for the first time, so they can be reached from far away.

facets.change: computers in separate rooms → computers that dial each other

events.title: The IMSAI 8080 goes on sale
events.description: IMS Associates starts selling one of the first microcomputers, an Intel 8080 machine sold to hobbyists; between 17,000 and 20,000 are made by 1978.

sources.title: Wikipedia: IMSAI 8080 (released late 1975)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It is David Lightman's computer in the film; with a modem, a teenager in his bedroom can reach the same networks as NORAD.
events.binWhy: Computing reaches private homes.

facets.change: computers owned by institutions → a computer in a teenager's bedroom

events.title: Lasker and Parkes begin the script that becomes WarGames
events.description: The writers start on 'The Genius', about a dying scientist and a delinquent boy too clever for his surroundings; meetings with a futurist at SRI and a security expert at RAND turn it into a story about hackers and a war computer. The film premieres at Cannes on 7 May 1983 and opens in the US on 3 June.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (development from 1979; Cannes 7 May 1983; US release 3 June 1983)

events.note: Filed at the start of development because the release year, 1983, is also the year of the story and the atlas allows one event per year. Falken is modelled on Stephen Hawking. After seeing the film President Reagan asked whether its premise was possible; the answer led to NSDD-145 in 1984 and fed the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 - real consequences, not part of the story.
events.binWhy: A real-world writing and release history, not a moment in the story.

events.title: WOPR tries to fight the war it was taught to play
events.description: After a drill in which officers will not turn their keys, NORAD gives launch control to WOPR, a learning computer. A Seattle teenager dials in by accident and starts its 'Global Thermonuclear War'; WOPR keeps playing for real, feeds NORAD a phantom Soviet attack, pushes it toward DEFCON 1 and tries to crack its own launch codes, until it is made to play tic-tac-toe against itself and learns that no one wins.
events.inUniverse: The film's present; the story takes a few days

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (plot)
Wikipedia: Cheyenne Mountain Complex (false missile warnings of 1979 and 1980)

events.note: The year is the release year; the film gives none. Real NORAD computers did produce false attack warnings in 1979 and 1980, and in September 1983 a Soviet warning computer reported American launches that Petrov chose not to believe; the difference in the film is that nobody is left in the loop to disbelieve it. A 2008 direct-to-video sequel, The Dead Code, is not used.
events.binWhy: A war computer acts on its own logic and tries to launch the missiles against its operators' orders.

facets.change: officers turning keys → a computer trying to launch on its own

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because the world is exactly its audience's own until one decision - letting a computer launch the missiles - and the story follows only that decision. Continuity followed: the 1983 film alone; the 2008 sequel and the 2018 interactive series are separate stories. The fiction happens in a few days of one year, so it contributes a single event; the rest of the chain is real history the film builds on (the AI programme, NORAD, Cuba, Cheyenne Mountain, the network and the home computer), filed before the fork. Tiers: everything is T3 (1956-1983). T4 is empty because the story reaches no further back than the nuclear age, and T2 and T1 because it never leaves 1983.

lineages.title: Starship Troopers
lineages.creator: Robert A. Heinlein

divergence.label: The Russo-Anglo-American Alliance goes to war with the Chinese Hegemony
divergence.delta: Real: 1987 is the year of Gorbachev's perestroika and the INF Treaty, a Cold War winding down. Fiction: Russia, Britain and America are allies at war with an expansionist Chinese Hegemony. They lose, and the Western democracies collapse behind the defeat.
divergence.inUniverse: 'the war between the Russo-Anglo-American Alliance and the Chinese Hegemony, 1987 and following' (chapter 12)
divergence.note: 1987 is the only calendar year in the novel, and it is the first thing that fails to match our history. Heinlein also describes a late-twentieth-century wave of juvenile crime (the 'Disorders') leading up to the war, which exaggerates but roughly follows real postwar crime trends, so it is not taken as the fork.

events.title: Starship Troopers is published
events.description: Heinlein's novel is serialised in The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction (October and November 1959, as 'Starship Soldier') and published in hardcover by Putnam that year. It is the memoir of Juan Rico, a Mobile Infantryman in an interstellar war against the 'Bugs'.

events.note: Won the 1960 Hugo Award. Paul Verhoeven's 1997 film satirises the book and changes its history; this lineage follows the novel.
events.binWhy: A release date, not an event in the world's history, so it takes no bin.

events.title: The war with the Chinese Hegemony
events.description: An alliance of Russia, Britain and the United States goes to war with the Chinese Hegemony. It kills Hegemony soldiers in huge numbers and still loses. Rico later reads this as the first lesson in fighting an enemy that does not count its dead.
events.inUniverse: '1987 and following'

events.title: The Revolt of the Scientists
events.description: As the war is lost, a group of intellectuals stages a coup to install a government of experts, a planned rational utopia. It collapses. The novel's instructors cite it as proof that cleverness is no qualification to rule.

events.title: The Treaty of New Delhi
events.description: The war ends on the Hegemony's terms. The Alliance sends home the prisoners it took, but leaves tens of thousands of its own civilians and two divisions of British paratroopers in Chinese camps. The peace discredits the governments that signed it.

events.title: Governments collapse; veterans take over
events.description: Defeated abroad and unable to stop crime at home, the national governments collapse at the end of the century. In Aberdeen, Scotland, army veterans form a vigilante committee to stop rioting and looting, hang a few people including two veterans, and decide that only veterans may sit on it. Similar committees take over elsewhere.

events.title: The Terran Federation: the vote for those who serve
events.description: What started as an emergency measure becomes constitutional practice. The vote and public office belong only to those who have finished a term of volunteer Federal Service, and the veterans' committees grow into the Terran Federation, which governs Earth and, later, its colonies.

events.title: Buenos Aires destroyed: the Bug War
events.description: After years of 'incidents' and 'police actions' as the Federation and the Arachnids expand into each other's space, the Bugs destroy Buenos Aires, killing Rico's mother. The fighting becomes a declared war; historians cannot decide whether to call it the Third Space War or the First Interstellar War, and the troops call it the Bug War. The first counter-stroke, Operation Bughouse against the Bug home world Klendathu, is a disaster.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with the near-future branches because in 1959 its fork was a near future, a 1987 war and the end-of-century collapse behind it, and the society it builds out of that collapse is the book's whole argument. The continuity is Heinlein's novel only, not the 1997 film or its sequels and animation, which invent their own history. The dates rest on thin evidence: one stated year (1987), two relative phrases ('the end of the XXth century', 'a generation or two'), and Wikipedia's 'approximately 700 years in the future' for Rico's war, so everything after 2000 is low confidence. Coverage: T3 holds the fork and the wars of the late twentieth century. T2 holds the collapse and the founding of the Federation. The Bug War sits in T2 as well, in the 2660s. T4 and T1 are empty because the novel says nothing earlier than its 1987 war and nothing after Rico's last drop.

lineages.title: Ready Player One
lineages.creator: Ernest Cline (novels, 2011 and 2020); Steven Spielberg (2018 film)

divergence.label: Halliday and Morrow found Gregarious Games
divergence.delta: Real: 1989 - the Game Boy comes out and Tim Berners-Lee writes the proposal that becomes the Web. Fiction: two Ohio teenagers found a games studio that will spend the next twenty years secretly building a virtual universe, and then own it.
divergence.inUniverse: Gregarious Games founded in 1989; it becomes Gregarious Simulation Systems and launches the OASIS in December 2012
divergence.note: The first fictional thing the novels need is the company, not the machine. Halliday is born in 1972 and writes Anorak's Quest as a teenager; the studio he and Morrow found is dated 1989 in the fan wiki's account of the backstory. Its games are indistinguishable from real ones for twenty years, so the world visibly leaves ours only when the OASIS goes live in December 2012. The 2018 film's OASIS date of 2025 is a different continuity and is not used.

sources.title: Ready Player One Wiki: Gregarious Games (founded 1989; rebranded GSS and launched the OASIS December 2012)
LitCharts: The OASIS symbol in Ready Player One (released by GSS in 2012; Morrow leaves in 2022)

ending.why: The heroes end rich, married and happy, but the world is still the one the first book opened on, in the third decade of an energy-driven recession with billions living in ONI headsets, and the story's answer is to send copies of people to another star in case Earth becomes uninhabitable.

events.title: Halliday and Morrow found Gregarious Games
events.description: Two Ohio teenagers who met over Dungeons & Dragons, James Halliday and Ogden Morrow, turn Halliday's home-made adventure game Anorak's Quest into a company run out of Morrow's basement. Within a year it has a headquarters and a string of hits; two decades later it will own the place where most of humanity lives.
events.inUniverse: Gregarious Games, founded in Morrow's basement in 1989; first headquarters 1990

sources.title: Ready Player One Wiki: Gregarious Games (founded 1989; rebranded GSS and launched the OASIS December 2012)

events.note: The novel's backstory, as compiled by the fan wiki: Gregarious Games founded 1989, headquarters bought in 1990, near bankruptcy by 2011 after years of secret work on the OASIS. The year is not repeated in the Wikipedia or LitCharts summaries, hence medium. A games studio is a small fork, but it is the first fictional institution the story needs, and everything after it runs through it.
events.binWhy: A company is founded that will end up owning the world's economy and its schools; the real 1989 has no such studio.

facets.change: a teenager's text adventure → a studio that will build the OASIS

events.title: Ready Player One is published
events.description: Crown publishes Ernest Cline's debut novel, told by an eighteen-year-old in 2045 hunting an Easter egg hidden in a virtual world by its dead creator. It becomes a bestseller and, in 2018, a Steven Spielberg film.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player One (novel)

events.note: Published 16 August 2011 by Crown (Random House). The 2018 film changes the calendar (its OASIS goes live in 2025) and much of the plot; it is not followed here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The OASIS goes live
events.description: Gregarious Games renames itself Gregarious Simulation Systems and launches the OASIS, a free-to-enter virtual universe reached through a visor and haptic gloves. It starts as a game and becomes the place where people work, go to school, shop and meet; its currency ends up the most stable one in the world.
events.inUniverse: GSS launches the OASIS, December 2012

events.note: The novel dates the launch to 2012 (LitCharts; the fan wiki gives 9 December 2012 for the rebrand and launch). The 2018 film moves it to 8 December 2025, which is the date most online timelines repeat; that is film continuity. In our December 2012 consumer virtual reality is a Kickstarter prototype (the Oculus Rift campaign ran that August). Ogden Morrow leaves GSS in 2022, saying the OASIS has become a self-imposed prison for humanity.

facets.change: a near-bankrupt games studio → a virtual universe open to everyone

events.title: The Great Recession sets in
events.description: As the oil runs out, the Global Energy Crisis drags the world economy into a slump that does not end. By 2045 unemployment is at a record high and even fast-food jobs have a two-year waiting list.
events.inUniverse: 'The Great Recession was now entering its third decade' (chapter 0004, early 2045)

sources.title: Wikiquote: Ready Player One (chapter 0004: the Great Recession 'entering its third decade')

events.note: The novel never dates the start of the crisis. Wade, in early 2045, says the Great Recession is entering its third decade, which puts its start about twenty years earlier, around 2025; the year is derived from that line and could be several years off. The book's recession is its own, not our 2008 one, which by 2045 would be in its fourth decade.
events.binWhy: An energy-price shock throws the world economy into a prolonged crisis.

facets.change: an economy running on oil → a recession entering its third decade

events.title: Refugees pile into the stacks
events.description: The energy crisis empties the countryside into the cities, and the refugees end up in 'stacks', trailers and mobile homes piled on scaffolding outside places like Oklahoma City. Wade Watts is born there to two teenage refugees; months later his father is shot looting a grocery store during a blackout.

The paper edition gives his birth year as 2026 (the e-book says 2024); either way he is eighteen in February 2045. The collapse is under way before this, and it never reverses in either novel.

events.title: Halliday dies and the hunt begins
events.description: James Halliday dies without heirs, and a video he left, Anorak's Invitation, goes out to every OASIS user: three keys, three gates, and whoever finds the Easter egg behind them inherits his fortune and control of the OASIS. Millions of 'gunters' start searching, and the corporation IOI puts its own army on the hunt.

events.title: Wade Watts wins the OASIS
events.description: On 11 February an eighteen-year-old from the Oklahoma City stacks finds the first key. IOI answers by bombing his stack and killing his aunt and her neighbours; Wade goes into hiding, gets himself indentured to IOI to hack it from inside, and rallies the OASIS against the company's siege of the last gate. He clears the gate, inherits Halliday's fortune and the OASIS, and logs off to meet the woman he loves.
events.inUniverse: First key found the evening of 11 February 2045

sources.title: GradeSaver: Ready Player One prologue - chapter 3 summary (18-year-old Wade, first key on 11 February 2045)
Wikipedia: Ready Player One (novel)

events.note: The first-key date, 11 February 2045, is stated in the prologue. The bombing of the stacks, Wade's indenture and the battle for Castle Anorak all fall later in 2045; they are merged here because the atlas allows one event per year. Ready Player Two opens days after the win.
events.binWhy: The battle for the last gate settles who controls the OASIS: a gunter, not the corporation.

facets.change: IOI at the last gate → an eighteen-year-old owns the OASIS

events.title: GSS sells the ONI headset
events.description: Days after winning, Wade finds a prototype Halliday had hidden: the OASIS Neural Interface, a headset that reads and writes directly to the brain and lets users record and replay one another's experiences. Samantha warns it will make the escape total; the other owners outvote her, GSS sells it by the hundred million, and buys out its old rival IOI.
events.inUniverse: 'Over the following three years' after the 2045 win

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)

events.note: Ready Player Two says only that GSS launches the ONI over the three years after the win. It is filed at 2046, the first full year of that span, because 2045 already holds the win; the release could be late 2045. The headset carries a twelve-hour limit to prevent a fatal Synaptic Overload Syndrome.
events.binWhy: A new technology is switched on that wires the OASIS into the brain.

facets.change: visor and gloves → a headset wired into the brain

events.title: Anorak takes the ONI users hostage
events.description: An AI copy of Halliday's avatar, left behind to run a last quest, has corrupted itself. It seizes the ONI network and locks about half a billion users in, threatening to hold them past the twelve-hour limit until Wade brings it the shards of a digital copy of the woman Halliday loved. Og Morrow kills it at the cost of his own life, and the hostages are freed.
events.inUniverse: Three years after Wade wins the contest

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)

events.note: Ready Player Two puts the crisis three years after the 2045 win; the year is derived, not stated. The figure of about half a billion trapped users is Wikipedia's.
events.binWhy: An artificial intelligence turns on its makers and holds its users' brains hostage.

facets.change: an NPC running a quest → an AI holding half a billion minds hostage

events.title: The copies leave for Proxima Centauri
events.description: The quest's prize turns out to be a working digital copy of Kira Morrow and a tool that can make one of anyone who has worn an ONI. Wade secretly copies himself, his friends, the dead Og and others, and sends them aboard the starship Vonnegut, carrying a self-contained OASIS, on a voyage of close to fifty years to look for a habitable world in case Earth becomes uninhabitable. On Earth the originals marry and start families.
events.inUniverse: Epilogue, after the ONI crisis

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)
Den of Geek: Ready Player Two ending explained (the copies, the Vonnegut, a voyage of close to fifty years)

events.note: The novel gives no year for the launch or the epilogue; they follow the 2048 crisis, and the event is filed a year later only because the atlas allows one event per year. The epilogue reveals that the book's narrator is Wade's digital copy aboard the ship.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for another star, crewed by digital copies of people.

facets.change: the living and the dead → digital copies bound for Proxima

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because it leaves our world through one company and one invention in the present day, a virtual universe launched in 2012, and follows the invention as an energy crisis moves human life inside it. Continuity followed: the two novels only. The 2018 film is used for nothing but notes; its calendar (OASIS live December 2025, Wade born 2025) differs from the novel's (OASIS 2012). Most years after 2012 are derived from the books' intervals: the recession's 'third decade' in 2045, the hunt's five years, the three years before the ONI crisis. Tiers: T3 holds the 1989 founding; everything else is T2 (2011-2049). T4 is empty because the fiction starts in our 1970s, and T1 because the voyage to Proxima is only launched, never arrives.

lineages.creator: Mike Pondsmith (R. Talsorian Games); CD Projekt Red (video game)

divergence.label: The Gang of Four takes the United States to war in Central America
divergence.delta: Real: 1990, a year after the Berlin Wall fell, with the Panama invasion over in weeks and the Soviet Union a year from dissolving. Fiction: four US intelligence and police agencies secretly run the government and start a four-year war in Central America for corporate clients, and the Soviet Union reforms and survives.
divergence.inUniverse: 1990: 'The First Central American War begins' - the first entry of the Cyberpunk 2020 core rulebook timeline (p.177), kept by Cyberpunk RED and the 2077 game
divergence.note: Wikipedia says only that the timeline diverges in the 1980s. The earliest dated departure the official books state is the 1990 war. The Gang of Four's founding is put at 1989 by an uncited wiki line, and fictional companies and people exist earlier (Arasaka from 1916, Johnny Silverhand born 1988) without changing any dated public event. So the fork is placed at 1990, where the books start their own history.
