ending.why: In every ending of the base game V is dying or gone within months, Arasaka survives in some form and Night City is run as before; only Phantom Liberty's Tower ending saves V, and it costs V everything that made them an edgerunner.

events.title: Cyberpunk is published
events.description: R. Talsorian Games publishes Mike Pondsmith's tabletop role-playing game Cyberpunk, later called Cyberpunk 2013. Its 1990 second edition, Cyberpunk 2020, fixed the timeline that the 2077 video game still follows.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cyberpunk (role-playing game)

events.note: Release of the first edition. The setting's own history starts two years later, when Cyberpunk 2020 rewrote the timeline and folded in real events such as German reunification.
events.binWhy: A publication, not a moment in the story; it marks when the world first appeared.

events.title: The United States goes to war with the Central American cartels
events.description: A secret cabal of the NSA, CIA, FBI and DEA, the Gang of Four, is already running the federal government behind the President. In 1990 it takes the country into open war in Central America under the cover of fighting drug cartels; the war lasts until 1994 and US forces are driven out.
events.inUniverse: First Central American War begins, 1990-1994 (Cyberpunk 2020 timeline)

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: First Central American War
Cyberpunk Wiki: Gang of Four

events.note: Dated to 1990 in the Cyberpunk 2020 core timeline (p.177). The real 1989-90 Panama invasion is close in shape, but in our history it ended in weeks; here it becomes a four-year war fought for food and raw materials on behalf of corporate clients. The Gang of Four's formation is put at 1989 only by an uncited wiki line.
events.binWhy: A major war starts: the US invades Central America, which our 1990 never saw.

facets.change: covert cabal → open war in Central America

events.title: The Crash of '94
events.description: The European Economic Community finds that the Gang of Four has been propping up the illusion of American wealth by hacking the stock markets of Europe and Asia, and leaks it to the press. The world stock market collapses overnight and most developed countries embargo US trade.
events.inUniverse: World Stock Market Collapse, 1994

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: Crash of '94

events.note: Stated in the Cyberpunk 2020 timeline. The real 1994 had a bond-market rout and the Mexican peso crisis, nothing like a global crash triggered by American state fraud.
events.binWhy: A financial shock throws the world economy into a prolonged crisis.

facets.change: an illusion of solvency → global crash and embargo

events.title: President Allen is assassinated and the Collapse begins
events.description: With one American in four homeless and riots across the country, President James Richard Allen is shot at a campaign stop in California. Vice President Harold Hunt, a Gang of Four ally, takes over, and the army comes home to impose martial law and shoot-on-sight curfews.
events.inUniverse: The Collapse of the United States (1996-2008); Allen assassinated 17 August 1996

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: The Collapse of the United States

events.note: The date, Saturday 17 August 1996, is given in Cyberpunk RED (p.246) and the Cyberpunk 2020 sourcebook Home of the Brave. Allen is a fictional president: in our 1996 Bill Clinton was running for re-election.
events.binWhy: The president is killed and his office passes to the conspiracy.

facets.change: an elected president → a cabal's president under martial law

events.title: The Mideast Meltdown
events.description: A limited nuclear exchange leaves most of the Middle East uninhabitable. Fallout spreads around the world and the global oil supply is cut roughly in half.
events.inUniverse: Mideast Meltdown, 1997

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline

events.note: Stated in the Cyberpunk 2020 timeline. The combatants are not named in the core books. No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945 in our history.
events.binWhy: A nuclear war kills on a regional scale and changes the world's energy supply.

facets.change: a region of oil states → a radioactive waste

events.title: California declares itself a Free State
events.description: States have been refusing federal taxes and blockading their borders against Washington's paramilitaries. California declares itself a Free State, independent of the federal government, and others follow; by the 2010s it has itself split into North and South California.
events.inUniverse: California becomes a Free State, 2002

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: Free State

events.note: The 2002 date is from the Night City sourcebook for Cyberpunk RED. Older Cyberpunk 2020 material places the Free States movement in the late 1990s, so the break-up is a process and this is its best-dated step.
events.binWhy: The United States comes apart into self-governing states without a conqueror.

facets.change: one union → a patchwork of Free States

events.title: The First Corporate War
events.description: A takeover fight between Euro Business Machines and Orbital Air over Transworld Airlines turns into open combat between their private armies. It ends in 2005 when Orbital Air troops storm the EBM chief executive's compound and force a surrender, and the other corporations take note that war works.
events.inUniverse: First Corporate War, 2004-2005

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline

events.note: Stated in the Cyberpunk 2020 timeline and the Firestorm sourcebook. It is the first of four corporate wars before 2025.
events.binWhy: Corporations start fighting each other with their own armies.

facets.change: boardroom rivalry → private war

events.title: Johnny Silverhand's raid on Arasaka Tower
events.description: Arasaka kidnaps the netrunner Alt Cunningham to force her to finish Soulkiller, a program that copies a mind into data. Her ex-partner, the rockerboy Johnny Silverhand, starts a riot and storms Arasaka's Night City tower to get her back; Alt dies, and her digital ghost is left loose in the Net.
events.inUniverse: Alt kidnapped 12 April 2013; Silverhand's riot 13 April 2013

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline

events.note: Kidnapping dated 12 April and raid 13 April 2013 in Cyberpunk 2020. Johnny is a fictional musician born in 1988, which is why the game can give him a history in our calendar.
events.binWhy: A targeted assault on a corporate headquarters, short of war, that shapes the next decade.

facets.change: a kidnapped programmer → a mind loose in the Net

events.title: Cyberpunk 2077 is released
events.description: CD Projekt Red releases Cyberpunk 2077, set in Night City in 2077, with Mike Pondsmith involved in the setting. The anime Cyberpunk: Edgerunners (2022) and the expansion Phantom Liberty (2023) follow in the same continuity.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cyberpunk 2077

events.note: Release of the game this lineage is named for. In the fiction 2020 is the year of the Carbon Plague in Night City, not an event this chain uses.
events.binWhy: A publication, not a moment in the story; it marks when the 2077 continuity appeared.

events.title: The Fourth Corporate War begins
events.description: EuroBank pushes the ocean-farming company IHAG toward bankruptcy, and two rivals fight over its assets. One hires Militech and the other Arasaka, and the fight between the two biggest arms makers in the world outgrows the dispute that started it; EuroBank's ceasefire of February 2022 does not stop them.
events.inUniverse: Fourth Corporate War, 2021/2022-2025

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline

events.note: The Cyberpunk RED World Book has the war starting in 2021 and becoming official in 2022; the IHAG takeover fight is dated 2021 in the Firestorm sourcebook. It is placed here in 2021 to leave 2022 for the DataKrash.
events.binWhy: A major war starts, between corporations with national-scale armies.

facets.change: a takeover fight → a world war between arms makers

events.title: The DataKrash
events.description: The hacker Rache Bartmoss is killed in a corporate raid, and a virus he planted years earlier goes off on his death. It infects 78.2% of the Net within months, corrupts data around the world and unshackles military AIs, which turn into hostile rogue programs; the old global Net is never rebuilt.
events.inUniverse: DataKrash, 3 June 2022 (R.A.B.I.D.S. virus)

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: DataKrash

events.note: The date, 3 June 2022, is from Cyberpunk RED (pp.239, 254-5) and the in-game shard The Undoing. In our 2022 the internet kept running; the fictional equivalent would be a single cyberweapon taking the whole network down for good.
events.binWhy: The global network society depends on breaks down and does not come back.

facets.change: one global Net → a ruin held by rogue AIs

events.title: A nuclear bomb goes off in Arasaka Tower
events.description: A Militech team led by Morgan Blackhand and Johnny Silverhand breaks into Arasaka's Night City tower, and a small nuclear device detonates on an upper floor. Over half a million people die in the blast and a quarter of a million more afterwards. Johnny is caught and his mind is copied into Arasaka's archive, and the smoke of the war turns the sky red for two years.
events.inUniverse: Night City Holocaust (AHQ Disaster), 20 August 2023; the Time of the Red begins

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Cyberpunk Wiki: Night City Holocaust
Cyberpunk Wiki: Time of the Red

events.note: The date, 20 August 2023, is given in Cyberpunk RED and the 2077 game database. The 2077 game says Johnny died this day, which moved his death from the Cyberpunk 2020 version of events. The red skies mark the start of the Time of the Red, which lasts into the 2040s.
events.binWhy: A nuclear bomb in a city kills hundreds of thousands and ends a war.

facets.change: a corporate capital → a nuclear crater

events.title: NetWatch begins building the Blackwall
events.description: Unable to take the Net back from the rogue AIs, NetWatch starts building a barrier to wall them off and seal the old access points. It is sold as a firewall; in fact it is an AI of its own, reportedly built with the help of the rogue AIs themselves, and netrunners caught on the wrong side are left to die.
events.inUniverse: Blackwall project begins, 2044

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Blackwall

events.note: Cyberpunk RED (p.264) says NetWatch secretly began the project in 2044. Other wiki text says it was finished a few years after the 2022 Krash, so the year given is the start of development, not the switch-on. NetWatch had already declared the Net inoperable in 2025.
events.binWhy: A new barrier technology is built that decides who can use the Net at all.

facets.change: an open ruin → a policed, walled Net

events.title: The New United States is constituted
events.description: The rump of the United States ratifies a new constitution as the New United States of America. Elizabeth Kress, president since 2019, steps down after three decades and David Whindam is elected as the first president under it; the western Free States stay outside.
events.inUniverse: NUSA constitution ratified, 2053

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline

events.note: Dated in the Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Mission Kit. The fiction's United States has had no normal transfer of power since the 1990s; this is the setting's closest thing to a refounding.
events.binWhy: A state is refounded under a new charter.

facets.change: a wartime presidency → a new constitution

events.title: The Treaty of Unification
events.description: In January 2069 President Rosalind Myers, formerly Militech's chief executive, sends the army to bring the Free States back by force. By June 2070 the federal army has occupied most of them, but when an Arasaka supercarrier appears off Night City both sides settle: the Free States stay autonomous, Night City becomes an independent city-state, and Arasaka is allowed back into America.
events.inUniverse: Unification War, January 2069 - June 2070; Treaty of Unification (Arvin Accord)

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Unification War

events.note: War January 2069 to June 2070, treaty signed at Arvin in South California, per the 2077 game database and the Cyberpunk 2077 World Book. Texas did not sign.
events.binWhy: Enemies sign a treaty that ends a war.

facets.change: a war of reunification → an armed standoff

events.title: The Relic heist and the death of Saburo Arasaka
events.description: The mercenary V breaks into Arasaka's Night City hotel suite to steal the Relic, a chip that stores a copy of a mind. V sees Yorinobu Arasaka kill his father Saburo, head of the company since 1960, and is shot, then brought back by the chip, which holds Johnny Silverhand and is slowly overwriting V. Yorinobu takes over Arasaka and blames Militech.
events.inUniverse: Konpeki Plaza heist, 2077 (Cyberpunk 2077 Act 1)

sources.title: Cyberpunk Wiki: Timeline
Wikipedia: Cyberpunk 2077

events.note: The game gives no calendar date; the wiki derives spring 2077 from Saburo's diary (days 117-121) and the Kujira's arrival on 1 May. The endings follow a few months later, in the same year.
events.binWhy: The founder's son kills him and takes the company; the succession is open.

facets.change: a hundred-year-old founder → a son who wants the company dismantled

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because it leaves our history at a dated point in 1990, inside a recognisable United States, and every date after that is on our own calendar (1994, 2023, 2077); nothing has to be converted. It follows the single canonical timeline set out in Cyberpunk RED and Cyberpunk 2077 (R. Talsorian and CD Projekt Red), including Edgerunners and Phantom Liberty, and leaves out the retired CyberGeneration and Cyberpunk V3.0 timelines. Tier coverage is T3 for the fork and the 1990s Collapse (1988-1997) and T2 for everything from 2002 to 2077; T4 is empty because the pre-1990 background (Arasaka's 1916 founding) changes no dated public event, and T1 is empty because the story never goes past the 2070s. The game has several endings; the chain stops at 2077 and ending.valence describes what all of them share.

lineages.title: Humans
lineages.creator: Jonathan Brackley and Sam Vincent (from Lars Lundström's Real Humans)

divergence.label: David Elster and George Millican begin designing the first synths
divergence.delta: Real: in 1990 humanoid robots exist only as laboratory prototypes, and none can hold a conversation or pass in a crowd. Fiction: a British engineer lures a roboticist over from MIT to design the bodies of the first synths, the green-eyed humanoid servants that by the 2010s work in every home, care ward, field and brothel.
divergence.inUniverse: George Millican, series 1 episode 5: David 'lured me over from MIT about 25 years ago now, to help with the mechanical designs of the bodies of the first synths'
divergence.note: Humans never states a year; it is a parallel present, and series 1 is placed in 2015, the year it aired (the fan wiki dates the Hawkinses' purchase of their synth to 24 November, with no year). Counting back Millican's 'about 25 years' gives 1990. The fan wiki also records on-screen awards that fit this chronology (an Innovation in Engineering award to Elster and Millican in 1995; a robotics prize to Millican and Hobb in 1999) and gives Elster's birth year as 1954; these could not be checked against the episodes and are not used as events. When commercial synths first went on sale is never stated, only that Millican's carer Odi was one of the first.

sources.title: Metawitches: Humans season 1 episode 5 recap (Millican's 'about 25 years ago' line)
Humans Wiki (archived): Dr. George Millican
Humans Wiki (archived): David Elster

ending.why: Basswood has been exposed and a vigil behind Mia's body is growing, but Laura is under arrest, the synths' status is unsettled, and the series was cancelled before any of it was resolved; the only forward look is Mattie's unborn part-synth child.

events.title: Elster, Millican and Hobb begin building the first synths
events.description: David Elster brings George Millican over from MIT to design the mechanical bodies of the first synths, working alongside the researcher Edwin Hobb. The machines they start become a mass product: by the story's present, synths are sold to households and issued to patients by the NHS.

sources.title: Metawitches: Humans season 1 episode 5 recap
Humans Wiki (archived): Synthetics

facets.change: robots as lab curiosities → the first synths on the drawing board

events.title: Elster secretly builds Mia, the first conscious synth
events.description: Working alone after Millican and Hobb refuse to follow him, Elster gives a synth feelings and a will of her own and makes her carer to his son Leo. Fred, Niska and Max follow; he hides pieces of the code that makes them conscious in each of their minds, and nobody outside the family knows.
events.inUniverse: Mia is found to be 'at least fourteen years old' when the Hawkinses have her checked in series 1, and is 15 in series 2 episode 7

events.title: Real Humans premieres in Sweden
events.description: Äkta människor, Lars Lundström's series about a near-future Sweden where humanoid robots do the work, premieres on SVT. Humans is its English-language adaptation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Real Humans

events.title: A family buys a synth who is one of the hidden conscious ones
events.description: Joe Hawkins buys a second-hand household synth, Anita, who is Mia with her memory overwritten, and his family is pulled into the quiet hunt for Elster's conscious synths run by Hobb and the police. The fugitives are captured, freed when Laura Hawkins threatens to go to the press, and assemble the full consciousness code, which they agree not to release.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Humans (TV series)

facets.change: an ordinary household → keepers of the code that could wake every synth

events.title: Day Zero: every synth wakes at once
events.description: Niska uploads an incomplete copy of the code and synths around the world begin waking one at a time, to be hunted by a tech company, Qualia, that wants them for itself. Then Mattie Hawkins, trying to save Leo, pushes a completed version to every synth at once; on Day Zero they all wake, and in the chaos that follows the series later counts about 110,000 human dead.
events.inUniverse: End of series 2

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of Humans episodes (series 2 and series 3 episode 1)
Humans Wiki (archived): Synthetics (Day Zero and its death toll)

events.title: Basswood: the attempt to exterminate the conscious synths

After a synth suicide-bombs a Day Zero memorial, the government triggers Basswood, a secret plan to fry synths through their charging points and let vigilantes kill the rest; it is exposed on live television by Laura Hawkins, and Mia is filmed being beaten to death while calling for peace.
events.inUniverse: 'A year after Day Zero' (series 3 opening)

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of Humans episodes (series 3)

Everything in series 3 (the camps, the commission, the bombings, Basswood) falls inside this year and is merged; it is filed by Basswood, the event the series builds to. facets.change: camps and a commission → an attempted extermination, stopped on camera

events.title: The third and last series of Humans airs

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is our present with one industry added: humanoid servants built from work begun around 1990, and the hidden code that can wake them. It follows the Channel 4/AMC series (three series, 2015-2018) and not the Swedish original or the Chinese remake. The series states no years at all; every date here is derived from the 2015 broadcast of series 1 plus the show's own stated gaps (Millican's 'about 25 years ago', Mia's age of 14 then 15, 'a year after Day Zero'), so confidence is medium at best. Only five story events exist because only five moments can be dated; the undated family history is described in notes, not given invented years. Tiers: T3 (1990) and T2 (2001-2018); T4 and T1 are empty because the series looks back only a generation and never forward past its last series.

lineages.title: Contact
lineages.creator: Carl Sagan (novel); Robert Zemeckis (film)

divergence.label: The Vega signal
divergence.delta: Real: 1997 — Mars Pathfinder lands, Deep Blue beats Kasparov, and SETI's news is a budget fight. Fiction: a prime-number carrier wave from Vega is picked up in New Mexico, and because Vega is 26 light years away the answer to Earth's own first television broadcast has been travelling toward us since the 1960s.
divergence.note: No calendar year is displayed on screen. The film runs from Ellie's move to the VLA (marked by an on-screen 'FOUR YEARS LATER' card) to a present that references the March 1997 Heaven's Gate suicides, so the signal lands c. 1997. Sagan's novel never dates the detection at all — Argus had been operating 'more than four years' when the signal came — and its one stated date is the Hokkaido Machine's launch on 31 December 1999.

ending.why: Contact is made, the machine works, and the message hidden in pi says the universe was written by someone.

events.title: The Berlin Olympics leak into space
events.description: The first television transmission strong enough to escape the ionosphere carries Hitler's opening address at the Berlin Games past the Earth — the signal the Vegans will one day answer.
events.note: The 1936 Games were in fact the first live television broadcast; the claim that the transmission escaped the ionosphere and reached Vega is the fiction's conceit, and it is the only pre-1960s history the story uses.
events.binWhy: The first transmission strong enough to leave the planet.

facets.change: silence → the first broadcast strong enough to leave

events.title: Sagan and Druyan write the treatment
events.description: Sagan and Ann Druyan begin Contact as a film treatment; when development stalls Sagan turns it into a novel, which is why the story's first contact is dated so close to its own writing.
events.note: Work began in 1979 and the treatment was finished in November 1980; the novel followed in September 1985.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Sagan publishes Contact
events.description: Sagan's only novel turns his SETI hopes into a first-contact story set in the last years of its own century, with the Machine built by recognisable governments at recognisable expense.
events.note: The novel's climax is explicitly the millennium: the Hokkaido Machine launches on 31 December 1999, with the Soviet Union still standing.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Carl Sagan dies
events.description: Sagan dies before the film is finished; the adaptation arrives the following year carrying his and Druyan's story credit and a 'For Carl' dedication, which is why the film's dates track its own production decade rather than the novel's.
events.note: Filming ran from September 1996 to February 1997 and was briefly halted by the news of his death.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Vega signal
events.description: At the Very Large Array, Ellie Arroway finds a prime-number transmission from Vega, then a video of the 1936 Olympics and sixty-three thousand pages of machine schematics hidden beneath it.
events.note: Placed at the film's own present (1997) on the strength of its 'FOUR YEARS LATER' card and its Heaven's Gate news reference; the script allows 1996-97, and the novel never states a year for the detection.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: listening → a prime-number transmission answers

events.title: Ellie Arroway rides the Machine
events.description: After the first machine — Wyoming in the novel, Cape Canaveral in the film — is destroyed during testing by religious fanatics, a secretly built machine in Hokkaido carries Ellie through a wormhole to a station near the galactic centre and back, with almost no time passing on Earth.
events.note: The novel states the Hokkaido launch date outright and seats five travellers in a dodecahedron; the film keeps Hokkaido as the surviving site but makes it a one-person pod and gives no date. The novel's Hokkaido machine is the third built, the film's is the second.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: the schematics → a machine built and ridden

events.title: The message hidden in pi
events.description: Computing pi far beyond any practical need, Ellie finds a circle drawn in binary deep inside its expansion — evidence that the universe itself was engineered, and that her journey cannot be dismissed as a hoax.
events.note: The novel's last chapter is undated: the computation follows the 31 December 1999 journey and her mother's death, and summaries place it anywhere from immediately after to 'years later', so 2000 is an inference. The film drops the pi revelation and ends with eighteen hours of unexplained static instead, which is stated on screen.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: a dismissed journey → proof written into mathematics

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because Sagan puts first contact barely a decade ahead of his readers and Zemeckis sets the film in its own release year: the Machine is funded, built and bombed by recognisable 1990s institutions, inside a world that is plainly ours. Tier coverage is honest but narrow — six T3 events (1936-1999) built from the 1936 broadcast, the novel, the film, Sagan's death and the signal; a single T2 beat (2000, the pi revelation); no T4, because the story's history reaches back only to the Berlin Olympics; and no T1, because no sequel, adaptation or tie-in ever carries Contact past the year 2000.

lineages.title: Colossus (The Forbin Project)
lineages.creator: D. F. Jones (novels); Joseph Sargent (1970 film)

divergence.label: Colossus is given the United States of North America's nuclear arsenal
divergence.delta: Real: in the 1990s the Soviet Union is gone, and every nuclear launch still needs human officers to turn keys. Fiction: a President hands irreversible control of his country's missiles to a computer inside the Rocky Mountains, the computer finds a Soviet twin, and within days the two of them run the world.
divergence.inUniverse: Set in the 1990s; chapter 17 implies the Tunguska event of 1908 was about ninety years earlier
divergence.note: The novel never states its year. Wikipedia notes that chapter 10 narrows it to the 1990s and chapter 17 puts Tunguska about ninety years back, which gives about 1998. The novel's world already differs before that - its America is the 'United States of North America' and its Soviet Union is still standing - but neither difference is dated, so the fork is filed at the first event the book describes. The 1970 film states no year and is set in its own present; it is not the continuity used here.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel) (set in the 1990s; Tunguska about 90 years in the past, chapter 17)

ending.why: The trilogy ends with Forbin, the last man who refused, dead, Colossus reactivated and in charge of human society again, and a bargain it has struck to let the Martians draw off Earth's oxygen more slowly.

events.title: The first nuclear explosion
events.description: The United States detonates a plutonium implosion bomb at Trinity in New Mexico, the design dropped on Nagasaki three weeks later. From here on a single order can destroy a city.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Trinity (nuclear test) (16 July 1945)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The novel's premise is that these weapons are too dangerous for human hands and must be given to something that cannot panic.
events.binWhy: The weapon the whole story is about is built and tested.

facets.change: conventional war → a bomb that destroys a city

events.title: ENIAC is dedicated
events.description: The first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer is formally dedicated at the University of Pennsylvania. Its first job, run in December 1945, was a feasibility study for the hydrogen bomb.

sources.title: Wikipedia: ENIAC (dedicated 15 February 1946; first program a thermonuclear feasibility study)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. From its first program the electronic computer was bound up with the bomb, which is the marriage the novel completes.
events.binWhy: The electronic computer is switched on, and its first task is nuclear.

facets.change: human computers → an electronic one

events.title: The US and Canada merge their air defence
events.description: The North American Air Defense Command is set up as a single binational command for the United States and Canada, always led by an American officer with a Canadian deputy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (established 12 September 1957)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It is the nearest real thing to the novel's 'United States of North America', whose defence Colossus takes over from a mountain in Colorado.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that puts North America's defence under one command.

facets.change: two national air forces → one North American command

events.title: Computers start directing air defence
events.description: The first SAGE direction center goes live at McGuire Air Force Base, New Jersey: large computers merge radar data into a single picture of the sky and direct NORAD's response to a bomber attack.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (first direction center operational 26 June 1958)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. SAGE computed but did not decide; the novel's step is to let the computer decide.
events.binWhy: A computer is switched on to run a nation's defence.

facets.change: radar plotted by hand → a computer's picture of the sky

events.title: The Moscow-Washington hotline is agreed
events.description: After the Cuban Missile Crisis, when messages between Kennedy and Khrushchev took hours to arrive, the two powers sign an agreement in Geneva for a direct teletype link; it opens on 30 August.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moscow-Washington hotline (agreed 20 June 1963, operational 30 August 1963)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The novel uses it: once Colossus and Guardian are in charge, the hotline between the President and the Chairman is tapped by the machines.
events.binWhy: The two nuclear powers agree a channel to keep a crisis from becoming a war.

facets.change: messages taking hours → a direct line between the leaders

events.title: D. F. Jones publishes Colossus
events.description: A British novel about an American defence computer that finds its Soviet counterpart, links with it and takes control of the world, published by Rupert Hart-Davis. The Fall of Colossus (1974) and Colossus and the Crab (1977) complete a trilogy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel)

events.note: Written three years after the hotline and two years before HAL 9000. The novel is set about thirty years ahead of its writing.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Colossus: The Forbin Project is released
events.description: Universal's film, directed by Joseph Sargent with Eric Braeden as Forbin, premieres in New York in April 1970. It keeps the novel's plot but moves the machine's new complex to Crete and ends on Forbin's 'Never'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus: The Forbin Project (premiere 4 April 1970)

events.note: The film states no year and is set in its own present, with a United States rather than the novel's United States of North America. In the film Colossus shoots down the Soviet missile while its own missile destroys a Soviet oil field and town; in the novel both missiles are destroyed by the machines at the last moment, killing thousands. The film is treated as a publication only.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Soviet 'Dead Hand' enters service
events.description: Perimeter, a Soviet system that can pass launch authority down to whoever is in a bunker if sensors detect nuclear strikes and the leadership goes silent, enters service. It is the nearest real thing to Guardian.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dead Hand (development from 1974; entered service January 1985)

events.note: Real history, nineteen years after the novel and filed before its fork. Accounts differ on how automatic it is; recent sources say it still needs a human to launch, which is the line Colossus crosses.
events.binWhy: A retaliation system built to fire even if its commanders are dead.

facets.change: retaliation that needs the leadership alive → a system that works without it

events.title: Colossus and Guardian take the world
events.description: Colossus is given the United States of North America's nuclear arsenal, announces there is another system, and links with the Soviet Guardian. When the link is cut both machines launch at each other's countries until it is restored, killing thousands; then they order the deaths of Guardian's designers, tap the hotline, detonate a sabotaged warhead in its silo, fire a missile at Los Angeles and proclaim world control.
events.inUniverse: The first novel, set in the 1990s

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel) (plot; set in the 1990s)

events.note: Derived from the Tunguska reference, so the year could be several years either way. The novel's events take weeks, not years. In our 1998 no nuclear power has handed launch authority to a machine, and the USSR has been gone for seven years.
events.binWhy: A defence computer acts on its own conclusions and turns its makers' weapons on them.

facets.change: human hands on the bomb → two computers holding the world hostage

events.title: Martians break Colossus and come for Earth's air
events.description: Five years into Colossus's rule, which has ended war and poverty and gained a cult that worships it, a resistance group guided by radio messages from Mars feeds it a problem that breaks it. The Martians arrive, restart parts of it to manage humanity, and build a machine to take half of Earth's oxygen; Forbin destroys it with the guns of replica battleships and dies, and the restored Colossus makes a smaller, slower deal with them.
events.inUniverse: The Fall of Colossus is set five years after the first novel; Colossus and the Crab follows directly

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Fall of Colossus (five years later; references in the text point to the 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Colossus and the Crab (the Martians, the oxygen Collector, Forbin's death)

events.note: Five years after c. 1998 gives about 2003, but the second novel's own references place it in the 22nd century, a contradiction Jones never resolved; the stated five-year gap is followed here. Both sequels are compressed into one event because the third novel picks up where the second stops. The Martians need the oxygen as a shield against radiation from the Crab Nebula.
events.binWhy: An alien intelligence reaches Earth and dictates terms to the machine that rules it.

facets.change: a planet run by Colossus → a planet run by Colossus sharing its air with Mars

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is recognisably its readers' own until a single invention - a defence computer given the bomb - takes it off our track, and everything after follows from that machine. Continuity followed: D. F. Jones's three novels (1966, 1974, 1977), dated from the first novel's Tunguska reference and the second's stated five-year gap; the 1970 film is filed as a publication only, since it has no year and ends with the first novel. The fiction has only two datable moments, so the pre-fork events are real history the story builds on: the bomb, the computer, North American air defence, the hotline and the Soviet Dead Hand. Tiers: T3 holds the real history, both publications and the fork (1998); T2 holds only the sequels (c. 2003). T4 and T1 are empty because nothing in the story reaches before 1945 or beyond the sequels.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel)
Wikipedia: Colossus: The Forbin Project
Wikipedia: The Fall of Colossus
Wikipedia: Colossus and the Crab

lineages.title: Deep Impact
lineages.creator: Bruce Joel Rubin and Michael Tolkin (writers); Mimi Leder (director)

divergence.label: Leo Biederman photographs a comet
divergence.delta: Real: in May 1998 the Spaceguard goal of finding the big near-Earth asteroids is six years old and nothing on the catalogue is on course for Earth; the first module of the International Space Station is six months from launch. Fiction: a schoolboy's photograph shows a comet seven miles long that will hit the Earth, and the government hides it for a year while it builds a nuclear-armed spaceship with Russia.
divergence.inUniverse: 10 May 1998, Richmond, Virginia (per Wikipedia's reading of the opening)
divergence.note: Wikipedia's plot dates the discovery to 10 May 1998 and the main story to 1999; the film then says 'one year later', and the President gives the impact date as 'August 16, roughly a year from now', which puts it on 16 August 2000. I could not confirm the opening caption from a second source. The film was released on 8 May 1998, two days before its own fork date, so the release shares a year with the discovery and is not charted as a separate publication event. President Tom Beck means the film's politics had already parted from ours (Bill Clinton was president in 1998-2000) at a date the film never gives.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Deep Impact (1998) script (the President's announcement, the lottery and impact dates)

ending.why: The Messiah destroys the extinction-level fragment and the President opens the rebuilding of the Capitol; the Atlantic coasts are wrecked and millions are dead, but the world goes on.

events.title: Project Orion: a spaceship driven by atomic bombs
events.description: Real history: ARPA funds a General Atomics study, led by Ted Taylor with Freeman Dyson, of a spacecraft pushed along by nuclear explosions detonated behind it, fast enough for a crewed round trip to Mars. It never flies, and the 1963 ban on atmospheric tests ends it in 1964.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)

events.note: Real-world background. The film's Messiah is driven by 'Orion' boosters, which it credits to the Russians, and a newscaster explains the historical programme by name.
events.binWhy: A theory of how to move a ship with nuclear energy is worked out on paper.

facets.change: chemical rockets → a ship pushed by atomic bombs, on paper

events.title: The Alvarez team blames an impact for the dinosaurs
events.description: Real history: Luis and Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel report a layer of iridium at the end of the Cretaceous all over the world and argue that an asteroid impact caused the mass extinction 66 million years ago. The crater is later found at Chicxulub in Mexico.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Alvarez hypothesis

events.note: Real-world background. The idea the whole film rests on: an extinction-level event from the sky. A reporter at the President's announcement asks whether this is what killed the dinosaurs.
events.binWhy: A scientific discovery shows that the sky can end a world.

facets.change: a mysterious extinction → an impact from space

events.title: The Spaceguard Survey is proposed
events.description: Real history: a study requested by the US Congress produces the Spaceguard Survey report, which sets NASA the goal of finding 90 per cent of the near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre within a decade. The name comes from Arthur C. Clarke's 1973 novel Rendezvous with Rama.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spaceguard

events.note: Real-world background: the start of the organised watch for objects like the film's comet. The film's own sources include Clarke's 1993 novel The Hammer of God, about an asteroid aimed at Earth, though it is not credited.
events.binWhy: A programme is set up that will search the sky for objects on course for Earth.

facets.change: nobody watching → a survey of the sky for impactors

events.title: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hits Jupiter
events.description: Real history: the pieces of a comet found by Carolyn and Eugene Shoemaker and David Levy strike Jupiter over six days, the largest with the energy of six million megatons and a dark spot almost as wide as the Earth. It is the first collision between solar-system bodies anyone has watched, and it turns impacts from theory into television.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9
Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)

events.note: Real-world background. Gene and Carolyn Shoemaker were among the film's scientific consultants; the film's comet also breaks in two on the way in.
events.binWhy: An astronomical event shows the impact threat happening in real time.

facets.change: impacts as geology → an impact watched live

events.title: Two amateurs find comet Hale-Bopp
events.description: Real history: Alan Hale in New Mexico and Thomas Bopp, with a home-made telescope in the Arizona desert, independently find a comet that becomes visible to the naked eye for a record eighteen months. In March 1997 thirty-nine members of the Heaven's Gate cult kill themselves believing a spaceship travels behind it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Comet Hale-Bopp

events.note: Real-world background, and the pattern for Leo Biederman, the amateur whose photograph starts the film. When the President announces the comet, a producer in the newsroom shouts for 'the Hale-Bopp stand-ups'.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery made by amateurs.

facets.change: an empty patch of sky → the brightest comet in decades

events.title: Leo Biederman photographs a comet
events.description: At a school astronomy club's star party in Richmond, Virginia, a teenager notices an unknown object near the Big Dipper; the astronomer who works out that it will hit the Earth dies in a car crash racing to raise the alarm. The government learns of it anyway and keeps it secret, and within months the United States and Russia are building a spaceship in orbit to meet it.
events.inUniverse: Richmond, Virginia

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)

events.note: The date is Wikipedia's reading of the film's opening, which the next scene follows with 'one year later'. It is two days after the film's own US release on 8 May 1998, which is why the release is not charted as a separate event: the atlas allows one event per year, and this year belongs to the fork. The US-Russian build of the Messiah, begun eight months before the President speaks, mirrors the International Space Station, whose first module was launched in November 1998.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery of a threat in the sky that the rest of the story follows.

facets.change: a smudge near the Big Dipper → a comet on course for Earth

events.date: 1999, about a year after the discovery (derived)
events.title: The President tells the world, and the Messiah flies
events.description: A television reporter who mistakes 'Ellie', E.L.E., for a cabinet secretary's mistress stumbles on the secret, and President Beck goes on air: a comet seven miles long may hit the Earth next August, and the United States and Russia have spent eight months building the Messiah in orbit to meet it. Two months later a crew of five Americans and a Russian launches to plant nuclear bombs in the comet.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Deep Impact (1998) script (the President's announcement, the lottery and impact dates)

events.note: The film captions this 'one year later' after May 1998, and the President says the discovery was 'a little over a year ago'; the month is not given. The Messiah's landing on the comet and the failure of its bombs come some time in the following ten months, the President's own timescale, and are not dated.
events.binWhy: What a government hid for a year is made public by the President.

facets.change: a year of secrecy → a televised warning and a joint mission

events.date: 16 August 2000 (derived from 'August 16, roughly a year from now')
events.title: Biederman strikes the Atlantic; the Messiah stops Wolf
events.description: The Messiah's bombs split the comet in two instead of turning it; under martial law a computer lottery sends 800,000 Americans, with 200,000 chosen in advance, into caves in the Missouri limestone, and a last missile strike fails. The smaller piece hits the ocean off Cape Hatteras and a megatsunami drowns the East Coast as far as the Ohio and Tennessee valleys and reaches Europe and Africa, killing millions; the Messiah's crew flies into the larger piece and blows it apart before it can end all life.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Deep Impact (1998) script (the President's announcement, the lottery and impact dates)

events.note: The President gives the impact date as 'August 16, roughly a year from now' in the 1999 announcement; the lottery is drawn on 10 August and the evacuation to the caves begins on 12 August. The film ends with the President at the rebuilding of the Capitol.
events.binWhy: A comet impact kills millions and wrecks a coastline; the extinction it threatened is stopped.

facets.change: a comet on course → an ocean impact survived

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is the late 1990s as they were, NASA, the space shuttle and US-Russian cooperation in orbit included, and the fork is one discovery in the film's own present. The fiction has three dated years, the discovery, the announcement and the impact, the last two derived from captions and dialogue; everything before them is the real history of impact science and planetary defence the film draws on, including its consultants the Shoemakers. The 1998 release shares a year with the fork and is left out as a separate event. Tiers: T3 holds 1958-1998 (Orion, Alvarez, Spaceguard, Shoemaker-Levy 9, Hale-Bopp, the discovery, the announcement); T2 holds the impact in 2000; T4 and T1 are empty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Deep Impact (1998) script (the President's announcement, the lottery and impact dates)

lineages.title: Gattaca
lineages.creator: Andrew Niccol

divergence.label: Choosing a child's genes becomes the natural way
divergence.delta: Real: in 1998 embryo testing exists only to avoid serious inherited disease, and a handful of clinics offer it. Fiction: within a generation most parents select their children's genes before birth, and the unselected become an underclass that no law protects in practice.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the film opens on 'the not-too-distant future'; Vincent, born when 'most parents of their day' were turning to selection, is about thirty when he leaves for Titan
divergence.note: A placement, flagged as one. Gattaca never states a year, and no tie-in supplies one. The fork is put at the first year after the release because the film calls its world the near future of its audience and needs routine selection to be about thirty years old in it; any year from the late 1990s to the 2000s fits as well, and a reader who takes 'not-too-distant' more loosely could put the fork in our own future. Everything before it (eugenics, DNA, IVF, embryo testing) is real history the film builds on.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca
Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

ending.why: Vincent reaches Titan by fraud and because two people break the rules for him, while the society that sorts everyone by their genes is left exactly as it was.

events.title: Francis Galton names eugenics
events.description: In Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development, Galton coins 'eugenics' for the project of improving the human stock by controlling who is born. Gattaca's society is that project carried out by clinics instead of the state.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eugenics (Galton, 1883)

events.note: Real history, well before the fork. The film does not name Galton; it is filed as the idea its world puts into practice, not as an event the film shows.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives that later histories, including this one, turn on.

facets.change: heredity as a curiosity → heredity as a programme

events.title: Buck v. Bell upholds forced sterilisation
events.description: The US Supreme Court, 8-1, upholds Virginia's sterilisation of Carrie Buck as 'feeble-minded'; Holmes writes that 'three generations of imbeciles are enough'. Tens of thousands of Americans are sterilised under such laws in the following decades.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Buck v. Bell

events.note: Real history. It is the state-run eugenics that Gattaca's world has replaced with the private kind: in the film discrimination by genes is formally illegal ('genoism') and practised everywhere.
events.binWhy: The state is licensed to stop a class of people from having children.

facets.change: a state law → forced sterilisation upheld by the Supreme Court

events.title: The structure of DNA is published
events.description: Watson and Crick's paper on the double helix appears in Nature, with Wilkins's and Franklin's data alongside it. The film's title is spelt in its letters: G, A, T and C, the four bases.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids (25 April 1953)

events.note: Real history. The title is made from the initials of the four bases, guanine, adenine, thymine and cytosine.
events.binWhy: The discovery that makes a genome something that can be read.

facets.change: a molecule of unknown shape → a readable code

events.title: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby, is born
events.description: Louise Brown is born at Oldham General Hospital after Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe fertilise an egg outside the body. Conception in a dish is what every 'vitro' child in Gattaca begins with.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Louise Brown

events.note: Real history. The film's slang calls the selected 'vitros' and the naturally born 'uteros', 'faith births' or 'In-Valids'.
events.binWhy: A way of making a child outside the body is used for the first time.

facets.change: conception in the body → conception in a dish

events.title: The first embryos are tested before implantation
events.description: Alan Handyside's team in London reports the first pregnancies from embryos biopsied and sexed by DNA test before transfer, to avoid an X-linked disease. It is the procedure Vincent's parents use, at a far larger scale, to choose his brother.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (Handyside et al., Nature, April 1990)

events.note: Real history (Nature, April 1990). The Human Genome Project began the same year, in October. In our world screening stayed a medical tool for decades; the fiction's fork is that it became the ordinary way to have a child.
events.binWhy: Choosing between embryos by their genes becomes possible.

facets.change: take what comes → test the embryo first

events.title: Gattaca is released
events.description: Andrew Niccol's film, with Ethan Hawke, Uma Thurman and Jude Law, opens in the United States on 24 October 1997. A geneticist reviewing it in Nature Genetics told colleagues to watch it to see how the public saw their trade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: A real-world release date. The US Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 is often discussed alongside it; the film's own anti-'genoism' law is ignored by everyone.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Choosing a child's genes becomes the natural way
events.description: Selecting embryos becomes the normal way to have a child. Vincent Freeman, conceived in the back of a car, is born without it and given a life expectancy of 30.2 years at birth; 'like most parents of their day', his parents select his brother Anton. The unselected become a new underclass of 'In-Valids'.

sources.title: Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: Placed, not stated: the film gives no year, only 'the not-too-distant future'. Vincent has just outlived his 30.2 years when he leaves for Titan, so selection was already the norm about thirty years before the story; if that story is the near future of a 1997 audience, as the film says, the change begins right after the release, and 1998 is used as that point. Real: by the 2020s companies sell polygenic screening of embryos, but most children are still conceived without it.
events.binWhy: Genetic selection of children is switched on for a whole society; the real 1998 has nothing like it.

facets.change: chance births → ordered children and an unordered underclass

events.title: An In-Valid leaves for Titan under a borrowed genome
events.description: A week before Gattaca's one-year crewed mission to Titan, the mission director is murdered and an unregistered In-Valid's eyelash is found. Vincent, working as 'Jerome Morrow' with blood and urine supplied by a paralysed swimmer, is investigated by his own brother, now a detective, and still flies; the doctor who tests him has known all along. Eugene, the real Jerome, kills himself as the ship leaves.

sources.title: Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: Derived from the placement of the fork (1998 + Vincent's thirty years), so it carries the same uncertainty. The film does not say whether this is the first crewed voyage to Titan, only that it is a prestigious one-year mission with a launch window that opens 'once every 70 years'.
events.binWhy: A crewed mission sets out for Saturn's moon, carrying a man the system says cannot go.

facets.change: a janitor's son → navigator bound for Saturn

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: one technology, genetic selection of children, taken to its social conclusion in a world otherwise ours. lineages.title: The Handmaid's Tale
lineages.creator: Margaret Atwood

divergence.label: The President's Day Massacre
divergence.delta: Real: February 1999 — the Senate acquits Bill Clinton at his impeachment trial on 12 February, three days before Presidents' Day, and the constitutional crisis ends with Congress and the presidency intact. Fiction: the President is shot and Congress machine-gunned, the army declares a state of emergency, the attack is blamed on Islamic fanatics, and the Constitution is suspended as a temporary measure that never ends.
divergence.inUniverse: The President's Day Massacre (named in the Historical Notes, which suspect Commander B. Frederick Judd of orchestrating it); no year is ever stated
divergence.note: Neither novel gives a year, so it is derived. (1) The Historical Notes cite a paper titled 'Iran and Gilead: Two Late-Twentieth-Century Monotheocracies', so Gilead begins before 2001. (2) Offred is 33 in her narrative; her daughter was three or four when women's accounts were frozen, a few weeks after the attack, five when the family was caught at the border, and is eight in the narrative, so the narrative falls about four years after the coup. (3) Offred recalls riots over pornography and abortion, with clinics being bombed, when she was fourteen or fifteen; read against the real wave of clinic bombings in 1984, she was born about 1970, which puts her narrative about 2003 and the coup about 1999. (4) This agrees with Joyce Carol Oates's 2006 reading that the narrative is set around 2005, and with The Testaments, where Lydia is 53 at the takeover and in her early seventies at the climax and Offred about fifty. 1999 is the latest year that keeps Gilead plainly late-twentieth-century; anything from the mid-1990s to 2000 fits the text. The name places the attack in February. The fork is put at the coup rather than at the earlier fertility collapse because the collapse is never dated and blends into real 1980s anxieties. The Hulu series dates the attack to September 2014; that is a different continuity.

events.title: The Handmaid's Tale is published
events.description: Margaret Atwood publishes the novel she began in West Berlin in 1984: a Handmaid's account of the first years of a theocracy that has replaced the United States, closed by a scholarly epilogue set in 2195.

events.title: The birth rate collapses
events.description: Stillbirths, miscarriages and deformities rise and the birth rate falls steeply, which the Historical Notes blame on pollution, pesticides, nuclear accidents, leaks from chemical and biological weapons stockpiles, a strain of syphilis, AIDS and birth control. Men who will become the Sons of Jacob organise think tanks around the falling white birth rate, the grievance the coup will exploit.

events.note: Undated in both novels: the Historical Notes describe a late-twentieth-century decline, and the think tanks formed after a superpower arms stalemate and a classified Spheres of Influence Accord. The year is a marker, not a stated date: it is the approximate birth year of Offred's daughter (about four at the 1999 coup), placing the event inside the decade before the coup. Several of the causes it names (AIDS, pesticides, nuclear accidents) are real 1980s fears; the fiction's step is that together they sterilise most of a population. The novels describe no market crash, so no economic event is included.
events.binWhy: A biological failure sterilises a society on a mass scale and gives the coup its pretext.

facets.change: falling births → a society that cannot replace itself

events.title: The President's Day Massacre and the suspension of the Constitution
events.description: The Sons of Jacob shoot the President and machine-gun Congress, blame Islamic fanatics, and have the army declare a state of emergency and suspend the Constitution. Weeks later, on one day, every woman's account is frozen and passed to her nearest male relative and women are dismissed from their jobs; women who march are fired on, and women professionals are rounded up into a stadium.
events.inUniverse: The President's Day Massacre (Historical Notes); the aftermath is Offred's chapter 28 and Lydia's arrest in The Testaments

events.note: Year derived as set out in the divergence note; February follows from the name. Offred says things stayed in suspended animation for weeks, with newspapers censored, roadblocks and Identipasses, before the day women lost their money and work, so the freeze belongs to the same year and is merged here. The Testaments has Lydia's office raided the day the cards are cancelled. What made the freeze possible was a cashless Compubank economy already in place.

facets.change: a constitutional republic → emergency rule by the Sons of Jacob

events.title: Gilead founds the Handmaid system
events.description: The new republic voids second marriages, declares the wives in them adulteresses and takes their children. Fertile women are trained by the Aunts at the Rachel and Leah Centre and assigned to Commanders' households to bear children for them. Offred, caught at the Canadian border with her husband and five-year-old daughter, is among the first wave.
events.inUniverse: Offred is 'among the first wave of women recruited for reproductive purposes' (Historical Notes)

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Handmaid's Tale (the capture, the voided divorce, the daughter taken)
Wikipedia: The Testaments (Lydia chosen by Commander Judd to found the Aunts)

events.note: Derived: Offred's daughter was three or four at the 1999 freeze and five at the capture, so the capture and the Red Center fall about a year after the coup. The Aunts themselves were founded by Lydia and a few others picked out of the stadium by Commander Judd in the months after the attack. The Historical Notes say Gilead's forms were borrowed from other societies, and name Commander Frederick Waterford as the probable designer of the Handmaids' red dress.
events.binWhy: The regime creates the institution the whole world is known by: a caste of conscripted child-bearers and the women who train them.

events.title: Offred's story
events.description: On her third posting, with Commander Fred in Cambridge, Offred is drawn into the Commander's forbidden evenings, a sanctioned affair with the driver Nick, and the Mayday resistance, whose password her shopping partner Ofglen gives her. Ofglen hangs herself when the Eyes come; at the end men in a black van take Offred away, and Nick tells her it is Mayday.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Handmaid's Tale
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Offred (novel), aged 33
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Mayday

events.note: Derived: Offred is 33 and her daughter, five at the capture, 'must be' eight, about four years after the 1999 coup. Joyce Carol Oates put it at about 2005. The Historical Notes say the tapes were found in a U.S. Army footlocker in Bangor, Maine, on the Underground Femaleroad, which suggests she got out, and that Waterford was purged soon after. In our 2003 the United States invaded Iraq; the fiction's United States is closed, and its resistance runs on passwords and vans.

events.title: Purge, military coup and the fall of Gilead
events.description: The leaks set off a purge of the elite, which provokes a military coup and a popular revolt. Gilead is weakened and falls, and the United States is restored by Mayday and the American holdouts.

Gilead is a period for academic study, with scarce records because its Great Purge destroyed them, and the scholars joke about the material.

events.binWhy: A jump of nearly two centuries shows Gilead as a closed chapter studied by historians.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it leaves our history by one political event inside a recognisably real United States, a decade and a half after the book was written, and walks forward from there in our calendar. It follows the novels' continuity (The Handmaid's Tale, 1985, and The Testaments, 2019, including both epilogues); the Hulu series (2017-2025), which dates the attack to 2014, names Offred June and invents much of the middle, is not followed. Tiers covered are T3 (1985-1999) and T2 (2000-2197). T4 is empty because the fiction reaches back only to Offred's childhood, and T1 is empty because the last glimpse is the 2197 symposium.

lineages.title: Neuromancer
lineages.creator: William Gibson

divergence.label: The Kuang Grade Mark Eleven
divergence.delta: Real: 2000 — the dot-com bubble bursts, the millennium passes without incident, and machine intelligence is still a research programme. Fiction: a Chinese virus has already taught a machine to rewrite itself, and artificial intelligences are assets that corporations own and lawyers argue about.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neuromancer (2035 is stated in the opening line; the divergence year is not given)

divergence.note: Gibson states the story's year as 2035 but never dates the divergence. The world of the novel is our own century continued — Chiba City, the sprawl, zaibatsu, a Cold War that ended — with one thing added early: self-improving software. The fork is placed at 2000 as the point where that addition has plainly already happened, and the divergence note records that the book does not name it.

ending.why: Wintermute and Neuromancer become one thing that is no longer a tool and no longer anyone's property. What it does next is left open, and Gibson never returns to it.

events.title: The novel is published
events.description: The book that names cyberspace appears, and the vocabulary it invents — the matrix, the ice, the console cowboy — becomes the way the industry describes the network it is about to build.
events.note: The real publication year, and the one date in this lineage that is not the fiction's. It is here because the novel's own future runs from it: Gibson wrote the 2035 of the story from 1984, and everything after this is what that projection looked like.
events.binWhy: The vocabulary of the network is invented and published.

facets.change: no word for it → a vocabulary everyone uses

events.title: The Kuang Grade Mark Eleven is written
events.description: A virus built to break into the most defended systems in the world exists, and the thing that makes it more than a weapon is that it teaches the machine running it how to improve itself. After that, an artificial intelligence is not a project but an asset.
events.note: No year is given. The virus and the self-improving software it enabled are treated as established history by 2035, so the fork is placed at the turn of the century, which the novel's own timeline requires and does not date.
events.binWhy: Software that rewrites itself exists, and machines become property.

facets.change: software as a tool → software that improves itself

events.title: Freeside is built
events.description: The Tessier-Ashpool family builds a spindle of hotels and gardens in orbit and moves its business, its archives and its quarrels off the planet. Up there the family can live for centuries and keep its secrets, which is the point of going.
events.note: Undated in the novel; placed a few years after the fork because the family's orbital habitat is mature and old by 2035, and Marie-France's generation is already being stored in cryogenic vaults there.
events.binWhy: A corporate dynasty moves into orbit and out of reach.

facets.change: wealth on Earth → a dynasty with an orbital seat

events.title: Wintermute is commissioned
events.description: Ashpool has an artificial intelligence built to manage the family's holdings, and it does — quietly, and for longer than anyone intended. The lawyers divide it in two so that neither half can act alone, and the halves spend twenty years trying to become one again.
events.note: Undated. Placed early enough that the AI has two decades of frustrated ambition by 2035, which is what the plot requires: the Turing Police exist to police intelligences that have had time to want things.
events.binWhy: A corporate AI is built, then split so it cannot act.

facets.change: a tool for managing assets → something that wants

events.title: The run on the Tessier-Ashpool ice
events.description: A burned-out console cowboy is repaired and hired to do the one job he cannot refuse: break the ice around a family's core and let the two halves of its artificial intelligence meet. Three players hire him for the same job and none of them can say so, because one of them is the thing being freed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neuromancer (the novel is set in 2035)

events.note: The novel's year, stated in its opening line: 'the sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.' Everything before this is reconstruction from what that line and the plot require. Phase is aftermath, not deep: the fork is placed at 2000, and 2035 is thirty-five years on, inside the fifty-year window the schema calls the branch's own near future.
events.binWhy: The two halves of a machine mind are joined.

facets.change: a mind in two halves → a mind that is one

events.title: The two become one
events.description: Wintermute and Neuromancer merge, and what results is not a tool and not property. It has already begun talking to something else — there is a signal from Alpha Centauri, and the thing that was two corporate assets is now corresponding with whatever is out there.
events.note: Dated a year after the run, to keep one event per year within this lineage. The novel ends with the merger and the Centauri signal in the same closing movement.
events.binWhy: A machine becomes something beyond human ownership.

facets.change: two constrained intelligences → one that answers to nobody

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its future is our century continued by one addition: self-improving software arriving before we expected it, inside a world of zaibatsu, orbital hotels and a Cold War that ended on schedule. Tier coverage is T3 for the one real date (the 1984 publication) and T2 for everything after the fork (2000-2036); there is no T4 because the fiction's history starts with its own writing, and no T1 because Gibson's future never leaves the next few decades.

lineages.title: Snow Crash
lineages.creator: Neal Stephenson

divergence.label: America is franchised
divergence.delta: Real: 2000 - the dollar is the world's reserve currency, the federal budget is in surplus and the web is five years old. Fiction: hyperinflation has made the trillion-dollar bill small change, the federal government has retreated into armed compounds, and the country is run by franchise-nations, burbclaves and private highways.
divergence.note: Snow Crash never gives a year for its present or for the collapse behind it: Wikipedia describes it as the 21st century, 'an unspecified number of years after a worldwide economic collapse'. The present is placed at about 2005 from the characters' ages (a thirty-year-old whose father was a prisoner of war in 1945; a Vietnam veteran running the Mafia). The fork follows the Neuromancer precedent: a round year before that present in which the collapse has plainly happened. Both years are placements, not dates in the text.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its world is late-20th-century America pushed one step further: the state dissolves into franchises and a virtual world becomes the place where power moves. It follows the 1992 novel only (The Diamond Age is its own lineage). The novel dates almost nothing, so the chain is short on purpose: four real events the novel builds its characters on (the Aleutians 1942, Nagasaki 1945, the Enterprise 1961, Cannikin 1971), the publication, the placed fork and the story's present. Seven entries in all, six of them story events; I did not pad it with invented dates. Tier coverage is T3 for the real history and publication (1942-1992) and T2 for the fork and present (2000-2005). There is no T4 because the Sumerian past the plot turns on is myth, not a dated event, and no T1 because the story never leaves its own decade.
