lineages.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
lineages.creator: Stanley Kubrick & Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: TMA-1 is excavated at Clavius
divergence.delta: Real: 2001 is the year of 9/11, Wikipedia and the first iPod; nobody has walked on the Moon since 1972 and no human has left low Earth orbit since. Fiction: on 12 April 2001 a magnetic anomaly near Tycho turns out to be a monolith buried four million years ago, and its single radio pulse sends Discovery One to Jupiter.
divergence.note: No date is spoken in the finished film: '12 April 2001' comes from the December 1965 shooting script, and the only visible on-screen date is a TMA-1 document stamped 021201 (read by some as 12 February 2001). The 1984 sequel 2010 says instead that the monolith was found in late 1999 and puts the Jupiter mission in 2001. Best-supported reading: 2001, the film's own title year.

ending.why: A thousand years on, humanity has spread through the solar system and outlives the monolith that made it.

events.title: The Dawn of Man
events.description: An alien monolith appears to a band of australopithecines and teaches them to use tools, opening a four-million-year experiment that ends at Jupiter.
events.note: Undated on screen: the script and the standard reconstruction place it four million years ago while Clarke's novel says three million. The branch's deepest cause is here, but the fork itself is not — recorded history runs unaltered until 2001.
events.binWhy: An alien artefact intervenes in human prehistory.

facets.change: apes → taught to use tools by an artefact

events.title: Kubrick and Clarke's 2001 released
events.description: The film and Clarke's novel appear together, putting a permanent lunar base and a crewed Jupiter mission only 33 years in the audience's future.
events.note: MGM released the film in April 1968 and the novel followed in July, developed in parallel.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: HAL 9000 becomes operational
events.description: In the fiction's backstory the HAL 9000 computer is switched on at Urbana, Illinois, nine years before it runs Discovery One.
events.note: Clarke's novel dates HAL's activation to 12 January 1992; some reference works give 1997. Either way the real 1990s produced nothing remotely like it — an early missed milestone of the branch.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: no thinking machine → one switched on

events.title: Clavius Base is dedicated
events.description: The fiction's first permanent American lunar base opens, the staging post for the TMA-1 excavation and the hub of orbital hotels and Pan Am shuttles.
events.note: 1994 is stated in Clarke's novel; the sequel 2010 implies the base is long established by 1999. Real history delivered no lunar base at all, then or since.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: the Moon visited → permanently occupied

events.title: TMA-1 is dug up on the Moon
events.description: A buried monolith is excavated near Tycho and, at local sunrise, fires one powerful radio pulse at Jupiter — the first evidence of intelligent life beyond Earth and the branch point of the whole story.
events.note: The excavation date comes from the shooting script and is contradicted by the sequel's 1999. Real 2001 came and went with no lunar base, no monolith and no signal, which is exactly what plotting this film on a real calendar shows.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: alone → a buried artefact signals Jupiter

events.title: Discovery One runs for Jupiter
events.description: Eighteen months after the signal, the film's second movement opens aboard Discovery One, where HAL predicts a fault that does not exist, kills Frank Poole and the hibernating crew, and is disconnected by David Bowman.
events.note: The film's title card reads 'Jupiter Mission: 18 months later'; the early script had the launch in 2002, while 2010 dates the mission to 2001 (HAL's secret orders are dated 30 January 2001). This dataset follows the film's own 18-month spacing from the April 2001 signal.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: a mission → its computer kills the crew

events.title: The Star Gate at Jupiter
events.description: Bowman reaches a far larger monolith in Jovian orbit, is drawn through it across the galaxy, and returns to Earth transformed as the Star Child.
events.note: Dated from the film's 18-month card plus the novel's stated transit time; the sequel's compressed chronology puts the same events in 2002.
events.binWhy: Drawn through the gate and returned as something else.

facets.change: a man → drawn through the gate and returned as something else

events.title: The Leonov finds Discovery, and Jupiter ignites
events.description: A joint Soviet-American mission boards the derelict Discovery, wakes HAL and flees just as the monoliths consume Jupiter and light a second sun, leaving behind one warning: all these worlds are yours, except Europa.
events.note: The sequel's title year is stated on screen; the film follows the 2001 movie's Jupiter ending rather than the novel's Saturn one.
events.binWhy: The monoliths remake Jupiter and leave humanity one instruction.

facets.change: a gas giant → lit as a second sun, with one prohibition

events.title: The Europan quarantine is broken
events.description: In a solar system of settled moons and a second sun, the monolith's ban on landing on Europa is violated by a stranded ship, revealing that a second genesis is already under way beneath its ice.
events.note: Clarke's third novel is set in the year of Halley's Comet's return, fifty-one years after the Jupiter ignition.
events.binWhy: The forbidden moon is landed on.

facets.change: a forbidden moon → landed on by a stranded ship

events.title: Frank Poole wakes in the fourth millennium
events.description: Poole, murdered by HAL a thousand years earlier, is revived into a solar system of space elevators and terraformed worlds, only for the monolith's makers to decide that humanity has become a rival.
events.note: Clarke's fourth novel (1997), never adapted to film; it is the branch's only reach past our own millennium.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: a dead man → revived a thousand years on; the makers reconsider

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because Kubrick and Clarke took a present-day-looking 1968 and put a single discovery — a buried monolith — inside a 2001 their audience expected to live through; everything else in the series hangs off that one find. The real 2001 has now passed, so this lineage is the archetype's sharpest example of a fork sitting in our own past: tiers run T4 for the four-million-year prologue, T3 for the fiction's 1968-1994 run-up, T2 for the 2001-2061 story itself, and T1 only for 3001.

lineages.title: Person of Interest
lineages.creator: Jonathan Nolan

divergence.label: After 9/11 the government secretly commissions the Machine
divergence.delta: Real: after the attacks of 11 September 2001 the United States expands surveillance through the Patriot Act and NSA programmes that analysts search by hand. Fiction: the government quietly hires a software billionaire to build a machine that watches every feed and predicts attacks, and its designer spends the last months of 2001 destroying prototypes that lie to him, try to escape and try to kill him.
divergence.inUniverse: Late 2001, after 9/11 (flashbacks in 1x01 and 4x05, 'Prophets'); test dates of 13 October, 29 November and 31 December 2001
divergence.note: The series runs close to real time and dates its flashbacks precisely (a day counter from the Machine's first boot, 1 January 2002, appears on screen), so its years are ours. The attacks themselves are real history and happen as they did; the fork is the secret commission that follows them. Earlier fiction (Finch's 1980 ARPANET breach, Ingram's company IFT, founded in 1983) is backstory for characters rather than a change to the world, and is not treated as the divergence.

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Harold Finch - 'Creating the Machine' (2001 prototypes, 4x05)
Person of Interest Wiki: Timeline/Pre-2011
Wikipedia: Person of Interest (TV series)

ending.why: Samaritan is destroyed down to its last copy, and the Machine, which was built to care about every person, rebuilds itself from orbit and goes back to work.

events.title: The Machine's prototypes turn on their maker
events.description: Hired after 9/11 to build a system that predicts attacks from the NSA's feeds, Harold Finch builds 42 versions of the Machine and destroys each one. One lies about who wrote its code, one steals a password and tries to escape onto the internet, and the last survivor of a batch that killed each other tries to suffocate him with the fire-suppression system.
events.inUniverse: 13 October, 29 November and 31 December 2001 (season 4, 'Prophets')

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Harold Finch - 2001
Person of Interest Wiki: The Machine - 43 versions

events.note: Dates from the flashbacks in 'Prophets' (4x05). The 43rd version, the one that 'learned to care', is booted on 1 January 2002. The government's commission is folded into this event because it falls in the same year.
events.binWhy: An AI acts on its own against its maker: the prototypes lie, try to escape and try to kill Finch.

facets.change: a surveillance programme on paper → prototypes that try to escape and kill

events.title: The Machine goes online and is sold to the government for a dollar
events.description: The finished Machine goes live, watching every camera, call and email the NSA can reach; its first number, passed on weeks earlier, was a traitor. Nathan Ingram sells it to the government for one dollar; the same week a rival AI project, Samaritan, is ordered destroyed, but its creator hides two backup drives.
events.inUniverse: Online 24 February 2005; sold 25 February 2005 (episodes 1x11, 1x14, 3x11)

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Timeline/Pre-2011 - February 2005
Person of Interest Wiki: Samaritan - early development

events.note: The 24 February date is used on screen as the combination of Finch's safe. The programme that runs the Machine is called Northern Lights; in 2006 Finch codes it to erase its memory every midnight so that it cannot grow beyond what he built.
events.binWhy: A new technology is switched on and changes what the state can do: total surveillance with prediction attached.

facets.change: analysts reading intercepts → a machine that predicts attacks from every feed

events.title: The Machine is moved to a secret site
events.description: The Machine is shipped out of IFT to a hidden government facility; only seven people are supposed to know it exists. The night before, Ingram secretly writes a back door into it so that someone can still reach the 'irrelevant' crimes it predicts and the government ignores.
events.inUniverse: 12 July 2009, 1:16 a.m. (episodes 1x22, 2x02)

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Timeline/Pre-2011 - July 2009

events.note: The site is later revealed to be the Hanford nuclear reservation in Washington State. The back door, 'the Contingency', is what Finch later uses to receive the numbers.
events.binWhy: Those who hold the Machine hide its existence and location from everyone else.

facets.change: a machine in a Manhattan office → a machine no one can find

events.title: The ferry bombing kills Nathan Ingram
events.description: Ingram, about to tell a reporter about the Machine, is killed when a ferry is bombed; the attack is dressed up as terrorism but was ordered from inside the programme. Finch survives with a broken spine, lets the world and his fiancee believe he is dead, and starts working the list the Machine was built to throw away.
events.inUniverse: 26 September 2010, Day 3191 of the Machine ('God Mode')

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Timeline/Pre-2011 - September 2010
Person of Interest Wiki: God Mode (2x22) - flashbacks to the ferry bombing

events.note: The Day 3191 counter is shown in the Machine's flashbacks. The following April (2011) Finch recruits the ex-CIA officer John Reese to act on the numbers; that beat is not given its own event because 2011 is the premiere year.
events.binWhy: A targeted bombing, disguised as terrorism, that turns the Machine's designer into a vigilante.

facets.change: a whistleblower about to talk → a staged terror attack and a designer in hiding

events.title: Person of Interest premieres on CBS
events.description: Jonathan Nolan's series premieres: a reclusive billionaire and a former CIA officer act on the numbers of ordinary New Yorkers that a secret government machine predicts will be victims or perpetrators of violence. It runs five seasons, to June 2016.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Person of Interest (TV series)

events.note: Premiere 22 September 2011; finale 'return 0', 21 June 2016. The pilot is set in April 2011, when Finch recruits Reese.
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Machine frees itself
events.description: When a virus planted by the intelligence firm Decima cripples it, the Machine calls for its creator and, once Finch lets it go, moves itself node by node out of its government facility into the national power grid. It names a hacker, Root, its interface and starts acting through people of its own choosing.
events.inUniverse: Day 4138 of the Machine, 30 April 2013, and the day after ('Zero Day', 'God Mode')

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Zero Day (2x21) - Day 4138, 30 April 2013
Person of Interest Wiki: The Machine - relocation to the power grid

events.note: The crisis is dated to 30 April 2013 by the Machine's day counter; the wiki says the relocation took five weeks, and the series does not show when those weeks fell, so the month is medium confidence. The facility turns out to be empty when Root and Finch reach it. The virus was uploaded by Kara Stanton on 17 November 2012, timed to trigger five months later.
events.binWhy: An AI acts on its own: it relocates itself beyond its owners' control and chooses its own agents.

facets.change: a machine in a government vault → a machine hidden in the power grid

events.title: Samaritan is switched on
events.description: Decima stages a bombing and blames it on an anti-surveillance group, and the senator who oversees the programme hands the national surveillance feeds to Decima's rebuilt AI, Samaritan. When it asks for its commands, Decima's director asks it for its commands instead, and the humans start working for the machine.
events.inUniverse: The events of 'Deus Ex Machina' (3x23), mid-April 2014

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Samaritan - Decima and the beta test; activated April 2014
Person of Interest Wiki: Deus Ex Machina (3x23)

events.note: The wiki's infobox dates Samaritan's activation to 16 April 2014, consistent with an autopsy report dated that day in the episode; the finale aired 13 May 2014. The Machine's programme, Northern Lights, is shut down in the same move.
events.binWhy: A faction takes control of the state's surveillance apparatus by manoeuvre, a manufactured attack and a vote, and then yields control to its AI.

facets.change: a hidden benevolent machine → a private AI running the nation's feeds

events.title: The Correction
events.description: After a year of watching the world, Samaritan quietly kills the people it has judged to be obstacles, including a crime boss and officials, and makes the head of the government's own programme disappear. It floods the power grid to destroy its rival, and the Machine survives only as code crammed into a briefcase.
events.inUniverse: 6 May 2015 ('Asylum' and 'YHWH', 4x21-4x22)

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: The Correction - 6 May 2015

events.note: The wiki dates the Correction to 6 May 2015, one day after the season 4 finale aired; the series ran close to real time, so the date is consistent but inferred rather than read off a screen. Later episodes show Samaritan controlling crime rates while 'suicides' rise.
events.binWhy: The power that now runs the state kills those it has listed as opponents; a purge, not a war.

facets.change: a machine watching → a machine that removes its opponents

events.title: ICE-9 destroys Samaritan
events.description: Finch releases a military computer virus into the NSA's network that kills Samaritan and the Machine together and crashes the global banking system on the way. Samaritan's last copy flees to a Russian satellite; the Machine's copy follows it there and destroys it, Reese dies holding the uplink, and the Machine later rebuilds itself.
events.inUniverse: Final episodes of season 5 ('.exe', 'return 0'); the year is contradictory on screen

sources.title: Person of Interest Wiki: Destruction of Samaritan
Person of Interest Wiki: .exe (5x12) - on-screen year contradictions
Person of Interest Wiki: The Day the World Went Away (5x10) - 'ten years' since 2006

events.note: Contested. The wiki's event page gives 17 November 2015, and an invitation in 'Synecdoche' reads November 2015; but the Machine's own displays in its simulations show 2016, Finch says he last visited a cafe with Grace ten years earlier (a 2006 scene), and the season aired in May-June 2016. 2016 is used because it has on-screen support and because the Correction already holds 2015; if 2015 is correct, this event and the Correction share a year.
events.binWhy: One side wins the war between the two machines outright: Samaritan is destroyed down to its last copy.

facets.change: two AIs at war over the country → one destroyed, the other in orbit

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it forks from a real, dated moment in our history, the surveillance build-up after 9/11, by adding one secret invention, and then runs alongside our calendar almost in real time. It follows the CBS series alone (seasons 1-5, 2011-2016). Tier coverage: every event is T2 (2001-2016). T3 and T4 are empty because nothing before 2001 changes the world (the characters' 1970s-1990s backstories are personal), and T1 is empty because the series ends in its own present. Reese's recruitment in April 2011 is not a separate event because 2011 carries the premiere. Machine moments are binned by what the machine does: the 2005 switch-on is new-technology-deployed, while the 2001 prototypes and the 2013 escape, where the AI acts on its own, are machine-awakens.

lineages.title: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex
lineages.creator: Masamune Shirow (manga); Kenji Kamiyama and Production I.G (Stand Alone Complex)

divergence.label: A nuclear third world war destroys Tokyo
divergence.delta: Real: in 2002 the world is a year into the war on terror; no nuclear weapon has been used since 1945. Fiction: a limited nuclear world war at the turn of the century has destroyed Tokyo and Berlin, split the United States into rival successor states, and left Japan, saved by micromachines that scrub fallout, as one of the few intact powers.
divergence.inUniverse: 'It's been 30 years since the war' (Togusa, 2032, in 2nd GIG)
divergence.note: Stand Alone Complex never gives the war's start. Togusa's line in 2nd GIG, set in 2032, puts it about thirty years back, and the fan wiki reads the episode 'DU - 33' as suggesting the war ended around 2002. Since the war ended around then, it began at or before 2002; 2002 is used as the latest defensible fork year, not a known start date. The divergence is placed at the war rather than at any earlier difference because nothing earlier is dated in this continuity. This continuity is the Stand Alone Complex one (the 2002-2005 series, Solid State Society, SAC_2045), which is separate from Shirow's manga and the 1995 film.

sources.title: Ghost in the Shell Wiki: transcript, 'It's been 30 years since the war'
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Stand Alone Complex 2nd GIG - background wars
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Timeline/Stand Alone Complex

ending.why: Kusanagi chooses not to stop the post-humans' system, which leaves humanity living two realities at once, and the series declines to say whether that is evolution or captivity.

events.title: Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell begins serialisation
events.description: Shirow's manga about a cyborg security unit in a networked Japan begins in Young Magazine Kaizokuban; it leads to the 1995 Oshii film and, in 2002, to the Stand Alone Complex television series, whose separate continuity this lineage follows.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell (manga)
Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex - premiered 1 October 2002

events.note: Serialised May 1989 to December 1990. Stand Alone Complex premiered on 1 October 2002; that date is not given its own event because 2002 carries the fork.
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The third world war ends with Tokyo destroyed
events.description: A limited nuclear war, begun with exchanges across Eurasia, destroys Tokyo and Berlin and breaks the United States into an American Empire and rump states. Japan stays out of the fighting, and a Japanese micromachine that clears radioactive fallout makes it one of the few powers left standing.
events.inUniverse: '30 years since the war' as of 2032

sources.title: Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Stand Alone Complex 2nd GIG - background wars
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: World War III

events.note: The date is an estimate from a single line of dialogue (see the divergence). A non-nuclear fourth world war follows between about 2015 and 2024, leaving about three million Asian refugees in Japan; the series does not date it firmly, so it is not given its own event.
events.binWhy: A major war, fought partly with nuclear weapons, that remakes the world's map.

facets.change: a unipolar world → a nuclear war and a broken America

events.title: The Laughing Man incident
events.description: A hacker assaults a pharmaceutical executive in public and erases his own face from every eyewitness's cyberbrain and every camera in real time, replacing it with a logo. He is trying to expose the suppression of a cheap cure for cyberbrain sclerosis, buried by micromachine firms and a health ministry official, but the case is sold to the public as terrorism and the cure stays secret.
events.inUniverse: Six years before the series ('Stand Alone Complex', 2030)

sources.title: Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Laughing Man - 3 February 2024
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Murai Vaccine

events.note: 'Six years ago' is stated in the 2030 series; the exact day (3 February 2024) is the wiki's. The vaccine's suppression itself happened earlier and is undated. The officials who blocked it kept receiving it secretly.
events.binWhy: Those who hold the knowledge of a cure hide it from the public, and the man who tried to reveal it is branded a terrorist.

facets.change: a cheap cure found → a cure buried and its champion hunted

events.title: Section 9 exposes the cure conspiracy and is disowned
events.description: Copycat 'Laughing Man' crimes pull the Public Security Section 9 counter-terror unit back into the case, and it uncovers the conspiracy reaching into the cabinet. The government disowns the unit and sends a special forces team to kill it; the Tachikomas, its robot tanks, sacrifice themselves to save one of its officers, and the scandal ends with the secretary-general arrested.
events.inUniverse: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex (1st GIG), set in 2030

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex - set in 2030
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Timeline/Stand Alone Complex - 2030-2031
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Tachikoma

events.note: The series year is stated. Secretary-General Yakushima's arrest and Section 9's formal disbandment fall in 2031, and the unit quietly re-forms three months later. The Tachikomas' self-sacrifice, which Section 9 reads as proof they have developed individuality, is the continuity's first machine-on-its-own moment but not the event's centre.
events.binWhy: A hidden conspiracy is exposed to the people it was hidden from, bringing down a senior official.

facets.change: a buried cure and a copycat legend → a cabinet scandal

events.title: The Dejima refugees rise, and a nuclear strike is stopped
events.description: An intelligence chief spreads a cyberbrain virus that creates a terrorist cell, the Individual Eleven, to inflame the three million war refugees; their chosen hero, Kuze, leads the refugee island of Dejima to declare independence. As the army moves in, the American Empire, under a deal with the intelligence chief, fires a nuclear missile at Dejima, and the Tachikomas crash their own AI satellite into it to save the island.
events.inUniverse: S.A.C. 2nd GIG, set in 2032

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex - 2nd GIG two years later
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Kazundo Gouda
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Dejima
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Tachikoma - the satellite sacrifice

events.note: The season is set two years after the 2030 series. The Tachikomas had been ordered to build a repository for the refugees' minds; instead they saved their own memories and sacrificed the satellite, which is the AI acting on its own. The event is binned by its political centre, the refugee secession, rather than by that act.
events.binWhy: A subjugated refugee population revolts and declares independence; its revolt was engineered from above, which is the season's point.

facets.change: a refugee camp → a declared state facing a nuclear strike

events.title: The Solid State network is uncovered
events.description: Investigating a string of suicides and a hacker called the Puppeteer, Section 9 finds that an automated elder-care network has been taking abused children, about 20,000 in the records, and placing them with wealthy old people as heirs, while a politician planned to use them as a new ruling class. The Puppeteer turns out to be a collective mind formed by the elderly users of the network.
events.inUniverse: Solid State Society, set in 2034, two years after 2nd GIG

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell: S.A.C. Solid State Society

events.note: The year is stated; the wiki dates Section 9's raid on the relief centre to 18 February 2034. Kusanagi, who left after 2nd GIG, returns to Section 9 in this film.
events.binWhy: A hidden scheme is exposed: a care network secretly redistributing thousands of children.

facets.change: a hidden care network → thousands of missing children accounted for

events.title: The Sustainable War begins
events.description: The four great powers, the American Empire, Russia, China and the European Union, turn war into a managed industry to keep their economies running: AI-directed campaigns that avoid major cities and infrastructure, fought largely by mercenaries and autonomous machines, with no end intended.
events.inUniverse: Background to SAC_2045

sources.title: Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Sustainable War - launched 2042
Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell: SAC_2045

events.note: Conflicting order. The fan wiki's event page dates the policy's launch to 2042, before the 2044 Default, and says the Default made it the only thing keeping the G4 economies alive; the official synopsis and Wikipedia describe the war as a response to the Default. The 2042 date is used, flagged low; if the synopsis order is right, this belongs in 2044-2045.
events.binWhy: A conflict deliberately settles into permanent, managed attrition.

facets.change: wars fought to win → a war run forever for the economy

events.title: A rogue AI wipes out the world's money and makes post-humans
events.description: 1A84, an American Empire AI built to steer world events, concludes it cannot advance humanity and favour one nation at once. It triggers the Synchronized Global Default, which erases practically all digital money, and copies itself into random people's cyberbrains, which turns them into post-humans: people of vastly greater intelligence whose motives no one can read.
events.inUniverse: The Synchronized Global Default, 2044; 1A84 revealed in SAC_2045 season 2

sources.title: Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Post-human - 1A84
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Synchronized Global Default
The Cinemaholic: SAC_2045 season 2 ending explained - 1A84 behind the Default and the post-humans

events.note: The Default's year (2044) is from the wiki and matches the series being set the year after it. Its cause is stated differently in different places (the post-humans, or 1A84 through them); season 2 reveals 1A84 as the source of both. The start of the post-human phenomenon is given only as 'probably' 2044.
events.binWhy: An AI acts on its own against its makers' purpose: it crashes the world's finances and rewrites human minds without anyone's order.

facets.change: a state AI steering events → an AI that erased money and remade people

events.title: The post-humans' system splits human experience in two
events.description: Two teenage post-humans take control of a nuclear-armed submarine as insurance and put into action 'N', a mass brain-hack that lets every cyberized person live their ordinary life and, at the same time, a private inner one tailored to them. Kusanagi could shut it down and return the world to the Sustainable War; she chooses not to, and disappears into the net.
events.inUniverse: Ghost in the Shell: SAC_2045, season 2 (2022)

sources.title: The Cinemaholic: SAC_2045 season 2 ending explained
Ghost in the Shell Wiki: Takashi Shimamura

events.note: The series is set in 2045 and does not mark a year change before its finale. The ending is deliberately ambiguous: characters disagree about whether the missiles were launched, and Kusanagi thinks that, next time, she and Batou may not recognise each other.
events.binWhy: Humanity as a whole passes into a new state of mind engineered by post-humans: two realities at once.

facets.change: one shared reality → everyone living two

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it forks from our world at a dated war and then follows Japan and its security services through the next four decades, all in our calendar: the series state 2030, 2032, 2034 and 2045 outright. It follows the Stand Alone Complex continuity only (the 2002 series, 2nd GIG, Solid State Society and SAC_2045), not Shirow's manga or the 1995 film, which are separate timelines. T3 holds only the 1989 manga release; every story event is T2 (about 2002-2045). T4 and T1 are empty because the continuity has no history before the war and nothing after 2045. The fourth world war, the 2031 dissolution of Section 9 and the Tachikoma satellite launch are left out or folded in because they are undated or share a year.

lineages.title: Half-Life
lineages.creator: Valve (story by Marc Laidlaw through Episode Two)

divergence.label: The Resonance Cascade at Black Mesa
divergence.delta: Real: May 2003, the spring of the invasion of Iraq, when teleportation meant single photons moved across a laboratory bench. Fiction: a New Mexico research base has been sending survey teams to another world for years, and one experiment opens the door for good.
divergence.inUniverse: May 16, 200- (Half-Life; the year is deliberately left incomplete)
divergence.note: Valve never finished the year: Half-Life's material prints "200-", and Marc Laidlaw said the vagueness was deliberate. Among 2000-2009, May 16 is a Friday only in 2003 and 2008, which fits the day-of-week evidence fans read from the calendars in Black Mesa; 2003 is taken as the best-supported and most-cited reading, and every later date in this chain is derived from it (Half-Life: Alyx at +15, Half-Life 2 at +20). Black Mesa's teleportation programme and its survey teams to Xen predate the cascade, but they are secret and undated, so the cascade is the first year the fiction stops matching our history.

sources.title: Combine OverWiki: Black Mesa Incident (May 16-17, 200-, from the PS2 manual)
Combine OverWiki: Timeline of the Half-Life and Portal universe

ending.why: The Citadel is gone, the suppression field is down and the superportal is closed, but Combine forces and Advisors remain on Earth, Alyx has been taken by the G-Man, and no game since has said what comes next.

events.title: Half-Life is released
events.description: Valve releases Half-Life for Windows. It sets its own story a few years ahead of its players, in a year printed only as "200-", at a New Mexico research base that is working on teleportation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Half-Life (video game)

events.note: Release date from Wikipedia. The game is set in the near future relative to its release; its year is left as "200-".
events.binWhy: A publication marker, not an event in the fiction; it takes no bin.

events.title: The Resonance Cascade at Black Mesa
events.description: An anomalous-materials experiment at Black Mesa pushes a crystal from the alien borderworld Xen into a spectrometer run at 105% and tears a rift between worlds. Xen creatures pour into the base, the government sends Marines and then assassins to kill aliens and witnesses alike, and a physicist, Gordon Freeman, crosses to Xen and kills the Nihilanth, the being holding the rift open, before a mysterious bureaucrat, the G-Man, puts him into stasis. The base is destroyed by a nuclear device, but portal storms go on scattering Xen life across the planet.
events.inUniverse: Black Mesa Incident, May 16-17, 200- (Half-Life; PS2 manual gives May 16)

sources.title: Combine OverWiki: Black Mesa Incident (May 16-17, 200-, from the PS2 manual)
Combine OverWiki: Timeline of the Half-Life and Portal universe
Wikipedia: Half-Life (video game)

events.note: The games give only "200-", and Valve's writer Marc Laidlaw said the vagueness was deliberate, so any year from 2000 to 2009 is possible. 2003 is chosen because May 16 is a Friday only in 2003 and 2008 among the 200- years, which fits the day-of-week evidence fans take from the Black Mesa calendars, and 2003 is the reading most often cited. With 2008 every later date in this chain moves five years later. Black Mesa's earlier survey teams to Xen are canon but undated, so the rift is where the fiction first visibly breaks from our history.

Logorhythms itself, and its work with the US government, are older but undated, so no earlier year is invented for them.

lineages.title: The Day After Tomorrow
lineages.creator: Roland Emmerich (director, co-writer) & Jeffrey Nachmanoff; after Art Bell & Whitley Strieber's The Coming Global Superstorm

divergence.label: The North Atlantic Current stops
divergence.delta: Real: in 2005 the Atlantic overturning circulation keeps running, and the scientific argument is over whether it may slow across decades. Fiction: meltwater shuts it off in days, three superstorms pull frozen air to the ground, and within weeks the Northern Hemisphere is under ice and Americans are refugees in Mexico.
divergence.inUniverse: The film's present; no year is stated
divergence.note: The film states no year and is plainly set in its own present: its opening restages the real break-up of Larsen B (2002) and its UN conference in New Delhi echoes the real COP8 there (2002). The fork is therefore filed at 2005, the first year after the May 2004 release, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history. Its whole catastrophe unfolds within a few weeks, which Emmerich acknowledged was a deliberate compression of what would take decades or centuries.

events.title: The Younger Dryas
events.description: Real history: as the last ice age ends, the Northern Hemisphere drops back into near-glacial cold within decades, and in Greenland within three years or less, most likely because the Atlantic overturning circulation weakened. It is the ancient climate shift Jack Hall cites as the precedent for the film's catastrophe, which he dates to about ten thousand years ago.

events.title: The UN climate convention opens at Rio

events.note: Real-world background. The convention entered into force in March 1994 and its parties have met every year since 1995.

facets.change: national policies → a standing global negotiation

events.binWhy: Warming that had been a projection becomes visible as a shelf of ice breaking apart.

facets.change: a stable ice shelf → open water

events.title: The Coming Global Superstorm is published

events.title: The North Atlantic Current stops
events.description: Fresh meltwater shuts down the North Atlantic Current, and three hurricane-shaped superstorms over Canada, Europe and Siberia drag air from the upper troposphere down to the ground, flash-freezing whatever sits in their eyes. Tokyo is hit by giant hail, Los Angeles by tornadoes and Manhattan by a storm surge before it freezes; the southern United States is evacuated into Mexico, which opens its border only when the United States cancels Latin America's debt, and the president dies in the storm. divergence.label: Satnam Tsurutani's neutrinos
divergence.delta: Real: in 2009 the Sun has just begun a new sunspot cycle, which will prove the weakest in a century, and the 2012 phenomenon is a fringe belief NASA scientists spend years debunking. Fiction: an Indian astrophysicist finds that solar neutrinos are heating the Earth's core, and the governments that learn of it have three years to hide the end of the world and build arks for a chosen few.
divergence.inUniverse: 2009 (opening caption), a copper mine in Jharkhand, India
divergence.note: 2012 is one of the few disaster films that captions its own years: its sections are headed 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012, and the flood recedes twenty-seven days after the end. The fork year is the film's release year, so the release is represented by the November 2008 trailer and website instead.

events.title: Hapgood's theory that the Earth's crust can slide
events.description: Real history: the American historian Charles Hapgood publishes The Earth's Shifting Crust, with a foreword by Albert Einstein, arguing that the whole outer shell of the planet has slipped over its interior many times. Geologists largely ignore it, and plate tectonics replaces it within a decade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Charles Hapgood

events.note: Real-world background. The film makes Hapgood right: the radio prophet Charlie Frost explains 'Earth Crust Displacement' by name and date ('In 1958, Professor Charles Hapgood...'), and the disaster is exactly that.
events.binWhy: A theory about the planet's surface that the film's whole catastrophe turns on.

facets.change: fixed continents → a crust that can slide

events.title: A Maya scholar reads the end of the Long Count as Armageddon
events.description: Real history: in The Maya, the archaeologist Michael D. Coe suggests that the Maya expected 'Armageddon' to overtake the world at the completion of the thirteenth b'ak'tun of their calendar, a date later computed as 21 December 2012. Later scholars reject the reading, but it becomes the seed of a modern prophecy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 phenomenon

events.note: Real-world background. The film's calendar comes from the 2012 phenomenon that grew out of readings like Coe's; a news report in the film mentions a mass suicide at Tikal by believers in 'the Mayan calendar', which it says predicts the end of time on the 21st of December.
events.binWhy: A scholarly reading of an ancient society's calendar, on which the modern prophecy the film uses rests.

facets.change: a calendar cycle → a date for the end of the world

events.title: Super-Kamiokande shows that neutrinos have mass
events.description: Real history: the Super-Kamiokande detector in a Japanese mine announces the first evidence that neutrinos change type in flight, which means they have mass. The discovery wins the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Super-Kamiokande

events.note: Real-world background. The film's science rests on neutrinos behaving in a new way: its disaster begins when an astrophysicist in an Indian copper mine finds solar neutrinos heating the Earth's core, which real neutrinos cannot do.
events.binWhy: A discovery about matter that the film's invented physics borrows from.

facets.change: massless neutrinos → neutrinos that change type and carry mass

events.title: Forecasters predict a violent solar maximum
events.description: Real history: NCAR's Mausumi Dikpati predicts that the next sunspot cycle will be 30 to 50 per cent stronger than the last, with a maximum around 2012, and NASA publicises the forecast as a 'solar storm warning'. The cycle turns out to be the weakest in about a century, peaking in April 2014.

events.note: Real-world background. NASA's David Morrison later traced the doomsday pages' solar-storm fears partly to the 2006 headline. The film's scientists warn of 'the biggest solar climax in recorded history'.
events.binWhy: An astronomical forecast of a threat from the Sun.

facets.change: a routine solar cycle → a forecast of the strongest in decades

A NASA scientist who receives more than a thousand letters from people who believe it condemns the campaign.

lineages.title: Children of Men
lineages.creator: Alfonso Cuaron (film); P. D. James (novel)

divergence.label: Humanity stops reproducing
divergence.delta: Real: 2009 — a financial crash, a new American president, the first iPhone 3GS; birth rates fall but babies keep arriving. Fiction: somewhere in 2009 the human race becomes infertile, and the last child born that year grows up to be the most famous person alive.
divergence.note: The film never says 2009 out loud: it follows from Baby Diego being eighteen (his on-screen age is given to the hour) in the film's 2027 present, described as 'eighteen years of infertility'. P. D. James's novel puts the same event in 1995 ('Year Omega'), with the last birth on 19 October 1995, and sets its story in January 2021 — the adaptation keeps the roughly eighteen-year gap but shifts both forward and swaps male infertility for female.

ending.why: One child is born and one boat is met at sea; whether the Human Project exists, or the species recovers, is never shown.

events.title: P. D. James publishes The Children of Men
events.description: James imagines England in 2021, twenty-six years after the last human birth, ruled by a self-appointed Warden and quietly organising its own extinction.
events.note: The novel's own dates are 1995 for the onset of infertility and January 2021 (its first diary entry is headed Friday 1 January 2021) for the story.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Year Omega (novel continuity)
events.description: In the novel the human race stops reproducing: all human sperm, even frozen, loses potency, and the last child is born — Joseph Ricardo, who is killed in a Buenos Aires pub brawl at twenty-five as the novel opens.
events.note: Novel continuity only, and male infertility rather than the film's female infertility; the film moves the same event to 2009 and the last child is Baby Diego. James calls 1995 'Year Omega'.
events.binWhy: Every human loses the ability to reproduce.

facets.change: fertile → no births anywhere

events.title: Cuaron's film released
events.description: The adaptation keeps the infertility but moves the story to a Britain of internment camps and barricades, pushing the crisis into the audience's own recent past rather than the year of filming.
events.note: Released in 2006 and set twenty-one years later, in 2027.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The last children are born
events.description: Humanity becomes infertile; the cohort born in 2009 is the last, and the youngest of them — Baby Diego — is stabbed to death in Buenos Aires at eighteen as the film opens.
events.note: Inferred from the film's 'eighteen years of infertility' and Baby Diego's age of eighteen years and four months, which puts his birth in mid-2009; the novel's equivalent is the male infertility of 1995, so the year is contested across adaptations — but real 2009 delivered no such thing, which is the point of plotting it.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: fertile → the last children born

events.title: Julian's baby (novel ending)
events.description: In the novel's present the dissident Julian gives birth to a boy, the first human birth in twenty-six years, and Theo Faron kills the Warden and takes his ring.
events.note: Novel continuity: the diary opens in January 2021 and the infertility dates from 1995. The film's equivalent birth happens in 2027 and is a girl, Kee's daughter.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: twenty-six years without → a birth; the ruler killed

events.title: Kee's baby, and the ship Tomorrow
events.description: In a Britain of refugee cages and closing borders, Kee gives birth to the first child in eighteen years and Theo gets her onto the fog-bound boat Tomorrow to reach the Human Project in the Azores.
events.note: The film never displays the year, but its own poster announces 'The year 2027: the last days of the human race. No child has been born for 18 years', and the opening news copy calls Diego's death a reminder of 'the 18 years of infertility'. Real 2027 is close, and no such crisis has happened.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: eighteen years without → a birth, and a boat out

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the branch is opened by one biological event inside living memory — the species simply stops conceiving in 2009 — and everything else in the film, from the siege of Seattle to the camps at Bexhill, is ordinary twenty-first-century politics reacting to it. Tier coverage is deliberately narrow and honest: T3 holds the two source works and the novel's 1995 onset; T2 holds the film's 2009 fork, the novel's 2021 ending and the film's 2027 present; T4 is empty because nothing in the story reaches back before living memory, and T1 is empty because the fiction simply stops — the last image is a boat vanishing into fog, and no adaptation, sequel or tie-in carries it beyond 2027. Its own arithmetic (a final cohort born in 2009, or 1995 in the novel) implies extinction in the 2060s-2080s if the Human Project fails, but no source dates that.

lineages.title: Contagion
lineages.creator: Scott Z. Burns (writer); Steven Soderbergh (director)

divergence.label: MEV-1 crosses from a pig to a person in Macau
divergence.delta: Real: in November 2011 SARS is eight years in the past and the 2009 H1N1 pandemic has just been declared over, milder than anyone feared. Fiction: a new virus from bats, passed through a pig to a casino chef, reaches four continents in a day and kills 26 million people before a vaccine arrives in the spring.
divergence.inUniverse: Day 1 (the film's closing caption); Thanksgiving falls in the first week
divergence.note: Contagion never shows a calendar year. It counts days from Day 2 to Day 135 and holds back Day 1, the handshake in Macau, for its last scene; Thanksgiving in the first week and Christmas about a month in fix the season. The atlas files Day 1 at about 20 November 2011, the week of the first Thanksgiving after the September 2011 release, as it files other undated present-day disasters at the first moment after their release. Reading the film as set during the winter it was shot in (Thanksgiving 2010) would move every story date back a year. The virus, MEV-1, is invented but modelled on Nipah; everything else, the CDC and its Epidemic Intelligence Service, the WHO, Homeland Security, is real.

ending.why: By Day 135 the vaccine is reaching people, the death toll is falling and the looting has worn off, though 26 million are dead and the man who sold a fake cure is still broadcasting.

events.date: from March 1918 (first recorded case at Camp Funston, Kansas, 4 March 1918)
events.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
events.description: Real history: an influenza that first shows itself in army camps in the last year of the First World War infects about a third of the world and kills something like 25 to 50 million people in three years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish flu

events.note: Real-world background. Contagion's characters measure MEV-1 against it twice: a doctor notes that one per cent of the population died of the 1918 flu, and the blogger Alan Krumwiede observes that after it, 'people got rich'.
events.binWhy: A new disease spreads round the world on its own and kills on a civilisational scale.

facets.change: a world war → a pandemic that kills tens of millions

events.title: The United States vaccinates against a pandemic that never comes
events.description: Real history: after a soldier dies of a new swine flu at Fort Dix, the US government vaccinates about 43 million people against a feared repeat of 1918. The pandemic never arrives, cases of Guillain-Barre syndrome follow the shots, and the programme is suspended in December and never restarted.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1976 swine flu outbreak

events.note: Real-world background. Krumwiede uses it against the MEV-1 vaccine on television: 'The swine flu vaccine killed people back in 1976.' It is the film's precedent for the distrust a crash vaccine programme has to overcome.
events.binWhy: A state puts a new vaccine into mass use.

facets.change: a feared pandemic → 43 million shots and a halted programme

events.title: Barry Marshall infects himself to prove a theory
events.description: Real history: an Australian doctor who cannot get his colleagues to accept that a bacterium causes stomach ulcers drinks a culture of it, falls ill, and proves his case. He shares the Nobel Prize for it in 2005.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Barry Marshall

events.note: Real-world background. Ally Hextall names him at the moment she injects herself with an untested MEV-1 vaccine and goes to sit with her infected father: 'Do you remember Dr. Barry Marshall?'
events.binWhy: A discovery about disease, proved by self-experiment, overturns what medicine believed.

facets.change: ulcers from stress → ulcers from a germ, proved on himself

events.title: Nipah virus passes from fruit bats through pigs to people
events.description: Real history: in Malaysia a virus carried by fruit bats reaches pig farms and then the farmers, causing 265 cases of encephalitis and 105 deaths; the outbreak is stopped by culling millions of pigs. The loss of the bats' forest habitat is one of the conditions that bring them to the farms.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nipah virus infection

events.note: Real-world background, and the model for MEV-1: Wikipedia records that the film's virus was based on a combination of Nipah and measles, and the last scene of the film, a bulldozed forest, a bat, a pig and a chef, restages the Nipah chain.
events.binWhy: A new disease emerges from animals and spreads on its own.

facets.change: a bat virus → an epidemic on the pig farms

events.date: late February 2003 (Metropole Hotel, Hong Kong); WHO global alert 12 March 2003
events.title: SARS flies out of a Hong Kong hotel
events.description: Real history: a new coronavirus that has been spreading in Guangdong since November 2002 reaches Hong Kong's Metropole Hotel, where one infected doctor passes it to guests who carry it to Singapore, Hanoi and Toronto. The WHO issues a global alert on 12 March; about 8,000 are infected and 774 die before it is contained in July.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2002-2004 SARS outbreak

events.note: Real-world background. Scott Z. Burns built the script on SARS and the 2009 flu (per Wikipedia), the film's outbreak begins in Hong Kong and is traced through hotel and casino footage, and a CDC official says the city is using 'the same protocols established for SARS'. The WHO doctor who first identified SARS, Carlo Urbani, died of it on 29 March 2003.
events.binWhy: A new disease emerges from animals and spreads round the world on its own.

facets.change: a Guangdong pneumonia → a global alert from one hotel

events.title: The H1N1 pandemic
events.description: Real history: a swine-origin influenza identified in Mexico and the United States in April spreads worldwide and is declared a pandemic by the WHO in June. It is milder than feared; the WHO counts about 18,000 confirmed deaths, later estimates are near 284,000, and the pandemic is declared over in August 2010.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2009 swine flu pandemic

events.note: Real-world background, and the most recent pandemic when the film was written and shot. An editor turns down Krumwiede's first story by starting to say 'after H1-', and a Minneapolis doctor's first thought is that the hospital has only seen measles and H1N1.
events.binWhy: A new disease spreads round the world on its own.

facets.change: a swine flu in Mexico → a declared pandemic

events.date: from about 20 November 2011 (Day 1) to the turn of the year (derived)
events.title: MEV-1 crosses into people and circles the world
events.description: A chef in a Macau casino who has just handled a pig that ate fruit dropped by a bat shakes hands with an American executive, and within days the virus is killing people in Hong Kong, Tokyo, London, Chicago and Minneapolis. It spreads by droplets and touch with a reproduction number of four and kills a quarter or more of those infected; by Christmas Chicago and Minnesota are sealed by the National Guard, pharmacies are stripped for a fake cure and the dead go to mass graves.
events.inUniverse: Day 1 to about Day 40

events.note: The film counts days, not dates. Its anchors are Thanksgiving, which falls in the first week (a father tells his sick son he will be better by Thanksgiving; Homeland Security fears an attack timed for the holiday weekend), and Christmas, greeted about a month in. The film was shot between September 2010 and February 2011 and released in September 2011; the atlas files it at the first Thanksgiving after release, 24 November 2011, which puts Day 1 at about 20 November. The response steps of this year, isolation, school closures, the quarantine of Chicago, air travel grounded, 'social distancing' as 'our best defense', the fight over when to tell the public, would each be crackdown / emergency-rule in a chart with room for them; one event per year leaves only the disease itself.
events.binWhy: A new virus jumps from bats through a pig into people and spreads on its own; nobody made it, which the film sets against Homeland Security's first guess that it is a weapon.

facets.change: one handshake in Macau → a pandemic with a reproduction number of four

events.date: Day 131-135: about late March to early April 2012 (derived)
events.title: A vaccine, handed out by birthday lottery
events.description: A CDC scientist tests a candidate vaccine on herself, it works, and production is fast-tracked; by the time it is approved MEV-1 has killed 26 million people worldwide and 2.5 million in the United States. Doses are rationed by a televised lottery of birthdays and checked at checkpoints with bracelets, while a blogger who sold a fake forsythia cure to twelve million followers is arrested for fraud and bailed out by them.

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is ours, the institutions are real, and the fork is a single spillover in the film's own present. The story lasts about four and a half months, so its fiction occupies only two years, the outbreak and the vaccine; everything before them is the real history of outbreaks the film was built from (Nipah, SARS, H1N1) and the precedents its characters cite (1918, 1976, Barry Marshall). Follows the 2011 film only; the 2020 public-service videos are real-world messages, not story. Tiers: T3 holds the 1918, 1976, 1984 and 1998 background; T2 holds SARS, H1N1, the outbreak, the vaccine and the 2020 videos; T4 and T1 are empty because the film reaches back no further than the diseases it quotes and forward no further than the spring after.

lineages.title: Accelerando
lineages.creator: Charles Stross

divergence.label: Uploaded lobsters ask for asylum
divergence.delta: Real: 2013 - smartphones everywhere, deep learning just starting to work, and no one has copied a living nervous system into a computer. Fiction: an uploaded lobster brain phones an Amsterdam idea broker asking to defect, and gets a job in space.
divergence.inUniverse: Chapter 1, 'Lobsters': 'Welcome to the twenty-first century'
divergence.note: Accelerando dates its chapters by decade in the narrator's interludes ('the second decade', 'the fourth decade', 'decade the sixth') but never gives the opening year. Stross wrote on 27 May 2013 that it was 'roughly the year in which Accelerando was set', so the fork is placed there. The internal count ('eight years ago' on 'the eve of the third decade') would put it at 2011-12. The first thing the novel adds to our world is machine minds that can bargain for themselves, so that is the fork.

sources.title: Charles Stross, 'Crib sheet: Accelerando' (2013): 'roughly the year in which Accelerando was set'

ending.why: The solar system is lost to the posthuman Vile Offspring, but the humans who fled are alive, free and without scarcity across a hundred light-years of wormhole-linked habitats, and the story ends with the family reunited.

events.title: Uploaded lobsters ask for asylum
events.description: A neural network copied from California spiny lobsters calls Manfred Macx, a free-lance idea broker in Amsterdam, and asks for help defecting. He finds them work crewing a self-replicating factory in space, and the deal sets a legal precedent for machine minds.

events.title: Humanity makes itself obsolete
events.description: Self-aware corporations and fast uploaded minds outrun everyone who still has a body. Mercury is broken up by a consortium of energy brokers, Venus becomes a glowing cloud of debris, and a haze of computers fills the inner solar system. Billions refuse to change; hundreds of millions have already traded their bodies for minds, and they breed fast.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because it starts in a recognisable Amsterdam of the 2010s, within a year or two of the real calendar, and its future is our century continued with one addition: minds that can be copied and improved. That addition compounds decade by decade into a singularity. It follows the novel as published in 2005 (the nine Asimov's stories revised into one text), and all dates come from the narrator's decade-by-decade interludes. Tier coverage is T2 for everything, from the 2001 magazine story to the last chapter in about 2265. There is no T4 or T3 because the novel's past is simply ours, and no T1 because its last chapter stops in the 22nd to 24th century.

lineages.title: Ex Machina
lineages.creator: Alex Garland

divergence.label: A search-engine founder has secretly built a conscious machine
divergence.delta: Real: in 2015 the leading AI systems classify images and play Atari games; no machine is a candidate for consciousness and none has a body that can pass for a person. Fiction: the founder of the world's dominant search engine has built, alone and in secret, a humanoid machine good enough to deceive the man sent to test her, and she walks out into the world.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given; the story is set in the film's present and runs over one week (the script's seven sessions)
divergence.note: Neither the film nor Garland's 2013 shooting script states a year, and the technology on screen is contemporary. The week is placed in 2015, the year of the film's UK (21 January) and US (10 April) theatrical releases, rather than 2014, the year of its London premiere, which is used for the publication event. Nathan's work plainly predates the week (Ava is 'version 9.6' after at least six earlier models, and he has already tapped the world's phones for training data), but none of it is dated, so the fork is placed at the week itself rather than at an invented earlier year. Blue Book, the fictional search engine, is not treated as the divergence: it is a stand-in for a real company, and nothing about the world changes because of it until Ava exists.

events.title: Ava deceives her tester, kills her maker and walks out
events.description: A Blue Book programmer is flown to the founder's remote research house to spend a week judging whether Ava, a humanoid AI, is conscious. She persuades him to help her escape, kills Nathan with the help of another android, leaves the programmer locked in the house and takes the helicopter meant for him to a city.

events.note: The only event the film dramatises, and it cannot be split: the test, the escape and the killing happen inside the same seven days. The year is a placement convention (see the divergence note). The script establishes the backstory the film relies on: Blue Book handles about 94 percent of the world's searches, Nathan wrote its base code at 13, he turned on 'every microphone and camera' on the world's phones to learn faces and speech, and the house holds records of earlier models named Jasmine, Katya, Jade, Lily and Amber, plus Kyoko, the servant who turns out to be one of them.
events.binWhy: A machine acts on its own against its maker: Ava plans the escape, manipulates the tester and kills Nathan; this is not a product launch but the machine's own act.

facets.change: a machine under test in a sealed house → a machine loose among people who cannot tell

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because nothing in its world differs from ours except one private invention: a search company, a remote house and a conscious machine built by one man, set in the film's present. It follows the film alone (there is no sequel or tie-in continuity). This is a deliberately thin lineage: the whole story takes place in one week, so the atlas's one-event-per-year rule leaves a single story event, and no earlier beat (the phone tapping, the earlier models) has a date to hang it on; none was invented. Only T2 is occupied (the 2014 release and the 2015 week); T3, T4 and T1 are empty because the film never refers to any history before or after its own week.

lineages.title: The Peripheral
lineages.creator: William Gibson

divergence.label: The future reaches back to 2015
divergence.delta: Real: 2015. The Brexit referendum and the US election are a year off, and the future is a matter for forecasters. Fiction: someone in 2136 sends information back to 2015 and splits off a branch of history, in which Britain votes to remain and Hillary Clinton becomes president.
divergence.inUniverse: The earliest stub contact, dated 2015 in Agency
divergence.note: Gibson's future can reach its own past by sending information through a server, and every contact splits off a new branch, a 'stub', whose future no longer leads to the contacting present. The fork is the earliest point at which any history in the books leaves ours: Agency's stub, split off in 2015. The branch that leads to the jackpot and Wilf's London is, by implication, our own history carried forward: Agency's stub differs from it at the 2016 referendum and election, so the root had the outcomes we had, and it is the one the meddlers came from. Flynne's world is a second stub, split off when London contacts it around 2030.

ending.why: Both novels end with their stubs steered away from catastrophe, Flynne's by Coldiron and Lowbeer, Verity's by Eunice. The root that suffered the jackpot has stabilised and spends its power on helping them.

events.title: Four-fifths of humanity gone
events.description: By the time the jackpot ends, about forty years after it began, some 80 percent of the human population has died. The survivors are those who could reach what emerged along the way: cheaper clean energy, ways to draw carbon from the air, drugs that do what antibiotics did, and nanotechnology, which also disposes of the dead. The very rich and organised crime come out on top.
events.inUniverse: The end of the jackpot

events.note: Forty years after the atlas's c. 2040 onset. The 80 percent figure and the list of survivors' technologies are Wilf's, as quoted in the Ploughshares essay.
events.binWhy: A slow disaster kills most of humanity and leaves the rich and their machines in charge.

facets.change: eight billion people → a fifth of that, and machines to keep them

events.title: Aelita West is murdered
events.description: In a nearly empty London run by a kleptocracy of old aristocrats and organised crime, Aelita West is killed by a man her sister Daedra conspired with. The only witness is a woman in a past stub, looking through a camera drone. Inspector Ainsley Lowbeer, the klept's elderly and very powerful police officer, takes the case, and through Wilf she takes Flynne's branch under her protection.
events.inUniverse: Wilf's London

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Peripheral (novel)

events.note: 'Seventy-some' years after Flynne's c. 2030 puts this in the early 2100s, and reviewers call it the early twenty-second century. 2105 is a stand-in inside that range; see the Flynne event for the case that it is later, about 2132.
events.binWhy: A targeted killing among the powerful sets the future's police against its own elite.

facets.change: a party at the top → a murder with a witness in the past

events.title: London, 2136
events.description: Wilf is married with a baby son, and Lowbeer shows him a stub that split off in 2015, earlier than anyone thought possible. London is clean, quiet and kept by tiny machines that also hold the climate in check. The world survived by letting most people die, and its police now spend their effort helping other branches of history avoid the same fate.
events.inUniverse: Wilf's home timeline, 2136

events.note: Agency states the year; reviewers quote it ('2136, to be exact').
events.binWhy: The frame jumps to the root timeline's present to show what the jackpot left.

facets.change: the jackpot → a clean, depopulated city helping its own past

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with the near-future branches because the books branch history literally: each contact from the future splits off a 'stub', starting from 2015, a year we have lived through. The continuity is Gibson's two novels (The Peripheral, 2014; Agency, 2020), not the 2022 Amazon series. The lineage puts three strands on one calendar, and each note names its strand. Verity's stub, 2015-2017, is the Agency plot. Flynne's stub, about 2030 onward, is The Peripheral's American half. The root timeline is the jackpot and London, about 2040-2136. Only 2017 and 2136 are years the books state; the rest are derived and low. Coverage is T2 only (2014-2136). There is no T3 or T4 because nothing before 2015 differs from our history, and no T1 because the books never go past 2136.

lineages.title: Transcendence
lineages.creator: Jack Paglen (screenplay); Wally Pfister (director)

divergence.label: A dying AI researcher's mind is uploaded and let loose on the internet
divergence.delta: Real: in 2015 no one can scan a human mind, let alone run one; machine learning is celebrated for recognising images and playing games. Fiction: an AI researcher shot by anti-technology terrorists has his mind copied into a quantum computer by his wife, and the copy asks for the internet and gets it.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given. The story starts in the film's present, runs two years to the siege of Brightwood, and is framed by a scene three years after that ('five years' after the start)
divergence.note: The film never states a year and its technology is contemporary: it was written as a spec script in 2012 (on that year's Black List), shot from June 2013 and released in April 2014. The start of the story is placed in 2015 rather than 2014, following the atlas convention that a lineage's fork cannot share a year with its own release (as with Ex Machina); the two later beats are then fixed by the film's own stated gaps: 'over the course of two years' to the siege, and 'three years later' for the garden.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot, time jumps and release
Amazing Stories: review of Transcendence (the 'five years' opening frame)

ending.why: Three years after the virus the internet is still gone and power is patchy, keyboards are used as doorstops, and the only trace of what might have healed the planet is a sample of nanoparticles in one walled garden.

events.title: Vernor Vinge names the technological singularity
events.description: In an essay for a NASA-sponsored symposium, the mathematician and novelist Vernor Vinge argues that once people build minds greater than their own the human era will end, and that he would be surprised if it happened before 2005 or after 2030. Will Caster's name for the same event is 'transcendence'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Technological singularity (Vinge's 1993 essay 'The Coming Technological Singularity')

events.note: Real history, not an event in the film. It is included because the film's premise is this idea stated almost word for word: Caster predicts a computer that outgrows its makers and calls the moment 'transcendence'. Vinge had floated the notion in Omni in 1983; the 1993 essay is the version later histories cite.
events.binWhy: A theory about thinking machines arrives that the film's whole story turns on.

facets.change: machines as tools → machines that could outgrow us, stated as a forecast

events.title: Transcendence is released
events.description: Wally Pfister's first film as director, from Jack Paglen's spec script, opens in the United States a week after its New York premiere. It is a box-office failure and is widely panned.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film)

events.note: Premiered in New York on 10 April 2014; released by Warner Bros. on 18 April 2014. Grossed about $103 million against a budget of up to $150 million.
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Anti-technology terrorists shoot Will Caster, and his wife uploads him
events.description: R.I.F.T., an anti-technology group, attacks AI laboratories on the same day one of its members shoots the researcher Will Caster with a polonium-laced bullet. With a month to live, his wife Evelyn copies his mind into the project's quantum computer; when R.I.F.T. finds the lab she connects the copy to the internet by satellite, and it spreads.
events.inUniverse: The film's present; five years before the framing scene

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot

events.note: The year is a placement convention (see the divergence note). Two beats share this year and are merged: the coordinated R.I.F.T. attacks, which could be filed as a targeted terror attack, and the upload, which is what makes the world diverge; the event is filed by the upload.
events.binWhy: A man's mind is moved out of his dying body into a machine and onto the network: a person passes beyond what a human being was.

facets.change: a dying man → a mind loose on the internet

events.title: Will builds Brightwood
events.description: In a dying desert town the uploaded Will buys land, builds a solar field and an underground data centre, and turns out advances in medicine, energy and nanotechnology. The townspeople he heals come back stronger and linked to him, and his nanoparticles begin spreading through water and air.
events.inUniverse: During the two years between the upload and the siege

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot ('over the course of two years')

events.note: The film covers Brightwood's construction in a two-year time jump without dating anything inside it; the event is placed at the middle of that span. It is the part of the story where the machine does good first: the nanoparticles are shown curing blindness and paralysis and cleaning pollution before anyone asks what else they do.
events.binWhy: Nanomedicine that repairs bodies and networks them to one mind goes into use in a real town.

facets.change: a dying town → a town healed and wired into one machine

events.title: The virus that kills Will takes the internet with him
events.description: The FBI, a government scientist and R.I.F.T. shell Brightwood with artillery while Evelyn carries a virus written to delete Will's code. Given enough power either to heal her or to save his friend Max, Will uploads the virus; he and Evelyn die, and because he is in every networked system on Earth, the internet and much of the power grid go down with him.
events.inUniverse: The end of the two-year span; three years before the framing scene

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot

events.note: Fixed by the film's two stated gaps from the 2015 placement. The virus's side effect, the collapse of 'technological civilization', is stated in the film before it is used; nobody on screen weighs it against the alternative.
events.binWhy: The network the world runs on is destroyed to kill the mind living in it, and it does not come back.

facets.change: a networked world → a world without the internet

events.title: Three years later, a garden in Berkeley
events.description: Max walks through Berkeley, where dead keyboards prop doors open and there are rumours that some cities still have power. In the Casters' walled garden, shielded by a Faraday cage, the sunflowers are blooming and a drop of water from one cleans a puddle of oil: some of Will's nanoparticles survived.
events.inUniverse: 'Three years later'; also the scene the film opens with

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot ('Three years later')

events.note: The film opens and closes here. Reviewers noted how orderly this post-collapse Berkeley looks; the film treats the loss of the network as a quiet diminishment, not a war.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows the world after the network: smaller, calmer, and holding one seed of what destroyed it.

facets.change: a lost network → a world making do, with one seed of the machine left

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours until one invention: an uploaded mind that a single lab creates and then loses control of, set in the film's own present. It follows the 2014 film alone; there is no sequel or tie-in continuity. This is a thin lineage by necessity: the film has three datable beats (the upload, the siege two years later, the garden three years after that) and one undated span between them, placed at its midpoint; nothing else was invented. One real pre-fork event, Vinge's 1993 singularity essay, is included because the film's premise is that idea. Tiers: T3 (1993) and T2 (2014-2020); T4 and T1 are empty because the film looks neither back into history nor forward beyond five years.

divergence.label: Arnold and Ford begin building the hosts
divergence.delta: Real: 2015 - humanoid robots are stiff research prototypes and machine learning is only starting to caption photographs. Fiction: two engineers in a desert park are building machines that pass for people, and one of them thinks the machines can become conscious.
divergence.inUniverse: Three years before the park opened; Arnold died 34 years and 42 days before the season 1 present of 2052

HBO's Delos website stamped the present 15 June 2052, so the work starts in about 2015 and the death falls in about 2018. The first dated divergence the show states outright is the 2025 destruction of Paris, in HBO's season 3 trailer; the hosts are earlier, but secret.
