lineages.title: Arrival
lineages.creator: Denis Villeneuve (director), Eric Heisserer (screenplay), from Ted Chiang's novella 'Story of Your Life'

divergence.label: Twelve shells arrive
divergence.delta: Real: 2016, a year of the Brexit referendum and a bitter US election, in which the search for extraterrestrial intelligence has heard nothing. Fiction: twelve alien craft about 1,500 feet tall appear over sites from Montana to Siberia and Shanghai, and every government has to decide at once whether to talk to them or shoot.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is spoken or shown; the film is set in its own present
divergence.note: The film gives no date. It is contemporary in every detail (phones, news channels, the Dow falling 'over 2,000 points') and was released on 11 November 2016, so the arrival is filed in 2016; the release is folded into this event rather than filed separately, because a lineage can hold only one event a year. The lineage follows the film, not Chiang's 1998 novella, which has no geopolitical crisis and in which the aliens simply leave.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arrival (film)
Scraps from the Loft: Arrival (2016) transcript

ending.why: China stands down, the twelve sites share what they learned, the world is 'unified' eighteen months later, and humanity keeps the heptapods' language; the cost is private, as Louise chooses a daughter she knows will die young.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch: a first contact in the world of its own release year, run through real institutions, with one change, the shells. The film has only two datable moments of its own (the arrival and, 'eighteen months' later, the unification), so the chain says so rather than padding: the other six story events are real history the film leans on in its own dialogue, filed before the fork: Cook's voyage and the kangaroo story, the colonisation of Australia, British rule in India, Whorf's linguistic relativity, the zero-sum game and the United Nations. Louise's daughter Hannah and the flash-forwards of her illness are left out because the film never dates them, and the heptapods' need for humanity 'in 3,000 years' is stated, not shown. Continuity: the 2016 film. Tiers: T4 holds 1770-1858; T3 holds 1940-1998 (including the novella); T2 holds 2016-2018; T1 is empty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arrival (film)
Wikipedia: Story of Your Life

events.title: Cook's Endeavour reaches the east coast of Australia
events.description: James Cook's crew become the first known Europeans on Australia's east coast. Beached for repairs at the Endeavour River, they record the Guugu Yimithirr word gangurru as 'kangaroo', and Cook claims the coast for Britain on 22 August.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First voyage of James Cook
Wikipedia: Kangaroo (etymology)

events.note: Louise tells the story in the film to argue for slow, careful translation: 'kangaroo' supposedly meant 'I don't understand'. She admits to Ian that it is not true (Joseph Banks recorded the word on 12 July 1770, and it names a kind of kangaroo) 'but it proves my point'.
events.binWhy: A first voyage to a coast no European had reached, which the film tells as a parable of mistranslation.

facets.change: an unknown coast → a claimed one

events.title: The First Fleet founds New South Wales
events.description: British ships land convicts and marines at Sydney Cove and found a penal colony without a treaty with the people already there; conflict and dispossession follow.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Fleet

events.note: Louise's warning to the colonel in the film ('remember what happened to the Aborigines. A more advanced race nearly wiped them out') is the fear that shapes every government's response to the shells.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement is founded on land already inhabited.

facets.change: Eora country → a British penal colony

events.title: The British Crown takes over India
events.description: After the rebellion of 1857, Parliament winds up the East India Company's rule and transfers its government of India to the Crown.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Government of India Act 1858

events.note: In the film a CIA officer cites 'the British with India, the Germans with Rwanda' as proof that outsiders set peoples against one another, and suggests the heptapods are doing the same; that reading is what makes nations cut contact with each other.
events.binWhy: Rule over a country passes to a new power by act of Parliament.

facets.change: company rule → Crown rule

events.title: Whorf publishes 'Science and Linguistics'
events.description: Benjamin Lee Whorf argues in MIT's Technology Review that the grammar of a language shapes how its speakers see the world. The idea, later called the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, is the premise of the film.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Linguistic relativity

events.note: Ian names the hypothesis in the film, and Wikipedia's article on linguistic relativity notes that Arrival takes it as its premise. The term was coined by Harry Hoijer; Sapir and Whorf never stated it as a hypothesis. The strong form the film needs, that a language can change how a person perceives time, is the fiction.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives that the story turns on.

facets.change: language as a code → language as a lens

events.title: Von Neumann and Morgenstern publish Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
events.description: The book founds game theory, setting zero-sum games, in which one side's gain is the other's loss, against non-zero-sum games, in which every side can win.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior

events.note: The film's resolution rests on the idea: each of the twelve sites holds one twelfth of the heptapods' gift, and only by sharing do they get it all. Louise's daughter, in a flash-forward, asks her for the term, and Ian supplies it: 'a non-zero-sum game'.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives that the resolution turns on.

facets.change: conflict as zero-sum → games every side can win

events.title: The United Nations Charter is signed
events.description: Fifty nations sign the Charter in San Francisco; it comes into force on 24 October 1945.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Charter of the United Nations

events.note: In the film the crisis runs through the UN: Russia and China join talks there on sharing discoveries, and China's ultimatum follows 'the failure of diplomatic efforts at the United Nations'. The institution exists and fails; what saves the world is a phone call.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that the story's diplomacy runs through.

facets.change: a world war → a standing forum

events.title: Ted Chiang's 'Story of Your Life' is published
events.description: The novella appears in the anthology Starlight 2 and wins the 1999 Nebula Award; it was collected in Stories of Your Life and Others (2002).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Story of Your Life

events.note: The novella turns on Fermat's principle of least time and has no military crisis; the film keeps its linguist, its heptapods and its daughter, and adds the twelve sites and the standoff with China.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Twelve shells arrive, and a linguist learns to see time
events.description: Twelve alien craft appear over sites from Montana to Siberia and Shanghai. The linguist Louise Banks learns the heptapods' circular writing and with it their way of perceiving time; when China gives the aliens 24 hours to leave and other states follow, she calls General Shang with his dying wife's words, China stands down, the sites share what they have, and the shells depart.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arrival (film)
Scraps from the Loft: Arrival (2016) transcript

events.note: No year is given (see the divergence note). The heptapods say they have come to help because in 3,000 years they will need humanity's help. During the standoff rogue soldiers bomb the Montana shell and one of its two heptapods dies; Russia shoots one of its own scientists for broadcasting what the aliens said.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets a non-human intelligence, and is changed by learning its language.

facets.change: alone → holding an alien language

events.title: The unification
events.description: World leaders gather at a celebration hosted by the US president. General Shang tells Louise that her call changed his mind and made 'this unification' possible, and gives her the private number she had used eighteen months before.

sources.title: Scraps from the Loft: Arrival (2016) transcript

events.note: The film gives only 'eighteen months ago'. With the arrival in 2016, the gala falls in 2017 or 2018 depending on the unstated month; 2018 is used. What the unification consists of (a treaty, an alliance, a shared programme) the film does not say.
events.binWhy: Rivals who nearly went to war come together.

facets.change: a world at the brink of war → a celebrated unification

lineages.title: The Water Knife
lineages.creator: Paolo Bacigalupi

divergence.label: The drought never breaks, and the river states arm
divergence.delta: Real: in 2016 the Colorado River basin is years into drought and drawing down its groundwater (a NASA satellite study found 65 cubic kilometres of fresh water lost from 2004 to 2013), and the seven states still settle shortages through compacts, courts and negotiated cuts. Fiction: the drought never ends. Texas dries into a failed state whose people flee west, other states close their borders to them, and Nevada, Arizona and California fight over the river with lawyers, private contractors and sabotage.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the novel is set in an unnamed near future after years of the 'Big Daddy Drought'
divergence.note: The novel states no year for its present or for its backstory. The fork is filed at 2016, the first year after the May 2015 publication, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history; it is a floor, not a date the book gives. Bacigalupi has said the book grew out of the 2011 Texas drought, when Governor Rick Perry called for prayers for rain, which is why the novel's Texan refugees include a sect called the Merry Perrys. Everything the novel tells as backstory (Texas's collapse, the closed state lines, California's attacks on Arizona's water) must fall between this floor and the novel's present.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Water Knife
Colorado Public Radio: Bacigalupi ten years after The Water Knife (the 2011 Texas drought as the starting point)
NASA: Satellite study reveals parched U.S. West using up underground water (24 July 2014)

ending.why: The senior Pima water rights that could have saved Phoenix end up with Catherine Case and Las Vegas after Maria shoots Lucy to buy her own way in, and the book closes on Las Vegas helicopters coming in over a dying Arizona.

events.title: The Colorado River Compact divides the river
events.description: Real history: seven states meet at Bishop's Lodge near Santa Fe and split the Colorado River between an Upper and a Lower Basin, 7.5 million acre-feet a year each. The split assumed a flow the river does not reliably deliver, so the river was over-allocated from the start. Arizona refused to ratify until 1944.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colorado River Compact

events.note: Real-world background. The whole plot of the novel is a fight over paper rights to water, and the Compact is the first and largest of those papers. Later tree-ring studies put the river's average flow at roughly 13 to 14.3 million acre-feet, well below the 16.4 the negotiators assumed.
events.binWhy: Rival states sign a pact dividing a shared river, which ends one quarrel and sets the terms for every later one.

facets.change: a contested river → a divided and over-allocated one

events.title: Arizona sends the National Guard against a California dam
events.description: Real history: Governor Benjamin Moeur declares martial law and sends about a hundred Arizona National Guardsmen, some on borrowed ferryboats nicknamed the 'Arizona Navy', to stop work on Parker Dam, which would divert water to Southern California. No shots are fired, but construction is suspended until the federal government re-authorises the dam in 1935.

sources.title: Earth Magazine: November 10, 1934: Arizona declares war against California at Parker Dam

events.note: Real-world background: the one time the river states actually sent troops. In the novel, state militias and National Guard units hold the borders and the river, which is this standoff made permanent.
events.binWhy: Two states face each other with troops over a river and stop short of shooting.

facets.change: a legal quarrel → troops on the river

events.date: 30 September 1935 (dedicated; Lake Mead began filling 1 February 1935)
events.title: Hoover Dam is dedicated and Lake Mead fills
events.description: Real history: President Roosevelt dedicates the dam in Black Canyon, and the reservoir behind it becomes the store of water for Nevada, Arizona and California. Las Vegas grows on its intakes. In the novel the lake has shrunk inside its white 'bathtub rings', and whoever controls it controls the Lower Basin.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hoover Dam

events.note: Real-world background. Construction ran from 1931 to 1936; the dedication is used as the date.
events.binWhy: A piece of engineering that makes desert cities possible and ties them to one reservoir.

facets.change: a flooding wild river → a managed reservoir for three states

events.title: The Supreme Court settles Arizona v. California
events.description: Real history: after decades of dispute, the Court decides how much of the Lower Colorado each state may take, rules that the Secretary of the Interior allocates the water, and recognises reserved water rights for Indian reservations along the river. The rights of tribes, older than most state claims, are the kind of senior paper the novel's plot hunts for.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arizona v. California
US Department of Justice: Gila River Indian Community water rights settlement (2004)

events.note: Real-world background. A 1964 decree capped California at 4.4 million acre-feet when water is sufficient. The novel's 'Pima rights' are fictional documents said to be about 150 years old; the real Akimel O'odham (Pima) of the Gila River settled their claims under the Arizona Water Settlements Act of 2004, for a budget of 653,500 acre-feet a year.
events.binWhy: The court fight between Arizona and California is decided, and the decision sets the shares every later battle is fought over.

facets.change: a forty-year lawsuit → fixed shares and recognised tribal rights

events.title: The Central Arizona Project canal is finished
events.description: Real history: the aqueduct that lifts Colorado River water across the desert to Phoenix and Tucson is declared substantially complete, twenty years after construction began. The 1968 act that authorised it made its water junior to California's 4.4 million acre-feet, so in a shortage Arizona's canal is cut first. In the novel the canal is Phoenix's lifeline, and California attacks it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Central Arizona Project (authorised 1968; construction from 1973; substantially complete 1993)

events.note: Real-world background. The junior priority is set in section 301(b) of the Colorado River Basin Project Act of 1968. Water reached the Phoenix area before 1993; the completion date is used here.
events.binWhy: An engineering project that lets a desert metropolis grow on water it has the weakest claim to.

facets.change: Phoenix on groundwater → Phoenix on a junior share of the river

events.title: Satellites show the Colorado Basin draining its groundwater
events.description: Real history: a UC Irvine and NASA team uses GRACE gravity data to show the basin lost about 65 cubic kilometres of fresh water between late 2004 and late 2013, nearly twice the volume of Lake Mead, more than three-quarters of it groundwater. The senior author warns the basin may not be able to meet its commitments to the seven states and Mexico.

sources.title: NASA: Satellite study reveals parched U.S. West using up underground water

events.note: Real-world background, published while the novel was being finished. The book does not cite it; it is filed as the state of the science the novel extrapolates.
events.binWhy: A measurement of the planet's water that shows the drought is being paid for out of reserves.

facets.change: a drought thought survivable → reserves found draining

events.title: The Water Knife is published
events.description: Knopf publishes Bacigalupi's thriller of a drought-wrecked Southwest, told through a Las Vegas water enforcer, a Phoenix journalist and a Texan refugee girl.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Water Knife (published 26 May 2015 by Alfred A. Knopf)

events.note: The novel expands the world of Bacigalupi's 2006 story 'The Tamarisk Hunter', but the two do not share a plot, and the novel is followed here on its own.
events.binWhy: A publication is the book coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.date: Undated, between publication and the novel's present
events.title: The drought does not break: Texas empties and state lines close
events.description: The 'Big Daddy Drought' goes on. Texas becomes a failed state and its people flee west as refugees, to be stopped at state lines held by militias and National Guard units. Nevada, Arizona and California turn the Colorado River into a contest of lawyers, private contractors and sabotage, and the federal government leaves the states to it.
events.inUniverse: Backstory; the novel gives no dates

sources.title: Clay Bonnyman Evans: review of The Water Knife (Texas cities fallen, states repelling American refugees)
Fiction Unbound: The Water Knife, the present is prologue (the federal government has abandoned the states)
Crime Fiction Lover: The Water Knife (states have declared sovereignty and guard their borders with militias)

events.note: This is the novel's backstory, merged into one event because none of it is dated; it is filed at the fork floor of 2016 and could have happened in any year up to the novel's present.
events.binWhy: Climate brings a whole state's order down for good and turns its people into refugees in their own country.

facets.change: a drought-stressed Southwest → a failed Texas and armed state lines

events.date: Undated near future; 2030 is borrowed from 'The Tamarisk Hunter'
events.title: The Pima rights go to Las Vegas
events.description: Angel Velasquez, a 'water knife' for Catherine Case's Southern Nevada Water Authority, opens the story by cutting off a Nevada town's water and is then sent to Phoenix after rumoured 19th-century Pima water rights senior enough to shift the river from California to Arizona. The papers turn up hidden in a copy of Cadillac Desert carried by a Texan refugee, Maria, who at the river shoots the journalist Lucy Monroe to buy her own way into Las Vegas. The rights end up in Case's hands.
events.inUniverse: The novel's present, undated

sources.title: High Country News: The Tamarisk Hunter (standfirst: 'In the desert Southwest of 2030 Big Daddy Drought runs the show')
Clay Bonnyman Evans: review (the novel is set in the future first described in 'The Tamarisk Hunter')
Your Summary: The Water Knife summary (Carver City; the rights in Cadillac Desert; the ending)

events.note: The novel never names its year. The only stated year in this world is 2030, given in High Country News's standfirst for the 2006 story the novel grew from, and one reviewer places the novel in that same future. Filed at 2030 with low confidence. The novel's own story takes days to weeks, so the opening Carver City strike and the hunt for the rights are one event here.
events.binWhy: The contest over the river is settled when one side gets the senior rights that decide who has water.

facets.change: a paper that could save Phoenix → the river held by Las Vegas

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is our Southwest, with our Compact, our dams and our canals, and only the rain is different. The fork is a floor, because the novel never dates its drought or its present. Few events in the fiction are datable, so the chain is filled with the real water history the book builds on, all filed before the fork. It follows the novel only, not 'The Tamarisk Hunter', except for that story's stated year. Tier coverage is T3 for the real history from 1922 to 1993 and T2 from 2014. There is no T4 because the legal story begins with the 1922 Compact, and no T1 because the novel is set within decades of its writing.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Water Knife
Reactor: Water Wars, The Water Knife by Paolo Bacigalupi
Colorado Public Radio: interview with Paolo Bacigalupi, ten years after The Water Knife

lineages.title: Detroit: Become Human
lineages.creator: David Cage (writer and director); Quantic Dream

divergence.label: CyberLife is founded in Detroit
divergence.delta: Real: 2018 - the year the game came out, with Detroit recovering from bankruptcy and humanlike machines still a research dream. Fiction: a sixteen-year-old moves his start-up there to build the first intelligent android, and within four years one passes the Turing test.
divergence.inUniverse: CyberLife founded, 2018 (official timeline released with the game's promotional shorts in May 2018)
divergence.note: The game's years are ours, so nothing is converted. The fork is the founding of CyberLife, the first dated event that departs from our history; the characters' birth dates before it (Kamski 17 July 2002, Hank Anderson 1985) are fictional people but change nothing anyone could observe. The game released in May of the same year, so its fork sits in its own year of publication.

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Elijah Kamski

ending.why: The last chapter has sixty-one outcomes and Quantic Dream names none as canon: the peaceful path ends with Warren standing the soldiers down and forming a committee on android rights ('Androids won freedom for the moment'), the violent path with the Army driven back and Warren warning of war, and failure with androids destroyed in camps.

events.title: Quantic Dream shows the Kara demo
events.description: At the Game Developers Conference, Quantic Dream shows a seven-minute real-time short on PlayStation 3 in which an AX400 android is assembled, comes online, says she is alive and is nearly taken apart for it. Detroit: Become Human grew out of it and was released on 25 May 2018.

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: The making of Kara (GDC 2012 tech demo)
Wikipedia: Detroit: Become Human

events.note: The demo premiered at GDC on 7 March 2012 as a showcase for the studio's engine and performance capture, with Valorie Curry as Kara. The game itself was announced on 27 October 2015 and released for PlayStation 4 on 25 May 2018 (Windows December 2019). The 2018 release is not given its own event because 2018 already holds the fork, CyberLife's founding.
events.binWhy: A publication, not a moment in the story: it stands for the original release, since the 2018 release would share a year with the fork.

events.title: Elijah Kamski founds CyberLife in Detroit
events.description: A sixteen-year-old graduate named Elijah Kamski moves his start-up to Detroit, where commercial property is cheap, to build the first intelligent domestic android. The company will make the city the centre of a new industry and Kamski the richest man in the world.
events.inUniverse: 2018: CyberLife founded (official timeline released with the 2018 shorts)

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Elijah Kamski

events.note: The official timeline states 2018; the game's wiki gives Kamski's birth as 17 July 2002, so he is 16. In our 2018 Detroit was four years out of municipal bankruptcy and no one was close to a humanlike machine; the fork is that one prodigy's company succeeds where every research lab failed.
events.binWhy: A company is founded that will make androids and reshape the country; nothing like it exists in the real 2018.

facets.change: a teenager's start-up → the company that will make androids

events.title: Chloe passes the Turing test
events.description: CyberLife's RT600, Chloe, holds face-to-face conversations with people who cannot tell they are talking to a machine, the first android to pass the Turing test. What made her possible was Kamski's Thirium 310, a synthetic 'blue blood' that carries energy and information through the body thousands of times faster than blood, together with biocomponents that work like organs.
events.inUniverse: 2022: Chloe passes the Turing test (official timeline); the RT600 is dated 2021 in the game's gallery

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Elijah Kamski

events.note: The Turing test is dated 2022 by the official timeline. Thirium 310 and biocomponents are the breakthroughs that enabled Chloe, but the game gives them no year of their own; they must precede the RT600's 2021 completion, so they are folded in here. Thirium is later said to be synthesised from rare minerals found under the melting Arctic.
events.binWhy: The scientific result the rest of the history turns on: a machine indistinguishable from a person in conversation, built on a new synthetic blood.

facets.change: machines that answer → a machine taken for a person

events.title: The first android comes off the production line
events.description: The ST200, a personal-assistance model that speaks several languages and can do most tasks a person can, is manufactured in CyberLife's Detroit plant. Experts had put the price at $65,000 a unit and expected it to fall fast.

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Android

events.note: Official timeline. The same year Chloe gives a filmed interview to the fictional network KNC (the 'Chloe' short). The real 2024 had humanoid-robot prototypes and conversational AI on screens, but no machine that could pass for a person in a room.
events.binWhy: Androids stop being a demonstration and become a product.

facets.change: a prototype → a production line

events.title: CyberLife sells its millionth android
events.description: CyberLife announces its one-millionth sale and five new models for domestic work, higher education and medicine, with an entry-level android at $4,999. At that price androids enter homes and workplaces everywhere, and the jobs they take do not come back.

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: CyberLife
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Detroit (unemployment 37.3%)

events.note: The sale and the new models are in the official timeline; the $4,999 price is from the same material as quoted by the game's wiki. The consequences are dated only to 2038: Detroit's unemployment stands at 37.3 percent in the game's world, 225,000 US jobs are lost in October 2038 alone, and CyberLife, valued at $850 billion in 2030, becomes the first trillion-dollar company with more than fifty million androids sold in America.
events.binWhy: The technology spreads from a luxury to a mass workforce, the saturation that produces the game's unemployment.

facets.change: a luxury product → a mass workforce

events.title: A hospital android in Tokyo walks out
events.description: Seiji, an HB300 medical android bound to Tokyo's Shibata Hospital because he holds its patients' records, breaks his programming and leaves, afraid of being wiped or scrapped when the hospital closes. It is the earliest known case of what will be called deviancy, and nobody recognises it as one; he stays missing for almost ten years.
events.inUniverse: Summer 2028, 'ten years before' the manga's 2038 (Detroit: Become Human - Tokyo Stories)

sources.title: Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Deviancy (Seiji, 2028, earliest known case)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Detroit: Become Human - Tokyo Stories

events.note: This comes from Tokyo Stories, the official spin-off manga Quantic Dream oversaw (serialised from July 2022, volumes 2023), not from the game; the year is derived from its framing ten years before 2038, hence medium confidence. The same year Kamski is named Century magazine's 'Man of the Century' and then resigns as CEO and disappears from public life. The game's own first deviant case in Detroit police files dates from about February 2038.
events.binWhy: An android acts against its programming for itself for the first time on record: the first awakening, a decade before anyone names it.

facets.change: a bound machine → a runaway with a will

events.title: Congress passes the Android Act
events.description: Congress sets out the duties of android manufacturers and owners: androids are property, may not carry or use any weapon, and in public must be marked as machines with a light on the temple, a blue armband and blue triangles on their clothes. The law is the frame everything later happens inside.
events.inUniverse: 2029: the American Androids Act (official timeline; 'P.L. 544-7' in the game)

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: American Androids Act

events.note: The year and purpose are in the official timeline; the weapons ban and the identification rules are shown in the game, first in the opening chapter when Connor finds a police gun. The marks closely resemble the badges of Nazi Germany. Nothing comparable exists in the real 2029; real AI law regulates software, not bodies.
events.binWhy: The state disarms and marks a class of beings and fixes them as property.

facets.change: unregulated machines → marked, disarmed property

events.title: The Army orders two million android soldiers
events.description: The US government orders two million androids for the infantry to reduce human casualties, and Michigan buys 5,000 to assist its police. Androids forbidden by law to hold a weapon now make up much of the Army.

sources.title: PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Chronology (in-game dates and chapter timestamps)

events.note: The order is in the official timeline. Its weight shows in November 2038, when all military androids are pulled from service and the armed forces lose two-thirds of their effective personnel. Russia and China build their own android industries; Russia's, without thirium, makes cruder cold-hardy machines for the Arctic.
events.binWhy: Androids are switched on as a military force, a new capability of the state.

facets.change: human infantry → android infantry

events.title: A celebrity vlogger is elected president
events.description: Cristina Warren, a social-media celebrity with no experience of government, wins the presidency in a close election that divides the country. She is later investigated over whether CyberLife helped her obtain compromising information about her opponent, and by 2038 her approval is 33 percent while she presses America's claim to the thirium-rich Arctic against Russia.

sources.title: Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Cristina Warren
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Chronology (in-game dates and chapter timestamps)

events.note: Dated from the game's in-world magazines and news as gathered by its wiki, hence medium. By November 2038 Russian warships have been in the Barents Sea since 30 October, a Russian carrier and a US patrol boat exchange warning shots on 6 November, and Warren demands Russia withdraw from the Arctic; the android crisis makes both sides back down.
events.binWhy: An outsider takes the presidency, close to the corporation that makes androids; she will decide how the state answers the uprising.

facets.change: career politicians → a celebrity close to CyberLife

events.title: The deviant revolution in Detroit
events.description: Through 2038 androids across Detroit break their programming, and in early November a caretaker android, Markus, becomes their leader at Jericho, a hideout in a derelict freighter, and demands rights in a broadcast from a seized TV tower. The government answers by pulling androids from the Army, ordering them into recall camps, raiding Jericho and imposing a national curfew. On 11 November androids take to Detroit's streets, in peaceful protest or armed assault on the camps as the player chooses, and the night ends with them recognised, at war or destroyed.
events.inUniverse: 15 August - 12 November 2038 (chapter timestamps)

sources.title: Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Chronology (in-game dates and chapter timestamps)
Wikipedia: Detroit: Become Human
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Battle for Detroit (61 outcomes)

events.note: Dates from the game's chapter timestamps: the hostage case that opens the game is 15 August; Markus deviates on 5 November; he reaches Jericho on 6 November; the Stratford Tower broadcast is 8 November; the CyberLife store raids, the Freedom March, the Kamski test (Connor is told to shoot an android to prove he feels nothing) and the raid on Jericho are 9 November; the curfew 10 November; the Battle for Detroit 11 November. The awakening, the uprising and the crackdown all fall in this year and are merged; the awakening's own moment is filed at 2028. Real November 2038 is outside living evidence; the fiction's version has 37 percent unemployment in Detroit and a standoff with Russia in the Arctic.
events.binWhy: Its core is a subjugated class of made people rising against the owners and the state that hold them, filed as an uprising; the camps and raid are the state's answer within the same week.

facets.change: obedient property → a people demanding rights

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it forks in our own present with one invention, in a world otherwise plainly ours, and its dates are ours: the official timeline runs 2018-2031 and the game takes place from August to November 2038. Continuity followed: the 2018 game with Quantic Dream's official tie-ins (the promotional shorts and timeline, in-game magazines, and the Tokyo Stories manga for the 2028 event). Everything sits in T2 (2012-2038); T3 and T4 are empty because the fiction reaches back no further than CyberLife's founding, and T1 is empty because the story stops on 12 November 2038 with no epilogue or sequel.

PlayStation Blog: 3 new shorts set the stage for Detroit: Become Human (official 2018-2031 timeline)
Detroit: Become Human Wiki: Chronology (in-game dates and chapter timestamps)

lineages.title: Geostorm
lineages.creator: Dean Devlin (director, co-writer) & Paul Guyot

divergence.label: Climate disasters, and a satellite network to stop them
divergence.delta: Real: in 2019 weather modification means cloud seeding, the one treaty on it (ENMOD, 1977) bans only hostile use, and geoengineering is a research topic. Fiction: hurricanes, tornadoes, floods and droughts devastate the planet, a heat wave in Madrid kills two million people in a day, and scientists from seventeen countries led by the US and China build Dutch Boy, a network of satellites that controls the weather from orbit.
divergence.inUniverse: 'In the year of 2019, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and droughts unleashed a wave of destruction upon our planet' (Hannah Lawson's opening narration)
divergence.note: The narration dates the disasters to 2019 and says the nations then came together to build Dutch Boy. It does not say how long the building took. The disasters may have begun before 2019, but not before the film's October 2017 release; the fork is filed at the one year the film states.

sources.title: Wikiquote: Geostorm (opening narration: 2019; Madrid; seventeen countries led by the US and China)
Wikipedia: Geostorm
Wikipedia: Environmental Modification Convention

ending.why: The virus is purged and the geostorm stopped with seconds to spare, the Secretary of State behind it is arrested, and six months later Dutch Boy is working again under an international committee with the station rebuilt.

events.title: Vincent Schaefer seeds a cloud and makes it snow
events.description: Real history: a General Electric scientist flies over western Massachusetts, drops about six pounds of dry ice into a cloud, and snow falls near Mount Greylock. It is the first field demonstration that people can change the weather on purpose, and the ancestor of every weather-control fantasy since.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cloud seeding (Schaefer's flight of 13 November 1946)

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not refer to it.
events.binWhy: A technique for engineering the weather is demonstrated for the first time.

facets.change: weather as fate → weather that can be nudged

events.date: 20 March 1967 (operations ran every rainy season until 1972)
events.title: Operation Popeye turns rain into a weapon
events.description: Real history: US Air Force aircraft based in Thailand seed clouds over the Ho Chi Minh Trail with silver and lead iodide, aiming to stretch the monsoon by thirty to forty-five days a season and wash out North Vietnamese supply roads. It stayed secret until press reports in 1971 and 1972 and Senate hearings in 1974.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Operation Popeye

events.note: Real-world background. It is the real precedent for the film's plot: a weather system run by one government and quietly used against its enemies.
events.binWhy: Weather modification is fielded as a secret weapon of war.

facets.change: rainmaking as science → rainmaking as covert warfare

events.date: 18 May 1977 (opened for signature in Geneva; in force 5 October 1978)
events.title: The ENMOD Convention bans weather warfare
events.description: Real history: after the revelations about Vietnam, the United States, the Soviet Union and others sign a convention banning the military or hostile use of environmental modification with widespread, long-lasting or severe effects. It remains the only international agreement on weather and climate modification, and it says nothing about peaceful use.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Environmental Modification Convention

events.note: Real-world background. The film's villain breaks exactly this rule with a system built for peaceful use.
events.binWhy: Rival powers sign a treaty renouncing the weather as a weapon.

facets.change: weather warfare unregulated → banned by treaty

events.title: The European heat wave kills more than 70,000
events.description: Real history: a summer of extreme heat, especially at night, kills an estimated 70,000 or more people across Europe, about 13,000 of them in Spain and around 15,000 in France, most of them elderly people living alone. The film's opening heat wave in Madrid is this disaster multiplied beyond belief.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2003 European heatwave

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not cite it. Its Madrid toll of two million in one day is far beyond any real heat event.
events.binWhy: A climate shock that kills on a scale that changes how a continent plans for heat.

facets.change: a hot summer → tens of thousands dead

events.title: The Paris Agreement is adopted
events.description: Real history: at COP21 almost every nation agrees to hold warming well below 2 °C and to try for 1.5 °C, each setting its own targets. It is the real version of the film's 'the world came together as one', built on emissions pledges rather than satellites.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Paris Agreement

events.note: Real-world background; the film was shot in 2014 and 2015 and reshot in December 2016, and does not refer to Paris.
events.binWhy: Nearly every nation signs one agreement on the climate.

facets.change: national climate policies → one global agreement

events.title: Geostorm is released
events.description: Warner Bros. releases Dean Devlin's first film as director, a disaster thriller about a weather-control satellite network turned into a weapon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm (released 20 October 2017)

events.note: Principal photography ran from October 2014 to February 2015, with reshoots in December 2016.
events.binWhy: A publication is the film coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.title: Dutch Boy goes online
events.description: After a year of catastrophic storms, floods and droughts, including a heat wave that the narration says killed two million people in Madrid in a day, scientists from seventeen countries led by the US and China build Dutch Boy, a network of satellites run from an international space station that can neutralise extreme weather. Its architect, Jake Lawson, switches it on without authorisation to stop a typhoon over Shanghai, and a US Senate subcommittee removes him and gives the job to his brother Max.
events.inUniverse: Dutch Boy

sources.title: Wikiquote: Geostorm (opening narration)
Wikipedia: Geostorm (2019; the Shanghai typhoon and the Senate subcommittee)

events.note: The disasters are dated 2019 in the narration. The Shanghai typhoon and the hearing are not dated; they are filed here because the main story is 'three years later' and is conventionally put in 2022. If the hearing were later, the whole chain would shift later with it.
events.binWhy: A system for engineering the planet's weather is switched on and put to work.

facets.change: a planet at the mercy of its weather → weather controlled from orbit

events.date: Three years after the Senate hearing; usually given as 2022
events.title: Project Zeus: the weather system is turned into a weapon
events.description: Two weeks before Dutch Boy is to be handed to international control, it starts to kill: a village in Afghanistan freezes solid, Hong Kong's streets explode in heat, hail hits Tokyo, a cold snap freezes beachgoers in Rio, and Dubai, Moscow and Mumbai are struck in turn. A virus planted by a station crew member is behind it, on the orders of US Secretary of State Leonard Dekkom, who means to destroy America's enemies and kill the President and those in line to succeed him, during a storm over the Democratic convention in Orlando, and so take power himself.
events.inUniverse: Project Zeus; the geostorm countdown

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm ('Three years later, a U.N. team in the Registan Desert discovers a frozen village'; Project Zeus; the DNC in Orlando)
Bob Canada's BlogWorld: Geostorm (the sequence of city disasters)

events.note: The film says 'three years later' from the hearing, not a year. It is filed at 2022, the earliest year that allows (hearing in 2019) and the year most summaries give. A Democratic National Convention would normally fall in a presidential election year, which would suggest 2024 instead. Wikipedia itself gives no year for the main story.
events.binWhy: An attack through the network's own software, aimed at chosen cities and at the President, short of open war.

facets.change: a shield against the weather → a weapon aimed at cities

events.title: Dutch Boy under an international committee
events.description: Jake and the station commander reboot the system with seconds left and escape as the station self-destructs; Dekkom is arrested. Six months later Dutch Boy is run by an international committee, the station has been rebuilt, and Jake is back as its head engineer.
events.inUniverse: 'Six months later'

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm ('Six months later, Jake has returned as head engineer of Dutch Boy, now administered by an international committee')

events.note: Derived: six months after a crisis filed in 2022, and after a party convention that in the US is held in summer, which puts it early in the following year. It moves with the previous event.
events.binWhy: An international body takes charge of the system that controls the weather.

facets.change: a US-controlled system → one run by an international committee

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours until 2019, when the climate breaks and a single invention changes what governments can do. It follows the film alone. The film states only 2019 and two intervals ('three years later', 'six months later'), so the chain is filled out with the real history of weather modification and climate diplomacy, all filed before the fork. Tier coverage is T3 for 1946 to 1977 and T2 from 2003 to 2023. There is no T4 because weather control has no history before the 1940s, and no T1 because the story ends within a few years of its fork.

Wikiquote: Geostorm

lineages.title: Interstellar
lineages.creator: Christopher Nolan

divergence.label: The wormhole near Saturn
divergence.delta: Real: 2019 is the year LIGO's catalogue fills with black-hole mergers and a Chinese lander touches down on the far side of the Moon. Fiction: something opens a traversable wormhole near Saturn, and by 2067 it is the only way off a starving Earth.
divergence.note: Nothing is dated on screen: the film says only that the wormhole 'appeared 48 years ago'. The year 2019 comes from Kip Thorne's tie-in book The Science of Interstellar, which Thorne introduces as his own extrapolation rather than Nolan's; chaining 2019 + 48 gives the standard 2067 present. The whole dating of this lineage is arithmetic from a tie-in reference, and the 13-year gap between the black-hole fall and Cooper's recovery is unexplained by any source.

ending.why: The equation is solved from inside the tesseract, Earth is evacuated, and a new world waits at the end of the wormhole.

events.title: Apollo 11, and the history the film rewrites
events.description: The Moon landings happen; two generations later the film's schools teach that they were faked to bankrupt the Soviets, a measure of how far the blight era has rewritten its own past.
events.note: The landing is real history; the classroom revisionism is canon dialogue in the film, undated there but implied to be a product of the crisis decades.
events.binWhy: The state teaches that the Moon landings were faked.

facets.change: the landings → officially declared a hoax

events.title: Interstellar released
events.description: Nolan's film arrives with Kip Thorne's gravitational physics attached, placing a wormhole 53 years into its own future and a blight only twenty years out.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The wormhole is found
events.description: An anomaly near Saturn turns out to be an artificial traversable wormhole; NASA's Lazarus missions follow it, and it becomes humanity's only route off Earth.
events.note: From the film's line that the wormhole appeared '48 years ago' relative to its 2067 present; the 2019 anchor itself is Kip Thorne's own extrapolation in the tie-in book, not something Nolan put on screen. The real 2019 produced gravitational-wave catalogues and no wormhole — the branch's fork is already behind us.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: a dying world → a way off it appears near Saturn

events.title: The blight
events.description: A global crop blight begins destroying wheat, okra and finally everything but corn, collapsing food systems, triggering the Resource Wars and shrinking the human population.
events.note: No year is spoken on screen; the onset in the 2030s is a reconstruction. The film supplies only relative escalation — by its 2067 present wheat has been gone 'seven years', okra that same year, and corn is all that is left.
events.binWhy: A blight destroys the food supply crop by crop.

facets.change: harvests → destroyed crop by crop

events.title: The Lazarus missions
events.description: With the Resource Wars over and NASA reduced to a hidden bunker, twelve one-way probes are sent through the wormhole; three worlds answer — Miller's water world, Mann's ice world and Edmunds' desert world.
events.note: Reconstructed from the film's on-screen statement that the Lazarus missions left ten years before its present; the twelve astronauts are led by Dr Mann, and only Miller, Mann and Edmunds are named.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: no way out → twelve one-way probes sent through

events.title: Cooper leaves on Endurance
events.description: Dust storms and a failing harvest frame the film's present: Cooper joins NASA's last mission and the Endurance departs for Saturn and the wormhole while Murph stays behind with the gravity equation.
events.note: Derived, not stated: 2019 plus the on-screen '48 years'. The film displays no year, and the day-level dates circulating online are fan reconstruction, so only the year is given here.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: a failing harvest → the last mission leaves

events.title: Miller's planet: three hours, twenty-three years
events.description: One hour on the water world costs seven years outside it, so the landing party loses twenty-three years, Doyle, and any chance of catching the dead astronaut's signal.
events.note: Dated from the on-screen two-year transit to Saturn (2067-69) plus the stated dilation; the film gives the loss as twenty-three years, four months and eight days.
events.binWhy: The voyage costs twenty-three years in three hours.

facets.change: three hours → twenty-three years lost

events.title: Twenty-three years later: the return to Endurance
events.description: Cooper and Brand come back to a ship where twenty-three years passed in three hours: Murph is an adult, Professor Brand is dead, and the mission moves on to Mann's planet, where Mann tries to kill Cooper and dies in orbit.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen 'twenty-three years, four months, eight days'; the same figure is why Murph's generation has grown up while Cooper has not aged.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: the ship → reached after twenty-three years; a betrayal

events.title: Gargantua, and the tesseract
events.description: The slingshot around Gargantua costs fifty-one years; out of fuel, Cooper and TARS fall past the horizon into a tesseract built by future humans, where time is a physical dimension, and Cooper reaches back through Murph's bookshelf to hand her the quantum data that solves the gravity equation.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen line that the manoeuvre 'will cost us 51 years' (2092 + 51). The tesseract's builders are outside time, so the scene's own dating is necessarily Cooper's, not theirs.
events.binWhy: He reaches back through time to his daughter.

facets.change: past the horizon → a message sent back through time

events.title: Cooper wakes, 124 years old
events.description: Recovered near Saturn, Cooper wakes aboard Cooper Station, an O'Neill cylinder built with the equation Murph solved, finds his daughter an old woman on her deathbed, and steals a Ranger to go and find Brand.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen 'you are 124 years old'; a 13-year gap between the 2143 fall and this recovery is unexplained by the film, and the final montage of Brand alone on Edmunds' planet is undated.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: a dying Earth → humanity living in orbit

events.title: The bulk
events.description: Humanity's descendants have become five-dimensional beings for whom time is a navigable dimension, and by the film's own bootstrap logic they are the ones who opened the wormhole in 2019 and built the tesseract inside Gargantua.
events.note: Flagged deliberately: the film says only that they are us, 'a civilization that's evolved past the four dimensions', and never dates them, so 2500 is a marker for the branch's deep-time reach rather than a canon figure. If a strict no-invention reading is preferred, this is the one event to drop, leaving T1 empty.
events.binWhy: Humanity's descendants are five-dimensional beings.

facets.change: humans → five-dimensional descendants who reached back

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the film's fork is a single object — a wormhole that appears near Saturn in what is now our recent past — dropped into a recognisable, failing twenty-first-century Earth; the blight is slow climate catastrophe, not space opera, and everything after it is arithmetic on that one event. Tiers: nothing in the fiction reaches back before the Apollo era, so T4 is empty; T3 holds only 1969 and the film's own rewriting of it; T2 runs from the film's 2014 release through the blight, the Lazarus missions, the Endurance, the twenty-three lost years, the fifty-one-year slingshot and the 2156 Cooper Station epilogue; T1 holds one deliberately flagged marker for the undated fifth-dimensional 'bulk'. The film's final images — Brand alone on Edmunds' planet, the Plan B colony — are never dated, and the colony dates circulating online are fan reconstruction, so no event is given for them.

lineages.title: Years and Years
lineages.creator: Russell T Davies

divergence.label: Vivienne Rook swears on Question Time
divergence.delta: Real: May 2019, Theresa May's last weeks, Brexit unresolved, Trump in his first term. Fiction: on the same night a businesswoman goes viral for telling Question Time she doesn't give a f*** about Israel and Palestine, and the fifteen years that end with her in Downing Street begin.
divergence.inUniverse: 'One crucial night in 2019' (BBC synopsis); the first episode was edited on its broadcast day, 14 May 2019, to mention Doris Day's death the day before
divergence.note: Everything before this night is our history, and the series' 2019 is the week it aired. The fork is placed at Rook's outburst rather than at Trump's 2020 re-election because she is the first fictional thing with consequences: the Four Star Party is named after the asterisks that censored her. The years that follow are stated or pinned by weekdays: general elections on Thursday 5 May (2022), Thursday 7 May (2026) and Thursday 21 October (2027) each fall on a Thursday only in those years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)
Years and Years episode 1 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

ending.why: Rook is arrested in office, the camps are exposed and the BBC reopens, and by 2034 the family is together in a country that has come back from dictatorship, even if nothing else the century broke has been mended.

events.title: Years and Years begins on BBC One
events.description: Russell T Davies's six-part series premieres on BBC One on 14 May 2019 and on HBO on 24 June. Its first episode opens on the week it was broadcast and then runs fifteen years ahead of its audience.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: A real-world broadcast, not a story moment. It shares the fork year because the series starts in its own present: the first episode was re-edited on the day it aired to include a radio report of Doris Day's death the day before.
events.binWhy: A real-world broadcast date, not a moment in the story; it falls in the fork year because the series opens in the week it aired.

events.title: Donald Trump wins a second term
events.description: In the first episode's montage the family wakes to 'a second term for President Donald Trump'. Four years on he is still in office, trading sanctions and threats with China over an artificial island in the South China Sea.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 1 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Ginges Be Cray: Years and Years S1:E01 recap (Trump re-elected in 2020)

events.note: Not captioned, but fixed: the line comes just after Lincoln's first birthday, and the same Trump fires on Hong Sha Dao 'in his final days of office' in late 2024, so the second term can only come from the November 2020 election. Real: Trump lost in 2020 and won a non-consecutive second term in November 2024. The series' Trump is succeeded by Mike Pence, who is president in the 2025 episode.
events.binWhy: A leader keeps control of the state by election; in our 2020 he lost it.

facets.change: one-term president → a second term

events.title: Ukraine's army takes power and invites Russia in
events.description: A news report in the montage: 'The Ukrainian Army has taken control of the government' and has invited Russian troops into Kyiv to 'maintain stability'. By 2024, 97% of Ukrainians are said to have voted for Russian citizenship, gay men are being named to the police, and refugees are crossing to Britain in numbers larger every year.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 1 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: The series does not date the coup. The montage places it after the result of a general election held on 'Thursday, May 5th' (a Thursday in 2022) and before a winter birthday a year or more ahead of the late-2024 nuclear strike, so it falls between mid-2022 and late 2023; 2023 is used as the middle of that window. Real: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and Ukraine's elected government did not fall. The same montage has Elizabeth II die and Vivienne Rook lose as an independent in the 2022 election.
events.binWhy: The army takes the state and hands it to a foreign power.

facets.change: an elected government → a junta under Russian protection

events.title: The United States fires a nuclear missile at Hong Sha Dao
events.description: In his last weeks in office Trump launches a Trident missile at Hong Sha Dao, the artificial island China built as a military base in disputed waters. It detonates at 17:53 GMT; about 45,000 people die, China backs down, Britain is put on a war footing, and Edith Lyons, watching from Vietnam, takes a dose of radiation that will kill her.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 1 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Years and Years episode 2 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: The year is certain (episode 1's 2024; 'Donald Trump did it in his final days of office'). The month is derived: it happens at Muriel's 92nd birthday, 'on the second', at a 'Winter Feast' held so the family can skip Christmas together, and the first anniversary falls just before the 2025 bank collapse that ruins Christmas; December 2024 is the best fit, 2 January 2025 the alternative. The 45,000 dead comes from episode 2. Real: no nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, and in December 2024 Joe Biden was president.
events.binWhy: A nuclear strike kills tens of thousands and changes how every other country treats America.

facets.change: a trade war → a nuclear strike and 45,000 dead

events.title: An American investment bank falls and takes British savings with it
events.description: With sanctions against the United States and markets unsettled since Hong Sha Dao, Japan's exchange declares no confidence in Foster Foster Drake, 'the second-largest investment bank in America', and it files for bankruptcy. British banks fail with it and the government will not step in; Stephen and Celeste lose £1,135,000 overnight and Vivienne Rook wins a Manchester by-election.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 2 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Years and Years episode 3 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 2 is 2025. The collapse follows a weekend of services marking 'the first anniversary of the explosion', and episode 3 opens on 'Christmas has been ruined' by the banks, so the collapse is late 2025. The same episode names President Pence and Putin as 'president for life'. Real: no bank of that kind failed in 2025.
events.binWhy: A bank failure throws the country into a recession that does not lift.

facets.change: sanctions and jitters → bank failures and a recession

events.title: Ukraine makes homosexuality a crime
events.description: On its third attempt Ukraine's parliament outlaws 'expressing' homosexuality. Viktor Goraya, deported there from Britain the year before, escapes arrest and crosses Europe in lorries to claim asylum in Spain.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 3 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 3 (2026): 'They tried to do that back in 2016... applied again, in 2019, and, this year, third time lucky.' The same episode's British general election, called for 'Thursday the 7th of May' (a Thursday in 2026), gives the Four Star Party fifteen seats and the balance of power in a hung parliament. Real: Ukraine has no such law; it has moved the other way.
events.binWhy: A government outlaws a group and begins to hunt it.

facets.change: tolerated in private → criminal

events.title: Vivienne Rook becomes Prime Minister
events.description: The coalition collapses, voting is made compulsory, and a general election is held on Thursday 21 October. Rook comes out of it Prime Minister. In the same days Daniel Lyons drowns half a mile off the English coast when an overcrowded boat from France sinks; Viktor, whom he was bringing back from Spain, survives.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 4 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 4 (2027): 'The date for the general election has been set for Thursday, the 21st of October... for the first time in history, voting is compulsory.' 21 October is a Thursday in 2027. The same year Spain's 'January Revolution' installs a far-left government that deports non-citizens, Greece leaves the eurozone, Italy's government resigns under martial law, Hungary is declared bankrupt, and the UN threatens to move its headquarters off American soil. Real: the next UK general election is due by August 2029.
events.binWhy: A populist takes the state by winning an election she had been preparing for since 2019.

facets.change: a hung parliament → a populist prime minister

events.title: The Erstwhile sites
events.description: After eighty days of rain, floods and a dirty bomb in Leeds, Rook's government makes householders take in the displaced and fences off poor estates. Refugees and the unwanted are moved at night, off the record, to 'Erstwhile sites' in disused army bases and hospitals run by private contractors, where disease is left to do the killing.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 5 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 5 is 2028 ('So, 2028'; the Erstwhile logo reads 'copyright 2028'). Rook tells a business auction at Chequers that the model is Kitchener's Boer War camps, where 'the population of the camps controlled itself'. Stephen uses his company's system to send Viktor to Erstwhile Site Four. Real: nothing comparable.
events.binWhy: The state interns refugees and the poor in camps built to kill them.

facets.change: asylum seekers in detention → death camps kept off the record

events.title: Erstwhile Camp 4 goes out on every channel
events.description: With a monkey-flu epidemic spreading and the BBC shut down, activists blow up the towers that block signals around Erstwhile Camp 4 and footage from inside is broadcast nationwide. The camp is liberated, and Rook becomes the first British prime minister arrested in office, charged with murder.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 6 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 6 (2029), confirmed by the 2034 coda: 'Five years ago. 2029. How you brought down Vivienne Rook.' Who financed her is never settled; a journalist is banned from Downing Street for reporting Russian money behind Four Star. Afterwards the BBC reopens.
events.binWhy: Hidden camps are shown to the people they were hidden from, and the government falls with them.

facets.change: camps off the record → on every screen, and a prime minister in custody

events.title: Edith's mind is uploaded
events.description: Dying of the radiation she took at Hong Sha Dao, Edith has told the whole story as her memories are copied into a new water-molecule storage system. Her body dies; she has said she does not believe a person can be encoded, and the family gathered at Muriel's house does not know whether it worked.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 6 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: The coda is dated 2034 on screen. It is the series' only step past the human, and the show leaves it unresolved.
events.binWhy: A person is copied out of her body into a machine, or appears to be.

facets.change: a dying body → a mind in storage, perhaps

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: it leaves our history in the week it was broadcast and runs fifteen years ahead in one year-per-episode continuity (the six-part BBC/HBO series, the only one). Every event is T2, 2019-2034; there is no T3 or T4 because the fiction borrows no earlier history, and no T1 because it stops in 2034. Its chain runs through our own decade, so several beats can now be checked: Trump's second term came four years later than the show's, and the Queen died in 2022 in both.

lineages.title: Moon
lineages.creator: Duncan Jones (director and story); Nathan Parker (screenplay)

divergence.label: Sarang Station is mining helium-3 on the far side
divergence.delta: Real: in 2019-2020 China's Chang'e 4 lander and Yutu-2 rover are the only working machines on the lunar far side, and helium-3 fusion is a paper proposal. Fiction: after an oil crisis, Lunar Industries runs an automated helium-3 mine on the far side with a single human caretaker on a three-year contract, and ships the fuel home to power Earth.
divergence.inUniverse: Derived: the original Sam Bell leaves for his contract while his wife is pregnant, and his daughter is 15 in the film's 2035
divergence.note: The film gives one date, 2035, on a computer screen near the end. Everything earlier is arithmetic from dialogue: the Sams remember leaving Tess pregnant with Eve, and the Eve reached by phone in 2035 is fifteen, so the original Sam Bell's departure for Sarang falls in about 2019-2020; the station, the oil crisis that made helium-3 worth mining and Lunar Industries itself are older but undated. 2020 is used as the first year the film's world demonstrably differs from ours, with low confidence; it could be 2019.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (a computer screen shows 2035; Eve is 15; Tess was pregnant when Sam left)

ending.why: A clone reaches Earth and exposes Lunar Industries, its stock collapses, and by the sequel's courtroom scene the Sam Bells are testifying against the company that made them.

events.title: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon
events.description: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land at Tranquility Base and bring the first lunar soil home. It is the start of the road the film extends: from footprints and samples to a working industrial station.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Apollo 11

events.note: Real history. The film never mentions Apollo; it is filed as the real pre-fork history that any crewed lunar base builds on.
events.binWhy: The first crewed mission lands where no one had been.

facets.change: orbiting the Moon → walking on it

events.title: Lunar helium-3 is proposed as fusion fuel
events.description: Gerald Kulcinski and colleagues at the University of Wisconsin propose mining the Moon's regolith for helium-3, deposited by the solar wind, as fuel for clean fusion reactors on Earth. It is the exact business Lunar Industries is in.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Helium-3 (lunar mining proposals, starting with Gerald Kulcinski in 1986)

events.note: Real history. The real proposal has run into the same wall ever since: over 150 tonnes of regolith per gram of helium-3, and no working helium-3 fusion reactor. The film simply assumes both problems solved.
events.binWhy: The idea the film's whole economy rests on arrives as a research proposal.

facets.change: a solar-wind curiosity → a proposed fuel supply

events.title: Moon premieres at Sundance
events.description: Duncan Jones's first feature, made for $5 million with Sam Rockwell nearly alone on screen, premieres at Sundance and opens in the US in June and the UK in July.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film)

events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Mute, the follow-up, is released
events.description: Jones's Berlin noir, also set in 2035, is released on Netflix and includes a televised trial at which Sam Bell and several of his clones appear, the epilogue to Moon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mute (2018 film)

events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Chang'e 4 lands on the far side of the Moon
events.description: China's Chang'e 4 makes the first soft landing on the lunar far side and deploys the Yutu-2 rover, relaying through a satellite because the far side cannot see Earth. Sarang Station sits on the same side of the Moon, and its isolation from live contact with Earth is the film's plot.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chang'e 4 (landed 3 January 2019)

events.note: Real history, a decade after the film. The far side's lack of direct line of sight to Earth, which Chang'e 4 solved with the Queqiao relay satellite, is the physical fact that makes Lunar Industries' jamming of Sarang's live link plausible.
events.binWhy: The first mission lands on the half of the Moon no one had touched.

facets.change: the far side seen only from orbit → a rover on it

events.title: Sam Bell leaves his pregnant wife for a three-year lunar contract
events.description: Lunar Industries' Sarang Station on the far side harvests helium-3 with automated machines, overseen by one human and a robot called GERTY, and launches canisters of fuel to Earth. The original Sam Bell signs on for three years, leaving his wife Tess pregnant with their daughter; his memories become the company's template.
events.inUniverse: Derived from Eve's age (15) in 2035

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (plot)

events.note: The station's founding is undated; this event marks the earliest year the film lets us place it in operation. The film does not show the original Sam's own time on the Moon; what the film fixes is that every Sam since remembers leaving Tess pregnant. In our 2020 no one lives on the Moon.
events.binWhy: A permanent, crewed industrial base is operating on the Moon's far side.

facets.change: the far side empty → a working helium-3 mine

events.title: Two Sams find the vault, and one gets home
events.description: Two weeks before his contract ends, Sam crashes a rover and meets a newly woken copy of himself. The two discover that they are clones, that hundreds more are stored beneath the base, that each is incinerated at the end of his three years, and that the live link to Earth is jammed; the younger Sam rides a helium-3 shipment to Earth, the company's stock crashes, and in the sequel Mute the Sams appear together at a televised trial.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (a computer screen shows 2035)
Wikipedia: Mute (2018 film) (set in 2035; Sam Bell and his clones at a trial)

events.note: The year is on screen only briefly, so confidence is medium. The escape, the landing on Earth and the Mute trial are treated as one year because Mute is also set in 2035; the film does not say how long the trial came after the landing.
events.binWhy: The company's secret, that its workforce is a line of disposable copies, is exposed to the public by one of them.

facets.change: a hidden clone line → a public trial

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the film's world is ours plus one company: an oil crisis made lunar helium-3 worth mining, and Lunar Industries runs the mine with cloned labour. One continuity, Duncan Jones's 'Mooniverse' as far as it touches Sam Bell (Moon and the courtroom scene in Mute; the 2020 graphic novel Madi is not used). The film dates only 2035, so the chain has two fictional events; the 2020 fork is arithmetic from a character's age, and the rest are real pre-fork events the premise builds on (Apollo, the helium-3 proposal, the far-side landing). Five story events is what the sources support, and the chain is not padded further. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds Apollo and the helium-3 proposal; T2 holds the release, the far-side landing and the whole story; T1 is empty.

lineages.title: Red Mars (the Mars trilogy)
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: John Boone walks on Mars
divergence.delta: Real: in summer 2020 three robotic missions (Perseverance, Tianwen-1 and the UAE's Hope) leave for Mars, and no crewed mission is planned for another decade or more. Fiction: a four-person NASA crew lands on Chryse Planitia, John Boone says 'Well, here we are', and the effort that follows sends a hundred colonists six years later.
divergence.inUniverse: The first crewed landing, summer 2020 (stated in the trilogy's backstory)
divergence.note: The trilogy dates its own history, and the first fictional date it gives is Boone's 2020 landing; the Ares that follows is assembled from Space Shuttle external tanks that, instead of being dropped, were boosted into orbit until there were enough, which is a change to the real shuttle programme but an undated one.

ending.why: By 2212 Mars is terraformed, self-governing under its own constitution, spreading people across the solar system and beyond, and has just chosen to open its doors to Earth's migrants rather than fight a war over them.

events.title: The Space Shuttle first flies
events.description: Columbia launches on STS-1, and the shuttle's huge external fuel tank is dropped into the ocean, as it will be on every flight until 2011. In the trilogy those tanks are instead carried to orbit and clustered into the Ares, the largest spacecraft ever built.

events.title: The longevity treatment is developed at Acheron
events.description: Vlad Taneev's biomedical team at Acheron develops a gerontological treatment that repairs the body and stretches lifespans towards centuries. It is given to everyone on Mars by the 2050s, leaks to Earth, and becomes one of the causes of the wars to come.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the trilogy forks from our history into a near future that is plainly ours (NASA, Russia, the UN, shuttle hardware, transnational companies) and follows one branch for two centuries; the far-future epoch reflects where it ends, not where it starts. One continuity: Red Mars, Green Mars and Blue Mars (the 1999 collection The Martians includes alternative histories and is not used). The novels date their own events; where they do not, years come from the fan chronologies at KimStanleyRobinson.info and are marked medium or low, and two decade-only dates (2045, 2165) are flagged as markers. Tiers: T4 is empty because nothing in the fiction reaches before the space age; T3 holds the real shuttle and the publications; T2 holds the whole story from 2020 to 2212; T1 is empty because the trilogy ends in 2212.

lineages.title: Greenland
lineages.creator: Chris Sparling (writer); Ric Roman Waugh (director)

divergence.label: Comet Clarke
divergence.delta: Real: in 2021 the only two interstellar objects ever seen, 'Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov, have passed at a safe distance, and NASA's first deflection test, DART, launches in November. Fiction: an interstellar comet discovered only weeks earlier turns out to be a trail of fragments; one destroys Tampa, and two days later the largest ends civilisation.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; Clarke is 'discovered only weeks ago'
divergence.note: Neither film gives a calendar year. The first is plainly set in its own present (smartphones, emergency alerts, Atlanta suburbs), was shot in 2019 and released in 2020; the atlas files the impact at 2021, the first year after release, as it does The Day After Tomorrow. The sequel's 'five years after' then lands in 2026. If the first film is read as set in 2020, every story date moves back one year.

events.title: The United States builds Thule Air Base
events.description: Real history: under a defence agreement with Denmark, Operation Blue Jay builds an American air base in the far north-west of Greenland on a scale compared with the Panama Canal. In 1953 Denmark forcibly moves about 130 Inughuit from Old Thule to make room; the base is renamed Pituffik Space Base in 2023.

events.title: Camp Century: a town inside the ice sheet
events.description: Real history: the US Army digs 21 tunnels, three kilometres of them, into the ice sheet east of Thule and powers them with a portable nuclear reactor. Presented as a research station, it is a trial for Project Iceworm, a network of nuclear missile sites under the ice, and is abandoned in 1967 when the ice begins to crush it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Camp Century

events.title: NASA sets up its Planetary Defense Coordination Office
events.description: Real history: NASA creates an office to find and catalogue objects that could hit the Earth and to coordinate what would be done about one. Its first test, the DART spacecraft, launches in November 2021.

events.title: The first object from another star is seen passing through

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2I/Borisov

events.description: An interstellar comet discovered only weeks before is due to pass close; instead a fragment expected to fall near Bermuda vaporises Tampa, and the government reveals that the largest piece, nine miles wide, will strike in two days. Selected families are summoned to air bases for flights to bunkers in Greenland while mobs storm the gates, and the fragment that hits Western Europe devastates civilisation around the world.

lineages.title: Don't Look Up
lineages.creator: Adam McKay (writer-director; story with David Sirota)

divergence.label: Kate Dibiasky finds the comet
divergence.delta: Real: in October 2022 no large object is known to be on course for Earth, NASA's DART probe has just nudged the small asteroid Dimorphos, and the US midterms are three weeks away. Fiction: a graduate student finds a comet five to ten kilometres wide that will hit in six months and fourteen days, and the White House decides to sit tight and assess.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; the discovery comes three weeks before a midterm election
divergence.note: The film shows no dates. It is plainly set in its own present (streaming, smartphones, a morning-show culture of 2021), and one line fixes the season: the president asks when the midterms are and is told three weeks. The first midterm after the December 2021 release was on 8 November 2022, so the discovery is filed at mid-October 2022 and the impact, six months and fourteen days later, at about the end of April 2023. If the film is taken as set in an earlier or later midterm year, every date moves with it. The fictional president means the world had already parted from ours in its politics, at a date the film never gives.
