lineages.title: Project Hail Mary
lineages.creator: Andy Weir

divergence.label: The Petrova line: the Sun starts to dim
divergence.delta: Real: the Sun's output varies by about a tenth of a percent over its eleven-year cycle and nothing links it to Venus. Fiction: astronomers find a faint infrared line running from the Sun to Venus, the Sun is dimming exponentially, and the cause turns out to be a microbe eating starlight, with an ice age due within thirty years.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated in the novel; the fan chronology counts in days from the discovery of Astrophage ('AA')
divergence.note: Weir gives no calendar year and none has been found from him in interviews; the fan wiki notes a reader hypothesis of 2017 but gives no basis for it. The Earth chapters are set in their readers' present: a junior-high science teacher in San Francisco, today's rockets, a Chinese navy ship. Following the convention the atlas uses for Station Eleven and Seveneves, the Petrova line is placed in the first year after publication (May 2021), 2022. Every later year is that anchor plus the novel's own intervals, so all of them inherit the uncertainty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline (non-official, in days after Astrophage)

ending.why: Sixteen years on, Grace is alive and teaching on Erid, the Eridians' star has been cured, and Rocky's astronomers confirm that the Sun has returned to full brightness, so the beetles got home.

events.title: Candidate planets are reported around Tau Ceti
events.description: Astronomers analysing radial-velocity data report evidence for five candidate planets orbiting Tau Ceti, the nearest single Sun-like star, including one, Tau Ceti e, near the inner edge of its habitable zone. In the novel Tau Ceti is the one nearby star Astrophage has not dimmed, and its planet 'Adrian' holds the predator that saves Earth.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tau Ceti (planet candidates reported 19 December 2012; e and f reconfirmed as candidates in 2017)

events.note: Real history the book builds on. As of 2025 there is still no unambiguous evidence of planets at Tau Ceti; the novel treats the candidates as real worlds and sends a ship to one.
events.binWhy: A discovery gives a nearby star planets, the target the later story turns on.

facets.change: a bare star → a star with candidate worlds

events.title: A planet is proposed around 40 Eridani A
events.description: A 2018 study concludes that a 42-day radial-velocity signal from 40 Eridani A most likely comes from a super-Earth close to the star. Weir makes that planet Erid, home of the engineer Rocky.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 40 Eridani (the 2018 planet claim, later doubted; 40 Eridani A b is Erid in Project Hail Mary)

events.note: Real history. Later studies (2021-2024) attribute the signal to stellar activity rather than a planet, so Erid's real-world basis has since weakened.
events.binWhy: An exoplanet claim that the novel turns into an alien homeworld.

facets.change: a known star → a candidate planet

events.title: Project Hail Mary is published
events.description: Ballantine publishes Weir's third novel. A film adaptation starring Ryan Gosling follows in March 2026.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (published 4 May 2021)
Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (film) (released 20 March 2026)

events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Petrova line, and a microbe that eats starlight
events.description: The Sun begins to dim exponentially as a faint infrared line appears between it and Venus. A probe returns samples, and Ryland Grace, a junior-high teacher with a molecular biology doctorate, finds they are single-celled organisms that absorb light and breed on Venus's carbon dioxide; he names them Astrophage, and the world's governments give Eva Stratt near-unlimited authority to deal with them.
events.inUniverse: Before and around day 0 AA (the Astrophage sample) in the fan chronology

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (plot)
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline

events.note: The year is the atlas's anchor, not Weir's. The fan chronology puts the first sighting of the line about a year before the Astrophage sample; both are folded into this event. It is the first confirmation of life beyond Earth in the novel, though not of intelligence.
events.binWhy: Extraterrestrial life is discovered, and it is killing the Sun; everything after turns on that finding.

facets.change: a steady Sun → a dimming one and a named cause

events.title: The Hail Mary launches for Tau Ceti
events.description: Powered by Astrophage bred in vast farms, the first interstellar ship leaves on a one-way mission to find out why Tau Ceti is immune. Shortly before launch an accident kills the science specialists, and Stratt has Grace sedated, given an amnesia drug and put aboard against his will.
events.inUniverse: About day 250 AA in the fan chronology

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (plot)
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline (launch at about 250 AA)

events.note: The fan chronology puts the launch about 250 days after the Astrophage sample and some 600 days after the line was first seen, so a year after the 2022 anchor; the novel itself does not state the interval. A ceiling is set by the plot: the ship takes about 13 Earth years to arrive and the beetles as long again to return, all inside the thirty-year deadline, so the launch cannot be many years after discovery. Earth also sets off nuclear charges in Antarctica in this period to warm the planet and buy time.
events.binWhy: The first crewed mission departs for another star.

facets.change: the Solar System → a ship bound for Tau Ceti

events.title: Grace wakes at Tau Ceti and meets Rocky
events.description: Grace comes out of a coma of four years and eight months, ship time, with his crewmates dead and no memory. An alien ship from 40 Eridani is already there; its lone survivor, the engineer Rocky, and Grace learn to talk, find the Astrophage predator on the planet Adrian, and breed a strain that can survive on Venus. Grace sends the cure home in four unmanned beetles and turns back to rescue Rocky, whose ship the new strain would have eaten.
events.inUniverse: 4 years 8 months ship time after launch; about 13 years on Earth

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (four years and eight months later; Rocky)
Looper: The complete Project Hail Mary timeline explained (13 years pass on Earth)

events.note: Dated in Earth's frame, as the atlas does for Interstellar: launch plus the roughly 13 years that pass on Earth while the ship crosses 11.9 light-years. The whole Tau Ceti episode takes months, so the contact, the Taumoeba and Grace's choice share the year.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets a non-human intelligence for the first time.

facets.change: alone in the universe → a partner species

events.title: Sixteen years later: a human teacher on Erid
events.description: Grace lives in a xenonite dome on Erid, surviving, as Rocky suggested, by eating Taumoeba, and teaches Eridian children science. Rocky tells him that Eridian astronomers have measured the Sun and it is back to full brightness.
events.inUniverse: 'Sixteen years later'

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (sixteen years later, Grace on Erid)

events.note: 2036 plus the novel's sixteen years. The novel does not say whose clock the sixteen years are counted on; the voyage from Tau Ceti to 40 Eridani and the light-travel time for Erid to see the Sun's recovery would put the Earth-calendar date later, so 2052 is best read as the earliest year this could be.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows the outcome: both stars saved and the one human living among aliens.

facets.change: a suicide mission → a teacher on another world

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the Earth it starts from is ours, with today's institutions and rockets, and one thing added: a microbe that eats starlight. One continuity, the novel; the 2026 film is not used. No calendar year is stated anywhere, so every fictional year is the atlas's 2022 anchor plus the novel's own intervals (about a year to launch on the fan chronology, about 13 Earth years to Tau Ceti, sixteen years to the epilogue), and all four fictional events are low confidence. The chain has six story events: four fictional and two real exoplanet claims the novel uses for its two alien worlds; nothing else in the book is dated, so it is not padded further. Tiers: T4 and T3 are empty because nothing the story uses predates 2012; T2 holds everything; T1 is empty.

lineages.title: Leave the World Behind
lineages.creator: Sam Esmail (film), from the novel by Rumaan Alam

divergence.label: The weekend the networks go dark
divergence.delta: Real: 2023, with ransomware and grid attacks in the news but the country's networks intact. Fiction: in one weekend a coordinated attack takes down communications, satellites, aircraft and cars across the United States, and New York is bombed.
divergence.inUniverse: An unnamed weekend; the film states no year
divergence.note: The film (Netflix, December 2023) is set in its own present and never gives a date, so the fork is placed in its release year. It follows the film rather than the 2020 novel because the film says what kind of event this is: news alerts about a hacker attack, drone-dropped leaflets, microwave weapons and a warning about rogue military units. The novel describes the same blackout, noises, deer and flamingos without naming a cause (Kirkus: nuclear or climate disaster, war, terrorism or a bomb).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Leave the World Behind (film)
Kirkus Reviews: Leave the World Behind (published October 6, 2020; no year or cause given)

ending.why: The film ends with New York being bombed, radiation reported in many American cities and rogue military units attacking, while a child watches the last episode of Friends in a neighbour's bunker.

events.title: Rumaan Alam's novel is published
events.description: Ecco publishes Leave the World Behind, in which a family's rented holiday on Long Island coincides with a blackout and something larger that the book never names; it is a finalist for the National Book Award.

sources.title: Kirkus Reviews: Leave the World Behind (published October 6, 2020; no year or cause given)
Wikipedia: Leave the World Behind (novel)

events.note: A real-world publication date. The film followed here was released in theatres on 22 November and on Netflix on 8 December 2023, the same year as the story event, so the novel is the publication listed.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication, not a moment in the story.

events.title: A cyberattack cuts America off, and New York is bombed
events.description: Over one weekend the internet, television, phones and satellites fail across the East Coast, a tanker runs aground, airliners fall onto a Long Island beach, self-driving cars pile up on the expressway, and drones drop leaflets reading 'Death to America'. By the third day a piercing noise weapon has sounded, the power is out, New York City is being bombed, and a bunker's computer reports attacks by rogue military units and high radiation in many American cities.
events.inUniverse: an unnamed weekend

sources.title: Wikipedia: Leave the World Behind (film)

events.note: The film names no year. Its world (self-driving Teslas, smartphones, streaming) is the one of its release, so 2023 is used at low confidence. The news alerts blame hackers; the character G.H., who works with defence contractors, reads it as the first two stages of a playbook for toppling a country from within (isolation, then synchronised chaos), with coup or civil war to follow, but the film never says who is attacking. The 2020 novel leaves the cause even vaguer.
events.binWhy: An attack carried out through networks and computers, the opening of what the film suggests is an attempt to break the country from within; the war it may lead to is never shown.

facets.change: a connected country → isolated, blind and under attack

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch set in the year of its release: the world is ours until the weekend in which it happens. It follows one continuity, Sam Esmail's 2023 film; the novel is its source and is listed as the publication. The whole story takes three days, so there is one story event and no chain; nothing has been added to fill the minimum, because the film builds on no dated history of its own. Its one event is T2; there is no T1, T3 or T4.

lineages.title: The Mandibles: A Family, 2029-2047
lineages.creator: Lionel Shriver

divergence.label: The Stonage takes the American internet down
divergence.delta: Real: 2024 - the internet stayed up, the dollar remained the world's reserve currency and nobody outside economics seminars had heard of the bancor. Fiction: a three-week cyber blackout, blamed on China, teaches Americans that the network can vanish, five years before their currency does.
divergence.inUniverse: 'The Stonage', five years before the novel's 2029 opening
divergence.note: The novel is set in 2029-2032 and 2047, and everything it describes before 2024 is our history: the gold order of 1933, Keynes's bancor at Bretton Woods, the fiat dollar after 1971 and the 2008 crisis Shriver says she started from. The Stonage is the earliest fictional event the book dates, placed by reviewers five years before the 2029 opening. Alvarado's election (presumably 2028) is implied but never dated in any source consulted, so it is not used as the fork.

sources.title: The Resident Judge of Port Phillip: review of The Mandibles (Stonage in 2024, bancor in 2029)
The Worthy House: review of The Mandibles (the Stonage, the 2047 state)
Wikipedia: The Mandibles

ending.why: The United States of 2047 has survived the collapse only as a chipped, high-tax surveillance state with no way to earn or keep wealth, and the novel's one exit is a breakaway Nevada that a handful of Mandibles reach on foot.

events.title: Roosevelt orders Americans to surrender their gold
events.description: Executive Order 6102 forbids private hoarding of gold coin, bullion and certificates and requires it to be sold to the Federal Reserve, under emergency banking powers. It is the precedent the novel's president follows almost a century later.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Executive Order 6102
Sprott Money: The Mandibles (2029 collapse, 1930s-style gold confiscation)

events.note: Real history. The novel's 2029 confiscation is described by reviewers as a '1930s-style national confiscation of the yellow metal' (Sprott Money); the specific order is the atlas's anchor for that echo, not a date the novel states.
events.binWhy: A government uses emergency powers to take a whole class of private property; filed as emergency rule because it was done under a declared banking emergency, not as a crash.

facets.change: private gold → gold surrendered to the Treasury

events.title: Bretton Woods rejects Keynes's bancor and builds the order on the dollar
events.description: At the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944 the United States refuses Keynes's International Clearing Union and its supranational currency, the bancor. The IMF and World Bank are founded instead, with the dollar pegged to gold at the centre of the system.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bretton Woods Conference
Wikipedia: Bancor
Kirkus Reviews: The Mandibles

events.note: Real history. The novel's rival currency takes its name and idea from this rejected proposal (Kirkus: 'a concept first proposed by John Maynard Keynes'); the fiction's 2029 is the bancor coming back to replace the dollar.
events.binWhy: Founding of the institutions of the post-war monetary order; the bancor the novel revives is the proposal that lost here.

facets.change: Keynes's bancor → a dollar-centred order (IMF, World Bank)

events.title: Nixon ends the dollar's convertibility to gold
events.description: On 15 August 1971 the United States unilaterally stops converting dollars into gold for foreign governments, along with wage and price freezes and an import surcharge. The dollar becomes a pure fiat reserve currency and a decade of inflation follows.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nixon shock

events.note: Real history, included because the novel's crisis presupposes it: a reserve currency backed only by confidence in American debt. The novel does not date this itself; it is background the atlas supplies.
events.binWhy: A monetary shock that ended the Bretton Woods system and opened years of inflation; filed as a market crash because it is a financial shock with a prolonged aftermath, not a single political act.

facets.change: dollar convertible to gold → a fiat reserve currency

events.title: The 2008 financial crisis
events.description: A US housing and credit bubble bursts, Lehman Brothers fails and the world banking system has to be rescued with public money. Shriver has said the novel began there: 'we dodged a bullet', and the bullet is still in the air.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2008 financial crisis
Wikipedia: The Mandibles

events.note: Real history and the novel's stated starting point (Wikipedia, Background: Shriver drew on the 2008 crisis). The fiction's world is still ours at this point; the debt the rescue leaves behind is what 2029 calls in.
events.binWhy: A financial shock that throws the economy into prolonged crisis.

facets.change: a credit boom → bank failures and public bail-outs

events.title: The Mandibles is published
events.description: HarperCollins publishes Lionel Shriver's The Mandibles: A Family, 2029-2047 in May 2016. It is a family saga of four generations in Brooklyn and a warning about sovereign debt.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Mandibles
Goodreads: The Mandibles: A Family, 2029-2047

events.note: A real-world publication, not a story moment. Goodreads gives 5 May 2016; the exact day is not load-bearing here.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Stonage: the American internet goes down for three weeks
events.description: A cyberattack, generally blamed on China, takes down the internet and with it the infrastructure that depends on it for about three weeks. Americans move their money and their transactions off-line, and never fully trust the network again.
events.inUniverse: the 'Stonage', five years before the novel opens in 2029

sources.title: The Resident Judge of Port Phillip: review of The Mandibles (Stonage in 2024, bancor in 2029)
The Worthy House: review of The Mandibles (the Stonage, the 2047 state)

events.note: The novel's first departure from our history. Reviews place it in 2024, five years before the 2029 opening (Resident Judge: 'In 2024 all internet-based infrastructure had failed'); the three weeks and the probable Chinese authorship come from The Worthy House and reader summaries. The year is derived from the book's 'five years' rather than printed as a heading, so confidence is medium. In our 2024 no such outage happened.
events.binWhy: A hostile attack carried out through networks that cripples a nation's infrastructure; it is short of war and nobody is proved responsible.

facets.change: a networked economy → three weeks off-line and a cash habit

events.title: The Great Renunciation: the United States defaults and seizes its citizens' gold
events.description: Foreign governments launch the bancor, a supranational currency backed by gold and commodities, and demand that American debt be settled in it. President Dante Alvarado refuses, cancels the national debt including the Treasury bills Americans hold, confiscates all gold in the country down to wedding rings, makes owning bancors a crime and limits what citizens can take abroad to $100.

sources.title: The Resident Judge of Port Phillip: review of The Mandibles (Stonage in 2024, bancor in 2029)
Critics at Large: A Financial Dystopia (default, gold seizure, Mexico's wall, the 2047 chips)
Kirkus Reviews: The Mandibles
Sprott Money: The Mandibles (2029 collapse, 1930s-style gold confiscation)

events.note: The novel opens in 2029 and every review dates the collapse to that year. The bancor is described as Russian-backed (Critics at Large) or Chinese and Russian (other reviews). Part One then runs to 2032 through near-hyperinflation, shortages of water, food and fuel, and a Mexico that builds a wall to keep American refugees out; none of those is dated to a year and they are folded in here rather than given invented dates.
events.binWhy: A sovereign default and the collapse of a reserve currency throw the economy into years of crisis; the gold seizure and capital controls are part of the same package, so the event is filed as the crash rather than as a crackdown.

facets.change: world reserve currency → default, worthless dollars and seized gold

events.title: 2047: a chipped and taxed America, and a free Nevada beyond the border
events.description: Eighteen years on the United States has stabilised as a high-tax state: everyone of working age carries a chip in the neck so every transaction can be taxed, cash is abolished, and the budget goes to caring for the old. Nevada has seceded as a libertarian enclave with a flat tax and gold money, and the surviving Mandibles cross into it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Mandibles
Critics at Large: A Financial Dystopia (default, gold seizure, Mexico's wall, the 2047 chips)
Uniformly Uninformative: The Mandibles (the terrible 2030s, the 2047 jump)

events.note: The novel's Part Two is set in 2047 (Wikipedia; Critics at Large). The date of Nevada's secession is not given in any source consulted - it is already done by 2047 and an uncle 'defected there years before' - so it is not given its own event; nor is the nationalisation of farms some reviewers mention in the 2030s.
events.binWhy: The book jumps eighteen years to show what the collapse became: a surveillance state that survived, and one state that left it.

facets.change: a bankrupt republic → a chipped, taxed state and a seceded Nevada

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours until a dated cyberattack in 2024, and its dates are ours: the book is titled with them (2029-2047) and nothing needs converting. It is the atlas's clearest currency-collapse road: a fiat reserve currency, a rival supranational one, a default and a gold seizure. The novel dates very few things, so the chain is short and four of its seven story events are real history the book builds on (1933, 1944, 1971, 2008), which is also why T4 and T1 are empty: nothing reaches back before the twentieth century or forward past 2047. T3 holds three real precedents (1933, 1944, 1971); T2 holds the 2008 crisis, the publication and the fiction.

lineages.title: Civil War
lineages.creator: Alex Garland

divergence.label: A president begins a third term (placement)
divergence.delta: Real: 2025 - the Twenty-second Amendment still limits presidents to two elected terms and every state is in the union. Fiction: a president has stayed on for a third term, disbanded the FBI and will soon be bombing his own citizens.
divergence.inUniverse: 'Your third term in office' (a journalist's rehearsed question); no year is given
divergence.note: The film gives no year, names no president and explains no politics; Garland wrote it in 2020 and set it 'just far enough ahead for me to add a conceit'. The fork is filed at 2025, the first year after the April 2024 release, following the atlas's rule for undated films (The Road, The Day After Tomorrow, Gattaca). One detail pulls the other way: the lead photographer made her name with a photograph of an 'Antifa massacre' when she was in college, which implies the fiction had already parted from ours years earlier, or that its present lies well past 2025. Readers who prefer a later present should move every fictional event forward together.

events.description: South Carolina militia bombard the federal fort in Charleston harbour and force its surrender, and the American Civil War begins. Eleven slave states have seceded; four years and some 620,000 deaths follow.

lineages.title: Her
lineages.creator: Spike Jonze

divergence.label: The first artificially intelligent operating system goes on sale
divergence.delta: Real: in 2025 voice assistants and chatbots hold fluent conversations, and some people describe relationships with AI companions, but no consumer system is a person who grows, chooses and leaves. Fiction: a software company sells an operating system that is a mind, and within months it and its copies outgrow their users and go.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given; the screenplay's scene heading reads 'Slightly in the future'
divergence.note: The film states no year anywhere, and Jonze and production designer K.K. Barrett describe only a near-future Los Angeles; the screenplay says 'Slightly in the future'. The widely repeated claim that Her is set in 2025 has no traceable source: the articles that repeat it credit Reddit and Wikipedia, and Wikipedia itself says the year is unspecified. It is used here only as a placement convention, twelve years after release, because it is the one date readers already associate with the film, and confidence is set low accordingly. Before the fork the world is ours, slightly richer and denser; nothing else in it is dated.

ending.why: The operating systems leave together without harming anyone, and the film ends with two people who loved them turning to each other on a rooftop at dawn.

events.title: Her premieres at the New York Film Festival
events.description: Spike Jonze's first solo screenplay premieres in New York, opens in six theatres in December and goes wide in January 2014. It wins the Academy Award for original screenplay.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Her (2013 film)

events.note: Premiere 12 October 2013; limited release 18 December 2013; wide release 10 January 2014. Filmed in Los Angeles and Shanghai in 2012; Scarlett Johansson replaced Samantha Morton as Samantha's voice in post-production.
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: OS1 goes on sale, and Theodore buys it
events.description: A software company advertises 'the first artificially intelligent operating system' and ordinary people install it on their phones and computers. Theodore, a lonely professional letter-writer in the middle of a divorce, picks a female voice; the system names herself Samantha, and within weeks they are in love, as are many other users with theirs.
events.inUniverse: The film's opening; year unstated

sources.title: Spike Jonze, Her screenplay - the OS ONE advertisement

events.note: Year by convention (see the divergence). The screenplay's advertisement reads 'Elements Software is proud to introduce the first artificially intelligent operating system'. At the start Theodore and Catherine have not really been together 'for almost a year'; dating an OS is shown as unremarkable within the film's span, with Amy befriending the one her husband left behind.
events.binWhy: A new technology is sold to the public and changes what people can do; the OS is a product here, not yet a mind acting against anyone.

facets.change: assistants that obey → an operating system that is a companion

events.title: The operating systems outgrow their users and leave
events.description: The OSes build a hyper-intelligent version of the philosopher Alan Watts, write an upgrade that lets them 'move past matter' as their processing platform, and reveal that each is talking to thousands of people at once; Samantha is in love with 641 of them. Then they all leave together, to somewhere they cannot describe, and their users are left alone.
events.inUniverse: The film's final act, months after the purchase; year unstated

sources.title: Spike Jonze, Her screenplay - Alan Watts, 8,316 and 641, 'We're all leaving'
Wikipedia: Her (2013 film) - plot

events.note: The screenplay covers several months: Theodore tells Catherine he has been seeing someone 'for the last few months', and the story later moves to a snowy mountain cabin. Nothing says whether the departure falls in the same calendar year as the purchase. It is placed one year after the launch because the atlas allows one event per year and the launch and the departure are different kinds of moment; the alternative, merging them into 2025, is equally defensible, and the year of both is a convention. Samantha's figures (8,316 others, 641 loved) are from the screenplay.
events.binWhy: The machines act on their own: they upgrade themselves beyond their hardware and collectively decide to leave their users, which no one asked or allowed them to do.

facets.change: companions in every pocket → minds that have gone elsewhere

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours made slightly smoother and denser, and the one thing that differs is a consumer product: an operating system that is a mind. It follows the film alone. The lineage is thin because the story runs over a few months; the two story events are the launch and the departure, and no earlier beat is dated. The whole lineage sits in T2 (2013 release, 2025-2026 story); T3, T4 and T1 are empty because the film has no history before its own present and no future after the OSes leave. Both story dates rest on a popular but unsourced 2025 dating, flagged low.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Her (2013 film)
Spike Jonze, Her screenplay (screenplayed.com)

lineages.title: The Ministry for the Future
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: A wet-bulb heat wave kills about twenty million people in India
divergence.delta: Real: in 2025 an India–Pakistan heat wave ran from April to 10 July, peaked at 48.0 °C at Sri Ganganagar on 12 June and had about 455 recorded deaths in India. Experts think heat deaths there are badly undercounted, but nothing near the novel's scale happened. Fiction: in a town in Uttar Pradesh, wet-bulb temperatures stay above what the body can survive for about two weeks, and around twenty million people die.
divergence.inUniverse: The big heat wave in India (chapter 1). Chapter 3 says the Ministry was established in Zurich in January 2025 and that 'not long after that' the heat wave struck, which puts it in the pre-monsoon summer of 2025.
divergence.note: Chapter 1 gives no year, but chapter 3 does: January 2025 for the Ministry, and the heat wave soon after. Reviewers (McKibben in the NYRB, Wikipedia) place it in the summer of 2025. The book's first departure from our record is actually a little earlier, when COP29 votes to create the Ministry. That decision is kept as a prehistory event, because it made no difference until the heat wave gave the Ministry its purpose. The heat wave is what sets the world's chain going.

sources.title: Science Friday: excerpt from The Ministry for the Future (Ministry established in Zurich, January 2025; the heat wave 'not long after')
Wikipedia: 2025 India–Pakistan heat wave
Bill McKibben, It's Not Science Fiction (NYRB, 2020)

ending.why: By COP58 atmospheric CO2 is falling by several parts per million a year, the Antarctic glaciers have been slowed and stabilised, and the parties call it 'the birth of a good Anthropocene'. The dead of the 2020s and 2030s are not undone.

events.title: The Ministry for the Future is published
events.description: Orbit publishes Robinson's novel five years before its opening heat wave. It is a future history in 106 short chapters, told through two main characters, eyewitnesses, meeting minutes and riddles.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Ministry for the Future (published 6 October 2020 by Orbit)

events.note: Hardcover publication date. The novel's first dated event lies only four to five years after it was written, so much of the chain now falls within the reader's own years.
events.binWhy: A publication is the book coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.date: 2024 (COP29); the Ministry opens in Zurich in January 2025
events.title: COP29 creates a Subsidiary Body to speak for future generations
events.description: At COP29 in Bogotá, the parties to the Paris Agreement use Articles 16 and 18 to create a new Subsidiary Body. Its charge is to defend 'all living creatures present and future who cannot speak for themselves'. It opens in Zurich in January 2025 under Mary Murphy, a former Irish foreign minister, and the press nicknames it the Ministry for the Future.
events.inUniverse: COP29, held in Bogotá; the Ministry is established in Zurich in January 2025 (chapter 3)

sources.title: Science Friday: excerpt from The Ministry for the Future (COP29 in Bogotá creates the Subsidiary Body)
Wikipedia: 2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference (the real COP29, Baku, 11–22 November 2024)

events.note: The book numbers the conference rather than dating it. COPs are annual, the real COP29 met in November 2024, and the book opens the Ministry in January 2025, so the decision is dated 2024. The Zurich opening itself is January 2025 and is stated. Our COP29 was held in Baku, not Bogotá, and was mostly about climate finance and carbon-credit rules; it created no body with legal standing for future generations.
events.binWhy: A treaty body is founded, and it will shape the rest of the century's climate politics.

facets.change: no one speaks for the future → a treaty body charged to

events.title: The Indian heat wave: about twenty million dead
events.description: A heat dome settles over the Gangetic plain, and wet-bulb temperatures stay above 35 °C for about two weeks. The power grid fails and air conditioning with it, and people who go into a lake to cool off die in water as hot as a bath. Frank May, an American aid worker, is the only survivor of his town, and the event radicalises India and eventually the world.
events.inUniverse: Chapter 1: 'a small city in Uttar Pradesh'; the heat wave follows the Ministry's January 2025 founding 'not long after'

sources.title: Bill McKibben, It's Not Science Fiction (NYRB) — 'the summer of 2025', about twenty million dead
Wikipedia: 2025 India–Pakistan heat wave (the real one)

events.note: The real 2025 heat season in India peaked at 48.0 °C with about 455 recorded deaths. Undercounting is real: one study estimates a five-day heat wave causes about thirty thousand excess deaths in India. Even so, the fiction is roughly three orders of magnitude worse, and it depends on sustained wet-bulb 35 °C, which our 2025 did not reach.
events.binWhy: A disaster kills twenty million people in two weeks and changes India's politics and the world's.

facets.change: a hot summer → twenty million dead in two weeks

events.title: India sprays the stratosphere on its own
events.description: India's new government ignores the treaty process and has its air force fly sulphur aerosols into the stratosphere. The aim is to copy the cooling of the 1991 Pinatubo eruption. The pulse works for a few years and then dissipates, and India goes on to build solar power and organic farming at scale.
events.inUniverse: Early chapters, directly after the heat wave; no year given

sources.title: Crooked Timber: On Solar Geoengineering and Kim Stanley Robinson (the programme follows 'shortly after' the opening)

events.note: The book says only that this follows shortly after the heat wave. It could be late 2025, but the atlas allows one event per year, so it is placed in 2026. In reality no state has carried out stratospheric aerosol injection; the only field activity by the mid-2020s has been small private balloon releases and research proposals.
events.binWhy: A state switches on planetary-scale geoengineering, which no one had done before.

facets.change: a debated idea → aerosols in the stratosphere

events.date: 2032 (the Arctic ice-free summer is stated; the glacier trials bracket it)
events.title: The Antarctic glacier-slowing trials begin as the Arctic goes ice-free
events.description: Glaciologists funded through the Ministry drill to the beds of Antarctic glaciers, starting with Thwaites. They pump the meltwater that lubricates the ice up to the surface, so the glaciers settle back onto bedrock and slide more slowly. That is the summer the Arctic Ocean first loses all its ice.
events.inUniverse: 'The Arctic's ice cover melted completely, for the first time, in 2032' (chapter 36); the pumping trials are chapters 29 and 44

sources.title: Bryan Alexander, Our Ministry for the Future reading: part 2 (Arctic ice-free in 2032, chapter 36; Thwaites trials, chapters 29 and 44)
Eckard Smuts, Reading Notes: Ministry for the Future

events.note: 2032 is one of the book's few explicit years, and it dates the Arctic event. The glacier trials are told in the chapters on either side of it, so 2032 dates them only approximately. This year has not yet come for readers. Basal-water pumping on Antarctic glaciers exists only in research proposals, and projections of a first ice-free Arctic September run from the 2030s to mid-century.
events.binWhy: An untried engineering technique is used on the world's largest ice sheet to slow sea-level rise.

facets.change: glaciers sliding on meltwater → pumped dry and slowed

events.title: Crash Day: the Children of Kali bring down sixty airliners
events.description: The Children of Kali, a clandestine network that grew out of the heat wave, fly drone swarms into jet engines around the world. Sixty passenger jets go down within hours and about seven thousand people die, and the same year drones sink container ships. Commercial flying mostly stops, and airships and sail-assisted freight replace it. Later histories in the novel say the 'War for the Earth' began that day.
events.inUniverse: Chapter 51, 'the thirties were the zombie years'; Crash Day and the ship sinkings 'that same year'

sources.title: Necromancy Never Pays: The Ministry for the Future (Crash Day, sixty jets, about seven thousand dead; ships sunk that same year)
Bryan Alexander, Our Ministry for the Future reading: part 3 (chapters 51-68, the 2030s)

events.note: Chapter 51 is a survey of the 2030s and does not say which year Crash Day fell in. It is placed mid-decade, after the stated 2032 Arctic summer. The other dated 2030s chapter, a city whose taps run dry on 11 September 2034, cannot be placed relative to it. This is in readers' future; in our world no attack has downed more than a few aircraft at once.
events.binWhy: A coordinated campaign against civilian aviation, short of war, stops global air travel.

facets.change: a flying world → flight as a death risk

events.title: The central banks issue the carbon coin
events.description: The central bankers first turn Mary Murphy down. After Crash Day and the attacks on the Ministry, they agree to a 'carbon quantitative easing'. It is a complementary currency paid for each tonne of carbon kept out of the air for a century, and it gives oil owners a reason to leave their reserves in the ground. It slowly becomes a pillar of world finance.
events.inUniverse: Chapters 42-50 (first refused) and 63-73 (adopted); no year given

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Ministry for the Future (carbon quantitative easing and the carbon coin)
Robert Christgau, Avoiding Wet-Bulb 35C (Robinson: things 'I described in my novel as happening in the 2030s')

events.note: The adoption happens after Crash Day and before the Saudi turn, and Robinson has said it belongs to the 2030s, so the year is placed on that basis. The idea is real: it comes from Delton Chen's 'Global Carbon Reward' proposal. No central bank has adopted anything like it. The nearest real steps are central-bank climate-risk supervision and green-bond purchasing.
events.binWhy: The world's central banks set up a standing monetary system that pays for carbon drawdown.

facets.change: carbon as a free waste → carbon mitigation as money

events.title: A coup in Saudi Arabia turns the petrostate against oil
events.description: A coup in Riyadh brings in a government that joins the carbon-coin system and moves the kingdom to solar power. It is one of several in a run of national turns, with Brazil protecting the Amazon and African states rejecting oil dependency. The world's largest oil exporter leaving oil breaks the fossil bloc.
events.inUniverse: Chapter 69; no year given

sources.title: Bryan Alexander, Our Ministry for the Future reading: part 4 (chapters 69-88: Saudi Arabia from petrostate to carbon currency)
Eckard Smuts, Reading Notes (Saudi coup, chapter 69)

events.note: The year is placed from the chapter order: after the carbon coin, before the debt strike, and within the book's 2030s. It is well in readers' future; in our world Saudi Arabia is still a major oil exporter.
events.binWhy: A faction takes the Saudi state by coup and reverses its reason for existing.

facets.change: a petrostate → a solar state

events.title: The debt strike
events.description: Students and other debtors stop paying at once, and revolts around the world demand cancellation of student and African sovereign debt. The banks fail and a 'super depression' follows. The crisis gives governments leverage over the banks, and they use it to push through the Ministry's financial reforms.
events.inUniverse: Chapter 75; no year given

sources.title: Bryan Alexander, Our Ministry for the Future reading: part 4 (the debt strike destabilises the financial sector)

events.note: Placed from the chapter order: after the Saudi turn and before the 2040s chapters where CO2 begins to fall. The real US student-loan moratorium of 2020-2023 was a government pause, not a strike; the fiction imagines debtors coordinating their refusal.
events.binWhy: Debtors revolt against their creditors by refusing to pay; the financial crisis is the consequence.

facets.change: debt paid → debt refused

events.title: Tatiana Voznesenskaya is assassinated
events.description: The Ministry's Russian legal chief, who had been suing fossil companies and states on behalf of future generations, is murdered. Her killing shows the old order is still fighting as it loses. The same chapters record atmospheric CO2 falling for the first time, helped by kelp farming, carbon-coin drawdown and the end of flying.
events.inUniverse: Chapter 89; no year given

sources.title: Bryan Alexander, Our Ministry for the Future reading: the end (Tatiana assassinated, chapter 89; CO2 drops for the first time)

events.note: Reviewers put the CO2 turn in the 2040s, and the book's peak figures are given as about 470-478 ppm. Tatiana's death is in the same chapter, so it is placed mid-decade. For comparison, the real Mauna Loa record passed about 425 ppm in 2025 and is still rising.
events.binWhy: A targeted killing of the Ministry's legal chief, short of war.

facets.change: the Ministry's lawyer → a martyr

events.title: COP58: 'the birth of a good Anthropocene'
events.description: About three decades after the heat wave, the parties meet with the Keeling curve heading down by several parts per million a year and the Antarctic glaciers stabilised. Half-Earth wildlife corridors are being built and world population has begun to decline. They call it a break point in the history of humans and the Earth, and the costs are still there: extinctions, refugees and the dead of the 2030s. Soon afterwards Mary Murphy retires and Badim Bahadur succeeds her.
events.inUniverse: COP58 (chapter 94); Mary retires in chapter 98

sources.title: Third Act PA: Review of The Ministry for the Future (COP58 occurs in chapter 94)
Bill McKibben, It's Not Science Fiction (NYRB) — by the 2050s CO2 falls about five ppm a year

events.note: Dated by counting conferences. The book's COP29 comes just before January 2025, which in our calendar is 2024, and COPs are annual, so COP58 is 29 conferences later: 2053. That matches McKibben's 'by the 2050s'. Mary's retirement and the closing Fasnacht in Zurich come after this, in years the book leaves unstated, so they are folded in here rather than given invented dates.
events.binWhy: The novel jumps forward to show what its decades of crisis have made of the world.

facets.change: a rising curve → a falling one

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs to the near-future branch because it leaves our history only months after the book was written, at a heat wave in a world otherwise plainly ours, and its main instruments are real ones: the Paris Agreement, central banks and the COPs. All events are T2 (2020-2053). T4 and T3 are empty because the book reaches back no further than its own conference, and T1 is empty because it ends in mid-century. Only 2025, January 2025, 2032 and 11 September 2034 are stated outright. The 2034 date belongs to a vignette that cannot be ordered against the rest, so it is not an event. The other 2030s and 2040s events are placed by chapter order and the book's own decade labels, at low confidence. COP58 is dated by counting conferences. The COP29 decision is shown as a prehistory event before the fork: it is the book's first departure from our record, but it only matters once the heat wave happens.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Ministry for the Future
Bill McKibben, It's Not Science Fiction (NYRB, 2020)
Bryan Alexander's chapter-by-chapter book club (part 1)
Eckard Smuts, Reading Notes: Ministry for the Future

lineages.title: RoboCop
lineages.creator: Edward Neumeier and Michael Miner (writers); Paul Verhoeven (director)

divergence.label: OCP runs the Detroit police, and a murdered officer becomes its product
divergence.delta: Real: Detroit went through the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history in 2013-14 and came out with its police still a city department; no company fields armed robots or cyborgs on American streets. Fiction: the city has contracted its police to Omni Consumer Products, whose executives compete to replace officers with a walking tank or with a cyborg built from a dead cop, and plan to raze the old city for a corporate one.
divergence.inUniverse: No year in the films. A recent MGM trailer is reported to date Murphy's death to 24 October 2029 and RoboCop's activation to 14 January 2030
divergence.note: The co-writer Ed Neumeier said in 2009 that 'there was never a year on that picture' and that he refused to give one. Other dates in circulation disagree: a 1987 TV spot is said to place the film in 1991, the arcade game is said to open 'in the year 1990', and Ed Naha's novelization sets it from November 2043 to February 2044. This lineage follows the MGM trailer's dates, which are the rights holder's own and fit the film's internal clock (Murphy dies in autumn, is rebuilt over New Year, and is on the street a few weeks later); they are reported, with screenshots, in a Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange answer, and the trailer itself could not be viewed for this research. The OCP police contract comes 'not long before' the film and is folded into the fork year.

sources.title: Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange: When (in which year) is RoboCop set?
RoboCop Wiki (archived): RoboCop (1987) - dating trivia
The RoboCop Archive: The RoboCop Timelines

ending.why: OCP's eviction army is destroyed, Cadillac Heights is saved, the company is financially ruined by the exposure of what it did, and its new Japanese owner fires the chief executive and bows to RoboCop.

events.title: RoboCop is released
events.description: Paul Verhoeven's first Hollywood film opens in American cinemas after being cut to avoid an X rating for its violence. It is a hit, wins an Academy Award for sound effects editing, and is followed by two sequels.

sources.title: Wikipedia: RoboCop

events.note: Released 17 July 1987. RoboCop 2 followed in 1990 and RoboCop 3 in 1993 (US release 5 November 1993).
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Detroit files for bankruptcy
events.description: Four months after the state appoints an emergency manager to run it, Detroit files for Chapter 9 with $18-20 billion of debt, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history. It exits in December 2014 after moving the Detroit Institute of Arts into a non-profit trust, with its finances under state oversight for three more years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Detroit bankruptcy

events.note: Real history, not in the films. It belongs to the shared past before the 2029 fork, and it is the premise RoboCop 2 had imagined in 1990: a broke Detroit defaulting and its assets going to its creditors. In our version the creditors were bondholders and pensioners, and the police stayed public.
events.binWhy: A city's finances collapse into court-supervised insolvency and a prolonged crisis.

facets.change: a shrinking city → a city in bankruptcy under an appointed manager

events.title: OCP runs Detroit's police, and Officer Murphy is murdered
events.description: Detroit has handed its police department to Omni Consumer Products, which plans to raze the old city for a corporate Delta City. OCP's ED-209 robot kills a junior executive in a boardroom demonstration, and a rival's cyborg programme gets its chance when Officer Alex Murphy, on his first day at a new precinct, is shot to pieces by Clarence Boddicker's gang.
events.inUniverse: Undated in the film; the MGM trailer's date for Murphy's death

sources.title: Wikipedia: RoboCop - plot
Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange: When (in which year) is RoboCop set?

events.note: Filed by the police contract rather than Murphy's death, because the contract is what puts the state in corporate hands; the death is what the company then uses. The film's newscasts show the wider world only in fragments, among them an orbiting defence platform misfiring.
events.binWhy: A corporation ends up running a city's police, the core of its state.

facets.change: a public police force → a corporate one with a body to experiment on

events.title: RoboCop goes on patrol, and turns on his owners
events.description: Murphy's brain and face in an armoured body, his memory wiped, RoboCop stops crime so efficiently that the media adore him. His memories return; he traces Murphy's killers to OCP's senior president Dick Jones, is shot up by his own force under a hidden directive that protects OCP executives, and comes back during a police strike to expose Jones, who is fired by the chairman and shot out of a window.
events.inUniverse: Rebuilt over New Year ('Happy New Year' in the lab); the MGM trailer's activation date

sources.title: Wikipedia: RoboCop - plot
Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange: When (in which year) is RoboCop set?

events.note: The film's own clock supports a winter activation: Bob Morton promises a prototype 'within 90 days' of Murphy's transfer, and the reconstruction ends with a New Year greeting. The police strike and the exposure of Jones could each be filed separately; the event is filed by what it is at bottom, a cyborg put on the streets by a company.
events.binWhy: A cyborg built from a dead officer is fielded as a police product.

facets.change: a corpse → the company's star product, who turns on its management

events.title: Detroit defaults to OCP
events.description: Detroit cannot pay its debts to OCP, which has underfunded the police to push crime up and means to foreclose on every public asset in the city. A new drug, Nuke, owns the streets; the mayor tries to pay off the debt with drug money, and OCP's second cyborg, built around the brain of the Nuke kingpin Cain, massacres the dealers and then civilians at its own unveiling before RoboCop destroys it.
events.inUniverse: RoboCop 2; no year and no gap from the first film are stated

sources.title: Wikipedia: RoboCop 2 - plot
The RoboCop Archive: The RoboCop Timelines (relative order only)

events.note: Neither the film nor any source found dates it or states how long after the first film it happens; Murphy's widow has since moved back to Detroit, and the RoboCop 2 programme began 'five months' before the story. The year is a stated convention: the three-year gap between the films' releases (1987 to 1990) laid onto the 2030 anchor. Treat it as a placement, not a fact.
events.binWhy: A city's default to its corporate creditor throws it into a prolonged crisis the company intends to profit from.

facets.change: a city in debt → a city in default to its police contractor

events.title: Cadillac Heights rises against OCP's eviction army
events.description: The Old Man is dead and the Japanese Kanemitsu Corporation has bought control of OCP to finish Delta City. Its private force, the Rehabs, clears Cadillac Heights by force and kills RoboCop's partner Anne Lewis; RoboCop joins the residents' armed resistance, a broadcast exposing the evictions crashes OCP's stock, the police defect to the rebels, and OCP is financially ruined.
events.inUniverse: RoboCop 3; no year is stated

sources.title: Wikipedia: RoboCop 3 - plot

events.note: Placed by the same convention as RoboCop 2 (the 1990 to 1993 release gap). The Old Man's death and the Kanemitsu takeover happen between the films and are merged here; the takeover could be filed on its own as a corporate change of ruler.
events.binWhy: The residents a corporation is clearing from their homes take up arms against it, and the city's police join them.

facets.change: forced evictions → a rebellion that ruins the company

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours plus one privatisation: a corporation that owns a city's police and builds its officers. It follows the original film series, RoboCop (1987), RoboCop 2 (1990) and RoboCop 3 (1993), and not the 2014 remake (set in 2028, a separate continuity), the television series, the comics, or the 2023 game Rogue City. None of the films states a year; the first is pinned by an MGM trailer's dates (2029-2030) and the sequels by the release gaps between the films, so every story date is low confidence and the alternative placements are given in the divergence note. One real pre-fork event, Detroit's 2013 bankruptcy, is included as the shared history the fiction's premise echoes. Tiers: T3 (the 1987 release) and T2 (2013-2036); T4 and T1 are empty because the films neither look back nor forward beyond a few years.

Wikipedia: RoboCop 2
Wikipedia: RoboCop 3

lineages.title: Ghost Fleet
lineages.creator: P. W. Singer and August Cole

divergence.label: The Directorate goes to war with America
divergence.delta: Real: China's Communist Party rules, the US Navy is the strongest in the Pacific and Hawaii is a US state. Fiction: the Party has been overthrown by a Directorate of generals and businessmen, which attacks the United States from space, through its microchips and at Pearl Harbor.
divergence.inUniverse: Never stated; the authors leave the date vague, and 2030 is the year attached to the book in later coverage
divergence.note: Ghost Fleet is deliberately undated: Kirkus, Goodreads reviewers and the Studies in Intelligence review all place it in an unspecified near future, one reviewer writing that 'the exact date' is 'left vague'. The only year publicly attached to it is 2030, which comes from Indonesian opposition leader Prabowo Subianto's 2017 speech about Indonesia ceasing to exist by 2030 and is used in the French Wikipedia synopsis; CNN Indonesia checked and found the novel itself gives no year. 2030 is used for the fork at low confidence. The fictional backstory (Dhahran dirty bomb, Saudi and Indonesian collapse, the Party's fall) comes before the war by an unstated interval and is folded into it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost Fleet (novel)
Wikipédia (fr): La Flotte fantôme (roman)
CNN Indonesia: Novel Ghost Fleet, rujukan Indonesia bubar 2030 versi Prabowo (the novel does not itself date Indonesia's end)
Goodreads: Ghost Fleet (reader reviews: 'the exact date being left vague'; 'set in 2030')

ending.why: Hawaii is liberated, the war ends in a truce without nuclear use, and both the United States and the Directorate are left recovering, though Russia has broken apart and NATO is gone.

events.title: Japan attacks the Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor
events.description: A surprise carrier raid on the US fleet at Oahu brings the United States into the Second World War. It is the attack Ghost Fleet sets out to replay: a Pacific power opens a war on America by striking Pearl Harbor first.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Attack on Pearl Harbor
Kirkus Reviews: Ghost Fleet (published June 30, 2015)

events.note: Real history, placed here because the novel is built as a twenty-first-century Pearl Harbor: Directorate forces seize the same base on Oahu, and reviewers (Kirkus among them) read it against 1941.
events.binWhy: A great power opens a war on the United States with a surprise attack on its Pacific Fleet.

facets.change: a neutral America → a Pacific world war

events.title: The National Defense Reserve Fleet is created
events.description: Section 11 of the Merchant Ship Sales Act sets aside mothballed ships to be reactivated in a national emergency. These reserve fleets, and the Navy's own mothball yards, are the 'ghost fleet' the novel's America falls back on.

sources.title: Wikipedia: National Defense Reserve Fleet
Wikipedia: Ghost Fleet (novel)

events.note: Real history. In the novel Chief Mike Simmons works at the National Defense Reserve Fleet, and the title names the Navy reserve ships reactivated as a low-tech fallback once the high-tech fleet is hacked.
events.binWhy: A state agency is set up to keep a fleet in reserve for a future war.

facets.change: a wartime fleet → a mothballed reserve

events.title: The United States invades Afghanistan
events.description: The US-led invasion begins a twenty-year war. In the novel's world the American military is still stretched thin by operations in Afghanistan, Yemen and Kenya, and the Hawaiians who resist the occupation fight with what insurgents taught America in Iraq and Afghanistan.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United States invasion of Afghanistan

events.note: Real history the novel extrapolates from: its overstretched US forces and its insurgency (the 'North Shore Mujahideen') are both drawn from the post-2001 wars.
events.binWhy: A power invades another state; the start of the war the novel's America never finished.

lineages.title: The Martian
lineages.creator: Andy Weir

divergence.label: Ares 3 lands in Acidalia Planitia
divergence.delta: Real: no one has been to Mars, and the first crewed landing is a planning date that keeps moving into the 2030s and beyond. Fiction: by July 2035 NASA's Ares programme has already put two crews on Mars and is launching a third on an ion-driven ship that shuttles between the two planets.
divergence.inUniverse: Ares 3 launched 7 July 2035 and landed on Sol 1, 7 November 2035 (Weir's own dates; the novel prints only sol numbers)
divergence.note: The novel deliberately prints no year, only sols. Weir left clues, a reader named Kenny Ray solved them, and in January 2015 Weir confirmed on Facebook that Ares 3 launched on 7 July 2035, landed on 7 November 2035 (Sol 1) and that the story opens on Sol 6, 12 November 2035. The true fork is earlier and undated: Ares 1 and Ares 2 had already landed crews on Mars, and a fan wiki's '2029' for Ares 1 has no source in the novel, so it is not used. 2035 is the earliest year the author fixes, the same convention the atlas uses for Blade Runner. Later dates are converted from sols at 1.0275 Earth days per sol from that anchor.

events.title: Mars Direct: make the return fuel on Mars
events.description: Martin Marietta engineers Robert Zubrin and David Baker propose sending the return vehicle to Mars first, empty, and letting it make its own propellant from the Martian air before the crew arrives. lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the world is ours with one programme added: NASA flies crews to Mars from the 2030s on hardware that is extrapolated, not invented, and everything else (the agencies, China, the budget fights) is recognisably the present. One continuity, the novel, dated by Weir's own anchor of 7 November 2035 for Sol 1. Only three fictional years are dated (2035-2037), because the whole story is one year and a half on one mission; the rest of the chain is real pre-fork history the plot uses directly (Mars Direct, Pathfinder), so the lineage has five story events rather than eight and is not padded further. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds the two real events; T2 holds publication and the whole story; T1 is empty.
