events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Neuroin reaches the streets, and its addicts' children see murders coming
events.description: An impure early form of the drug neuroin spreads, and the children of addicts are born with severe brain damage; most die before they are twelve. Iris Hineman, treating them, finds that the survivors dream of murders before they happen.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: Hineman: 'This was 10 years ago, when neuroin first hit the streets', said in the film's 2054, which gives 2044. It sits badly with Agatha being an adult in 2054, so the interval is loose. Real: no such drug or ability.
events.binWhy: A discovery the whole later history turns on: that murder can be seen before it happens.

facets.change: a drug epidemic → children who foresee murder

events.title: Precrime is founded with a federal grant
events.description: According to the program's own advertising, Precrime begins with a federal grant. The three surviving precogs, Agatha and the twins Arthur and Dashiell, are kept sedated in a nutrient pool and wired to a system that turns their visions into a victim's name, a killer's name and a time.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

events.note: Stated by an advert in the film: 'The Precrime program began in 2046 with a federal grant. And now, nine years later...' Nine years from 2046 would be 2055, one more than the film's 2054, so the advert and the dialogue ('six years') do not quite agree; 2046 is read here as the founding and 2048 as the start of arrests.
events.binWhy: A police department is founded around three people who can see the future.

facets.change: a research subject → a police department

events.title: Precrime starts arresting people for murders they have not committed
events.description: With the capital's homicide rate at 'epidemic proportions', Precrime begins arresting future killers in Washington, D.C.; within a year murder in the city stops. Around the same time John Anderton's six-year-old son Sean is taken from a Baltimore public pool, and Anderton joins the unit because of it.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: Derived from the film's 'six years' ('in the six years of our experiment there hasn't been a single murder'; 'Just six years ago, the homicide rate had reached epidemic proportions'; the epilogue's 'six-year Precrime experiment') counted back from 2054. Sean was taken 'six years ago, Baltimore'. Real: predictive policing arrived as statistics, not visions.
events.binWhy: A police force switches on a way to punish crimes before they happen.

facets.change: arrest after the fact → arrest before it

events.title: Precrime is exposed and abandoned
events.description: Days before a national vote on taking Precrime nationwide, the system names its own chief, Anderton, as a future killer. On the run he learns that the precogs sometimes disagree and the dissenting 'minority reports' are destroyed, and that the program's director, Lamar Burgess, murdered Agatha's mother, Anne Lively, and used the system to hide it. Burgess kills himself, the experiment is abandoned, and every prisoner is pardoned.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: 2054 is stated in the epilogue: 'In 2054, the six-year Precrime experiment was abandoned. All prisoners were unconditionally pardoned and released.' The adverts call the vote for 'Tuesday, April 22'; 22 April is a Tuesday in 2053 and a Wednesday in 2054, a small slip. Anne Lively's murder is not dated beyond happening years earlier, after Precrime began.
events.binWhy: The flaw a system was built to hide is exposed, and the system falls.

facets.change: an infallible system → a discredited and abandoned one

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: a single invention (seeing murder before it happens) in a Washington that is otherwise recognisably ours, with dates that are ours. It follows the 2002 film only; Dick's 1956 story has a different world and ending, and the 2015 Fox series, a sequel set in 2065, is left out. The film dates very little, so the chain is short: four story beats between 2044 and 2054, all T2, plus the story's 1956 publication at T3. There is no T4 or T1.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)
Wikipedia: The Minority Report (1956 novelette)
Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

lineages.title: New York 2140
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: The First Pulse: the sea rises ten feet in a decade
divergence.delta: Real: in 2017, when the book appeared, the IPCC's 2013 assessment put this century's likely sea-level rise at about 1.5 to 3 feet, and a 2016 study had only just argued that Antarctic ice cliffs could collapse fast enough to make multi-metre rise thinkable. Fiction: in the mid-century, collapses in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets raise the global sea by ten feet in about ten years, and every coastal city on Earth floods at once.
divergence.inUniverse: The First Pulse. The book gives it as history told by its 'citizen' narrator, not as a dated scene; reviewers place it in the 2050s or the 2060s.
divergence.note: The novel dates its catastrophes by decade and through its chorus-narrator, not by year, and its readers disagree by a decade. Robert Kopp, a Rutgers sea-level scientist writing in March 2017, puts the First Pulse in the 2050s; Mal Warwick's review puts it in the 2060s; A Green Man Review says 'about 2060'. Robinson's own description on Living on Earth (ten years of fast rise, then about thirty quiet years, then a worse second pulse) fits Kopp's 2050s best if the Second Pulse begins in the 2080s. The fork is filed at 2050, the start of the earliest decade any source gives. Nothing earlier in the book is known to contradict our history: its political argument is built on the real 2008 crash and its drowned Manhattan on Hurricane Sandy.

sources.title: The Conversation: Robert Kopp, New York 2140: a novelist's vision of a drowned city that still never sleeps (First Pulse in the 2050s; Second Pulse late in the century)
Mal Warwick on Books: New York 2140 (First Pulse in the 2060s; Second Pulse 2085 to 2100)
Living on Earth: New York 2140 (Robinson interviewed on the two pulses)

ending.why: After the hurricane and the debt strike, the Fed's bailout comes with conditions that make the Treasury majority owner of the banks, a wave of radical Democrats including Charlotte Armstrong is elected, and the proceeds go to health care, education and housing, though the narrator warns that such gains are transient and capitalism has only been squeezed.

events.title: Lehman Brothers fails and the banks are bailed out
events.description: Real history: a housing bubble built on speculative lending bursts, Lehman Brothers files the largest bankruptcy in US history, and Congress authorises $700 billion to buy toxic assets and bank stock. Robinson wrote New York 2140 in response to this crash, and the novel's plot is built to answer it: a second crash in which the public does not simply pay.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2008 financial crisis (Lehman 15 September; TARP 3 October)
Peter Frase: Marx and the Two Crises in New York 2140 (Robinson wrote it in response to the crash of 2007-8)

events.note: Real-world background. The novel's 'citizen' chapters return to 2008 repeatedly as the model of what a bailout does; Kopp remarks that the book's political fantasy 'seems more rooted in 2008 than 2140'.
events.binWhy: A speculative bubble bursts and throws the economy into years of recession; the bailout that follows is what the novel sets out to undo.

facets.change: a housing bubble → a banking collapse paid for by the public

events.title: Hurricane Sandy floods Lower Manhattan
events.description: Real history: Sandy comes ashore near Atlantic City and drives a storm surge into New York Harbor that floods streets, subway lines and road tunnels in Lower Manhattan. It kills 160 people in the United States and does about $65 billion of damage. It is the flood the novel extrapolates into a permanently drowned downtown.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hurricane Sandy
3 Quarks Daily: Through a 3D Glass Starkly, New York 2140 Redux (Sandy and 2008 as the novel's present)

events.note: Real-world background. Kopp notes that grid switching stations flooded by Sandy had been sited more than a century earlier, the same kind of inherited vulnerability the novel's New Yorkers live with. The death toll is modest for this bin; it is filed here because it is the event that made a flooded Manhattan a thing people had seen.
events.binWhy: A storm surge floods the lowest part of the city and changes how New York thinks about the sea; the atlas's nearest bin is a disaster that kills.

facets.change: a city that assumed it was dry → flooded tunnels and a new fear of the sea

events.title: A model says Antarctica could add more than a metre by 2100
events.description: Real history: Robert DeConto and David Pollard publish a model in Nature in which Antarctic ice shelves break up and the ice cliffs behind them collapse under their own weight. Under high emissions the continent alone adds more than a metre of sea level by 2100 and more than fifteen by 2500. It was the most discussed climate paper of the year, and the kind of fast ice-sheet collapse the novel's two Pulses dramatise.

sources.title: Carbon Brief: Studies shed new light on Antarctica's future contribution to sea level rise (DeConto and Pollard 2016)
The Conversation: Kopp on the ice-cliff study and the novel's scenario

events.note: Real-world background, a year before publication; Kopp cites 'a recent study that incorporated the collapse of ice cliffs'. Later work has argued the 2016 projections were too high, and the authors themselves lowered some of them. Robinson's fifty feet by 2100 still goes well beyond even the 2016 paper.
events.binWhy: A scientific result about the ice sheets that makes rapid, multi-metre sea-level rise a serious hypothesis.

facets.change: a slow Antarctic melt assumed → a fast collapse thinkable

events.date: 14 March 2017 (US, Canada, Australia); 16 March in the UK
events.title: New York 2140 is published
events.description: Orbit publishes Robinson's novel of a half-drowned Manhattan, told in alternating chapters by eight residents of the MetLife Tower and a sardonic 'citizen' who narrates the history.

sources.title: KimStanleyRobinson.info: New York 2140 (published 14 March 2017)
Wikipedia: New York 2140

events.note: Hardcover, ebook and audiobook release date.
events.binWhy: A publication is the book coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.title: The First Pulse
events.description: Collapses in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets raise the world's oceans by about ten feet in ten years. Robinson calls it a profound shock: every coastline is redrawn at once, ports and shipping are thrown into disorder, and the people of the drowned shores become refugees.
events.inUniverse: The First Pulse

sources.title: The Conversation: Kopp (First Pulse in the 2050s, ten feet in a decade)
Living on Earth: New York 2140 (Robinson: 'raising sea level by 10 feet in 10 years')

events.note: Dated by decade only, and the sources split between the 2050s (Kopp, Grokipedia) and the 2060s (Warwick); filed at 2050, the start of the earlier decade. No death toll is given in the sources consulted; the bin is chosen for the scale of displacement.
events.binWhy: A climate disaster on a planetary scale that redraws every coast in a decade.

facets.change: coastal cities → ten feet under in a decade

events.title: The food crisis
events.description: In the decade after the First Pulse, food runs short worldwide. Together the two shocks finally make the world cut greenhouse emissions in earnest: electricity moves to renewables, container ships give way to wind-driven clippers, and airships replace aeroplanes.
events.inUniverse: The food crisis of the 2070s

sources.title: The Conversation: Kopp (the First Pulse and the food crisis of the 2070s as focusing events)

events.note: Only the decade is given, and only in Kopp's summary; filed at 2070. The energy transition it sets off is described without dates, so it is folded in here rather than filed separately.
events.binWhy: A resource shock, food this time, that throws the world economy into crisis and forces it to change how it runs.

facets.change: a flooded but carbon-burning world → rationed food and a forced energy transition

events.title: The Second Pulse
events.description: The cuts come too late. Melting begins in the Aurora Basin of East Antarctica and cascades through the world's ice sheets, adding another forty feet of sea over about fifteen years. Lower Manhattan becomes an intertidal zone, flooded at high tide, and the city's poor move into the half-drowned towers.
events.inUniverse: The Second Pulse

sources.title: Mal Warwick on Books: New York 2140 (forty feet over the fifteen years from 2085 to 2100)
The Conversation: Kopp (Second Pulse at the end of the 21st century, driven first by the Aurora Basin)

events.note: Warwick gives 2085 to 2100; Kopp says 'the end of the 21st century'; A Green Man Review says about fifty years after the first. Filed at 2085, where the one explicit range begins. The total rise by 2140 is about fifty feet.
events.binWhy: A second, larger climate disaster that drowns the world's coasts for good.

facets.change: a ten-foot flood adapted to → a fifty-foot sea and an intertidal city

events.title: Two coders rewrite the market's rules, and vanish
events.description: Two programmers living in the MetLife Tower slip a batch of code into the financial system that rewrites the rules governing it, then disappear; they are later found held in a shipping container on the harbour floor. Meanwhile speculation in the drowned 'intertidal' property of lower Manhattan is running as a bubble, and someone is trying to buy the tower out from under its co-op.
events.inUniverse: The novel's opening year

sources.title: A Green Man Review: Kim Stanley Robinson's New York 2140 (the hack on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange; the buyout attempts)
Stories for Earth: New York 2140, summary and analysis (the story runs about three years; the rescue from the underwater container)

events.note: The title year is taken as the year the story opens; the sources say it runs for about three years from there. Summaries describe the hack as an attack on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange's systems and as code revising the rules of the financial system; its effect was short-lived.
events.binWhy: An attack on the financial system carried out through its own networks.

facets.change: a market no one can touch → a hack, and two coders gone

events.title: Hurricane Fyodor, and the everybody strike
events.description: Hurricane Fyodor batters New York for three days, destroys the intertidal zone and drives thousands of homeless people into a refugee camp in Central Park; weeks later, with luxury towers standing empty, the camp riots. The Householders' Union calls on everyone to stop paying mortgages, rents and insurance, the intertidal bubble and the banks collapse, and this time the bailout makes the Treasury their majority shareholder while a wave of radical Democrats is voted into Congress.
events.inUniverse: Hurricane Fyodor; the Householders' Union's debt strike

sources.title: Progress in Political Economy: Everybody strike! The urban environmental politics of New York 2140 (a 2142 hurricane; the strike; the Treasury as majority shareholder)
Living on Earth: New York 2140 (Hurricane Fyodor and the householders' union)

events.note: The PPE Sydney essay and Grokipedia put the hurricane in 2142; one search summary gave 2141. The strike follows within weeks, and the election and nationalisation follow from it, so hurricane and strike are filed together at 2142. A US congressional election falls in an even year, which fits 2142.
events.binWhy: A mass of unarmed people withhold payment together and force a change in who owns the banks; it is a strike, not an armed revolt.

facets.change: bailouts for the banks → the banks owned by the public

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours, with our banks, our Fed and our 2008, until the ice sheets give way in mid-century; the rest of the history follows from two floods and one old financial habit. It follows the novel alone. Tier coverage is T2 throughout, from the 2008 crash to the strike of 2142. There is no T3 or T4 because the book's history begins with the crash it answers, and no T1 because it never leaves the twenty-second century. The fork and both Pulses are dated only by decade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: New York 2140
KimStanleyRobinson.info: New York 2140
The Conversation: Robert Kopp on New York 2140

lineages.title: The Expanse
lineages.creator: James S. A. Corey (Daniel Abraham & Ty Franck)

divergence.label: The first permanent settlement on Mars
divergence.delta: Real: no human has walked on Mars, no permanent settlement there is on any agency's schedule, and the Moon has only temporary visitors. Fiction: a permanent Martian colony is founded in 2050, and within two centuries Mars is terraformed, sovereign, and fielding its own navy against Earth.
divergence.note: The year comes from the TV series' production design guide (the books say only 'colonised in the 21st century'); the same source puts a permanent lunar colony in 2025. The invention everyone remembers, the Epstein Drive, comes later, in 2213-14, and is what opens the Belt — but the Mars settlement is the first fork.

ending.why: Humanity survives the ring gates, the empire and the things that ate the gate-builders; a thousand years on it is still here and still plural.

events.title: The ring builders seed Phoebe
events.description: A galaxy-spanning civilisation parks a protomolecule payload inside an interstellar asteroid aimed at the primitive Earth, which Saturn captures and which becomes the moon Phoebe.
events.note: Canon states roughly two billion years; this is the deep backstory that the whole branch eventually detonates, and the only pre-modern material the series has.
events.binWhy: An alien civilisation touches the primitive Earth without anyone knowing.

facets.change: an empty system → seeded by a civilisation long gone

events.title: Leviathan Wakes published
events.description: The first Expanse novel appears, set in a solar system that is what ours becomes if fusion travel arrives: an overpopulated Earth, a terraforming Mars, and a Belt that does the work and gets none of the gravity.
events.note: The series grew out of the authors' tabletop setting, which was literally named '2350' — the origin of the series-present date used here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The first permanent lunar colony
events.description: In the fiction the Moon is permanently settled in 2025, becoming the shipyard and launch pad for everything that follows.
events.note: Design-guide date (the RPG says only 'the 2000s'). Real 2025 passed with robotic landers and the Artemis Accords and no permanent base — the branch's first missed milestone, and the reason this lineage is plottable against our own decade.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: visits → the Moon permanently settled

events.title: The first permanent settlement on Mars
events.description: Humanity's first permanent settlement on another planet is founded, beginning both the Martian project of making a dead world live and the long resentment of the world that claims to own it.
events.note: Design-guide date; the novels give no year, only 'the 21st century' and 'about three generations' before the Epstein Drive.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: one world → the first settlement on another

events.title: Eros becomes a deep-system base
events.description: The Mars-crossing asteroid Eros is occupied and used as a staging base for exploration of the outer system, the first foothold beyond the inner planets.
events.note: Design-guide date; the same asteroid is later the site of the protomolecule catastrophe, which gives the early colonisation its retrospective weight.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: inner planets → a foothold in the outer system

events.title: Mars starts rejecting Earth rule
events.description: A century after the first colony, Martian society begins openly refusing United Nations authority, and the Earth-Mars cold war that frames the series takes shape.
events.note: Design-guide date; canon stresses that the split is generational rather than a single act, and the formal independence demand follows around 2200-2213.
events.binWhy: A colony begins refusing the homeworld's authority; a cold war forms.

facets.change: a colony → openly refusing the homeworld's authority

events.title: The Epstein Drive, and Martian independence
events.description: Solomon Epstein's modified fusion drive makes continuous-thrust travel possible and turns the Belt and outer moons into places people can live; Mars trades the drive to Earth for sovereignty and the Martian Congressional Republic is proclaimed the same year.
events.note: Contested: on screen the drive is dated 137 years before the series' 2350s present (2213-14), the wiki's prose rounds it to c. 2213, and the TV design guide says 2200. The independence trade is dated to the same year in the wiki's reconstruction.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: slow travel → continuous thrust; independence bought with it

events.title: The Belt fills up
events.description: The drive triggers a gold rush: hundreds of settlements, stations and ships across the Belt, Ceres as its port city, and functioning settlements on the major moons of Jupiter and Saturn.
events.note: Reconstructed from the wiki's era table; the novels describe the Belt's settlement in detail but never date it.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: empty rock → hundreds of settlements

events.title: The Vesta Blockade
events.description: A UN blockade over Martian terraforming supplies becomes the closest thing yet to open war: one MCRN cruiser cripples five UNN destroyers, and half the UN fleet burns for Mars before cooler heads prevail.
events.note: TV continuity: Avasarala dates it 'forty years' before the series' 2350s present.
events.binWhy: A blockade brings the two powers to the edge of war and no further.

facets.change: cold war → a blockade brings the fleets to the edge

events.title: The Anderson Station massacre
events.description: UN forces storm a Belt station over a water protest and kill the people inside; the officer who gave the order, Fred Johnson, defects to the Belt and becomes the face of the Outer Planets Alliance.
events.note: The novels place it four years before the 2340 Pallas revolt, which is a decade before Leviathan Wakes, so c. 2336; the TV continuity's table gives 2339.
events.binWhy: State forces kill protesters over water; the massacre creates the opposition.

facets.change: a protest → the state kills everyone inside

events.title: The alien substance on Phoebe
events.description: A Martian survey of the moon Phoebe recovers something that is not geology; Mars brings in the Protogen corporation to study it in secret, and the protomolecule enters human history.
events.note: Design-guide/wiki dating (the books' relative era 0-1 XTE corresponds to c. 2342-43); the Mars-Protogen base on Phoebe follows in 2345.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: geology → something alien, studied in secret

events.title: Leviathan Wakes: the Canterbury and Eros
events.description: The series opens with the ice hauler Canterbury destroyed and Julie Mao dying of protomolecule exposure on Eros; the Mormon generation ship Nauvoo is hijacked and thrown at the station, and its hundred thousand people are driven into Venus.
events.note: The series never prints a year: 2350 comes from the authors' original RPG (named 2350), the wiki's reconstruction and ScreenRant's timeline; the official RPG map is marked 2351 because it is set in the gap between books one and two.
events.binWhy: A ship is destroyed and a hundred thousand people are killed on a station.

facets.change: cold war → a ship destroyed, a station's people fed to an experiment

events.title: The ring gate opens
events.description: The protomolecule's growth on Venus becomes a vast ring beyond Uranus; when a Belter slingshotter flies through it the gate activates and more than thirteen hundred habitable systems open at once.
events.note: TV dating (ring forms 2352, fleet arrives 2353, '187 days later'); the books' Abaddon's Gate corresponds to c. 2354, so the books run a year or two later than the show.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: one system → thirteen hundred open at once

events.title: The bombardment of Earth
events.description: Marco Inaros's Free Navy throws stealth-coated asteroids at Earth, killing millions and dusting the sky, while the colony systems beyond the gates begin to break away from the inner planets.
events.note: TV: the strikes fall in 2355 and the Free Navy war ends in late 2356; the novels' Nemesis Games and Babylon's Ashes cover the same ground c. 2359-60.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: the homeworld → struck by asteroids; the colonies break away

events.title: Laconia takes the gate network
events.description: Thirty years after the Free Navy war, the renegade Martian fleet that vanished through a gate returns as the Laconian Empire and seizes the slow zone with ring-builder technology.
events.note: Persepolis Rising jumps 'thirty years' past Babylon's Ashes; the wiki's reconstruction lands c. 2390, with Tiamat's Wrath c. 2393-94 and Leviathan Falls c. 2395.
events.binWhy: A returned fleet seizes the gate network by force.

facets.change: a vanished fleet → returns as an empire and seizes the network

events.title: The gates close
events.description: The war against Laconia ends with the ring network destroyed, stranding all thirteen hundred colony systems from one another and from Earth.
events.note: Leviathan Falls (2021); the year is reconstructed from the wiki's relative chronology, not printed in the novel.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: an empire → defeated by destroying the network itself

events.title: A thousand years later: the Thirty Worlds reach Earth
events.description: In the epilogue humanity has built its own faster-than-light drive; a delegation from the Thirty Worlds crosses to a depopulated Earth and is met by Amos Burton, still alive.
events.note: Wikipedia's plot summary states the epilogue is set a thousand years after Leviathan Falls and that the gate collapse stranded 1,300 colony systems; the novel prints no year, so c. 3395 is arithmetic from the reconstruction above.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: stranded colonies → return to a depopulated homeworld

lineages.groupingNote: The cleanest case in this group: no aliens arrive and no history is rewritten — this is what our own solar system becomes if one propulsion breakthrough lands, so the branch is drawn entirely in the fiction's own future. Tiers: T4 holds only the ring builders' two-billion-year-old payload; there is no T3 material, because the branch's history only starts in the twenty-first century; T2 carries the lunar and Martian settlements, the Epstein Drive and the Belt gold rush; T1 carries the whole series present, the ring gate, the Free Navy war, the Laconian conquest and the millennium after the gates close.

lineages.title: The Diamond Age
lineages.creator: Neal Stephenson

divergence.label: A stolen Primer reaches a four-year-old
divergence.delta: Real: 2060 is thirty-four years from now. Fiction: nations have given way to phyles, tribes chosen by culture; every home has a matter compiler fed atoms by a Feed the Neo-Victorians control; and the Chinese coast is divided into leased enclaves on artificial diamond islands.
divergence.note: The Diamond Age dates nothing. Its world has plainly diverged well before its first scene: nation-states have dissolved into phyles and nanotechnology is universal. But no earlier year can be fixed, so, as in the Blade Runner entry, the fork is the earliest point the story lets us place. That is placed at about 2060 through Miss Matheson, the aged ex-skateboarder usually read as Snow Crash's Y.T. Low confidence throughout.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Diamond Age
Wikiquote: The Diamond Age (Miss Matheson: 'I used to be a thrasher')

ending.why: The Coastal Republic has fallen, the Seed that could end the Feed's monopoly is nearly within the Celestial Kingdom's reach, and Nell's new tribe of Primer-raised girls has just been born; the book stops before any of them shows what it will become.

events.title: The Treaty of Nanking
events.description: The First Opium War ends with Qing China ceding Hong Kong Island to Britain and opening five ports to foreign trade and residence. It is the first of the foreign enclaves on the China coast that the novel's Leased Territories deliberately echo.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Treaty of Nanking
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history. The novel's Leased Territories around Shanghai, and the anti-foreign rising that ends it, replay the century of treaty ports and concessions that began here.
events.binWhy: A defeated state cedes territory and opens its ports to the victors.

facets.change: a closed coast → ports held by foreigners

events.title: The Boxer Uprising
events.description: The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists rises in north China against foreigners and Christians and besieges the foreign legations in Beijing, before an eight-nation army crushes it. The novel's Fists of Righteous Harmony take the name and stage the rising again, this time against the Feed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Boxer Rebellion
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history (September 1899 to September 1901). The Diamond Age's Fists are a deliberate replay: an anti-Western wing of the Confucian Celestial Kingdom rising against the foreign-run Feed.
events.binWhy: An armed rising against the foreign powers that hold the coast.

facets.change: resentment of foreign enclaves → an armed rising against them

events.title: Engines of Creation
events.description: K. Eric Drexler's book proposes molecular assemblers that build anything atom by atom. With Ralph Merkle's case for diamond as the material they would make most easily, it is the idea the novel treats as settled engineering. Both men are named in the novel.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Engines of Creation
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history. Wikipedia on the novel notes that Drexler and Merkle receive an honorary mention in it, and takes the title from Merkle's line about a coming 'Diamond Age'.
events.binWhy: A theory of building matter atom by atom, which the novel's world turns on.

facets.change: chemistry in bulk → manufacturing atom by atom, on paper

events.title: The Diamond Age is published
events.description: Neal Stephenson's fourth novel, subtitled 'A Young Lady's Illustrated Primer', appears. It wins the 1996 Hugo and Locus awards.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real-world publication (Bantam Spectra, February 1995).
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: A stolen Primer reaches a four-year-old
events.description: A Neo-Victorian Equity Lord commissions an interactive book to raise his granddaughter to think for herself. Its engineer, John Percival Hackworth, secretly compiles a second copy for his own daughter and is mugged on the way home. The copy ends up with Nell, a four-year-old with no tribe in the slums of the Leased Territories.
events.inUniverse: Nell is four when Harv gives her the Primer

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Diamond Age
Wikiquote: The Diamond Age (Miss Matheson: 'I used to be a thrasher')

events.note: The novel gives no year. Its head teacher, Miss Matheson, is an old woman in a wheelchair who says she 'used to be a thrasher' on skateboards; she is widely read, and teased by Stephenson, as Y.T. from Snow Crash, fifteen in that novel's present (about 2005 in this atlas). That puts the start around 2060, as reviewers also guess ('the 2060s or so'). The Y.T. link is a hint, not a stated fact.
events.binWhy: The child on whom the rest of the story turns receives the thing that will shape her.

facets.change: a book for a lord's granddaughter → a book raising a slum child

events.title: Primers for hundreds of thousands of abandoned girls
events.description: Dr. X, a black-market engineer, reveals that he is hiding hundreds of thousands of abandoned infant girls and asks Hackworth to give each of them a Primer. The price of the arrangement is that Hackworth disappears for ten years into the Drummers, a submarine hive mind that is growing the Seed, a nanotechnology no one can meter.

sources.title: GradeSaver: The Diamond Age summary (Dr. X's abandoned girls; ten years with the Drummers)
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Derived: Hackworth's decade with the Drummers ends at the climax, about eleven years after Nell receives the Primer, so it begins about a year in.
events.binWhy: An adaptive teaching machine goes into use on a mass scale.

facets.change: one stolen tutor → a quarter of a million children raised by machines

events.title: The Fists overrun the Coastal Republic
events.description: The Fists of Righteous Harmony, the anti-Western wing of the inland Celestial Kingdom, overrun the Coastal Republic. Shanghai's foreign enclaves are besieged and refugees flee by sea. Nell, now grown, is found by the army of Primer-raised girls and becomes the head of a new tribe, as Hackworth comes back from the Drummers, whose Seed is close to being made; Nell rescues Miranda before the Drummers can use her to make it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Diamond Age
GradeSaver: The Diamond Age summary (Dr. X's abandoned girls; ten years with the Drummers)

events.note: Derived: about ten years after Hackworth goes to the Drummers (see the previous event). Nell is in her teens.
events.binWhy: An armed rising overruns the foreign-backed coastal state; it is the 1900 rising staged again.

facets.change: coastal enclaves fed by the Feed → a coast overrun and the Feed's monopoly in doubt

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its future is our globalised century carried forward by one technology, molecular manufacturing, until nations dissolve into tribes of choice and China's coast is carved into foreign enclaves again. It follows the 1995 novel alone; it is loosely continuous with Snow Crash, which is its own lineage. The novel dates nothing, so the chain is short and honest: three real events it is built on (the 1842 treaty ports, the Boxers, Drexler's 1986 book), the publication, and three placed years for the story, all low confidence. Seven entries, six of them story events. Tier coverage: T4 for 1842, T3 for 1900-1995, T2 for the story (2060-2071); no T1, because the story covers about eleven years.

Wikiquote: The Diamond Age (Miss Matheson: 'I used to be a thrasher')
GradeSaver: The Diamond Age summary (Dr. X's abandoned girls; ten years with the Drummers)

lineages.title: Rendezvous with Rama
lineages.creator: Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: An asteroid destroys Padua, Verona and Venice
divergence.delta: Real: the last large impact near people was Chelyabinsk in 2013, which injured about 1,500 and killed none, and planetary defence is a small survey programme and one test deflection. Fiction: on 11 September 2077 a meteorite wipes out three Italian cities, and the world builds Spaceguard.
divergence.inUniverse: 11 September 2077 (chapter 1, 'Spaceguard')
divergence.note: Clarke's future history is ours up to this morning: it opens with the real Tunguska (1908) and Sikhote-Alin (1947) falls as the warnings the world ignored. Between 1973 and 2077 the novel names no year, so nothing in that span contradicts us; by 2131 the planets are settled and governed by a United Planets, but the novel dates none of it. The Po Valley strike is the first dated event our history does not contain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

ending.why: The missile is disarmed, the crew comes home, Rama leaves the solar system unharmed and unharming, and humanity is left with a lesson in its own smallness and the hint that the Ramans do everything in threes.

events.title: James Cook's Endeavour sails for the Pacific
events.description: HMS Endeavour leaves Plymouth to observe the transit of Venus and look for the southern continent, and over three years charts New Zealand and the east coast of Australia. It is the voyage Norton models himself on, and the ship his own is named after.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First voyage of James Cook (Endeavour sails from Plymouth, August 1768)
This Is Not Where I Live: Rendezvous with Rama, chapters 15-17 (Norton and Captain Cook)

events.note: Real history. The novel's commander, Bill Norton, is a devotee of Cook who has read the journals and asks himself what Cook would do; the solar survey ship sent to Rama is the Endeavour. Included because the novel frames its first contact as an exploring voyage in Cook's mould, not a war.
events.binWhy: The original of the voyage the novel restages: a crew sent past the edge of the charts to see what is there.

facets.change: the edge of the charts → a ship sent past it

events.title: Something explodes over the Siberian taiga
events.description: An air burst over the Podkamennaya Tunguska flattens some 2,150 square kilometres of forest and kills at most a handful of people. The novel opens on it: had it come a few hours later, it would have taken a city.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tunguska event (30 June 1908)
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

events.note: Real history, and the first line of the novel's history: Clarke uses Tunguska and the 1947 fall as the two twentieth-century warnings the world did not act on. The real death toll is estimated at up to three.
events.binWhy: The first proof in modern times that the sky can destroy a city; it is a warning, not a catastrophe, which is why it is filed as a discovery about the sky rather than as mass death.

facets.change: a harmless sky → a forest flattened from above

events.title: An iron meteorite falls in the Sikhote-Alin mountains
events.description: A shower of iron fragments lands in the Russian Far East, about 440 km north-east of Vladivostok. It is the novel's second warning, and again nothing is done.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sikhote-Alin meteorite (12 February 1947)
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

events.note: Real history. The novel counts it as the century's second great meteorite and notes how near it came to Vladivostok; Wikipedia puts the fall about 440 km from the city. The Sea Lion Press review of the novel's future history mentions the 1908 and 1940s strikes as its opening.
events.binWhy: A second astronomical near-miss, recorded and forgotten; the novel's case that people do not guard against a threat until it has killed them.

facets.change: one near-miss → a second, nearer a city

events.title: Rendezvous with Rama is published
events.description: Arthur C. Clarke's novel is published in June 1973 and goes on to win the Nebula, Hugo, Campbell, Locus and BSFA awards.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama

events.note: A real-world publication event. Clarke later co-wrote three sequels with Gentry Lee (1989-1993); they are a different kind of book and are left out of this chain.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Spaceguard Foundation is founded in Rome
events.description: Astronomers found an international body to find and track near-Earth objects, taking the name of the novel's fictional project. NASA's own 1992 Spaceguard Survey report had already borrowed it, with Clarke's permission.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spaceguard Foundation (founded in Rome, 26 March 1996)
Wikipedia: Spaceguard (the name adopted from the novel)

events.note: Real history, after the novel's publication and before its fork: the real world adopting the book's own institution. The 1992 US Congressional study produced the 'Spaceguard Survey Report' and the goal of finding 90% of kilometre-sized near-Earth asteroids; the Foundation followed an IAU workshop in 1995. That the real Spaceguard began in Italy, the country the novel's asteroid destroys, is a coincidence.
events.binWhy: A body is founded to watch the sky for impacts, and it is named after the book; the novel's institution arrives eighty years early and without a catastrophe to prompt it.

facets.change: a name in a novel → a real watch on the sky

events.title: The first interstellar object is seen passing through the solar system
events.description: The Pan-STARRS telescope in Hawaii picks up an elongated object on a hyperbolic path that came from outside the solar system. Before it got its Hawaiian name, astronomers suggested calling it Rama.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 'Oumuamua (discovered 19 October 2017; 'Rama' was suggested as its name)

events.note: Real history. 'Oumuamua was found on 19 October 2017; Breakthrough Listen pointed the Green Bank Telescope at it in December and heard nothing. In the novel the equivalent object is fifty kilometres long and hollow; the real one was a few hundred metres at most and inert. Included because it is the event of our century that most resembles the book's premise.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery of exactly the kind the novel begins with: an interstellar visitor detected by a sky survey. Nothing about it proved artificial, which is where our history and the novel's part.

facets.change: no visitor ever seen → one passes through

events.title: An asteroid destroys Padua, Verona and Venice
events.description: A meteorite strikes the Po Valley in northern Italy, wiping out Padua and Verona and sinking what is left of Venice. Hundreds of thousands die in minutes, in the first impact since 1908 to hit a populated place.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama
Skulls in the Stars: review of Rendezvous with Rama (gives the detection as 2130)

events.note: Dated in the novel's first chapter to 11 September 2077. In our world there is no such impact on record and no 2077 has happened; the fiction's history is ours until this morning. The strike is the reason everything else in the book exists.
events.binWhy: An impact that kills on a mass scale; the disaster itself, not the institution it later produces.

facets.change: two warnings ignored → three cities gone

events.title: Project Spaceguard begins
events.description: The world resolves that no impact large enough to cause catastrophe will ever get through again, and turns the skills of old missile defence to watching every rock that could come near. The survey radars that later find Rama are Spaceguard's.

sources.title: Your Summary: Rendezvous with Rama chapter summary (2077 strike, detection of 31/439, Sita seven weeks later)
Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama

events.note: The novel says Spaceguard was begun after the 2077 strike and gives no year. It says the project justified itself about fifty years after it began, when it found Rama in 2131; c. 2081 is derived from that and is only as good as the novel's round number. The real Spaceguard, begun in the 1990s, is the book's name without the book's catastrophe.
events.binWhy: A standing body is founded to guard a whole planet against one kind of threat; it is what the rest of the story runs on.

facets.change: an unwatched sky → every rock catalogued

events.title: Spaceguard finds Rama, and the Endeavour goes inside
events.description: An object catalogued as 31/439 turns out to be a hollow cylinder fifty kilometres long, and the survey ship Endeavour is the only crewed vessel able to meet it. Norton's crew explore a world built for someone else while the colony on Mercury sends a nuclear missile, which one of them disarms; then Rama uses the Sun to turn and leaves without noticing anyone.
events.inUniverse: 31/439, detected by Spaceguard in 2131

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama
Your Summary: Rendezvous with Rama chapter summary (2077 strike, detection of 31/439, Sita seven weeks later)
Skulls in the Stars: review of Rendezvous with Rama (gives the detection as 2130)

events.note: Wikipedia and most summaries give the detection as 2131, which matches the catalogue number 31/439 (year, then order of discovery); some reviews say 2130 for the detection and 2131 for the expedition. The whole encounter, the Hermian missile and the departure fall inside a few months, so they are one event here. In our world no crewed ship has flown beyond the Moon; the fiction's 2131 has colonies on Mercury, Mars and the moons of Jupiter and Saturn under a United Planets.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets the work of a non-human intelligence face to face. The builders never appear and never take notice, but the contact is real, which puts it here rather than among discoveries of old artefacts.

facets.change: a catalogue of rocks → a ship built by someone else

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is plainly ours, extended, and the fork is a single dated catastrophe that sets up the institution the rest of the book depends on. The 1973 novel alone is followed; the Clarke and Gentry Lee sequels (Rama II, The Garden of Rama, Rama Revealed) change the tone and the answers and are left out. The novel dates very little: the 2077 strike, the start of Spaceguard (derived) and the 2131 encounter, which happens within a few months and is one event. The minimum is filled with real history the book builds on or that has since echoed it: Cook's voyage, the 1908 and 1947 falls, the real Spaceguard of the 1990s and 'Oumuamua in 2017. Tier coverage: T4 for Cook (1768), T3 for 1908-1996, T2 for 2017-2131. T1 is empty because the novel ends in 2131.

Wikipedia: Spaceguard (the name adopted from the novel)

lineages.title: Elysium
lineages.creator: Neill Blomkamp

divergence.label: The rich move to an orbital habitat
divergence.delta: Real: in our world orbital habitats are still the 1975 Stanford drawings, and the richest people visit space for minutes. Fiction: by the late 21st century Earth is ruined and its wealthy live permanently in a ring in orbit, with medicine that no one on the ground can reach.
divergence.inUniverse: 'In the late 21st century, Earth was diseased, polluted and vastly overpopulated. Earth's wealthiest inhabitants fled the planet to preserve their way of life' (opening titles); the story is set in 2154
divergence.note: The film gives one year, 2154, and one range, 'the late 21st century', for the flight to Elysium; 2080 is a placeholder inside that range. The decline that drives the flight is not dated either, so everything before it is treated as ours. Dates are ours; nothing is converted.

sources.title: Newcity Film: review of Elysium (opening titles over Saudi Arabia)
Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

ending.why: The reboot makes every person on Earth a citizen of Elysium and its medical ships are sent to Earth, ending the division the film is built on.

events.title: NASA's summer study designs the Stanford torus
events.description: At the 1975 NASA Summer Study at Stanford, a team led by Richard Johnson and Charles Holbrow designs a rotating ring habitat for 10,000 people at the Earth-Moon L5 point, published in 1977 as Space Settlements: A Design Study. Elysium is that ring, moved into Earth orbit and given to the rich.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stanford torus
Looper: Elysium facts (Stanford torus illustration; Syd Mead)

events.note: Real history the film is built on: Blomkamp has said the film took shape when he saw a National Geographic illustration of the torus, and he hired Syd Mead to design the station. Nothing like it has been built.
events.binWhy: A design for living in space arrives that later histories, including this one, build on.

facets.change: space as a destination → space as a place to live

events.title: Elysium is released
events.description: Neill Blomkamp's second feature, with Matt Damon and Jodie Foster, opens on 9 August 2013. Its Los Angeles of 2154 is a Spanish-speaking slum policed by robots, under a station where illness can be cured in seconds.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

events.note: A real-world release date. The film was read, and meant, as commentary on the present: immigration, health care, worker exploitation and class.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The wealthy leave Earth for Elysium
events.description: With Earth 'diseased, polluted and vastly overpopulated', its wealthiest inhabitants leave for Elysium, a ring habitat in Earth orbit with lawns, mansions and home med-bays that cure any disease in seconds. Armadyne, the arms company, built it, and Earth is left to robot police and parole officers.

sources.title: Newcity Film: review of Elysium (opening titles over Saudi Arabia)
Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

events.note: The opening titles say only that this happened 'in the late 21st century'; 2080 stands for that range (roughly 2067-2099) and is not a date the film gives. Delacourt's line to Armadyne's CEO ('So you built the torus') is the evidence that Armadyne built it. The titles place the words 'Earth's wealthiest inhabitants' over Saudi Arabia.
events.binWhy: A permanent habitat is founded in orbit, and the people who can afford it move there.

facets.change: one planet for everyone → a habitat for the rich above a planet for the rest

events.title: Max reboots Elysium and makes everyone a citizen
events.description: Given five days to live after a radiation accident at the Armadyne plant, Max Da Costa takes a job stealing data from the company's CEO and ends up carrying a program Defence Secretary Delacourt ordered for a coup. He fights his way onto Elysium past her black-ops agent Kruger and runs it: the reboot registers every person on Earth as a citizen, and the station's medical shuttles are sent down. Max dies doing it.

sources.title: Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

events.note: 2154 is the film's stated year. Delacourt's coup and Kruger's attempt to take the station for himself happen in the same days and both fail. Max was raised in an orphanage in Los Angeles where he promised a friend, Frey, he would take her to Elysium; the film gives no year for his childhood.
events.binWhy: The people on the ground break into the station and rewrite who counts as a citizen.

facets.change: citizens above and illegals below → everyone a citizen

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch in a world that is ours plus one long decline and one space station, with its dates ours. The film states almost nothing: one range for the fork and one year for the story, so the chain is short and says so rather than filling in. T3 is the real 1975 torus design it is built on, T2 the release, the placed fork and the 2154 story; there is no T4 or T1. One continuity: the 2013 film.

Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

lineages.title: Avatar
lineages.creator: James Cameron

divergence.label: The first probes land on Pandora
divergence.delta: Real: Alpha Centauri is 4.37 light years away and nothing has been sent there; in 2025 the James Webb Space Telescope imaged a candidate gas giant around Alpha Centauri A, and whether it has moons is unknown. Fiction: by 2084 humanity has found a living moon, Pandora, around a gas giant there, and interstellar ships have dropped robot rovers onto it.
divergence.inUniverse: 2084 (Pandora ROVR, a 2009 tie-in game, as summarised by Looper); no film gives a year before 2148
divergence.note: 2084 is the first year the official chronology names, not the first year the fiction differs. Earlier, and undated, the Resources Development Administration is founded in the early twenty-first century, and Pandora is discovered by telescope in the late twenty-first century (Looper; Slashfilm puts the discovery between 2050 and 2077). The RDA's founding would not by itself contradict our history; Pandora does, but no source dates its discovery, so the fork is placed at the first dated mission and marked low. The real 2025 JWST candidate planet at Alpha Centauri A (Wikipedia: Pandora) makes the setting's premise less fanciful than it was in 2009, but it is not Polyphemus and nothing is known of any moon.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Slashfilm: The entire Avatar timeline explained
Wikipedia: Pandora (Avatar), including the 2025 JWST candidate planet at Alpha Centauri A

ending.why: The Na'vi have won every decisive battle of two wars, but the RDA has come back to settle rather than to mine, and the third film ends with its forces beaten, not gone from Pandora.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch rather than space opera: one company, one colony and one moon, reached from an Earth that is recognisably ours ruined, with no galactic society and no alien powers beyond Pandora. The lineage follows the three films (2009, 2022, 2025); where they are silent, it takes dates from tie-ins as gathered by Looper and Slashfilm (the 2084 probe, Grace Augustine's school, the 2152 massacre), marked medium or low, and it leaves out the plot of the game Frontiers of Pandora (2023). Every event is T2: the fiction adds nothing to the record before the late twenty-first century (the Na'vi legend of the first Toruk Makto, about three thousand years before the first film, is Pandoran history, not ours), and no released film goes past 2170. Avatar 4 (due 2029) is to open with an eight-year jump.

Wikipedia: Avatar (franchise): the second film set in 2170, the third shortly after

events.title: Avatar is released
events.description: James Cameron's film, developed from a 1994 treatment, opens in the United States and becomes the highest-grossing film ever made.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Avatar (2009 film), set in 2154

events.note: It premiered in London on 10 December 2009.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Avatar: Fire and Ash

events.title: Robot rovers land on Pandora
events.description: Interstellar ships drop remotely operated rovers onto Pandora, a moon of the gas giant Polyphemus in the Alpha Centauri system, for the first survey of another star's world.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far

events.note: The date comes from Pandora ROVR, a promotional browser game released with the first film, as summarised by Looper; no film states it. Which organisation sent the rovers is not given; the RDA later holds the monopoly on Pandora, so it is assumed here.
events.binWhy: The first mission reaches a world around another star.

facets.change: a telescope image → rovers on the surface

events.title: The first humans reach Pandora and meet the Na'vi
events.description: Human explorers arrive on Pandora and find a moon whose life is linked in one planetary network, and a people, the Na'vi, three metres tall and armed with bows. Under their land lies unobtanium, a superconductor that becomes the backbone of Earth's economy at twenty million dollars a kilogram.

sources.title: Slashfilm: The entire Avatar timeline explained
Pandorapedia: Unobtanium

events.note: Derived: Cameron has said the first film takes place 35 years into the colonisation, which puts the first explorers at about 2119 (Slashfilm); no film dates the first landing, and the first meeting with the Na'vi is not dated separately. Pandorapedia gives the unobtanium price.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets a non-human intelligence for the first time.

facets.change: rovers' images → humans among the Na'vi

events.title: Grace Augustine opens a school for Na'vi children
events.description: The botanist who runs the RDA's avatar programme teaches English and science to Omaticaya children from her avatar body, the nearest thing the colony has to diplomacy.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Pandorapedia: Dr. Grace Augustine

facets.change: no common language → a school

events.title: Jake Sully takes his dead brother's place
events.description: When the scientist Tom Sully is killed, his twin Jake, a paraplegic former Marine, is recruited because his genome matches the avatar grown for Tom. He leaves Earth on the ISV Venture Star for a crossing of nearly six years.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Wikipedia: Avatar (2009 film), set in 2154

facets.change: a disabled veteran on a dying Earth → an avatar driver bound for Pandora

events.title: RDA security kills Grace's students, and the school closes
events.description: Grace's students, led by Neytiri's sister Sylwanin, attack an RDA bulldozer; security forces kill them, and the Omaticaya break with the humans.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Slashfilm: The entire Avatar timeline explained

facets.change: a school → a massacre and a broken relationship

events.title: Hometree falls, and the Na'vi drive the RDA off Pandora
events.description: The RDA destroys the Omaticaya's Hometree to reach the unobtanium beneath it. Jake Sully, now one of the clan, unites the Na'vi clans; with Pandora's wildlife they defeat the company's assault on the Tree of Souls, the RDA is expelled, and Jake passes permanently into his avatar body.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Avatar (2009 film), set in 2154
Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far

events.note: The film states 2154; Looper dates Jake's arrival to 19 May and his training to May-August. A few humans are allowed to stay. The real 2154 is far beyond forecasting; the film is an old colonial war fought on a new frontier.
events.binWhy: The native side wins the battle that ends the first war and expels the company.

events.title: The RDA comes back to stay
events.description: Starships burn a swath of forest to land and build a new colony city, Bridgehead. This time the company's aim is not only unobtanium but settling Pandora; Jake leads the Omaticaya in a guerrilla war against it, while a Marine colonel reborn in a Na'vi body hunts him.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Wikipedia: Avatar: The Way of Water

Wikipedia's plot says the RDA 'returns to colonize Pandora'; the RDA's aim of making Pandora humanity's new home because Earth is becoming uninhabitable is confirmed by Wikipedia's article on the RDA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDA_(Avatar)).
events.binWhy: The second war with the RDA begins with an invasion.

facets.change: sixteen years of peace → an invasion and a colony city

events.title: The war reaches the reef and the ash lands
events.description: The Sullys take refuge with the Metkayina reef clan; the RDA hunts the whale-like tulkun to draw them out, and the Sullys' eldest son is killed. Soon after, the colonel allies with a hostile Na'vi clan, the Mangkwan, until Pandora's wildlife turns on the company's forces and he throws himself from a floating rock; the films end without the company leaving.

Wikipedia: Avatar: Fire and Ash

events.binWhy: The war becomes a long struggle across the whole moon that neither side can end.

lineages.title: Altered Carbon
lineages.creator: Richard K. Morgan

divergence.label: The first Martian datasystems are decoded
divergence.delta: Real: Mars has been searched for ruins since the Viking photographs of 1976, and has shown only rock. Fiction: by 2089 a dig at Bradbury on Mars has found the remains of a starfaring culture as old as humanity, and its archives include charts of the habitable worlds it once settled.
divergence.inUniverse: 'Bradbury, 2089 precolonial reckoning' - the heading of a passage in Broken Angels on the decoding of the first Martian datasystems
divergence.note: The novels give almost no Earth-calendar dates. 2089 is the one stated year that marks a change of history: Broken Angels (pp. 332-33) dates the decoding of the first Martian datasystems to '2089 precolonial reckoning', after which humans know which stars to send ships to. Altered Carbon also mentions the Hendrix hotel opening in 2087, and the dig at Bradbury is older than 2089 but undated; neither is a departure of substance, so the fork is placed at the decoding.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Takeshi Kovacs (cites Broken Angels pp. 332-36: '2089 pre-colonial reckoning', 'over four centuries of archaeology'; the novels are set in or around the 26th century)
Bram reads books: Broken Angels review (quotes the 'Bradbury, 2089 precolonial reckoning' passage)

ending.why: Woken Furies ends with Quellcrist Falconer's recorded mind alive in another woman's body, a link to the Martian orbital guns and a dormant gene weapon aimed at the ruling families, and stops before the revolution is fought.

events.title: Viking 1 lands on Mars and photographs a 'face'
events.description: Viking 1 becomes the first spacecraft to land and work on Mars, on 20 July 1976. Five days later its orbiter photographs a two-kilometre mesa in Cydonia that looks like a human face, and the idea of ruins on Mars gets its most famous picture.

events.title: The 'face on Mars' is shown to be a hill

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is ours until a single discovery inside this century - a dead civilisation's archives on Mars - and everything after, from the colony worlds to the trade in bodies, follows from what those archives made possible. Continuity followed: Morgan's three novels only; the Netflix series (2018-2020) dates itself differently (2384 and about 2414) and rewrites Kovacs and Falconer, and is not used. Only 2089 is a stated year: the later dates are chained from 'over four centuries of archaeology' in Broken Angels and the novels' thirty-year gaps, and all are low confidence. The pre-fork events (1976, 1996, 2001) are real history the premise rests on. Tiers: T3 holds the real history and the 2002 publication; T2 holds everything in the story (2089-2520). T4 is empty because the fiction has no pre-industrial history, and T1 because the trilogy stops around 2520.

lineages.title: Battlestar Galactica
lineages.creator: Ronald D. Moore (developer), from Glen A. Larson's 1978 series

divergence.label: The Thirteenth Tribe leaves Kobol
divergence.delta: Real: around 152,000 BCE anatomically modern humans live in small foraging groups in Africa, with no farming, writing or metal. Fiction: on Kobol, a world elsewhere in the galaxy, a starfaring human civilisation already exists, and its thirteenth tribe, which is in fact a people of humanoid machines, leaves to found a world it calls Earth. It is not our Earth; ours enters the story only at the end.
divergence.inUniverse: ca. 4,000 years before the Fall of the Twelve Colonies (radiocarbon dating of the Temple of Five, 'The Eye of Jupiter')
divergence.note: Conversion, stated explicitly. The series finale ('Daybreak', aired 20 March 2009) cuts from the fleet's arrival on our Earth to modern New York with the title '150,000 years later'; the modern scene is taken as 2009, the year it aired, so the arrival is 2009 - 150,000 = 147,991 BCE (year -147991). The fleet reaches the first, dead Earth about three years after the Fall ('Three years ago I promised to lead you to a new home', 'Revelations') and our Earth some weeks or months later, so the Fall is placed three years earlier, at year -147994, and dates given as 'N years before the Fall' (Battlestar Wiki's BCH) convert as -147994 - N. The single-year precision is an artefact of that arithmetic: '150,000 years' is a round figure. The date of the exodus itself is contradictory on screen: Tyrol's radiocarbon estimate gives at least 4,000 years, Elosha says all thirteen tribes left about 2,000 years ago ('Kobol's Last Gleaming'), and Cottle ties a virus to the Thirteenth Tribe's departure 'over 3,000 years ago' ('A Measure of Salvation'). The earliest figure is used because the fork has to precede everything fictional; Kobol's own history is older still and undated.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the space-opera archetype for its fleets, colonies and a war across star systems, but like Star Wars it runs in reverse: the finale's '150,000 years later' cut to modern New York places the whole story in our deep past, so epoch is deep-past. It follows the 2003 miniseries and the 2004-2009 series (with the season-4 revelations and the wiki's reconstructed day counts); the prequel Caprica is used only for context in notes. Tier coverage is lopsided by construction: every story event is T4 (about 152,000 to 148,000 BCE), the three T2 entries are the two releases and the 2009 epilogue, and T3 and T1 are empty because nothing happens between the landing and the present, and nothing after it. Phases are derived from the divergence; everything after the Thirteenth Tribe's exodus is 'deep' because the fork precedes the main story by about 4,000 years. Two machine uprisings are binned machine-awakens (the first Earth's and the Colonies'); the Fall itself is mass-death, because by then the Cylons are an established enemy, not a newly woken one.

lineages.title: Halo
lineages.creator: Bungie (2001-2010), then 343 Industries / Halo Studios; Forerunner prehistory by Greg Bear (novels, 2011-2013)

divergence.label: An ancient human civilisation is already spreading between the stars
divergence.delta: Real: around 150,000 BCE anatomically modern humans live in Africa as hunter-gatherers with stone tools, and nobody has left the planet. Fiction: an earlier humanity has an interstellar civilisation spreading along the Orion Arm, on its way to a war with the Forerunners that will end with its survivors stripped of their technology and exiled to Earth.
divergence.inUniverse: c. 150,000 BCE (Halopedia's earliest dated statement about the ancient human civilisation; its rise is not dated)
divergence.note: The UNSC story starts in the 2160s, but Halo's history leaves ours much earlier. In the canon as it now stands, today's humans descend from an interstellar people who fought the Flood and the Forerunners, were defeated around 106,445 BCE, devolved and confined to Earth, and were returned to Earth again after the Halo Array fired around 97,445 BCE. None of that is in our archaeological record, so under the rule that anything fictional comes after the fork, the fork has to sit in deep prehistory. No source dates the ancient civilisation's beginning; c. 150,000 BCE is the earliest year Halopedia attaches to it, and all these deep dates are approximate. Between 97,445 BCE and 2160 the Halo record is to all intents ours (its twenty-first-century entries are trivia, such as an engineering society founded in 2021 and a book in the 2004 alternate-reality game), so a reader interested only in the UNSC chronology can treat March 2160 as a practical second threshold.

sources.title: Halopedia: Human-Forerunner wars (c. 107,445-106,445 BCE; human civilisation on the Orion Arm c. 150,000 BCE)
Halopedia: Halo universe (overview of the canonical timeline)

ending.why: Humanity has won the Covenant War and outlived Cortana's rule, but as of Halo Infinite (2560) the UNSC Infinity is wrecked, the Banished hold Zeta Halo, and the war with them is unfinished.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in far-future space opera: a human interstellar state of hundreds of colonies at war with a multi-species alien theocracy, among the ruins of an older galactic civilisation. The continuity is the games' canon as maintained by 343 Industries / Halo Studios and catalogued by Halopedia, which folds in the novels (Greg Bear's Forerunner Saga supplies the ancient past). The Paramount+ television series (2022-2024) is a separate continuity and is not used. Tiers: three T4 events in deep prehistory (c. 150,000 to c. 97,445 BCE), all approximate; T3 is empty, because the fiction adds nothing to the twentieth century; T2 holds the two releases and the twenty-second and twenty-third centuries (the Interplanetary War, the Unified Earth Government and the slipspace drive); T1 holds everything from the colonisation of Reach in 2362 to Zeta Halo in 2559.

lineages.title: Star Wars
lineages.creator: George Lucas

divergence.label: The founding of the Galactic Republic
divergence.delta: Real: 23,023 BCE is the Upper Palaeolithic - no cities, no writing, no metals, no wheels. Fiction: in that same era a Galactic Republic is founded that will last 25,000 years, hold a galaxy together through a Jedi Order, fall to an Empire, and be succeeded by a First Order. The fork is not a change to our history; it is an entire galactic civilisation inserted into our Stone Age.
divergence.inUniverse: 25,000 BBY (BBY/ABY = years before/after the Battle of Yavin)
divergence.note: Conversion, stated explicitly: the Battle of Yavin (year 0 of the BBY/ABY system) is mapped to 1977, the release year and story present of the original film, so real = 1977 - BBY before Yavin and 1977 + ABY after it. The founding figure is the one printed and current-canon sources give: The Star Wars Book and Star Wars: Timelines place the Old Republic's founding at c. 25,000 BBY, as did the Legends reference books (The Essential Guide to Warfare, The New Essential Chronology, The Essential Atlas). The frequently quoted 25,053 BBY is web-only Legends material traced to a Star Wars: The Old Republic HoloNet entry and could not be found in any printed reference book - the live and archived HoloNet pages say only 'more than twenty thousand years' - and it would move this date 53 years earlier, to 23,076 BCE. Note the direction, which is the opposite of what an early draft of the brief assumed: 25,000 BBY is 23,023 years BEFORE the 1977 anchor, so the whole branch lies in our deep past, which is exactly what 'a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away' asserts. Nothing in Star Wars canon ties the BBY/ABY calendar to Earth - canon has no Earth and no Milky Way - so this is a placement convention, not a continuity claim.

ending.why: Empire, Republic, First Order: the galaxy keeps relapsing into tyranny and keeps throwing it off; the saga as told ends with the tyrant's second fall.

events.title: The Galactic Republic is founded
events.description: A Republic of member worlds is founded and its capital eventually settles on Coruscant; over the next 25,000 years it grows into a galaxy-spanning state guarded by a Jedi Order, and its origins fade into legend.
events.note: No film dates this. Printed reference books and the current canon chronology both give c. 25,000 BBY; a web-only Legends figure of 25,053 BBY is noted in the divergence note.

facets.change: member worlds → one republic

events.title: The Ruusan Reformations and the fall of the Sith
events.description: The last Jedi-Sith war ends with the Sith destroyed at Ruusan, the Republic disarmed and its Supreme Chancellor's powers cut back, and the Sith survivor Darth Bane taking the order underground under the Rule of Two - the rearrangement the prequel-era Republic inherits a thousand years later.
events.inUniverse: c. 1,032 BBY (canon); 1,000 BBY (Legends)
events.note: Contested across canon levels. Canon dates the end of the Jedi-Sith War and the restoration of the modern Republic to 1,032 BBY (Star Wars: Timelines; The Star Wars Book) but gives the Ruusan Reformations no date at all; Legends reference books date the Reformations to 1,000 BBY, where the Republic Measures and Standards Bureau reset the calendar's year zero to the battle. I use the canon 1,032 BBY, which converts to 945 CE; the Legends date would be 977 CE.

events.note: One of the few genuinely odd places in Star Wars dating. Star Wars: Galactic Atlas: Updated Edition (2025) and Timelines (2023) put Alderaan's destruction in 1 BBY and the Battle of Yavin in year 0, even though in the story the two are days apart; the 2016 Galactic Atlas and the Legends continuity put both in 0 BBY. I follow the current canon numbering and keep them as separate years, which is why they are two events here rather than one.

events.inUniverse: 29 ABY

events.description: The First Order destroys the New Republic's capital system with Starkiller Base and is destroyed in turn within days; the galaxy is at war again, and the last Jedi goes into exile.
events.inUniverse: 34 ABY

facets.change: cold war → the capital system destroyed

lineages.groupingNote: The group's inverse case and its most popular one: everything the archetype asks for - a founding rupture no longer remembered, a 25,000-year-old Republic, a fall into empire, a dark age, a return - happens not downstream of us but upstream. Star Wars is 'a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away'; it never claims to be Earth's future, so it cannot be converted into our years by continuity, only by convention, and the convention used here (0 BBY = 1977, the original film's story present) places the entire saga in our past. That produces the one genuinely surprising shape in this group: the lineage has no T1 events at all, because even its furthest future converts to 2011 CE. Its deep history (the Republic's founding, the Ruusan Reformations, the High Republic) is T4; its film-era present is overwhelmingly T3 - eight events - because pinning each film's story present to the 1977 anchor drops them into the 20th century; and only the First Order's rise and war reach T2. Empty tiers are left empty rather than padded, and the fiction is silent about Earth entirely: there is no T4 material about our own history to record because Star Wars never touches it. phaseIsAuthored is set on this lineage because a single divergence year cannot classify a branch that runs 25,000 years: the fork is the Republic's founding, which on the real axis is also the Upper Palaeolithic, and every later beat is deep in the branch's own history even when it lands in our recorded 20th century; phases are assigned by that narrative judgement rather than derived.

lineages.title: The Culture
lineages.creator: Iain M. Banks

divergence.label: The Culture is founded
divergence.delta: Real: c. 7600 BCE - the early Neolithic, with farming villages spreading across the Fertile Crescent, and nobody anywhere has built anything more complicated than a house. Fiction: on the far side of the galaxy, several humanoid species and their thinking machines join into a single spacefaring civilisation that will still be there ten thousand years later.
divergence.inUniverse: '10,000 years before' The Hydrogen Sonata (c. 2375 CE); 'about 9,000 years before the events of novels'
divergence.note: Banks dates the Culture against the Earth calendar: Consider Phlebas's appendix fixes the Idiran War at 1327-1375 CE, and the later novels count from it. The founding itself has no stated year. It is derived from The Hydrogen Sonata's '10,000 years' before c. 2375, which gives c. 7625 BCE; the looser 'about 9,000 years before the novels' would put it one or two thousand years later. The galaxy has older fictional history (the Sublimed, the builders of the airspheres), but none of it is dated to a year, so the fork is the Culture's own beginning.

events.title: The Excession, and a war arranged on purpose
events.description: The black sphere reappears at the edge of Culture space and resists every attempt to probe it. events.title: A Culture ship studies Earth and leaves it alone
events.description: The Contact ship Arbitrary spends months studying Earth: its broadcasts, its weapons and its politics. One of the crew argues for contact to repair the mess humanity has made; another wants to wipe the species out. The Culture leaves the planet alone, and no one on Earth learns that it was there.

Banks said in a 2010 interview that it is set about 800 years after Look to Windward (c. 2967-70). I use the first, most specific textual anchor.
events.binWhy: The conflict over the Hells is settled: the Hells are destroyed and the anti-Hell side wins.

facets.change: a war over the dead fought in simulation → the Hells destroyed in reality

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's post-scarcity utopia: an interstellar civilisation of humans and artificial Minds that intervenes, covertly and at a scale of centuries, in the societies it meets. It belongs here because its drama is galactic politics and war over thousands of years. It follows Banks's published chronology, taking the novels' own cross-references (the Consider Phlebas appendix's 1327-1375 CE for the Idiran War, then the later books' 'N years after the war') as the Wikipedia Culture-series table and the Wertzone chronology lay them out. The anchors are Consider Phlebas (1327, 1331, 1375), The Player of Games (c. 2083-88), The State of the Art and Use of Weapons (1977 and 2092), Excession (c. 1867 and c. 633 BCE), Look to Windward (c. 2167), The Hydrogen Sonata (c. 2375) and Surface Detail (c. 2767). Matter (c. 1887 or 2167, self-contradictory) and Inversions (undated) are left out. Tier coverage: T4 for the founding, the first sighting of the Excession, the Idiran War and Excession; T3 for Earth in 1977 and the 1987 publication; T2 for Azad, Earth contact and Masaq' (2087-2167); T1 for the Gzilt Subliming and Surface Detail (2375-2767).
