events.title: The Horus Heresy begins
events.description: The Isstvan III atrocity opens the civil war: the Warmaster and half the Legions turn on the Emperor, and the nine years that follow burn the Imperium's best armies and end the Great Crusade.
events.note: Lexicanum dates the Heresy 005.M31-014.M31 and labels the dates approximate; Games Workshop's own timeline has the Isstvan III betrayal running 005-006.M31.
events.binWhy: Civil war begins with half the legions turning.

facets.change: crusade → half the legions turn on the throne

events.title: The Siege of Terra and the Golden Throne
events.description: The siege ends with Horus dead and the Emperor entombed on the Golden Throne; the Imperium becomes a deathless theocracy that will spend the next ten thousand years waiting for its god to wake.
events.binWhy: The siege ends with the traitor dead and the Emperor entombed.

facets.change: civil war → the traitor dead, the ruler entombed alive

events.title: The War of the Beast
events.description: An Ork empire led by the Beast nearly takes Terra a thousand years after the Heresy; the Imperium survives, and the political reckoning that follows - the Beheading of 546.M32 - reshapes its ruling institutions.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: stability → an alien empire nearly takes the capital

events.title: The Age of Apostasy: the Reign of Blood
events.description: Goge Vandire seizes both spiritual and temporal power and the Imperium tears itself apart in a century of religious civil war, from which the Adepta Sororitas and the modern Ecclesiarchy emerge.
events.note: Lexicanum dates the Age of Apostasy to M36 only; the ca. 200.M36 start of the Reign of Blood comes from the Fandom timeline. Finer precision does not exist.
events.binWhy: One man seizes both spiritual and temporal power.

facets.change: divided offices → one man seizes church and state

events.title: The Fall of Cadia and the Great Rift
events.description: The 13th Black Crusade breaks Cadia and the Great Rift opens across the galaxy, splitting the Imperium in two and ending the long stalemate of the 41st millennium.
events.binWhy: The fortress world falls and the empire is cut in two.

facets.change: long stalemate → the fortress falls and the realm is cut in two

events.title: The Indomitus Crusade and the Plague Wars
events.description: Roboute Guilliman's Indomitus Crusade and the Plague Wars that follow: the setting's present, in which the Imperium holds half a galaxy and the date itself is in dispute.
events.note: The Plague Wars are dated ca. 012.M42 in the Dark Imperium novel; the Indomitus Crusade's length was retconned in 2021 from about a century to about twelve years, and Games Workshop still bills the setting as 'the 41st Millennium', so 'M42' is a wiki convenience: the Chronostrife makes the present deliberately undecidable.
events.binWhy: Wars without end in the setting's present.

facets.change: a realm cut in two → wars without end

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's terminal case: forty thousand years of human history whose founding rupture is not merely forgotten but suppressed - the Imperium does not know what the Dark Age of Technology was - and whose calendar is nevertheless our own. Warhammer 40,000 is the one branch here that needs no projection: Imperial dates are Anno Domini on the Gregorian calendar (year N of millennium MN is (N-1)x1000+N AD, so 999.M41 = 40,999 CE and 2025 = 025.M3), and the lore's Age of Terra explicitly includes real human history, which is why this lineage has both a T4 event (the Emperor's birth in 8,000 BC, hidden inside our prehistory) and a T3 one (the game's own publication in 1987) before its fork. Where it forks is arguable and no source names a date: some material settles the Sol System in the late 2nd/early 3rd millennium and launches sublight colony ships in the mid-to-late M3, the Dark Age of Technology's start is M15 in the 6th-edition rulebook but M21 in the 3rd-edition 'Keeper Cripias' account, and the rupture the setting remembers is Old Night in M25. I take M15, the first era boundary in the current timeline that is not our history, and record the alternatives in the divergence note. Because the fiction's beats are spaced by millennia, T2 is empty - between the game's publication and the 15th millennium the branch has no near-future events to chart - and T1 carries thirteen of the fifteen events, which is exactly what a setting whose present is the 41st millennium should look like.

lineages.title: Dune
lineages.creator: Frank Herbert

divergence.label: The Butlerian Jihad
divergence.delta: Real: the year 16,000 is empty - no human being has ever lived then and our record stops in the 21st century. Fiction: in the same era humanity turns on the thinking machines that had come to rule it, and the two-generation crusade that follows becomes the founding rupture of a galactic civilisation. Its commandment, 'Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind', still governs the Imperium ten thousand years later, and the Guild calendar that dates every event below is counted from the settlement that ended it.
divergence.inUniverse: 201 B.G. (Before Guild; the calendar's year zero is the Spacing Guild's monopoly)
divergence.note: A projection, and flagged as one. No Frank Herbert text, appendix or interview gives a real-world year for Dune: the novel's own glossary defines the epoch (B.G./A.G. = before/after the Spacing Guild's monopoly) and Appendix IV dates the story to 10,191 A.G., but nothing bridges that to Earth. The bridge used here is the non-canon Dune Encyclopedia, the only reference work with a Terran chronology: it dates the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588 CE) to 14,512 B.G. and the first use of atomics in war (1945 CE) to 14,255 B.G., which puts the calendar epoch at roughly 16,100-16,200 CE. I take A.G. 0 = 16,200 CE, so the Jihad begins at 15,999 (rounded to 16,000 here), the novel's 10,191 A.G. falls at 26,391 and Chapterhouse at 15,240 A.G. at 41,440. Uncertainty is about a century from the Encyclopedia's own disagreeing anchors alone, and much more if the non-canon material is rejected: the canon-only reading is that interstellar travel had been underway for 'one hundred and ten centuries' before the Jihad, which supports 'tens of thousands of years in the future' and fixes no date. Standard Years are also some twenty hours shorter than Terran years, worth centuries of drift across 10,191 of them. Herbert himself never said.

ending.why: Herbert died with Duncan and Sheeana fleeing into an unmapped universe while the Honored Matres and the Bene Gesserit merge; nothing is settled.

events.title: Terran atomics, dated from the far end
events.description: The Dune Encyclopedia's Terran chronology dates the first use of atomics in war to 14,255 B.G. - our own 1945 - and threads Alexander, the Armada and a Golden Age of Invention through the same B.G. sequence. It is the only place in Dune reference material where our history is given a date in the fiction's own calendar.
events.inUniverse: 14,255 B.G. (Dune Encyclopedia)
events.note: Non-canon and internally shaky: the Encyclopedia's Terran anchors imply a calendar epoch of 16,100 CE from the 1588 entry and 16,200 CE from the 1945 entry. Its inclusion here is deliberate - it is the single thread tying this branch back to our era - but no canon source dates Earth history at all.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: conventional war → atomics used

events.title: Dune is published
events.description: Frank Herbert's Dune appears, the real-world origin of the branch and the anchor without which none of these dates could be plotted at all.
events.note: A real-world publication event, not an in-universe one; it sits in the branch's prehistory because the fiction's history has not forked from ours in 1965.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Butlerian Jihad
events.description: Humanity turns on the thinking machines: the crusade against computers, thinking machines and conscious robots runs for two generations, ends with the injunction 'Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind', and becomes the founding rupture of all later human civilisation - the Orange Catholic Bible, the Great Convention and the Guild's monopoly all grow out of it.
events.note: The in-universe dates are canon (the novel's own glossary dates the Jihad 201-108 B.G.); the real-world year is the projection described in the divergence note.
events.binWhy: Humanity rises against the machines that governed it.

facets.change: machine rule → machines destroyed and forbidden

events.title: The Battle of Corrin
events.description: The space battle near Sigma Draconis settles the ascendancy of House Corrino over the last armies of the Jihad and the remnants of the machine empire; the Corrino Empire begins eighty-eight years before the Guild's calendar does.
events.note: 88 B.G. is canon (novel glossary). The real year follows the projection.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: post-jihad struggle → one house ascends

events.title: The Spacing Guild takes its monopoly
events.description: The Guild's monopoly on space travel, transport and interstellar banking begins and is taken as year zero of the Imperial calendar; CHOAM is chartered in the same settlement. No ship moves without the Guild's consent for the next ten thousand years, and every date in Dune is measured from here.
events.inUniverse: 0 A.G.
events.note: The epoch is canon by definition (novel glossary: 'The Guild monopoly ... is taken as the beginning point of the Imperial Calendar'). The Dune Encyclopedia adds that the Guild existed as an organisation from 78 B.G., so the monopoly and the founding are different events.
events.binWhy: One body takes a monopoly on all travel and banking.

facets.change: open travel → one body's monopoly on all movement and banking

events.title: House Atreides takes Arrakis
events.description: House Atreides is given Arrakis and destroyed within the year: Leto I dies, Paul and Jessica flee to the Fremen, and Alia is born. It is the opening of Dune and the hinge on which the Imperium's ten-thousand-year-old order turns.
events.note: 10,191 A.G. is canon: Appendix IV dates Leto I (10,140-10,191) and the novel's chapter epigraphs give the same year. The real year is projected.
events.binWhy: The Duke is killed within the year and his house destroyed; the heir flees.

facets.change: a great house → given a planet and destroyed within the year

events.title: Paul Muad'Dib becomes Emperor
events.description: Shaddam IV abdicates and Paul takes the throne; his Fremen legions carry a jihad across the Imperium that kills billions in his name and breaks the Corrino-Guild-CHOAM settlement that had held the peace for ten thousand years.
events.note: The A.G. year comes from the Dune Encyclopedia and wiki chronologies, not from the novel, which gives only the sequence; the real year inherits that plus the projection.
events.binWhy: The prophet takes the throne and his legions carry a jihad.

facets.change: emperor → a prophet takes the throne; his legions carry a jihad

events.title: Dune Messiah
events.description: Twelve years into Paul's reign a conspiracy of the Bene Gesserit, the Guild and the Tleilaxu breaks the prophet; Paul walks blind into the desert and the Imperial centre of gravity shifts to his sister and his twin children.
events.note: The twelve-year interval is stated in the novel; the A.G. years are reference-book reconstructions.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: prophet-emperor → broken by conspiracy, walks into the desert

events.title: Children of Dune: Leto II takes the throne
events.description: Leto II begins his metamorphosis into the sandworm and becomes Emperor; his reign will run for three and a half thousand years and will end the spice's dependence on a single planet.
events.note: Nine years after Dune Messiah per the novel; the A.G. year is a reference-book reconstruction.
events.binWhy: The heir takes the throne and begins his transformation.

facets.change: regency → the heir takes the throne and begins to change

events.title: The death of the God Emperor
events.description: Leto II dies after 3,500 years as the God Emperor; his death releases the Scattering, in which trillions of humans flee beyond the Imperium's reach, and no single power can ever again hold the species.
events.note: The 3,500-year reign is canon; the end year is not agreed - the Dune Encyclopedia has 13,724, wiki chronologies 13,727-13,728, and 10,219 plus 3,500 gives 13,719. Herbert's own books also contain a contradictory epigraph ('ten thousand years since Leto II began his metamorphosis') in Heretics.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: 3,500 years of one ruler → dies; humanity scatters

events.title: The Honored Matres return
events.description: The Honored Matres come back from the Scattering and burn Arrakis; fifteen hundred years after Leto II's death the Bene Gesserit face a force bred in the wilderness beyond the old Imperium.
events.note: The 1,500-year interval is stated in reference material; the A.G. year is wiki-derived.
events.binWhy: An enemy returns from beyond the frontier and burns the capital.

facets.change: scattered humanity → returns as an enemy and burns the capital

events.title: Chapterhouse: Dune
events.description: The Bene Gesserit, holding the last sandworms on Chapterhouse, fight the Honored Matres to a standstill and begin building a new sisterhood and a new Arrakis from scratch - the last point Frank Herbert's own chronology reaches.
events.note: Weakest date in the lineage: wiki-derived only.
events.binWhy: The sisterhood fights the invaders to a standstill.

facets.change: invasion → fought to a standstill; a new order begins

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's darkest case and its clearest remembered rupture: a galactic civilisation twenty-odd thousand years downstream of us whose founding event - the Butlerian Jihad against thinking machines - survives only as religious commandment, and whose calendar never touches our own. The real-world years here are a projection and are flagged as one everywhere they appear: no Herbert text gives an Earth date, so the anchor is the Dune Encyclopedia's Terran chronology, the only reference work that maps Terran events onto B.G. dates; anchored on 1588 CE = 14,512 B.G. and 1945 CE = 14,255 B.G. it puts A.G. 0 at roughly 16,100-16,200 CE, and I take 16,200, which sets the Jihad at 16,000, the novel's 10,191 A.G. at 26,391 and Chapterhouse at 41,440. Everything carries about a century of uncertainty from the Encyclopedia alone, and far more if non-canon material is rejected. Tier coverage follows the projection: no T2 events, because the fiction jumps from its founding straight to the novel ten thousand years later, and T4 consists of one Terran touchstone the Dune Encyclopedia preserves plus the 1965 publication, which is where this branch's real-world anchor actually lives.

lineages.title: Foundation
lineages.creator: Isaac Asimov

divergence.label: The founding of the Galactic Empire
divergence.delta: Real: the year 35,000 is empty - no human being has ever lived then and our record stops in the 21st century. Fiction: the same year is where the Galactic Era calendar begins, as the Trantorian Empire finishes absorbing the galaxy and is proclaimed the Galactic Empire - a state that stands twelve thousand years, then falls in a single lifetime, and whose fall Hari Seldon's psychohistory is built to shorten from thirty thousand years of barbarism to one thousand.
divergence.inUniverse: 1 G.E. (Galactic Era; 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E.)
divergence.note: A projection, flagged as one, and resting on an inference as well. No Asimov text gives a real-world year for G.E. 1, and none states outright that G.E. 1 is the Empire's founding - that identification is reference-work inference from Frankenn I being called the first Emperor in Pebble in the Sky. The projection used is the only one Asimov himself published: his notebook chart in Thrilling Wonder Stories (Winter 1955) puts the hyperspatial drive at about 5,000 CE, 'Trantor becomes the Galactic Empire officially, about 35,000', Seldon's birth at about 47,000 and the Second Galactic Empire at 48,000. That scheme is corroborated twice by in-universe numerals - Seldon born 11,988 G.E. and the plan's thousand years counted from 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E. - so I use real = G.E. + 34,999, giving 12,069 G.E. = 47,068 and the Second Empire's due date at 48,067. It is flatly irreconcilable with the Robot/Foundation merger Asimov wrote in 1982-86, which implies G.E. 1 at about 11,600-12,100 CE and would move every date here back by some 23,400 years; the alternative is a different dataset row, not a rounding error, and is not blended in. Asimov's own comment on his dating was that it was 'made up ad hoc'.

ending.why: Asimov left the choice between a Second Empire and Galaxia open; the Plan is on schedule and its ending is deliberately unwritten.

events.title: 'Foundation' is published
events.description: The first story of the series appears in Astounding Science Fiction, written from August 1941 after Asimov's meeting with John W. Campbell; the fix-up novel follows in 1951 with 'The Psychohistorians' written last, to open a book whose first part was the last written.
events.note: The only real-world event in this lineage. It matters to the dating because the stories were written 1941-1949 as a far-future history with no real-world anchor at all; Asimov published a real-world scheme only in 1955.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Galactic Empire is founded
events.description: The Trantorian Empire becomes the Galactic Empire: Frankenn I is crowned, the Galactic Era calendar begins, and the Empire will hold the galaxy for twelve thousand years - the long peace whose end Seldon spends his life calculating.
events.inUniverse: 1 G.E.
events.note: Real year projected; the identification of G.E. 1 with the Empire's founding is reference-work inference, not an Asimov statement.
events.binWhy: Independent powers become one polity.

facets.change: expanding kingdom → galactic empire proclaimed

events.title: Pebble in the Sky
events.description: The Empire is still expanding at fifty new provinces a day, and Earth - the forgotten homeworld, its crust still radioactive from wars nobody remembers - is a backwater prison world where a man from the 20th century wakes up. It is the one Empire novel that prints a Galactic Era date.
events.note: The numeral is in the text ('in the Year of the Galactic Era 827'), which makes the in-universe date unusually solid; the real year is projected. The same novel is internally inconsistent, having a character estimate he was thrown 50,000 years forward.
events.binWhy: An empire still adding fifty provinces a day.

facets.change: empire → still adding provinces; the homeworld forgotten

events.title: Prelude to Foundation: Seldon comes to Trantor
events.description: Hari Seldon arrives on the imperial capital and presents psychohistory at the Decennial Convention - the moment the science that could save the galaxy becomes visible to the Empire that will want it suppressed.
events.note: 12,020 G.E. is Prelude's date. An early draft of the research brief attributed it to 'The Encyclopedists'; it belongs here, and the Encyclopedists belong at 50 F.E.
events.binWhy: Psychohistory is presented to the Empire and becomes visible.

facets.change: the fall unforeseen → a science that predicts it is presented

events.title: Seldon's trial and the exile to Terminus
events.description: Hari Seldon is tried by the Commission of Public Safety and exiled with his Encyclopedists to Terminus at the rim of the galaxy; the Foundation is founded there as a cover for the thousand-year plan to shorten the coming dark age from thirty thousand years to one.
events.note: The anchor is printed in the novel's own epigraph: Seldon 'born in the 11,988th year of the Galactic Era; died 12,069', the latter given as 'the year 1 F.E.'. The trial's year, 12,067, is the standard reading (Wikipedia and the chronologies agree). Real year projected.
events.binWhy: The Foundation is founded on Terminus under cover of exile.

facets.change: the scientist tried → exiled; the plan begins under cover

events.title: The Encyclopedists: the first Seldon Crisis
events.description: Fifty years after the founding, Terminus faces annexation by the neighbouring kingdom of Anacreon and survives it not by force but by playing its rivals off against each other - the pattern for every crisis to come, and the first proof that the plan works.
events.note: The story prints no G.E. numeral, only 'fifty years' since the Foundation was established; 50 F.E. follows from the epigraph's 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E. The brief's 'The Encyclopedists opens around 12,020 G.E.' is a mix-up: 12,020 is Prelude to Foundation, and 12,050 G.E. has no Encyclopedists connection in any source.
events.binWhy: Annexation is survived by diplomacy, not force.

facets.change: annexation threatened → survived by playing rivals off

events.title: The Mayors: religion instead of arms
events.description: Salvor Hardin breaks the Four Kingdoms by religion rather than by arms and the Foundation becomes the spiritual centre of its barbarian neighbours - 'violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.'
events.note: The F.E. year is fan-chronology rather than text; real year projected.
events.binWhy: Control of the neighbouring kingdoms is taken by religion rather than by arms.

facets.change: neighbours by arms → neighbours by religion

events.title: The Mule
events.description: A mutant outside psychohistory's equations conquers the Foundation and the remains of the Empire in five years, and the plan's first millennium looks lost - the one event Seldon's mathematics could not predict.
events.note: Fan-chronology year; real year projected.
events.binWhy: An enemy no one predicted conquers the Foundation in five years.

facets.change: the plan on course → an unpredicted mutant conquers everything

events.title: The Second Foundation is found
events.description: Search by the Foundation: the Second Foundation at Star's End is located and apparently destroyed, and the plan is restored - at the cost of the First Foundation believing itself alone in the galaxy.
events.note: Fan-chronology year; real year projected.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: hidden guardians → found, and apparently destroyed

events.title: Foundation's Edge: Trevize's choice
events.description: Five hundred years on, the two Foundations are on a collision course and Golan Trevize is made to choose the galaxy's future - Galaxia, a single group mind, over either of them.
events.note: Wikipedia dates the novel 'five hundred years after the establishment of the Foundation'; the F.E. numeral is fan-chronology.
events.binWhy: One man chooses a group mind for the galaxy.

facets.change: two foundations on collision → one man chooses a group mind

events.title: Foundation and Earth: the radioactive homeworld
events.description: Trevize's search ends on a radioactive Earth, the lost planet of origin, where he learns that the robot Daneel Olivaw has guided humanity for twenty thousand years and that the plan was never only Seldon's.
events.note: The 'twenty thousand years' is the novel's own wording - 'twenty thousand perhaps - since the people of the Galaxy have concerned themselves with Earth' - and it is the line that welds the Robot novels to the Foundation era, and therefore the line that makes Asimov's published 35,000 CE projection irreconcilable with the 1982-86 merger.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: origin lost → the homeworld found, and the hidden guide revealed

events.title: The Second Empire is due
events.description: The terminus of Seldon's plan: a Second Galactic Empire is to be founded a thousand years after the fall, thirty thousand years of barbarism compressed into one. The published stories stop five hundred years short of it.
events.inUniverse: 1,000 F.E. (projected)
events.note: Not a depicted event: this is psychohistory's own projection, the far end of the plan, included because it is the only date the fiction sets for its own future.
events.binWhy: The plan's terminus: a second empire a thousand years after the fall.

facets.change: thousand-year interregnum → a second empire due

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's 'history as engineering' case: an empire twelve thousand years old, a science that predicts its fall, and a plan to shorten thirty thousand years of barbarism to one thousand. It belongs here because its whole drama is the shape of a galactic civilisation's decline, and because its calendar is pure far-future: Galactic Era 1 is the founding of the Galactic Empire, and no Asimov text gives a real-world year for it, so every date here is a projection and is labelled as one. The projection used is the only one Asimov himself published - his 1955 notebook chart, which puts the Empire at about 35,000 CE, Seldon's birth at about 47,000 and the Second Empire at 48,000 - and it is corroborated twice by in-universe numerals (Seldon born 11,988 G.E.; 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E.). It cannot be reconciled with the Robot/Foundation merger of 1982-86, which implies G.E. 1 at about 11,600-12,100 CE; that alternative belongs in a different row and is recorded in the divergence note rather than averaged in. Tier coverage reflects the projection: one T3 event (the 1942 first publication, the lineage's only real-world event), no T4 and no T2 events at all, and everything else in T1 between 35,000 and 48,000 CE. The fiction is silent about our own era by construction - its Earth survives only as a radioactive legend at the galaxy's edge, and no book dates it - which is why the lineage's contact with real history is a magazine issue rather than an event.

worlds.setting: Present-day America, exactly as it looks, with one addition. Under Cheyenne Mountain the Air Force runs a device found at Giza in 1928 that opens wormholes to thousands of worlds. Humans live on many of them, taken from Earth long ago by the Goa'uld, parasites who posed as the gods of Egypt and still rule much of the galaxy. Earth's teams go through every week, and the public has no idea.
worlds.conflict: The Goa'uld want Earth back as a source of hosts and slaves, and the SGC is the only thing in their way: a handful of teams, a borrowed alien ally and whatever technology they can steal. At home the fight is over secrecy, as rogue agencies, politicians and corporations each want the gate for themselves. Later come enemies who are worse than the Goa'uld.
worlds.politics: A classified US military programme answering to the President and a few senators, later shared with the great powers under an international oversight body, and harassed by rogue intelligence agents who think it is too soft.
worlds.technology: An alien gate older than humanity, captured weapons and ships, and eventually starships of Earth's own, all run from a bunker with 1990s computers.
worlds.mood: Confident, adventurous and wry. It is a military procedural in which the gods turn out to be frauds, and it rarely takes itself too seriously.

whereToStart.title: Stargate
whereToStart.blurb: The original film, self-contained.

whereToStart.title: Stargate SG-1: Children of the Gods
whereToStart.blurb: The series pilot, which sets up the whole programme.

connections.note: The same government that keeps the truth from the public, here fighting on humanity's side.
A secret organisation at the heart of the ordinary world handling aliens nobody else sees.
Emmerich and Devlin's next film: the aliens come to us instead.
An alien gate network left by a vanished older race, and humans racing to understand it.

worlds.setting: Not our world. Lyra's Oxford has colleges, gas lamps and a river, and the year is roughly ours, but the Reformation never broke the Church's power: John Calvin became Pope, the Magisterium still governs, and there was no scientific or industrial revolution. Every person is accompanied by a daemon, an animal-shaped soul that speaks, changes shape in childhood and settles at puberty. Power is liturgical, fuel is anbaric, and the North is a frontier of zeppelins, witches, armoured bears and experimental stations.
worlds.conflict: The Church teaches that Dust, a particle visible only to instruments and attracted to conscious beings, is evidence of original sin, and it is prepared to sever children from their daemons to prevent it. Against that stands a child whom the witches' prophecy concerns, and the question the trilogy asks is whether knowledge and desire are pollution or the whole point of being alive.
worlds.politics: The Magisterium rules Lyra's world: doctrine is law, and it has courts, spies and experimental stations of its own. Everything else sits outside it or under it, from the colleges of Oxford to the Gyptians on the canals and the witch clans of the far north, who owe the Church nothing.
worlds.technology: No electronics, no screens, no computing. Zeppelins, anbaric lamps, naphtha, hand-written reports, glass instruments and the alethiometer, a compass-like device that answers questions in symbols and is read by intuition rather than calculation. The world is industrious without being industrial: it can build airships and cannot build a radio, and it possesses photographic plates while lacking the thought that would make them mundane.
worlds.mood: Wonderful and dreadful at once. It reads as a children's adventure written in the language of theology, where the villains are sincere, the scholarship is dangerous and growing up is the most serious event in the universe.

locations.name: Jordan College, Oxford

factions.name: The Magisterium
factions.blurb: The Church as government: doctrine, courts, spies and scientific bureaux.

factions.name: The witches

factions.name: The armoured bears

Mirror images: a federation built on inquiry, and a church that burned the inquiry down.

worlds.setting: The present day, mostly 2006 and 2007, spread across New York, Odessa in Texas, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Tokyo and India. Ordinary people discover they can fly, heal, read minds, paint the future or stop time, and each learns that others like them have been watched for decades by a company hidden behind a paper business, founded by survivors of a 1961 government camp.
worlds.conflict: Scattered strangers with powers try to stop visions of catastrophe from coming true, a nuclear explosion in New York first among them, while a serial killer hunts them for their abilities and the Company and later the government try to keep them hidden, caged or registered. The underlying question is whether the gifted should hide, rule or simply be seen.
worlds.politics: Power is the Petrelli family's: a matriarch who co-founded the Company, a son who flies into Congress and then the Senate, and a hidden bargain with the President that becomes a round-up. The public record shows elections and explosions; the machinery behind them is private.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, except for what is in the blood: a biological source of powers, a formula that can give them, a virus that can take them away, and a Company with tracking tags, memory-erasing agents and a sub-basement prison. Everything else is 2006: phones, paintings and comic books.
worlds.mood: Earnest, sprawling and comic-book bright, with a dread of foretold futures running underneath and a fondness for the ordinary person who decides to be brave.

worlds.setting: The United States between 1953 and the late 1980s, seen one ordinary life at a time: small towns, army bases, Southern courthouses, rock clubs and suburban kitchens, each for a few days. Behind them is Project Quantum Leap, a secret complex at Stallion's Gate, New Mexico, in the 1990s, where a hologram, a vain computer and a skeleton crew try to track the man they lost.
worlds.conflict: Sam Beckett is trapped in the past, leaping into strangers and able to go on only after he fixes something that went wrong in their lives: a death, a wrong verdict, a marriage, a race riot. The question underneath is who is doing the leaping, and whether a good man's wish to fix the world can ever let him go home.
worlds.politics: Mostly the politics of the street and the family: segregation, the Klan, Vietnam, women's rights and prejudice, each seen from inside one person. The federal government appears only as the funder that wants results and can shut the project down.
worlds.technology: One machine, the Quantum Leap accelerator, and its supports: Ziggy, a hybrid computer with an ego and access to every record, and a hand-link that tells Al the odds. Everything else is period: whatever the year of the leap has.
worlds.mood: Warm, humane and episodic, a weekly morality play with comedy and music, darkening at the edges when a leap cannot fix everything.
themes: putting right what once went wrong
the cost of changing the past

worlds.setting: An island somewhere in the South Pacific that cannot be found without its exact bearings and sometimes moves: jungle, a beach camp of plane-crash survivors, the abandoned bunkers and yellow houses of a 1970s research colony, a community of ageless natives called the Others, and at its heart a pool of light that the Island's guardians say holds back something worse. Off the Island, the world believes Flight 815 went down with everyone aboard.
worlds.conflict: Survivors of a crash try to get home, then try to understand where they are, then learn they were brought there as candidates to replace the Island's guardian. Two immortals, Jacob and the Man in Black, have fought for centuries over whether people are good, and the survivors must decide whether to leave, to stay, or to take a side.
worlds.politics: Power on the Island is hereditary and hidden: a guardian who chooses his successor, leaders of the Others who answer to him through an ageless intermediary, and a billionaire exile who wants the Island back. Off it, the Oceanic Six's lie becomes the official account.
worlds.technology: Mostly 2004 and 1970s DHARMA hardware: bunkers, film reels, a computer that must be fed a code every 108 minutes, a sonar fence and a submarine. Underneath lie a frozen wheel that moves the Island through space and time and an energy that no instrument explains.
worlds.mood: Mysterious and emotional, a survival story that becomes a puzzle box and then a parable, with long flashbacks into the lives that brought each passenger to the plane.

worlds.setting: Hill Valley, a fictional county seat in the Sierra foothills of California, seen in four years: a new railroad town in 1885, a busy courthouse square in 1955, a downtown hollowed out by the mall in 1985, and a revived, gadget-filled town in 2015. The courthouse clock, stopped by lightning in 1955, ties the eras together, and the same few families, McFlys and Tannens above all, keep turning up in each one.
worlds.conflict: A teenager and his inventor friend keep changing the past and then have to repair what they changed: first his parents' meeting, then a bully's stolen fortune, then a friend's death in the Old West. The fight is less against a villain than against consequence itself, and the question is whether a person's future is fixed by what already happened or can still be chosen.
worlds.politics: Small-town politics seen from the kerb: a Black busboy in 1955 becomes the mayor of 1985, the courthouse passes from law to ruin to shopping mall, and in the erased 1985A one rich bully buys the police and turns the town into his casino. National politics appears only in jokes and in that alternate version.
worlds.technology: One impossible machine among ordinary ones: a stainless-steel DeLorean with a flux capacitor, powered first by stolen plutonium, then by a bolt of lightning, then by a kitchen fusion unit, and finally rebuilt as a flying steam locomotive. Around it, 2015 has hoverboards and flying cars, and 1885 has the telegraph and the railroad.
worlds.mood: Comic, fast and warm, with a streak of dread: the jokes are about embarrassment and near-misses, and the nightmare is a version of home where the wrong man won.
themes: parents as they were at seventeen
the small town across a century

worlds.setting: Winden, a small German town with a forest, a cave system and a nuclear power station due to close in 2020, seen in 1888, 1921, 1953, 1986, 2019, 2020 and 2053. Four families, the Kahnwalds, Nielsens, Dopplers and Tiedemanns, live there in every period, and a tunnel in the caves joins each period to the one thirty-three years away. In the town's archives the story looks like missing children and unsolved crimes; underneath, the same people travel between the years and are their own ancestors.
worlds.conflict: Children keep vanishing from Winden, and each disappearance is a step in a loop. Adam, an aged Jonas, and Eva, an aged Martha, lead rival secret societies, one trying to end the loop and one keeping it going, while the families try to save the people they have lost. The apocalypse of 27 June 2020 is the event they are all converging on.
worlds.politics: Almost none on the surface: a police station, a town council, a plant manager, a school principal. The real power is held by two secret societies, Sic Mundus and Erit Lux, who plan across centuries and treat the townspeople as pieces to place. After 2020 there is only a sealed plant, military patrols and whoever has guns.
worlds.technology: Each era's own, from 1888 clocks to 1986 cassette players and 2019 smartphones. The fantastic technology is small and hand-built: a brass device, a steel chair, a tunnel in a cave, a glowing sphere of matter in the ruined reactor. There is no future gadgetry; the nuclear plant is the most advanced thing in town, and it is what ends the world.
worlds.mood: Cold, rain-soaked and fatalistic, with a mourning score and a sense that every choice has already been made.
themes: families as knots of cause and effect
grief that refuses to accept a death
the nuclear age as original sin

worlds.setting: A present-day American city, 'the City', where a gothic mansion houses what is left of a famous childhood superhero team. In 1989 forty-three women gave birth without having been pregnant; an alien billionaire adopted seven of the children, numbered them and trained them to save the world. Now adults and estranged, they return for his funeral. The series also goes to 1960s Dallas, to the Kennedy assassination and to an office outside time that edits history.
worlds.conflict: Every season ends the world, and every ending is the family's fault: a sister's suppressed power, a time jump gone wrong, a paradox made by visiting their father in 1963. A time-policing agency, the Commission, wants history to run as written; their father wants to use them to bring back his wife. The siblings keep saving the world without knowing they are why it keeps ending.
worlds.politics: Hidden authority everywhere: a billionaire who is not human, Majestic 12 inside the US government in 1963, and the Commission, which keeps history on schedule by assassination. Public politics barely appear; the celebrity team is the only public face of the hidden world.
worlds.technology: Mostly the present, with steampunk touches: an android mother, a chimpanzee butler who can talk, a time-travel briefcase, a moon base and a hotel built around a button that resets the universe. Powers come from marigold, a substance from Reginald's home world.
worlds.mood: Sardonic family drama with a pop soundtrack, broken up by time-travel farce and very violent fights.
themes: the family that caused the apocalypse
a father who raised weapons, not children
history kept on schedule by assassins
saving the world by ceasing to exist

worlds.setting: The surface is an unremarkable 1990s America: federal offices, motels and small towns, a country that has officially stopped believing in flying saucers. Underneath it, the government has known since 1947 that something non-human is here, and a small group of officials has spent fifty years managing that fact in secret. The X-Files office holds the cases nobody wants filed. Knowing costs you: the record is simultaneously true and officially discredited, and the people who keep it tend to lose their careers, their families and their lives.
worlds.conflict: Mulder believes the truth is knowable and suppressed; Scully demands evidence that would survive a courtroom. Both are right. The government is in a standing arrangement with visitors it cannot fight, made by men who priced a few generations of silence as a fair trade for the species. Every case asks whether exposure would save anyone, or would end the arrangement that keeps humanity alive.
worlds.politics: Agency politics on the surface, a shadow cabinet underneath. A handful of powerful men decide what the public may know, and the Bureau's official position is that Mulder's work is a waste of money.
worlds.technology: The tech is deliberately mundane: filing cabinets, payphones, rental cars, autopsy rooms. The aliens have what we cannot build, the conspiracy has only what it can steal and reverse-engineer, and none of it reaches the public. You notice the absence of the ordinary things that would prove anything, such as a working camera or a witness who stays alive.
worlds.mood: Paranoid, melancholy, claustrophobic. It is a show about two people doing careful work in a building that has already decided the answer, and about how lonely it is to be the only one asking.

worlds.setting: Hawkins, Indiana, between 1983 and 1987: bicycles, basements, walkie-talkies, a new shopping mall and a Department of Energy laboratory at the edge of town that everyone drives past. Behind its fence the lab has been running psychic experiments on children since 1959. Under it, from November 1983, is a passage to a cold, spore-filled copy of the town, and beyond that a realm the children call the Upside Down. The adults who find out mostly keep quiet, and the government covers each disaster as an accident.
worlds.conflict: A boy who went missing in 1983 is the first sign the laboratory has opened something it cannot close. Every year after, something comes through: a predator, a hive mind, a Soviet attempt to reopen the gate, and finally the lab's first subject, Henry Creel, who wants to merge his realm with Hawkins. Children and a few adults fight it while the state hunts the girl who can stop it.
worlds.politics: Cold War secrecy. The Department of Energy lab, the Soviets beneath Starcourt and the army that quarantines Hawkins in 1986 all want the same thing: the power of the gate and the children who can open it. Local authority is either complicit, like the mayor, or overwhelmed, like the police chief. The only people telling the truth are teenagers, a pirate radio station and a conspiracy journalist nobody believes.
worlds.technology: The public side is ordinary 1980s America: CB radios, cassette recorders, arcade games, Eggo waffles and a new mall. The secret side is sensory-deprivation tanks, LSD sessions, blood transfusions to spread powers and a Soviet machine that punches through into another world. The monsters are organic and connected by a hive mind; the humans have radios, flamethrowers and nail-studded bats.
worlds.mood: Warm nostalgia with horror underneath: friendships, first loves and summer holidays, interrupted by disappearances and a government that lies about all of them.
themes: the state that experiments on its children
trauma and the monster that feeds on it
growing up in a town that is being lied to

worlds.setting: New York looks like New York: traffic, tourists, hot dog carts, a news cycle about nothing. Underneath it, roughly fifteen hundred aliens live disguised among humans, and a small agency runs their arrivals, paperwork, disputes and deportations. Both films and cartoon spin-off are consistent about one thing: the extraordinary here is administered. The surface stays beautifully ordinary because a neutral zone is only neutral while nobody notices it. The cost of knowing is exacted by machine: one flash and you lose the memory, one signature and you lose your name.
worlds.conflict: The agency's mandate is to keep Earth a neutral zone, which makes immigration control and public relations more important than firepower. Every incident that risks exposure is a catastrophe, whether a hostile alien or a human demanding proof causes it. The comedy comes from procedure; the tension from the fact that procedure is all that stands between the planet and everyone who wants it.
worlds.politics: An unofficial department with no congressional oversight, no public budget line and no accountability to anyone outside itself. It answers to no electorate, and the only check on it is its own sense of restraint.
worlds.technology: Chrome sidearms and sunglasses are the visible kit, but the real technology is discretion: neuralysers that erase memory, disguises that hide a body, doors that fold space. Nothing is designed to impress, only to be forgotten. What is missing is any interest in improving human life. The agency could change the world and has decided, for excellent reasons, not to.
worlds.mood: Deadpan, breezy, faintly sinister. A galaxy-threatening emergency is handled like a lost-luggage claim, and the joke is that this is exactly how it should be handled.

worlds.setting: China and then the whole Solar System, from the Cultural Revolution to the end of the universe. At a secret radio base in the northern mountains, a persecuted astrophysicist invites an alien civilisation that lives on a planet thrown between three suns. Their fleet will take four centuries to arrive. In the meantime, particles smaller than an atom lock human physics and watch everything. Earth passes through eras named for the ways it tries to survive: Crisis, Deterrence, Broadcast, Bunker.
worlds.conflict: Humanity against Trisolaris at first, and then against the universe itself. The galaxy turns out to be a dark forest, where every civilisation hides and destroys any other it finds. The war is fought with secret strategies, deterrence and broadcast coordinates more than with fleets. Its turning points depend on individuals, Ye Wenjie, Luo Ji and Cheng Xin, making choices for the whole species.
worlds.politics: A UN Planetary Defense Council that gives unaccountable power to Wallfacers and later to a single Swordholder, an Earth-Trisolaris Organization of human traitors, periods of defeatism and of false optimism, and in the end a Solar System federation of bunker cities.
worlds.technology: Sophons (protons unfolded into computers), Staircase nuclear-pulse probes, controlled fusion, strong-interaction droplets, gravitational-wave broadcasting, curvature (lightspeed) drives, black domains of lowered lightspeed, photoids and dual-vector foils that make space two-dimensional.
worlds.mood: Cold and vast; history seen from far above, with individual choices weighed against the fate of the species and the heat death of everything.
themes: the dark forest: cosmic sociology as a war of all against all
trust, betrayal and a species' faith in itself
deterrence and the person who must hold the switch
deep time and the end of the universe
what the Cultural Revolution did to a generation of scientists

connections.note: Both are about a radio message from the stars; here the answer is a warning, not a gift.
Both show the Solar System's politics under an alien threat that humanity cannot match.
Both use relativity and higher dimensions to stretch human lives across deep time.
Both have secret plans carried out over centuries; the Wallfacers are Seldon plans kept in one person's head.

worlds.setting: Boston and New York in the 2000s and 2010s, seen from the basement laboratory at Harvard where Walter Bishop, released from a mental hospital, works for an FBI unit that investigates the impossible. The cases are scientific horror: flesh-dissolving toxins, shape-shifters, men who walk through walls. Behind them is a second universe a crossing away, where the Twin Towers stand and airships fly, and which is coming apart because of what Walter did in 1985. From 2015 the whole Earth is occupied.
worlds.conflict: Walter's crossing to save a dying boy broke the wall between two universes, and the damaged side wants revenge. The FBI's Fringe Division fights their cases, then their agents, then the men behind both. Watching the whole time are the Observers, bald men in hats who, it turns out, are scouting for an invasion from 2609.
worlds.politics: At first, bureaucratic: an FBI unit whose remit nobody wants to know about, and a corporation, Massive Dynamic, with its own agenda. The other universe is a security state that seals damaged areas in amber, bystanders included. After 2015 the Observers rule directly, with human Loyalists branded on the cheek, a Ministry of Science and a native population policed by what is left of the FBI.
worlds.technology: Mostly the present: laptops, FBI cars, an old Harvard laboratory with a cow in it. The fringe science is chemistry and biology gone wrong, plus machines that cross between universes and amber that freezes whole city blocks. The Observers bring time travel, mind-reading and devices that age a man years in seconds.
worlds.mood: Procedural, melancholy and family-centred: every case is a horror story, and the arc is about a father who broke the world for his son.
themes: what a father will do for a child
two versions of the same people
love as the thing that cannot be erased

connections.note: An FBI unit, a sceptic and a believer, and cases the government would rather not file: Fringe is its direct descendant.
Both turn on crossing between parallel worlds and on the damage every crossing does.
Both have a ruined future that reaches back into the present to change what caused it.

worlds.setting: Ordinary Britain in the 1990s: suburbs, comprehensive schools, the evening news, a country with no idea. Laid over the top of it is a parallel magical Britain with the same postcode, hidden behind enchantment, misdirection and memory charms. It has its own civil service, newspaper, prison, bank and class system, and it is small enough that everyone knows everyone. The cost of knowing is the cruellest of the five worlds: the Muggle side of your family is not supposed to be told.
worlds.conflict: Two wars, twenty years apart, over whether magic belongs to everyone or only to those born to it. Powerful families and the movement they fund want a pure-blood order restored; the Ministry wants calm above all else, which makes it the enemy of anyone trying to warn it. Because the world is concealed, the war is fought in spaces the ordinary one never looks at.
worlds.politics: The Ministry of Magic governs the concealed population: an elected minister, a permanent bureaucracy, a court, and one seat of contact with the Muggle Prime Minister. It is a small civil service with a small civil service's instincts, which is why it spends its worst year denying a war rather than fighting one.
worlds.technology: Magic replaces almost every modern convenience, and nothing is built: no computers, no electronics, no industry, only wands, quills, enchanted objects and a steam train to school. Wizards conjure what Muggles manufacture, treat Muggle engineering as a curiosity, and cannot easily fix a problem that magic does not solve. The result is a world with 1990s politics and medieval infrastructure.
worlds.mood: Cosy and parochial on the surface, genuinely frightening underneath. The emotional register is boarding-school warmth, petty snobbery and real grief, all in the same corridor.

locations.name: Hogwarts

whereToStart.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire

connections.note: Contemporaries and deliberate opposites: one affirms a hidden magical order, the other burns religious authority down.
Both are 1990s adolescence split between an ordinary life and a secret, lethal duty.
One hidden world is bureaucratic and the other magical, and both hide a whole population next door.
Both run a hidden ministry their national government half-knows about and never mentions.

worlds.setting: Sunnydale, California, late 1990s: stucco houses, a mall, a high school, a nightclub called the Bronze, and a death rate the local paper never asks about. The town sits on a Hellmouth, a weak point between worlds, which is why so much happens here and why the adults explain none of it. The show's real structure is high school as horror: the monsters are literal and the metaphors are adolescent. To know about it is to be drafted, and the drafting is lifelong.
worlds.conflict: One girl in each generation is given the strength to fight vampires and demons, and the fight never ends for her. Buffy wants an ordinary life and is not allowed one; her friends insist on helping and are always in danger because of it. The engine is that the power is real, necessary, isolating and unfair, and each season makes her pay more for it.
worlds.politics: A secret council of Watchers trains and directs the Slayer, treats her as an instrument, and controls what she is told. The town authorities, the police and the school board are innocent, corrupt or wilfully blind. Everything is informal: the real decisions are made by a teenager, her librarian and her friends.
worlds.technology: Deliberately analog and cheap: stakes, crossbows, a card index in a school library, research done by hand, and no mobile phones worth relying on. Magic exists and is expensive to use. The conspicuous absence is any adult institution that could help, and any weapon that does not have to be swung by a person at close range.
worlds.mood: Wry, adolescent, genuinely sad. The jokes land fast, the horror is practical and physical, and grief is treated as the actual cost of the job.
themes: the loneliness of the only one

worlds.setting: Surrey and London in an Edwardian June, a few years after 1900. The narrator is a writer on philosophy living near Woking; his brother is a medical student in London. Mars is an older, cooling world whose inhabitants, all brain and hands, have watched Earth for generations. Their cylinders fall on commons and heaths in the Home Counties, and the story follows the two brothers through the collapse of the most powerful city on Earth.
worlds.conflict: Beings as far above humanity as humanity is above animals arrive with heat-rays, poison smoke and three-legged fighting-machines, and the British army cannot stop them. There is no hero and no plan: the narrator hides, flees and watches, and the invaders are finally killed by bacteria, the smallest things on Earth.
worlds.politics: The empire at the height of its confidence, facing what it did to Tasmania done to itself. Government dissolves within days: the army is broken, London empties, and people become refugees on their own roads. An artilleryman the narrator meets imagines a new society living in the drains; the narrator does not join him.
worlds.technology: Victorian England's best: railways, telegraphs, field artillery and the ironclad Thunder Child. Against it the Martians bring the Heat-Ray, the Black Smoke, tripod fighting-machines, handling-machines and a flying-machine, all worked by creatures who feed by injecting human blood.
worlds.mood: Calm, reportorial and appalled; a story of ordinary roads and villages told as if it happened last week.

Both are English home-counties catastrophes told through ordinary people as order dissolves around them.

worlds.setting: London and its outskirts in AF 632, about 2540, six centuries into a World State that dates its calendar from Henry Ford. People are grown in bottles at the Central London Hatchery, sorted before birth into castes from Alpha to Epsilon, and conditioned to love their place. Everyone is kept busy with work, sport, casual sex and the drug soma. Outside the state are the Savage Reservations, such as the one in New Mexico, where people still give birth, marry and grow old.
worlds.conflict: Bernard Marx, an Alpha who does not fit, brings John the Savage from the Reservation to London. John was raised on an old volume of Shakespeare and cannot accept a world that has traded art, religion, love and suffering for stability. The book's real argument is the long debate between John and Mustapha Mond, the Controller who knows exactly what was given up and why.
worlds.politics: Ten World Controllers rule a peaceful, stable world state. Caste, consumption and pleasure are engineered, and dissent is handled by exile to islands, not by prisons. The motto is 'Community, Identity, Stability'. The past, the family and old religion have been abolished, but the Controllers keep forbidden books in their safes.
worlds.technology: Ectogenesis and Bokanovsky's Process, which makes up to ninety-six identical twins from one egg. Hypnopaedia and Neo-Pavlovian conditioning. Soma. Feelies, films with touch as well as sound. Rocket planes and helicopters for the upper castes. Science itself is kept under control, because real discovery would threaten stability.
worlds.mood: Bright, clean and sterile, a satire that turns into tragedy: the jokes are about happiness, and the ending is a man alone in a lighthouse.
themes: the abolition of the family and the past

connections.note: Humanity kept content inside a system it does not question.
A state that takes reproduction out of private hands, by bottle or by force.
Pleasure manufactured to order, and a figure from outside the system who cannot bear it.

worlds.setting: The Second World War ended in an Axis victory in 1947, and by 1962 the United States no longer exists as a power. Japan governs California and the west coast as the Pacific States; the Rocky Mountain states sit between the empires as a neutral buffer; the South and the eastern seaboard are run from Berlin through a puppet American government. Hitler is alive, hidden and dying, Germany and Japan are rivals, and in San Francisco a novel about an Allied victory is passed around.
worlds.conflict: The engine is the gap between what people believe and what is true. Everyone performs loyalty to an empire that won, and nobody thinks the arrangement is permanent: Berlin despises Japan, Japan thinks Germany vulgar, and occupied Americans sell each other antiques and forged pedigrees. A banned book describing an Allied victory circulates as contraband, and its readers begin asking which version of history they are living in.
worlds.politics: Bormann ran the Reich as acting chancellor until his death in 1962; Hitler is incapacitated, Goebbels is named chancellor and is planning a nuclear strike on Japan under the code name Dandelion, and Heydrich's SS is moving to stop him. In the Pacific States, Japanese administrators govern through cooperative American officials, and the Rocky Mountain states answer to nobody.
worlds.technology: German technology is the visible proof of who won: jet aircraft, rocket launches, colour television and a space programme that already talks about leaving the planet. The Pacific States still run on ordinary mid-century American appliances, which is exactly the humiliation. Nothing here is futuristic except the Reich's rockets, and the I Ching is consulted to make decisions a computer would make elsewhere.
worlds.mood: Polite, anxious, counterfeit - a world of exquisite manners laid over an arrangement that everyone knows is a swindle.

whereToStart.title: The Man in the High Castle
whereToStart.blurb: The Amazon series: a separate continuity with a different war ending and a literal multiverse.

connections.note: The other great Axis-victory novel, but Harris writes a detective story where Dick writes metaphysics.
Both fork the twentieth century in the 1930s and follow an America that never became itself.
Both hide a true world behind a false one; Dick's nested realities are the Matrix's ancestors.

worlds.setting: It is October 1985 and Richard Nixon is still president, the two-term limit having been repealed. Costumed adventurers were real, were a licensed American institution for decades and were outlawed in 1977, so the survivors are retired, employed by the government or outlaws. New York is filthy and tense; the Soviet Union is losing a Cold War it cannot win, and the only thing holding the two sides apart is a man who no longer thinks like a person.
worlds.conflict: The Cold War is a countdown and the only thing slowing it is a superhuman drifting away from humanity. Meanwhile the masked people who used to fight crime are aging, outlawed and mostly useless, and one of them has been murdered. The engine is the question the costumes never answered: what does a person with power over the whole world owe it, and what may be done to save it?
worlds.politics: Nixon governs a United States that wins its wars because it has a god on the payroll: Vietnam was finished in two months once Doctor Manhattan was sent, and is now the fifty-first state. The Keene Act of 1977 made freelance vigilantism illegal, so masks now belong to the government, and real authority sits with whoever can direct Doctor Manhattan; the Soviet Union is the desperate party.
worlds.technology: This is 1985 with one impossible addition. Electric cars, airships and advanced medicine exist because a man who transmutes matter builds them, while ordinary life runs on payphones, newsprint and CRT screens: no personal computers, no mobile phones, no internet. The cutting edge is a single person, and everyone else is living in the twentieth century.
worlds.mood: Sour, weary, apocalyptic - a murder mystery in a world that has already decided how it ends, told by people who keep putting the costume back on anyway.
themes: the costumed hero as a real institution
the price of saving the world

connections.note: Both rewrite the twentieth-century United States from a 1930s-40s fork.
Both are murder investigations that unpick a state conspiracy: Nixon's New York, Nazi Berlin.
Both make 1980s Cold War dread literal: Moore's doomsday clock, Cameron's Judgment Day.

worlds.setting: London in November 1941, nine months after Britain surrendered. The SS runs Scotland Yard, the King is a prisoner in the Tower, and Churchill has been shot. A puppet government sits under an Emergency Powers Act, the Soviet Navy has Scottish bases under the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and an American journalist flew in on the first Lufthansa service from New York. Detective Superintendent Douglas Archer still investigates murders.
worlds.conflict: Archer, a widower with a young son, takes a murder case that turns out to involve a British atomic scientist and the German bomb programme. He is caught between the SS chief Kellermann and the Berlin envoy Huth, the Army and the Abwehr, the Resistance and the Americans, each using him and the King for their own ends.
worlds.politics: An occupation run by a German military commander and an SS police apparatus, with a collaborating British Parliament and Prime Minister. The SS, the Army and the Abwehr fight each other. The United States is neutral, Roosevelt still president, and a government in exile under Rear-Admiral Conolly Abel Smith struggles for recognition in Washington.
worlds.technology: Real 1941 technology: radio, telephones, forensic microscopes, prosthetic limbs made in prisoner camps. The one step ahead is atomic research at Bringle Sands in Devon, where the Germans are further along than anyone in our 1941.
worlds.mood: A grey, rationed police procedural in which everyone is compromised and survival is a series of small collaborations.
themes: the atomic bomb as the prize of the war
the monarchy as a symbol worth more dead

Another occupied English-speaking country after a German victory.
A different way for Britain's and America's 1940 to turn.

worlds.setting: Weequahic, the Jewish neighbourhood of Newark, New Jersey, from June 1940 to late 1942, seen by a boy named Philip Roth between seven and nine. Charles Lindbergh, the aviator, has beaten Roosevelt for the presidency on a promise to keep America out of the war, and has made peace with Hitler. Nothing on the street changes at first; then the government starts sorting Jewish families out of the cities.
worlds.conflict: The Roths watch their country turn: Herman, the father, defends American democracy aloud; Sandy, the older brother, joins the government's Just Folks programme and admires Lindbergh; cousin Alvin goes to war in Canada and comes back without a leg. Homestead 42 relocations, Walter Winchell's campaign, the pogroms and the October crisis bring the history into the family.
worlds.politics: Democracy is formally intact while it is emptied out: an elected president with Nazi sympathies, treaties with Germany and Japan, an Office of American Absorption that breaks up Jewish communities, a Jewish rabbi who lends it respectability, and an FBI that watches Jewish families. When Lindbergh vanishes, his vice president tries martial law and mass arrests, and the First Lady brings him down.
worlds.technology: The real 1940s: radio broadcasts, newsreels, the Spirit of St. Louis, trains, telephones and stamp collections. Nothing is invented but the politics.
worlds.mood: Intimate dread recalled by an adult: a child's fear, ordinary family life under pressure, and a history that could have gone either way.

locations.name: Washington, D.C.

An American democracy hollowed out from inside, seen by a family caught in it.

worlds.setting: It is April 1964 and Berlin is being dressed for Hitler's seventy-fifth birthday. The Greater German Reich runs Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals; Britain made peace in 1944, the United States is a rival superpower negotiating a detente, and Russia survives east of the mountains as a guerrilla war that never ends. The extermination of Europe's Jews is not remembered because it is not known: the camps were demolished, the records burned, and every witness is being killed before the American president arrives.
worlds.conflict: A Berlin detective investigating a drowning finds a list of names, then finds the men on it dying one by one. The Reich is staging a state visit that must look like a triumph, and the only surviving proof of the Holocaust is a set of conference minutes that would humiliate the regime. A totalitarian state's weakest point is its paperwork, and one official is honest enough to read it.
worlds.politics: Hitler is Führer, reclusive and increasingly invisible, and the real politics of 1964 is the succession: Heydrich, Reichsführer-SS since Himmler's death in 1962, is the probable heir, and every faction in the party, the army and the ministries is positioning. Germany is a one-party police state ruling an occupied continent, and Washington deals with it as a fact.
worlds.technology: The Reich's technology is the boast of a winning power: jet airliners, autobahns, colour television, a rocket programme at Peenemünde and nuclear submarines at Trondheim. Consumer comfort is genuine and is meant to be evidence that the system works. The novelty of the age is the Cold War apparatus itself - files, bugs, surveillance - and the fact that a telephone call in Berlin is never private.
worlds.mood: Orderly, oppressive, suspended - a prosperous police state where the worst crime in history has been reduced to a filing problem and one man keeps pulling the file.

worlds.setting: London in 1984, or about then, the chief city of Airstrip One, a province of Oceania, which covers the Americas, the British Isles, Australasia and southern Africa. The city is shabby and bomb-damaged, with rotting nineteenth-century houses under four huge white Ministries. Telescreens watch every Party member at home and at work. Oceania is always at war with one of the other two superstates, Eurasia and Eastasia, and always allied with the other.
worlds.conflict: Winston Smith rewrites old newspapers for the Ministry of Truth and privately hates the Party. He keeps a diary, has an affair with Julia, and looks for the Brotherhood, the resistance run by the Party's official enemy, Goldstein. O'Brien, the man he trusts, is Thought Police. The Party's aim is not just to punish him but to make him believe whatever it says.
worlds.politics: Ingsoc (English Socialism) is a one-party oligarchy: a small Inner Party, a larger Outer Party of functionaries, and the proles, 85 per cent of the population, left alone in poverty. Big Brother is its face and may not exist. The four Ministries are Truth (propaganda), Peace (war), Love (police and torture) and Plenty (rationing). The permanent war uses up surplus production and justifies the emergency.
worlds.technology: Deliberately stalled, apart from war and surveillance. Two-way telescreens, hidden microphones, speakwrites, pneumatic tubes and memory holes that feed the Records Department's furnaces, Floating Fortresses, rocket bombs falling on London, and the atomic bomb that all three powers stockpile but have not used since the war. Newspeak, a language being cut down so that dissent cannot be put into words.
worlds.mood: Grey, cold and airless: gin, boiled cabbage and fear, with brief warmth in a rented room above an antique shop, then the long, clinical cruelty of the Ministry of Love.
themes: control of the past as control of the present

worlds.setting: Two Americas. One is the late 1950s and early 1960s as Jake Epping lives them: root beer at ten cents, Maine mill towns, Florida bookies, a small Texas town called Jodie where he teaches English, and Dallas, where Lee Harvey Oswald moves between shabby apartments. The other is the 2011 he comes back to after saving Kennedy: Lisbon Falls in ruins, radiation sickness, gangs, earthquakes, a sky that seems to be tearing, and a United States that has lost Maine to Canada.
worlds.conflict: A dying diner owner has found a doorway to 1958 and a reason to use it: stop Oswald, and Vietnam and the assassinations of the 1960s might never happen. Jake takes on the mission, falls in love in Jodie, and finds that the past pushes back against every change in proportion to its size. When he succeeds, Sadie dies, and the future he made is worse.
worlds.politics: The novel's alternate history is a lesson in unintended consequences: a surviving Kennedy loses the civil-rights fight, Vietnam goes worse, George Wallace wins in 1968 and uses the atomic bomb, and nuclear weapons become ordinary. The politics of 1958-63 are real and carefully researched, from Oswald's marriage to the Walker shooting.
worlds.technology: Period detail is the point: party lines, Sunliner convertibles, typewriters, reel-to-reel recorders, a parabolic microphone for spying on Oswald. The only impossible device is a pantry step that leads to 1958. In the ruined 2011, electricity and fuel are scarce and radiation is everywhere.
worlds.mood: Nostalgic, suspenseful and elegiac: a love story and a thriller in a past that smells better than it was, and a warning about wanting to fix it.

worlds.setting: Melbourne and the seaside town of Falmouth in the southern summer, autumn and winter after a short nuclear war. The Northern Hemisphere is silent; petrol is gone, so people cycle, ride horses and pull cars with bullocks. The last American nuclear submarine, Scorpion, lies at Williamstown under Australian command. Everyone knows the fallout is drifting south and has a date, about September, and they go on sailing, fishing and planting gardens.
worlds.conflict: There is no enemy left to fight. The conflict is between denial and acceptance: Commander Towers buying presents for a family he knows is dead, Mary Holmes refusing to hear how to give her baby the pill, Moira drinking and then learning shorthand. Scorpion's voyage north tests the one hope, that the radiation might thin out, and disproves it.
worlds.politics: An Australia still governed from Canberra, orderly and polite to the end. The government keeps services running as long as it can and then issues free suicide pills. The war's causes, cheap bombs in small countries and decisions made in minutes by commanders whose governments were dead, are explained once over drinks.
worlds.technology: Late-1950s: a nuclear submarine that needs no oil, cars without petrol, a restored Ferrari racing car, radio, and the cobalt and hydrogen bombs that caused it all. Radio reports track the line of sickness as it moves south, city by city.
worlds.mood: Quiet, restrained and mournful; people behave well and die politely, which is what makes it hard to read.
themes: how people meet an end they cannot change
the innocent paying for a war elsewhere

worlds.setting: One day in the early 1960s, in three rooms. Burpelson Air Force Base, where General Ripper has sealed the gates and confiscated the radios; the cockpit of Major Kong's B-52, flying low over the Soviet Union with its radio shot out; and the Pentagon War Room, where President Muffley, General Turgidson, the Soviet ambassador and the former Nazi scientist Dr. Strangelove sit at a round table under the Big Board and try to stop a war nobody ordered.
worlds.conflict: The President has to recall 34 bombers that will only obey a code Ripper alone knows, while helping the Soviets shoot down his own planes. Every safeguard designed to stop a sneak attack now protects the attack. When the Soviet ambassador reveals a Doomsday Machine that fires automatically, stopping the last bomber becomes the survival of the species.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union in the Cold War balance of terror. American civilian authority exists but is powerless against procedures written to work without it; the military men argue for seizing the moment. The Soviet premier is drunk, the Soviet state kept its deterrent secret, and the only plan that survives is the mineshafts.
worlds.technology: Real early-1960s hardware: B-52 bombers on airborne alert, thermonuclear bombs, SAC codes and a CRM 114 discriminator that blocks any message without the right prefix, a telephone hot line. The one invention is the Soviet Doomsday Machine: buried cobalt-thorium G bombs wired to fire on attack or tampering.
worlds.mood: Black comedy played straight: documentary camera work on the base, expressionist gloom in the War Room, and an ending set to 'We'll Meet Again'.
themes: machines and procedures that remove human choice

worlds.setting: A secret history of the Cold War and after, told across fifty years of covert operations. It moves from the Soviet jungle of 1964 to a Caribbean mercenary platform in 1974, Afghanistan and Central Africa in 1984, the mercenary states of Outer Heaven and Zanzibar Land in the 1990s, an Alaskan nuclear site in 2005, New York Harbor in 2007 and 2009, and the private-military battlefields of 2014.
worlds.conflict: A legendary soldier, Big Boss, and his cloned sons fight over one question: whether soldiers can be free of the governments that use them. Behind them is the Patriots, a secret group founded by his old comrades that turns into artificial intelligences controlling what the world knows, and walking nuclear tanks called Metal Gear.
worlds.politics: Public history runs as recorded, but a hidden layer decides it: the Philosophers, then the Patriots (Cipher), who choose presidents and stage crises. Against them stand stateless armies, from Militaires Sans Frontières and Diamond Dogs to Outer Heaven and Zanzibar Land, which offer soldiers a nation of their own. By 2014 war is a regulated market run by private military companies.
worlds.technology: Metal Gear, walking tanks that can launch nuclear weapons from anywhere, each new model leaked or stolen. Alongside it: AI weapons and an AI that edits digital information, cloning and gene therapy for soldiers, nanomachines that regulate soldiers' emotions and weapons (the SOP system), and parasites engineered as weapons.
worlds.mood: Operatic and self-aware: stealth thriller, Cold War melodrama and anti-nuclear sermon, mixing very long cutscenes with jokes and grief.
themes: soldiers used and discarded by states
inheritance: genes, memes and what parents pass on

worlds.setting: One day in 1967, told from the rooms where nuclear war is managed. SAC's war room in Omaha, the Pentagon, the President's bunker under the White House, and the cockpit of Colonel Grady's Vindicator bomber over the Arctic. A routine alert over an unidentified aircraft ends, but one bomber group has received a real attack code, and by the time anyone notices it is past the point where it can be recalled.
worlds.conflict: The President must stop his own bombers or persuade Khrushchev that the attack is an accident. Every safeguard now works against him: Grady is trained to ignore voices that tell him to turn back, and the fighters cannot catch him. When one bomber is certain to reach Moscow, the President offers the only proof of good faith he has, New York.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union at the height of mutual deterrence, with leaders who can speak directly but do not trust what they hear. The civilian strategist Groteschele argues for using the accident to win; the generals and the President resist. The ending is a bargain between two men over the heads of both cities.
worlds.technology: The real SAC system of the early 1960s, slightly projected: supersonic 'Vindicator' bombers (shown with B-58 Hustler footage in the film), a fail-safe box that transmits attack codes, radar warning lines, jamming, air-to-air missiles, and 20-megaton bombs. The failure is a single electronic component.
worlds.mood: Tense, claustrophobic and procedural; the film plays in close-up with no music, and ends on New Yorkers frozen in the frame.
themes: automation that removes the chance to stop
the strategist who wants to win a nuclear war
