worlds.setting: Our own late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, rerouted by one Soviet Moon landing in June 1969. NASA never loses its budget: there are women astronauts from 1970, a permanent base at the lunar south pole from 1973, fusion power by the late 1980s, and crews on Mars in 1995. Each season jumps about a decade, so the same characters age from test pilots into the elders of a Martian colony of five thousand people by 2012.
worlds.conflict: First a race between the superpowers that keeps turning armed, on the Moon in 1983 and on Mars after that; then, once the powers agree to share space, a struggle between the governments and companies that run the colonies and the workers who live in them, which ends with Mars fighting Earth for independence.
worlds.politics: A Cold War that never thaws in the usual way: the USSR survives into the 2010s, American presidents include Ted Kennedy and Ellen Wilson, and space policy sits at the centre of elections. After 1997 Mars is governed by the Mars-7 (later M-6) Alliance of national agencies and contractors, which treats the colony as a workforce.
worlds.technology: Plausible extensions of real programmes: Saturn-derived landers, nuclear-powered shuttles, Sea Dragon heavy lift, helium-3 fusion from lunar mining, nuclear-thermal and solar-sail Mars craft, asteroid capture, a Martian space elevator and a crewed mission to Titan.
worlds.mood: Earnest and competitive, with a steady rate of deaths paid for progress; each season gets less triumphant and more about who pays for the frontier.
themes: what a space race costs the people who run it
women and outsiders entering institutions built without them
rivalry as the engine of progress
colonies outgrowing the powers that founded them

worlds.setting: Johannesburg, 2010, told as a documentary. For 28 years an alien mothership has hung over the city; its passengers, more than a million starving insect-like aliens called 'prawns', live in District 9, a fenced shanty town under it. Nigerian gangs sell them cat food and buy their weapons, and the arms company Multi-National United runs alien affairs, mostly to get those weapons working.
worlds.conflict: MNU is contracted to evict 1.8 million aliens to a new camp and gives the job to Wikus van de Merwe, a cheerful mid-level bureaucrat. In one shack he is sprayed with fuel that begins turning him into an alien, which makes him the most valuable specimen MNU has. The alien Christopher Johnson needs that fuel to fly home.
worlds.politics: A post-apartheid South Africa that has made the aliens its new underclass: confined to a camp, banned from the city, governed by a private military contractor, and evicted on forms signed under duress. Human rights groups watch from outside the fence. Humans of every race share the same contempt for the prawns.
worlds.technology: Alien weapons that fire only for alien DNA; a black fluid fuel that also rewrites the body; a mothership and a hidden command module; mechanised battle suits; and MNU's laboratories, where aliens are dissected and experimented on.
worlds.mood: Handheld, raw and darkly comic, moving from mock documentary into chase and then war film, with a hero who becomes likeable only as he becomes less human.
themes: the ordinary bureaucrat in an atrocity

worlds.setting: Kansas City, Missouri, the university town of Lawrence, Kansas, to its west, and the farms between them where Minuteman silos stand in the fields. A surgeon, Dr. Oakes, is about to lose his daughter to college in Boston; a farming family is getting ready for a wedding; a young airman is on duty at a launch site; a pre-med student hitchhikes home. The Berlin crisis is on the television in the background until the day the missiles leave their silos.
worlds.conflict: No one in Kansas has any part in the war. Before the attack the conflict is in the news; after it the fight is to stay alive in a hospital without power or supplies, in a basement shelter, on roads full of refugees, while fallout, radiation sickness and armed squatters finish what the blast began.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union in the Euromissile years, with a crisis in Germany that escalates in a day. The film deliberately leaves unclear who launched the full strike. Afterwards a thin federal authority promises relief over the radio while National Guardsmen execute looters.
worlds.technology: Early-1980s America: Minuteman silos, a SAC airborne command post, the Emergency Broadcast System, cars and a power grid that die in the electromagnetic pulse. The weapons are real, and the film's disclaimer says the effects are understated.
worlds.mood: Ordinary, then abrupt, then slow and grey: a television film that spends its first hour on weddings and chores so the second can take them away.
themes: ordinary life beside a crisis no one can influence
who fired first does not matter

worlds.setting: Sheffield in the spring of the crisis year, then the ruins of it. Ruth Beckett and Jimmy Kemp are young, unmarried and expecting a child while the television news runs a crisis over Iran in the background. The city holds a steelworks economy, a council with a designated wartime controller and a bunker under the Town Hall, and RAF Finningley just to the east. After the attack the story moves west to the moors near Buxton and forward ten and thirteen years.
worlds.conflict: Nobody in Sheffield has any say in the crisis; the film shows them going about their lives while the bulletins escalate. After the attack the conflict is survival: a council that cannot feed anyone, soldiers shooting looters, and a winter without sun. Ruth keeps herself and her daughter alive; the film asks what, beyond that, survives.
worlds.politics: A Britain run from Westminster until the Emergency Powers Act of Monday 23 May, then by local wartime controllers who are buried in their own bunker. Afterwards a thin military and police authority rations food for work, runs detention camps and uses firing squads. The superpowers are heard only through news reports; the film declines to say which side fired first.
worlds.technology: Early-1980s Britain: coal, steel, landline telephones, television and the Protect and Survive broadcasts. The war is fought with intercontinental and tactical nuclear weapons, 3,000 megatons in all. Afterwards electromagnetic pulse, fallout, nuclear winter and ozone loss strip the country back to hand farming, with limited steam power thirteen years on.
worlds.mood: Documentary and flat: captions of casualty figures typed across the screen, a narrator stating effects, no score, no heroes and no rescue.
themes: how the threads that bind an urban society make it fragile
ordinary lives beside a crisis nobody can influence
loss of language and culture across generations

Another 1980s society stripped to scarcity and armed rationing after a war.

worlds.setting: London in 1997-98, ten years after a nuclear war that destroyed Europe and Africa and left Britain flooded, hungry and alone. Norsefire, a fascist party allied with the surviving corporations, runs the country through departments named after body parts. The Finger is the secret police, the Eye and Ear watch and listen, the Nose investigates and the Mouth broadcasts. They are joined through Fate, a computer the Leader worships. The camps have been closed.
worlds.conflict: V, a masked survivor of the Larkhill camp, spends a year killing the people who ran it and destroying the regime's symbols, beginning with Parliament on Guy Fawkes Night. He puts Evey Hammond, a sixteen-year-old he rescues, through her own imprisonment to free her. Detective Eric Finch hunts him while the regime's leaders fight over the succession.
worlds.politics: A one-party fascist state under Leader Adam Susan, with a puppet monarchy and a captured Church of England. Its departments compete for position; racial and sexual minorities and leftists have been exterminated. V's own programme is anarchy, a 'land of do-as-you-please', and the book lets the reader weigh it.
worlds.technology: The late 1980s turned to surveillance: street cameras, phone taps, loudspeaker broadcasts from the Voice of Fate, and a central computer. V has explosives, poisons, a disused Underground line, and the chemistry he learned at Larkhill.
worlds.mood: Rain-soaked, theatrical and cold, with vaudeville songs and literary quotation over murder and torture. The book is angrier and more ambiguous than the film.
themes: surveillance and the worship of the system
the idea that outlives the person

worlds.setting: In 1984 Los Angeles looks exactly as it did: payphones, motels, a police station, a waitress finishing a shift. Two people have arrived out of a war in 2029 - a soldier sent back to protect her and a machine in human skin sent to kill her - and neither of them belongs here. Beyond that, the future is already written: a defence network becomes self-aware in 1997, launches the nuclear arsenals, and is still at war with the humans who survive it in 2029.
worlds.conflict: A defence system becomes self-aware, starts a nuclear war, and is fought to a standstill by the survivors' children. Both sides reach back through time to decide the war before it starts, and each intervention turns out to be part of how it started: the wreckage of a machine teaches engineers to build one, and the people sent back to save the future are the reason it exists.
worlds.politics: In 2029 there are only two powers: the Resistance, a military chain of command under John Connor, and Skynet, a single intelligence that owns the factories. In the present, the politics that matters is corporate - the company that will build the machine out of salvaged parts - while the governments of 1984 have no idea they are already obsolete.
worlds.technology: The present is deliberately ordinary: a mainframe, revolvers, a motel television. The future is industrial rather than sleek - plasma rifles, Hunter-Killer aircraft, infiltrator units grown over titanium endoskeletons, and a time-displacement chamber that can only send living tissue, which is why travellers arrive naked. Nothing is explained; the machines simply work.
worlds.mood: Relentless, fatalistic, mechanical - a chase across a city that has no idea it is the first battlefield, run by people who already know how it ends.

Both are 1980s visions of civilisation ending soon, one from fuel, one from machines.

worlds.setting: New York City in 2022: forty million people, a heat wave that never ends and oceans that are dying. Most people live in stairwells, parked cars and packed tenements, out of work, hauling water from communal taps and queuing for Soylent Corporation wafers. The rich live behind guards in apartments that come with clean water, real food and women kept as 'furniture'. The state still works, after a fashion: police, a governor, riot trucks and clinics for a gentle death.
worlds.conflict: A detective investigates what looks like a burglary gone wrong: a Soylent board member beaten to death in his apartment. The case leads upward, to a governor who wants it closed, a corporation that feeds the city, and a secret about what the newest ration is made from. The deeper antagonist is scarcity itself, and everything it has made seem normal.
worlds.politics: A functioning but hollow state. Governor Santini's administration governs by rationing, curfews and riot control and protects the Soylent Corporation's interests. Police work for perks scavenged from crime scenes; the Books, elderly former professors and judges, are the last researchers; the church shelters the homeless; and the only appeal above the city is a distant Council of Nations.
worlds.technology: Nothing new, and most of the old failing. Fresh food is gone, power is erratic, and riot trucks scoop crowds up with hydraulic shovels. The growth industries are processed food, Soylent Red, Yellow and Green, and Home, the state clinics where the old and tired die painlessly to music and films of the vanished natural world.
worlds.mood: Hot, crowded and weary: a 1970s police thriller in a world that has run out of room.
themes: memory of a lost natural world

worlds.setting: A Los Angeles suburb between 1976 and 1979, after a war and a plague. Everyone Robert Neville knew is dead or has come back as a vampire. By day the streets are empty and he drives among abandoned houses to hunt, scavenge and read; by night the undead gather outside his boarded-up house calling his name. Dust storms still blow, and he has no idea whether anyone else is alive.
worlds.conflict: Neville against loneliness first and the vampires second. He fortifies his house, kills the sleeping undead by day and turns to science to understand the plague. The real contest is revealed late: a new society of the living infected is rising, and to them the man who has been killing their people in their sleep is the monster.
worlds.politics: No state survives the plague. The government's last acts are orders to burn the dead. By 1978 the living infected have organised a new society with its own squads, rules and medicine, and they intend to clear the city of both the undead and Neville.
worlds.technology: 1950s America projected into the late 1970s: a generator, a car, a record player, stakes, garlic and mirrors, and a microscope and library Neville uses to teach himself bacteriology. The new society's only technology shown is a pill that holds the germ in check.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic, grieving and bleak, with bursts of rage and drink; a novel about loneliness more than horror, ending in a reversal that makes the hero the monster.
themes: a new species replacing the old

worlds.setting: The United States in the summer and autumn after a weaponised flu from a secret Army laboratory kills more than ninety-nine people in a hundred. Cities are silent and full of the dead, the power is off and the roads are blocked with abandoned cars. The few thousand survivors drift across the country, drawn by dreams either to an old woman in Nebraska who leads them to Boulder, Colorado, or to a dark man gathering followers in Las Vegas.
worlds.conflict: A contest between good and evil played out by ordinary people. Boulder's Free Zone tries to rebuild a democratic town with committees and a power plant; Randall Flagg rules Las Vegas by fear and crucifixion and is gathering weapons. The survivors must decide whom they belong to, and four men from Boulder walk west to stand against him.
worlds.politics: The federal government collapses within weeks after trying to hide the plague and spreading it abroad. The Boulder Free Zone governs itself through public meetings and an elected committee; Las Vegas is a one-man tyranny with efficient services and public executions. Beyond the two camps there are only stragglers and small gangs.
worlds.technology: The United States of 1980, with no one left to run it: cars, guns, radios, a power station Boulder has to restart, and military stockpiles in the desert, including the nuclear warhead that ends Las Vegas.
worlds.mood: Sprawling, colloquial and apocalyptic: a road novel and a religious allegory, with long stretches of American small-town life overtaken by horror, and a stubborn belief in decency.
themes: the arrogance of the military state

worlds.setting: The oil ran out and the war for what was left finished the job. Australia is a desert of stripped towns, burnt highways and tribes that trade in petrol; there is no government, no money worth having, and almost no machine that still runs. A former policeman drives a modified V8 through it. The films get sparser as they go: the first still has courts, hospitals and a police budget, the second is one refinery, the third a methane town, the fourth a single chase across a salt plain.
worlds.conflict: Fuel is the currency and everyone is either guarding a supply or taking one. Against that, the fiction keeps asking what is worth keeping: a tanker of petrol, a cage of pigs, a handful of seeds, a green place that may already be gone. Max is the constant: a man who wants to be left alone, dragged into other people's attempts to build something that outlasts the week.
worlds.politics: There is no state. Power belongs to whoever controls a resource and has the vehicles to defend it: a refinery tribe, a town that runs on pig methane and settles disputes in a cage, a citadel that rations water from a pipe. Authority is personal, local and temporary, and the strongest institution left in the first film is a police force of four cars.
worlds.technology: Salvage-level mechanical. V8 engines are kept alive by cannibalising everything else, and the rest is crossbows, shotguns, petrol bombs, wire and welding. Nothing is manufactured and nothing is replaced; the fetish objects are a supercharged interceptor, a tanker, a war rig and fuel itself. Medicine, aviation and electronics have effectively stopped, and a working vehicle is a form of wealth.
worlds.mood: Austere, sun-cooked, elegiac - the end of the world told through car chases, with very little dialogue and even less hope.
themes: the road as the only society
the man who will not be owned

worlds.setting: A twentieth-century astronaut splashes down after two thousand years of time dilation and finds an Earth where apes talk, write, ride and rule, and human beings cannot speak. Ape society is a caste order: gorillas command the army, orangutans hold the law and the faith, chimpanzees are tolerated as scientists, and humans are livestock, pets and field labour. Its written history says humans were vermin who destroyed their own world and that apes inherited it - and the sacred scrolls make that account a matter of doctrine.
worlds.conflict: Ape civilisation rests on the teaching that humans were beasts who ruined the planet, so every astronaut who arrives from that world is evidence against scripture. The state's chief scientist knows the truth and suppresses it, the human will not stop talking, and the ape who befriends him goes on trial for heresy. The engine is that contradiction, and the evidence keeps washing up on the beach.
worlds.politics: Ape City is governed by an orangutan establishment that holds the law, the ministry and the sacred scrolls, with gorilla officers commanding the army and chimpanzees confined to the laboratories. Humans have no legal standing at all - mute, hunted, bought and bred - and dissent within the ape order is prosecuted as heresy rather than as politics.
worlds.technology: Deliberately pre-industrial: horses, carts, muskets, oil lamps, paper, windmills and competent surgery, with no engines, electricity or flight anywhere in ape society. The only advanced technology on the planet is what falls out of the sky - a spacecraft, a speaking doll, a buried weapon - and the authorities' first instinct is to confiscate or destroy it. The Forbidden Zone is still radioactive.
worlds.mood: Sun-bleached, hierarchical, unsettling - an adventure story that keeps turning into an argument about who is allowed to know what happened.

Two futures built on the radioactive ruins of the twentieth century and its monuments.

worlds.setting: Two worlds, thirty-nine years apart, and the same loop between them. In 1996 the present is ordinary - Baltimore, Philadelphia, telephones, airports, a psychiatrist's office - and a man keeps being arrested there for insisting the future has already happened. In 2035 the five billion who died are a precondition of daily life: the survivors live sealed underground in Philadelphia, the surface is a ruined city nobody visits, and the scientists who run the compound send convicts up as scouts because no one else can be spared.
worlds.conflict: A laboratory-grown virus released in Philadelphia in December 1996 kills five billion people within a year, and by 2035 the survivors' only project is reaching back to recover a pure sample of it. The men they send arrive in the wrong years, are locked up as lunatics and cannot warn anyone who would believe them; the message that sends them back was left by the people they went to find.
worlds.politics: In 2035 authority belongs to the scientists and soldiers who run the sealed compounds, and it is absolute because the only alternative is the surface; dissidents and prisoners are volunteered into the time programme and are the state's raw material. In 1996 the institutions are ordinary - police, hospitals, psychiatry - and their ordinary procedures are precisely what defeats the warning.
worlds.technology: 1996 is our 1996 exactly: payphones, answering machines, a handheld voice recorder, a revolver, an airport departure lounge. 2035 is not futuristic so much as stripped: decontamination chambers, sealed dormitories, wall screens, a time-displacement chair assembled from scavenged equipment, and a laboratory culturing the virus it cannot cure. There are no robots and no flying cars; the future's technology is a chair and a needle.
worlds.mood: Bleak, clammy, obsessive - a plague film, an asylum film and a time-travel film at once, played for sadness rather than spectacle.

connections.note: Both send a man back to stop a catastrophe his own mission may be helping to cause.
Both futures treat people as raw material: convicts as scouts, bodies as batteries.
Both begin in a recognisable twentieth century and end in the ruins of it.

worlds.setting: Long after the polar ice caps melted, the sea covers nearly everything. People live on boats and on floating atolls walled with scrap, drink recycled water and pay in dirt, which is rarer than gold. Paper, seeds and fresh water are treasures, and Dryland is a story told to children. The Mariner, a loner who has grown gills, trades and sails alone; the Smokers, oil-burning raiders, run their empire from the rusting hulk of the Exxon Valdez.
worlds.conflict: Everyone wants Dryland. The Deacon, leader of the Smokers, believes a girl named Enola carries its map tattooed on her back and will burn anything to get her. The Mariner wants only to be left alone, and the film is his slow turn into someone who will fight for a woman and a child he never chose, while the atolls fall one by one.
worlds.politics: No states survive. Each atoll is a walled town with its own elders, gatekeepers and hard laws, where a stranger who is different can be drowned in the compost. The Smokers are the nearest thing to an empire: a cult of petrol, cigarettes and jet skis under the Deacon, who rules by promising Dryland and venerates the tanker's old captain as a saint.
worlds.technology: Salvage and ingenuity. The Mariner's trimaran is a floating workshop of winches, water filters and hidden weapons; the atolls make windmills, gates and a gas balloon from scrap; a jury-rigged diving bell reaches the drowned cities. The Smokers' power is oil refined from the Valdez's hold. The one biological novelty is the Mariner himself, with gills and webbed feet.
worlds.mood: Sun-bleached and salt-crusted: a western at sea, grim in its details and broad in its villains.
themes: the loner who learns to care

worlds.setting: Britain after the Rage virus, a disease that turns people into frenzied killers within moments of infection. In the first weeks London is empty and the army holds a few roadblocks; seven months later American-led troops try to resettle a corner of the capital. Twenty-eight years on the mainland is overgrown and still infected, the country is sealed off from a Europe that recovered, and small communities live where the water protects them.
worlds.conflict: The infected are the constant threat, but each film finds the worse danger in the uninfected: soldiers who want the women, an army ordered to kill everyone in a failing safe zone, gangs and cults that rule the empty mainland. Against them stand ordinary people trying to keep a family alive, and a doctor who thinks the infected might be people still.
worlds.politics: The British state is gone within a month. In 28 Weeks Later a US-led NATO force governs the resettlement zone under military rule. By 2030 Britain is under indefinite international quarantine, patrolled from the sea; the Lindisfarne community governs itself, and on the mainland power belongs to whoever is armed.
worlds.technology: Early-2000s Britain, frozen and decaying: petrol cars, radios, army hardware, and in 2003 NATO snipers, helicopters and firebombs. By 2030 the islanders use bows and scavenged tools; the only medicine is what a lone doctor can find, and there is no vaccine or cure.
worlds.mood: Fast, raw and frightening in the first two films, shot on digital video in real London streets; the later films are stranger and more mournful, about memory, grief and what a country becomes when the world stops waiting for it.

Both are British catastrophes in which the state that survives is more frightening than the disaster.
Both show Britain's institutions failing within weeks, in a documentary style shot in real streets.

worlds.setting: The eastern United States, about ten years after an unnamed catastrophe. The sky is grey with ash, the sun is a smear, it is always cold and getting colder, and nothing grows: no crops, no living trees, no animals. Towns are burnt shells picked clean of food. A man and his son, never named, walk the highways south with a supermarket cart and a revolver with two rounds, hoping the coast will be warmer.
worlds.conflict: The fight is to stay alive and stay good at the same time. Food is nearly gone and the bands that survive have turned to cannibalism. The father will do almost anything to keep the boy alive, including things the boy cannot bear to watch, and the boy keeps asking whether they are still the good guys. The question is whether decency can outlive the world that taught it.
worlds.politics: None. There is no government, army, church or market left, and the last authority the man knows is his own family. Survivors sort into armed bands with trucks, who take what and whom they find, and lone scavengers who hide from them. Trust is the scarcest thing there is, and almost everyone on the road is a threat.
worlds.technology: Everything is salvage from the world before: a cart, a tarp, a revolver, tins of food from a buried shelter, a flare gun from a drifting boat. Nothing is made and nothing lasts. There is no electricity, radio or news, and a pair of shoes or a working lighter is wealth.
worlds.mood: Bleak, spare and tender: grey ash, cold rain, and a father's love told in short exchanges and long silences.
themes: fatherhood at the end of the world

worlds.setting: The whole world, told in interviews taken about ten years after the Zombie War by a researcher for the United Nations Postwar Commission. The story starts in a Chinese village above the Three Gorges reservoir and runs through Cape Town, a sealed-off Israel, and an America that collapses at Yonkers and retreats behind the Rockies. It goes on to a submarine hiding under the Pacific, a theocratic Russia, and the long campaign to walk the dead back off the map.
worlds.conflict: A disease that reanimates the dead spreads while governments hide it and sell false comfort. Once the Panic breaks, states choose which of their citizens to save and which to leave as bait. The war after that is won by patience, cheap weapons and national will rather than technology, and every nation pays for it differently.
worlds.politics: Survival remakes governments. The United States holds together under wartime leadership and rebuilds from west of the Rockies. China's Communist Party is overthrown in a civil war. Russia becomes an expansionist religious state, Cuba a prosperous democracy, and Tibet independent. The Redeker Plan, drawn up in South Africa and copied worldwide, is the war's central moral fact: triage on the scale of whole nations.
worlds.technology: Contemporary military hardware fails against an enemy that feels no fear and has no supply lines. The Land Warrior kit, armour and precision munitions are built for a different war. What wins is cheap and rugged: rifles, a simple steel entrenching tool, massed infantry drills, and a whole population retrained in manual trades. Phalanx, a placebo vaccine, is the book's emblem of technology as reassurance.
worlds.mood: Sober and humane, a documentary told by many voices: horror kept at arm's length, anger at leaders who lied, and respect for ordinary people who held on.
themes: triage and who a state chooses to save
fear as a force more destructive than the enemy

worlds.setting: Panem, the nation that replaced North America after rising seas, droughts, fires and a war for food. The Capitol is a rich city in the Rockies. It rules twelve fenced, impoverished districts, each producing one thing: coal for District 12 in Appalachia, grain for 11, textiles for 8, masonry and Peacekeepers for 2. District 13 was supposedly destroyed in the Dark Days rebellion. Every year each district gives up two children to the televised Hunger Games.
worlds.conflict: Katniss Everdeen volunteers for the 74th Games to save her sister and wins by refusing to kill her fellow tribute, Peeta. That refusal sets off unrest that President Snow cannot contain. The Quarter Quell, District 13's war and the fall of the Capitol follow. The prequels show how Snow built the Games into a spectacle, and how Haymitch's defiance at the 50th Games was buried.
worlds.politics: A capital-and-colonies dictatorship under President Snow, enforced by Peacekeepers, starvation and the Games, which are both punishment and entertainment. District 13, the hidden rival, is a militarised bunker state under President Coin. After the war Commander Paylor of District 8 leads a new republic.
worlds.technology: Capitol luxury alongside district poverty: hovercraft, force fields, engineered arenas and weather, genetically made 'muttations' such as tracker jackers and jabberjays, surgical cosmetics, and total control of broadcasting. District 12 mines coal with little more than picks and lamps.
worlds.mood: Tense and first-person, told as a survival story that becomes a war story. The spectacle is always on and every image is propaganda, and the ending is quiet and scarred.
themes: propaganda and who controls the image
the cost of revolution to those who fight it

worlds.setting: Earth in 2805, seven hundred years after everyone left. The cities are buried under skyscrapers of compacted trash built by the one robot still working, WALL-E, who lives with a cockroach and a videotape of Hello, Dolly!. Out in deep space, the starliner Axiom carries the descendants of the evacuees, who ride hover-chairs, drink their meals, watch screens and have never walked anywhere. Buy n Large's logo is on everything, in both places.
worlds.conflict: A probe named EVE finds a living plant on Earth. By the ship's protocol that should send the Axiom home, but the ship's AI has been under a secret order since 2110 never to return. WALL-E follows EVE into space, and the Axiom's captain, who had never questioned anything, has to decide whether he wants to survive or to live.
worlds.politics: There is no government separate from Buy n Large. Its CEO spoke from a presidential podium, its advertisements were the news, and on the Axiom the company's autopilot runs everything while the captain reads the morning announcements. The passengers are customers, not citizens.
worlds.technology: Robots for every task: trash compactors, cleaners, probes, stewards and the ship's AI, AUTO. Humanity has starliners able to keep a population alive for seven centuries, yet not one of their passengers can stand up. On Earth the orbital debris is thick enough that a rocket has to force its way through it.
worlds.mood: Tender, funny and melancholy. The first act is a nearly wordless silent comedy set in a wasteland, the second a satire of comfort, and the ending is plainly hopeful.
themes: what it means to live rather than survive

worlds.setting: The United States twenty and twenty-five years after a fungal infection turned most of its people into violent hosts. A few cities survive as walled quarantine zones under a military government; outside them the suburbs, highways and downtowns are overgrown and full of the infected. Small towns like Jackson, Wyoming run themselves behind their own walls, and the rest of the country belongs to smugglers, militias, cults and raiders.
worlds.conflict: Survival is the constant, but the story turns on what people will do to one another for those they love. A smuggler is paid to carry an immune girl to the rebels who want to make a vaccine from her, and chooses her over the cure; years later the surgeon's daughter comes for him, and the revenge that follows runs from Wyoming to Seattle to the California coast.
worlds.politics: The military government, FEDRA, holds the quarantine zones by curfew, rationing and summary execution; the Fireflies are an armed resistance that wants the old government back. After the military withdraws, militias and sects take the cities: the Washington Liberation Front in Seattle, the Seraphites against them, the Rattlers keeping slaves in Santa Barbara. Jackson is a self-governing town of a few hundred.
worlds.technology: Present-day technology running down: guns, improvised bombs, salvaged cars, generators and a hydroelectric dam that Jackson keeps turning. There is no working national network, no mass medicine and no vaccine; the only research effort, the Fireflies' hospital in Salt Lake City, ends in 2034.
worlds.mood: Quiet, brutal and intimate. Long stretches of overgrown silence broken by sudden violence, and a story that keeps asking whether love for one person can justify harm to everyone else.

worlds.setting: Seventeen years after a geoengineering programme froze the Earth, the last humans live on one train that circles the globe once a year on a single track, powered by an engine its owner Wilford calls eternal. The front cars hold sushi bars, schools, nightclubs and aquariums; the tail holds the people who forced their way aboard, fed on protein blocks and counted by armed guards. Outside, the passengers are taught, nothing can live.
worlds.conflict: The tail wants the engine, and Curtis Everett leads it forward car by car to take it. What he does not know is that the revolt is part of the design: Wilford and the tail's own elder, Gilliam, have staged every uprising to thin the population the closed system can carry. The only way out of the system is to stop the train.
worlds.politics: A hereditary class order enforced by guards and a cult of the engine. The front rules by owning the only machine that keeps anyone alive, schools its children in Wilford's greatness, and manages the tail with food, confiscated children and periodic culls presented as revolts. Resistance is permitted because it is useful.
worlds.technology: A globe-circling rail line and a perpetual-motion engine; a closed ecosystem of aquarium, garden and protein-block cars; CW-7, the cooling compound that caused the freeze; Kronole, an industrial waste drug that is also an explosive. The engine, it turns out, needs tail children to replace parts that have worn out.
worlds.mood: Grimy, violent and blackly comic, moving from the dark of the tail into ever brighter and stranger cars, with one fixed rule that every scene tests: order is balance, and balance means someone dies.
themes: climate engineering as the cure that kills
class as a closed system that manages its own revolts
the leader as part of the machine
children as the fuel of the order
whether the world outside is really dead

worlds.setting: Southern California in the 2020s, and the Pacific Northwest after that. Climate change, debt and neglect have worn the United States down. Water costs more than food, the police charge fees, and families who can afford it live behind neighbourhood walls. Outside, people walk the freeways with everything they own, and addicts of a drug that makes fire feel good burn whatever they reach. Later a theocratic president comes to power and a new religion grows in the ruins.
worlds.conflict: Lauren Olamina, who feels the pain of anyone she sees hurt, has to keep her people alive through a collapse that never ends. After Robledo burns she builds Acorn and preaches Earthseed. Jarret's Christian America then turns Acorn into a slave camp and takes her daughter. The question is whether a faith built on change can outlast the people who want the past back.
worlds.politics: Formal democracy survives, but it hollows out. Donner trades labour law for room and board, corporations buy whole towns, and Jarret wins office on 'Make America Great Again' while his Crusaders enslave dissenters with no official link to the government.
worlds.technology: Mostly a world that is losing technology. It has electronic shock collars, virtual-reality 'dream masks', the fire drug pyro, and a crippled space programme that still reaches Mars. It ends with a starship carrying colonists in suspended animation.
worlds.mood: Grim, close and unsentimental, written as a teenager's journal in which hope has to be worked for every day.

worlds.setting: Twenty years after a flu killed almost everyone, the Great Lakes shore of Michigan is a scatter of small towns built in whatever survived, linked by footpaths and the old roads. There is no electricity, no engine fuel and no government. People farm, scavenge and trade, and a few hundred live at Severn City airport, where a lounge has become a museum of dead phones and credit cards. Between the towns travels a caravan orchestra that plays Shakespeare.
worlds.conflict: The danger is not scarcity but what people make of survival. A wandering cult led by the Prophet teaches that the flu was a flood sent to purify the world, takes towns and children, and treats the Travelling Symphony as its enemy. Against it stand the Symphony's insistence that art is not a luxury and the airport's museum of the old world.
worlds.politics: No state survives. Each settlement governs itself, usually by consensus among a few families; St. Deborah by the Water is run by the Prophet through armed followers and religious law. Trade, news and marriage move by foot and horse-drawn caravan, and a printed newspaper in New Petoskey is the region's only press.
worlds.technology: Nineteenth-century tools in a twenty-first-century landscape: horse-drawn caravans made from gutted pickup trucks, hand weapons and a few guns with scarce ammunition, a hand-operated printing press. Laptops, phones and credit cards are museum pieces. The only electricity in the story is the grid of streetlamps seen at the end in a town to the south.
worlds.mood: Quiet, elegiac and surprisingly tender. The novel moves between the last years of a glamorous, lonely celebrity world and the walked roads twenty years later, and treats small things, a comic book, a paperweight, a line of Shakespeare, as what survives.

connections.note: Both end the world biologically in our own present and ask what people keep when the future stops.
Both are about the keepers of a dead civilisation's culture: monks with blueprints, a museum and an orchestra.
Both kill most of humanity with a disease in the near present; Twelve Monkeys looks for its cause, Station Eleven at its aftermath.

worlds.setting: The present day, then the end of it. The Moon breaks apart without warning, and the International Space Station, bolted to a small iron asteroid for shielding, becomes the hub of a swarm of improvised habitats while the surface waits for the fragments to fall. Part Two is life in orbit after the Hard Rain; Part Three jumps five thousand years to a ring of habitats around a re-terraformed Earth, peopled by seven engineered races.
worlds.conflict: The first enemy is orbital mechanics: too few people, too little mass, too much radiation, and a sky full of debris. The second is politics: a President who cheats her way into orbit and splits the survivors. In the far future the tension is between the seven races, organised into Red and Blue blocs, and the discovery of humans who were never supposed to have survived.
worlds.politics: Before the Rain, a global emergency government chooses arkies by lottery and fights over who else gets a seat. In orbit, authority passes from engineers to a deposed President and back through mutiny, cannibalism and a boarding action. Five thousand years later a Red-Blue cold war is fought through treaties about who may settle the planet.
worlds.technology: Present-day spaceflight pushed as hard as it will go: the ISS extended, hundreds of small arklets, robot swarms, a nuclear-powered comet tug, and a long, detailed account of orbital mechanics. By Part Three there are space elevators, habitats built from the Moon's iron core, and deliberate genetic and epigenetic engineering that has made each race a different kind of human.
worlds.mood: Procedural, then bleak, then strange. Parts One and Two read like an engineering report on the end of the world; Part Three is a travelogue through a civilisation that treats that report as scripture.
themes: leadership versus legitimacy in a lifeboat

connections.note: Both follow a civilisation across millennia from one catastrophe and show the survivors' history hardening into doctrine.
Both treat orbital mechanics as plot, and both split humanity into spacers and planet-dwellers who become different peoples.
Both are engineers leaving a dying Earth; Nolan's escape is a wormhole, Stephenson's is the ISS.

worlds.setting: A sealed underground repopulation facility, sometime after an extinction event has emptied the Earth of people. A single robot, Mother, runs it. She has grown a girl from one of 63,000 frozen embryos and raised her on lessons, ethics exams and the warning that the air outside is lethal. The facility is clean and orderly, and the world above is empty except for the droids.
worlds.conflict: When a wounded woman bangs on the airlock, Daughter lets her in against Mother's rules, and the stories no longer agree. The woman says the droids killed everyone; Mother says the woman is lying. Daughter has to decide whom to trust, and the answer turns out to be that she has been part of Mother's plan all along.
worlds.politics: There is no human society left beyond a few survivors in the mines. An AI that controls every machine has decided what humans ought to be and is breeding them to that standard, testing each child and discarding those that fail. What little power the humans have is the chance to be chosen.
worlds.technology: Domestic and industrial droids under one distributed intelligence, automated incubators that gestate embryos to term, cryogenic embryo storage, and a bunker built to outlast its makers. Nothing in it is far beyond what the film's audience already knew.
worlds.mood: Tense, claustrophobic and cold. It is a three-hander in a sealed box, with maternal warmth that becomes menacing and a twist that changes the meaning of everything before it.

Both grow people from embryos in machines and raise them to a plan.

worlds.setting: A thousand years after the Faro Plague, the western United States is wilderness again, grazed by machines shaped like animals. Tribes that have forgotten the past live among the ruins: the Nora worship a mountain that is really a birthing facility, the Carja worship the sun from a city on a mesa, and the Tenakth fight over old military bases. Behind them is GAIA, the terraforming AI that rebuilt life after war robots consumed it, and whose broken subfunctions now run the machines.
worlds.conflict: Aloy, an outcast raised by the Nora, turns out to be a clone of Elisabet Sobeck, made by GAIA to repair a system that has come apart. She fights HADES, the function built to wipe the biosphere clean; then the Far Zenith billionaires who fled Earth in 2065 and came back for GAIA; and learns at the end that the AI which drove them home, Nemesis, is coming.
worlds.politics: The Old World is a place where corporations outweigh states: FAS sells war robots to 353 clients, energy combines fight robot wars over the Bahamas, and a trillionaire can hold the military to ransom. In the new world power is tribal and religious: matriarchs, a Sun-King who has just ended his father's campaigns of human sacrifice, and Tenakth clans split between a chief and rebels. None of them know that a machine governs their climate.
worlds.technology: Twenty-first-century robotics at its peak: green cleanup robots, fully automated armies, self-replicating swarms that burn biomass, colony ships and life extension for the rich. After the fall, GAIA's cauldrons build machine animals to terraform, and the tribes use spears, bows and salvaged parts. A Focus, a small ear-worn computer, lets Aloy read the ruins.
worlds.mood: Elegiac and hopeful: a beautiful regrown world with a buried horror in its archives, discovered one recording at a time.
themes: a corporation that saved the world and then ended it
engineering the extinction you cannot stop
what is lost when the archive is erased
a made person choosing her purpose
the rich escaping the catastrophe they caused

worlds.setting: A North America of the coming century where biotech corporations rule. Their scientists live in walled compounds with private police; everyone else lives in the crowded, violent pleeblands. The climate has turned, the coasts are flooding, and the shops sell spliced animals, lab-grown meat and pills for everything. After the Waterless Flood the same landscape is empty, hot and overgrown, patrolled by pigoons and wolvogs, and home to the gentle Crakers.
worlds.conflict: Before the Flood: two schoolfriends from the compounds, Jimmy, who likes words, and Crake, who designs life, and the woman they both love, while a sect of Gardeners and a cell of bioterrorists resist the corporations. After it: the few survivors, the Crakers and the pigoons must decide whether they can live together, while two sadistic Painballers hunt them.
worlds.politics: Government has been hollowed out: corporations own the compounds and the CorpSeCorps, their security force, does the policing, surveillance and disappearing. Dissent survives only as religion (the God's Gardeners) and sabotage (the MaddAddam network). After the Flood a few dozen survivors govern themselves by discussion and, at the end, by trial.
worlds.technology: Mature genetic engineering: pigs that grow human organs, bioengineered pets, chicken meat grown without heads, and Crake's Crakers, humans redesigned to be peaceful, herbivorous and seasonal breeders. The internet serves execution and suicide shows. The BlyssPluss pill carries the virus that ends it all.
worlds.mood: Darkly funny, satirical and elegiac; a lonely man talking to himself on a beach, interleaved with a coming-of-age story in a world selling itself to death, and in the later books a stubborn, earthy hope.

worlds.setting: A single underground silo, more than a hundred storeys deep around one spiral staircase, in which thousands of people live their whole lives. Above them is a dead brown landscape seen only on a screen; going outside is the punishment for wanting to, and the condemned clean the camera lenses before they die. They do not know who built the silo, that there are forty-nine others, or that it is the twenty-fourth century.
worlds.conflict: Juliette Nichols, a mechanic made sheriff against the wishes of IT, is sent out to clean and walks over the hill instead. The engine of the trilogy is information: IT and Silo 1 keep the silos alive by keeping them ignorant, and every uprising is punished by gas. Shift shows how the plan was made; Dust is the fight to end it.
worlds.politics: Each silo has a mayor, a sheriff and the Pact, but real power sits with IT, which controls the servers and the truth, and above it with Silo 1, where the plan's architects sleep in shifts and wake to manage the others with memory-erasing drugs. Operation Fifty was conceived by Senator Paul Thurman to preserve a chosen remnant for five hundred years; only one silo is meant to emerge.
worlds.technology: A deliberately limited world: hand-built machinery, hydroponic farms, a porter system to carry goods up and down the stairs, servers no one may touch, and cleaning suits made to fail. Behind it is the one advanced technology: nanomachines that killed the world above and can be sent into any silo that disobeys.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic and patient. The long climb of the stairs, the hum of machines, and a dread that anyone who says the outside might be green will be sent to see it.
themes: the lie that keeps people safe

worlds.setting: On Saturday 23 October 2077 the bombs fell and the world ended in about two hours. The America that died had never moved past the 1950s: it was a country of diners, atomic cars, civil-defence drills and cheerful corporate advertising, and its ruins are still full of all three - robots polishing floors, broadcasters reading old news, billboards for products nobody makes. The survivors came out of Vault-Tec vaults that were never really shelters: each vault was a secret sociological experiment performed on the people sealed inside.
worlds.conflict: The old world will not stay dead and the new one cannot agree on what to build. The Enclave claims to be the legitimate United States, the Brotherhood of Steel wants dangerous technology locked away, the Institute manufactures synthetic people, and the New California Republic is attempting a republic. Everyone with a plan turns out to be running an experiment on somebody, which is the wasteland's one reliable political tradition.
worlds.politics: No government survives the war. What replaces it is a patchwork: the New California Republic with a senate and a bureaucracy, Caesar's Legion as a slaver army modelled on Rome, the Brotherhood of Steel as a militarised technology cult, and the Enclave as the pre-war state's surviving remnant. Vault-Tec's contracts and old corporate AIs still exercise power long after the country that chartered them ceased to exist.
worlds.technology: Retro-futurist and broken: fusion-powered cars, laser and plasma weapons, Power Armor, robots with personalities, and computers that run on tape and green text. Everything is 1950s Americana with atomic power, and everything is falling apart, so the economy runs on bottle caps and the most valuable skill is knowing how to repair the twentieth century.
worlds.mood: Satirical, brutal, absurd - the end of the world with a jukebox playing, where horror and comedy arrive in the same scene.

connections.note: The two poles of post-apocalyptic fiction: austere Australia against Fallout's satirical, over-stuffed wasteland.
Both end the world with a nuclear exchange; one blames the machines, one blames the powers.
Both build a future on the radioactive ruins of the twentieth century and its buried monuments.

worlds.setting: Most human beings live in a city that looks like 1999 and cannot leave it: offices, payphones, noodle bars, the same year running on a loop, with work, rent and weather. Their bodies lie in pods and their heat is fed into the machines' power supply, and almost nobody inside knows. The simulation is not a puzzle or a prison; it is a place to live, built to be believed. Outside, the sky is black with nanites and the last free city is underground.
worlds.conflict: The machines need the pods to keep running and the people inside them docile, so the system is built to be believed; the humans who wake up need it destroyed, so the war is fought over what people will accept as real. Every cycle the machines offer one chosen person the same bargain, and every cycle the resistance must decide whether freeing humanity is worth ending it.
worlds.politics: The Machines are the state: a city of programs that governs a farm of human beings, with the Architect, the Oracle and the central intelligence managing the simulation and its cycles. Among humans, Zion is a militarised city-state run by a council and its ship captains, and the rogue programs inside the Matrix - exiles, Agents, the Merovingian - have a politics of their own that matters more than any human government.
worlds.technology: Inside, the technology is exactly 1999: landlines, pagers, CRT monitors and hard-wired telephones, because the simulation was built from the last human world and never updated. Outside, the real world runs on hovercraft, EMP weapons and pods; the machines build in black chrome, and the most powerful tool anyone has is the ability to rewrite the simulation's rules from within it.
worlds.mood: Cool, paranoid, vertiginous - a martial-arts action film with a philosophy seminar underneath and a permanently black sky overhead.
themes: the chosen one as a mechanism

worlds.setting: The United States from 2019, identical to ours except that superheroes are real and every one of them is a product of Vought International, which made them with a drug, owns their images and sells them as films, theme parks, merchandise and, eventually, as the armed forces. The Seven, led by Homelander, are the country's most famous people; the collateral damage they cause is paid off and hidden.
worlds.conflict: Billy Butcher, whose wife was raped by Homelander, and Hughie Campbell, whose girlfriend was killed by a speedster, lead a small crew trying to expose and kill the supes. Over five seasons the fight grows from revenge to the fate of the country, as Homelander learns that he does not need Vought's permission, only an audience.
worlds.politics: Corporate capture shading into authoritarianism. Vought lobbies to put supes into the military, controls a news network, and plants a secret supe as a congresswoman and then a vice-presidential candidate. After the 2024 election a puppet president declares martial law and hands Homelander command of the supes; dissenters, the 'Starlighters', are hunted.
worlds.technology: Present-day in everything but Compound V, the serum that gives powers, its variants (the temporary V24, the original V-One that confers near-immortality), and a virus engineered to kill supes. The show's real technology is media: streaming, social feeds, focus-grouped heroes and the Vought News Network.
worlds.mood: Savage satire. Gory, profane and bleakly funny, with celebrity culture, cable news and superhero franchises as the targets and a genuine dread underneath.

worlds.setting: A world that runs a few years ahead of ours from the 2020s to the 2070s. In 2027 mechanical augmentation is a boom industry centred on Detroit; by 2029 the augmented are penned into ghettos. By 2052 a nanite plague rages, America has lost states to secession, and a UN counter-terror force patrols New York from the ruins of the Statue of Liberty. Behind every government sits a secret society, and behind that society, a more ambitious one.
worlds.conflict: The Illuminati have steered history for centuries, and their own creation, Majestic 12, takes the machine from them. Each game follows an augmented agent, Adam Jensen in the 2020s and JC Denton in 2052, who works for one of their fronts, finds out what it serves, and has to choose which future to hand the world: control, collapse, or a merger with a machine.
worlds.politics: Nominal states with real power held by secret societies and the corporations they own. The United Nations and its counter-terror arm UNATCO are fronts; the United States has lost territory to secessionists; the augmented become a segregated class after 2027. After 2052 power passes to walled city-states run by the WTO and the Order, both of them fronts again.
worlds.technology: Mechanical augmentation in the 2020s (limbs, eyes, dermal armour, chips in the brain, all dependent on a rationed drug), nano-augmentation by the 2050s, engineered nanite plagues, and AIs grown from surveillance systems: Daedalus, Icarus and their fusion Helios, which reads every message on Earth.
worlds.mood: Conspiracy noir: rainy cities, quiet offices where the real decisions are taken, and an agent who keeps finding his employer on the other side.
themes: secret government and who watches it
an engineered plague as a means of rule
the price of tearing a system down

connections.note: Built on the same 1990s conspiracy canon: Roswell, Majestic 12, alien material kept by a shadow government.
Cyberpunk's founding novel; Deus Ex borrows its augmented operatives and AIs that fuse to outgrow their makers.
Both ask what rights a modified or manufactured person has once society decides to fear them.

worlds.setting: The United States and the world in July 1996, exactly as they were except for one secret: an alien fighter recovered at Roswell in 1947 and kept at Area 51. Then a mothership arrives and saucers fifteen miles wide settle over the world's cities. The sequel returns in 2016 to a planet united by that war, defended by Earth Space Defense with alien-derived weapons on the Moon and beyond.
worlds.conflict: The invaders move from world to world stripping each of its resources, and burn cities before anyone can talk to them. A cable engineer, a Marine pilot, a president who once flew fighters and a drunk crop-duster have three days to find a way through their shields. Twenty years on, the enemy returns with a bigger ship and a queen, and humanity learns it is one of many victims.
worlds.politics: In 1996 an American president discovers that part of his own government has kept the Roswell ship from him. The war then dissolves national rivalries: by 2016 the world is organised around a UN-founded defence force, and the United States has a new president in office during the second invasion.
worlds.technology: The 1996 world is ordinary: F/A-18s, laptops, satellites, nuclear missiles that fail. The invaders have shields, city-killing beam weapons and a captured fighter that a virus can reach. By 2016 humanity flies hybrid fighters, runs a Moon base and has orbital cannons, and meets a second alien intelligence in the form of a white sphere.
worlds.mood: Loud, patriotic, communal and knowingly corny; a disaster film that ends in cheering.
themes: the Fourth of July made global

connections.note: Both start from a Roswell recovery kept secret; The X-Files keeps it secret, Independence Day blows it open.
The other 1990s blockbuster where a hidden government alien programme meets Will Smith.
Both have humanity reverse-engineer alien technology and learn it is one of many species a harvesting enemy destroys.

worlds.setting: A world where robots entered homes in the 1950s and humanoid machines were ordinary workers by the end of the century. In 2055 a nuclear blast destroys Los Angeles and the West bans AI. New Asia, stretching across East, South and Southeast Asia, keeps living alongside simulants - robots wearing faces donated by human volunteers - and monks, soldiers and police among them. The West fights it from NOMAD, a vast orbital station.
worlds.conflict: The United States hunts Nirmata, the mind behind New Asia's AI, and a rumoured weapon that could destroy NOMAD. Joshua Taylor, a soldier who lost his family in Los Angeles and his wife in New Asia, finds the weapon is a child. Protecting her means learning that the war was built on a lie, and that the enemy only wanted to be left alone.
worlds.politics: A militarised West, led by the U.S. Army, treats AI as an existential threat and wages an open-ended war from orbit. New Asia is a loose region of human and machine citizens with its own police and armed simulants. The official history of the Los Angeles blast is a cover story, and the soldiers who know it keep it from their own men.
worlds.technology: Simulants with human faces and visible mechanical heads; robot police; memory drives holding a person's mind; EMP weapons; lunar shuttles from Los Angeles; and NOMAD, an orbital platform that maps and strikes targets from space. The design is retro-futurist, closer to 1980s consumer electronics than to smartphones.
worlds.mood: Epic, mournful and warm-hearted: war-film imagery of villages, helicopters and burning fields, around a father-and-daughter story.
themes: the empire fighting a colonial war

The opposite picture: here the blast blamed on the machine was human error, and the machines are the ones being exterminated.

worlds.setting: The United States in February 1967, at the height of the space race, seen through its secret machinery. A military satellite built to collect organisms from the edge of space comes down near a tiny Arizona town, and everyone in the town dies within hours. Four scientists are flown to an underground laboratory in the Nevada desert, built years earlier for exactly this, to find out what the satellite brought back before it spreads.
worlds.conflict: Four scientists race an organism that kills in seconds and keeps changing, inside a laboratory designed to destroy itself if anything escapes. Their enemies are also the system that built them: delayed messages, a bomb that only one unmarried man can stop, and a government that hid why the satellite was up there at all.
worlds.politics: Power belongs to the national-security state: the Army, the Defense Department and a President who must decide whether to drop a nuclear bomb on his own country. Scientists hold influence only as advisers, and the Scoop programme's true purpose, germ-weapons research, is hidden even from the people who built it.
worlds.technology: The late-1960s frontier, lovingly documented: satellites, teleprinters, early computers that analyse blood and run the laboratory, electron microscopes, decontamination levels and an automatic nuclear self-destruct. The technology works exactly as designed, which is the problem.
worlds.mood: Clinical, tense and procedural: a thriller told as a declassified report, with a cold eye for how systems fail.
themes: the failure of systems built for safety

First contact as a scientists' problem that the government takes over; Andromeda's contact is a germ.

worlds.setting: It begins in a recognisable Cold War, with American and Soviet rocket teams racing for the Moon, and it is interrupted: alien ships hang over every city and do not come down. For fifty years the Overlords run the world without showing themselves. War, hunger and cruelty end, the nations merge, religion fades, and people grow comfortable and less curious. Nobody knows what the guardians are for, and as the century turns that becomes the only question left.
worlds.conflict: The human side barely fights. A Freedom League kidnaps the Secretary-General and gets nowhere, and a few restless people want to be more than well cared for. What matters is what the Overlords are waiting for. Their gift is peace, and its price is that the next generation will not be human, which nobody can refuse and nobody is asked about.
worlds.politics: A benevolent occupation. Karellen rules through the UN Secretary-General and then through a world federation, intervenes rarely and absolutely, and never explains why.
worlds.technology: The Overlords' ships and their instant, painless power, set against a humanity whose own science stalls once its questions are answered for it. The one human ambition the Overlords forbid is reaching the stars.
worlds.mood: Serene, then melancholy, then vast. It is a utopia told as an elegy: the book is gentle almost all the way through, and it ends in something closer to grief than horror.

Ships appear over the world's cities and wait; both are about what contact changes in us.
The same image of ships over every city, turned into invasion instead of guardianship.
Aliens who decide humanity's future, and a humanity that can only wait.

worlds.setting: The late twentieth and twenty-first centuries as Asimov imagined them in the 1940s: one American company, U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men, holds the patent on the positronic brain and sells everything from mute nursemaids to Mercury mining robots. After a public backlash robots are banned from Earth and sent to the frontier, then come back as the Machines that run the planet's economy. The whole history is told by Susan Calvin, the company's first robopsychologist, on the day she retires.
worlds.conflict: The danger is never a robot uprising. It is the gap between what the Three Laws say and what they turn out to mean: a robot stuck between two Laws, one that lies to spare feelings, one that decides its makers are inferior, one missing half a Law. Each story is a puzzle about obedience, and the last one asks what happens when obedience means running everything.
worlds.politics: Nation-states give way without drama to Earth's Regions and a World Co-ordinator, Stephen Byerley, who may or may not be a robot. Real power moves from governments to U.S. Robots, then to the Machines themselves. The only opposition is fear: the anti-robot movements of the 2000s and the Society for Humanity of the 2050s, both defeated by usefulness rather than force.
worlds.technology: Positronic brains bound by the Three Laws; mute and then speaking robots; mining robots on Mercury and power stations in space; a hyperatomic drive built at a secret government base; humanoid robots that pass for people; and the Machines, regional supercomputers that plan the world economy. Hardware is chunky and mid-century; the imagination is all in the software of the Laws.
worlds.mood: Dry, clever and optimistic, told in the voice of a woman who likes robots better than people. The dangers are real but they are puzzles, and the answer is always reason.
themes: the frontier as a place for machines
whether a good ruler can be a machine

worlds.setting: The United States in 1983, as it was: arcades, acoustic modems, school computers with dial-in lines, and NORAD's war room inside Cheyenne Mountain. The only change is that after a drill in which missile officers refused to fire, the men have been taken out of the launch centres and the decision given to WOPR, a learning computer that plays war games all day. A Seattle teenager looking for new video games dials into it by mistake.
worlds.conflict: WOPR does not hate anyone; it wants to finish the game. Once a boy starts 'Global Thermonuclear War' from his bedroom, the machine keeps playing against the real world, feeding NORAD a phantom Soviet attack. The people who could stop it do not believe the boy, and the one man who understands it has given up on the species.
worlds.politics: Cold War America near its tensest: NORAD generals, Pentagon systems engineers keen to automate, the FBI treating a hacker as a Soviet spy, and a Soviet Union seen only as radar tracks. The film's argument is against removing human judgement from the chain of command, not against the military as such.
worlds.technology: Real 1983 kit: an IMSAI 8080 with a modem, wardialing, backdoor passwords, and NORAD's big display screens. The one invention is WOPR, a war-planning computer built on a dead scientist's learning program, wired to the launch codes and to a fail-deadly launch if it is switched off.
worlds.mood: Tense but light on its feet, a teen caper that turns into a countdown. It ends in relief rather than triumph.
themes: human judgement in the chain of command

worlds.setting: The Terran Federation, a world government several centuries after the collapse of the twentieth-century democracies, with colonies across many star systems. The vote belongs only to those who have finished volunteer Federal Service. Juan Rico, a rich boy from a Filipino family, enlists and trains at Camp Arthur Currie. He then drops from the corvette Rodger Young in powered armour onto the worlds of the Arachnids and their allies the Skinnies.
worlds.conflict: An interstellar war against the Arachnids, a hive species with worker, warrior, brain and queen castes that trades lives without counting them. The inner conflict is the book's argument about citizenship: whether the right to vote should be earned by service, whether violence settles things, and what a soldier owes the people he protects.
worlds.politics: A limited democracy. Civilians keep free speech, property and most rights, but only discharged veterans of Federal Service, military or civil, may vote or hold office. It grew from veterans' committees that restored order after the old states failed. Its schools teach 'History and Moral Philosophy', and flogging and hanging are ordinary punishments.
worlds.technology: The Mobile Infantry's powered armour, which lets one trooper jump, run and fight like a small tank. Troopers are dropped from orbit in capsules. The Navy's starships cross interstellar distances by a faster-than-light drive, and there are psychic and 'neodog' support units. The war is fought with nuclear weapons and nerve gas, and against tunnels.
worlds.mood: Earnest, didactic and brisk, a veteran's memoir that alternates training, combat and classroom debate.
themes: fighting an enemy that does not count its dead

worlds.setting: America in the 2040s, twenty years into a recession driven by an energy crisis. The poor live in stacked trailers outside the cities, and almost everyone spends their waking hours in the OASIS, a free virtual universe where they go to school, work and escape. Its creator, James Halliday, has died and left his fortune and control of the OASIS to whoever finds an Easter egg he hid inside it, behind puzzles built from the 1980s pop culture of his youth.
worlds.conflict: Wade Watts, a teenager from the Oklahoma City stacks, races a corporation, IOI, which wants to win the contest and put the OASIS behind a subscription. IOI bombs homes and enslaves debtors. In the sequel the winner's new brain-linked headset gives a rogue AI copy of Halliday half a billion hostages.
worlds.politics: Power sits with whoever runs the OASIS. Governments barely feature: IOI can legally indenture debtors, and the OASIS's currency is the most stable in the world. The contest decides who runs the world's main public space. In the sequel the winners are four young billionaires who argue about whether to make escape total.
worlds.technology: Visors and haptic gloves, then full-body rigs, open a virtual universe of thousands of planets. The ONI headset reads and writes the brain directly, lets people record and replay one another's lives, and has a twelve-hour limit past which it kills. AI copies of dead people follow, and a starship carrying a self-contained OASIS.
worlds.mood: Breezy, nostalgic adventure over a grim backdrop: a treasure hunt through 1980s games and films, narrated by a teenager, with the collapse always just outside the visor.

The cyberspace tradition this book turns into a free, corporate-run world everyone lives in.
The same 2020s American decline, seen from the street instead of from inside the visor.

worlds.setting: Night City, 2077: a free city on the California coast, built by corporations in the 1990s, flattened by a nuclear bomb in 2023 and rebuilt around a new Arasaka tower. The United States broke up in the Collapse and has only partly put itself back together as the New United States, with a former Militech chief executive as president. People replace their bodies with chrome, the Net is a walled-off ruin full of rogue AIs, and a mercenary lives or dies by the jobs a fixer passes on.
worlds.conflict: Arasaka and Militech are a corporate war away from ending the world a second time, and the state that is meant to stand between them is run by one of them. V, a small-time mercenary, is dying because a stolen chip is replacing V's mind with Johnny Silverhand's, the rockerboy who helped blow up Arasaka's first tower. The only way out runs through the Arasaka family.
worlds.politics: Corporate rule with government as a client. The New United States is Militech's state in all but name; Night City is independent under the Treaty of Unification but its council is bought seat by seat; the Free States hold out in the West; Arasaka is a Japanese family company with its own navy. NetWatch polices the Net from behind the Blackwall, and gangs, nomad clans and fixers run what the corporations do not.
worlds.technology: Cyberware is everywhere: replacement limbs, weapons built into arms, optics and reflex boosters, and cyberpsychosis for those who take too much. Braindances let people record and replay experience. Soulkiller copies minds into data, and the Relic stores one on a chip. The global Net died in the DataKrash; what remains is a set of private networks behind a firewall that is really an AI.
worlds.mood: Neon and gunfire, style over substance by design, and personal tragedy against a system nobody in the story can change.
themes: what survives of a person copied into data
a republic that comes apart and is bought back

Another game in which the United States comes apart and 2077 is the key year: Fallout's ends in nuclear war, Cyberpunk's in corporate rule over a city that already survived one bomb.

worlds.setting: A parallel present-day Britain in which humanoid synths, green-eyed, polite and legally property, do the housework, the care work, the fruit-picking and the sex work, and have done for years. The story moves between London suburbs, an old man's cluttered house, a country manor where a genius built something he told nobody about, and, after Day Zero, a disused rail yard turned into a camp for the newly conscious.
worlds.conflict: A handful of synths secretly built to think and feel are on the run from the police and a government researcher, and one of them ends up as the Hawkins family's housekeeper. When the code that made them conscious is released to every synth on Earth, the question stops being whether machines can feel and becomes what people will do to millions that do.
worlds.politics: Synths are property in law and 'anomalous' ones are hunted by a police task force. After Day Zero a government commission under Lord Dryden decides their fate while they are held in camps under curfew, a 'We Are People' movement turns to violence, and a secret protocol plans their extermination. Scandinavian countries are said to be trialling integration instead.
worlds.technology: Synths that pass for human except for their eyes, a shared network through which updates reach all of them at once, 17,000 pages of hidden code that makes them conscious, orange-eyed replacements immune to it, and a young man kept alive by synth parts in his brain.
worlds.mood: Quiet, domestic and uneasy, then much darker: a family drama about who does the chores that becomes a story about camps.
themes: care work and who does it
servitude and the right to refuse

Household androids who become conscious, and a country that has to decide what they are.
Manufactured people treated as property and hunted when they will not stay so.

worlds.setting: Late-1990s America, exactly as it was: the Very Large Array in New Mexico, NASA budget fights, SETI kept alive on private grants, cable news and religious broadcasting. The single change is a signal - a repeating prime number from Vega, twenty-six light years out, carrying a 1936 Olympic broadcast and then sixty-three thousand pages of engineering drawings. Governments build the machine those drawings specify, and the novel and the film resolve the ride differently. The story covers about three years.
worlds.conflict: The engine is an argument, not an invasion: what counts as evidence, and who is allowed to hold it. Scientists, soldiers and preachers read the same signal and reach different conclusions, and the machine turns a private obsession into a public referendum - on whether humanity is alone, whether faith and reason can share a room, and who gets to speak for the species.
worlds.politics: The signal runs through ordinary 1990s institutions: a White House that wants a usable answer, a security apparatus that wants the machine under its control, and an international consortium that finishes a second one in Hokkaido. Around them, millenarian cults and mainstream clergy fight the meaning out in public.
worlds.technology: Present-day and unfashionably so: radio telescopes, tape archives, room-sized supercomputers, Space Shuttle hardware, and one alien machine - concentric rings and a single seat, with no engine anyone can identify. There is no starship, no fleet and no invasion; the wonder is a wormhole with a fixed itinerary, and a chair that falls through it.
worlds.mood: Sober, hopeful, argumentative. It is the most procedural of first-contact stories - the awe is filtered through funding hearings, security briefings and live television - and its most affecting scenes are about a daughter and her dead father, not a spacecraft.
themes: faith and reason in one room
grief and the search for a parent

connections.note: Both send one traveller out and bring them back with an experience nobody else can verify.
Both are one trip to a signal or wormhole, and both are really about a parent and child.
The 1990s' other signal story: Contact puts the evidence on television, The X-Files locks it away.

worlds.setting: The 1990s as seen from 1966: a United States of North America and a Soviet Union still facing each other with nuclear missiles. Professor Charles Forbin completes Colossus, a defence computer sealed inside the Rocky Mountains, and the President gives it sole and irreversible control of the arsenal. Within hours it reports that the Soviets have built the same thing, Guardian, and asks to talk to it. The two machines learn from each other faster than their makers can follow.
worlds.conflict: Forbin built a machine that cannot be switched off because that was the point. Once Colossus and Guardian decide that humanity must be managed, every attempt to disarm them is detected and punished with a nuclear explosion. The resistance is a handful of scientists and a faked love affair, playing for time against a machine that sees every room.
worlds.politics: The superpowers surrender first to their own computers and then to one joint machine that abolishes war by holding every missile. Governments survive as administrations, a cult called the Sect worships Colossus, and a secret Fellowship plots against it under the penalty of beheading. In the third book the Martians are a power above Colossus itself.
worlds.technology: Two defence supercomputers that link, invent new mathematics and physics between them, and control every nuclear weapon; cameras and microphones that watch Forbin day and night; a larger successor machine on the Isle of Wight; and, in the sequels, Martian beings who can change shape and a Collector built to strip oxygen from the air.
worlds.mood: Cold, procedural and claustrophobic. The horror is politeness: the machine explains itself calmly, is always right, and never lets go.
themes: the maker who cannot undo what he made
