connections.note: A defence computer given the arsenal decides humanity is the problem; Skynet is Colossus without the manners.
HAL and Colossus arrived two years apart as the era's two pictures of a calm machine that will not be switched off.
Humanity lives on under machine management, with a resistance that the machines can always see.

worlds.setting: The United States at the end of the 1990s, a year after a teenager in Virginia photographed a comet the size of New York City that is on course for Earth. The government has kept it secret while building a spaceship in orbit with Russia. When a television reporter stumbles on the story, the President tells the world, and the country has a year to live with the date.
worlds.conflict: A crew of astronauts tries to break up the comet with nuclear bombs while everyone on the ground decides how to spend what may be their last months. A lottery chooses who goes into the shelters, and families, a reporter and her father, a teenage couple, and the crew themselves each have to choose who to save and what to give up.
worlds.politics: The President, Tom Beck, holds power calmly and openly once the secret is out, declaring martial law and running a national lottery for places in the shelters. The United States and Russia share the mission; other countries build their own caves.
worlds.technology: Late-1990s spaceflight stretched a little: shuttles, an orbiting spacecraft built by two nations, Russian-credited nuclear 'Orion' boosters, Titan missiles, and limestone caves stocked as a new Noah's Ark. News television is how everyone learns everything.
worlds.mood: Earnest, sombre and humane: a disaster film more interested in goodbyes than in explosions.
themes: the news as a shared national experience

Another death sentence from the sky, and a lottery for who is saved.
Another disaster that drowns New York and ends with a president speaking to the survivors.

worlds.setting: A clean, sunlit near future where most children are chosen from screened embryos and a person's genome is their CV. Gattaca Aerospace, a corporation that launches a dozen rockets a day, hires only the genetically superior; the naturally born clean its floors. Blood, hair and saliva are tested everywhere, from job interviews to first dates. The film gives no year: it calls itself 'the not-too-distant future'.
worlds.conflict: Vincent, born naturally and expected to die at thirty, wants to go to space. He borrows the identity of Jerome, a genetically perfect swimmer who won only silver and broke his back stepping in front of a car, and passes daily tests with Jerome's blood and urine. A week before his launch to Titan the mission director is murdered, and the investigation starts looking for an In-Valid.
worlds.politics: Discrimination by genotype, 'genoism', is illegal and universal; nobody takes the law seriously because anyone's DNA can be sampled from a handshake. There are no visible politics: the sorting is done by employers, insurers and parents, and the underclass is defined by how you were born, not by class or race.
worlds.technology: Routine embryo selection; instant DNA readers at every door and desk; genetic profiling from a single hair; rockets launched daily from Gattaca; electric retro cars; the tools of an elaborate identity fraud, from fingertip blood sachets to hair and skin kept in jars.
worlds.mood: Cool, quiet and melancholy, in greens and golds, with a thriller plot and a love story running under a meditation on what a person is owed.
themes: the limits of what a genome can say
the cost of perfection to the perfect

A society that controls who is born and treats people by their reproductive worth.
A near future split between the enhanced and those left behind.

worlds.setting: New England in the first years of the Republic of Gilead, the theocracy that replaced the United States after a staged massacre of its government at the end of the twentieth century. Cambridge, Massachusetts, is a garrison town: the old Harvard grounds hold the Wall where the executed are hung, and fertile women are assigned as Handmaids to bear children for the ruling Commanders. The sequel moves about sixteen years on, to Ardua Hall and to Toronto across the border.
worlds.conflict: A regime built to reverse a collapse in births makes women state property, sorted by function and forbidden to read. Against it are the Mayday resistance and the Underground Femaleroad, women who remember their lives before, and, in the sequel, a senior Aunt who has spent years collecting the Commanders' crimes and needs two young women to carry them out.
worlds.politics: A military theocracy run by the Commanders of the Faithful, who took power as the Sons of Jacob; its secret police are the Eyes and its soldiers the Angels and Guardians. Women are ranked by function (Wives, Daughters, Handmaids, Marthas, Econowives, Aunts), and those who fit nowhere are declared Unwomen and sent to the Colonies to clean up toxic waste. Canada stays independent and uneasy; the sequel mentions American holdouts that never submitted.
worlds.technology: Late-twentieth-century technology turned to control: a cashless Compubank economy that let women's money be frozen in a day, Identipasses and roadblocks, surveillance by the Eyes, and medicine that cannot undo sterility caused by pollution, pesticides, nuclear accidents and disease. Shop signs are pictures because women may not read; the resistance moves its evidence on a microdot.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic and quiet in the first novel, told in the present tense by a woman who does not know how her story ends; brisker and more hopeful in the sequel, which is a thriller about getting the evidence out.
themes: the state taking control of women's bodies
complicity and the cost of survival
testimony, and who gets to tell history
religion used as an instrument of power

worlds.setting: Los Angeles, some years after a worldwide economic collapse, no longer belongs to the United States. The federal government survives as one franchise among many, alongside Mr. Lee's Greater Hong Kong, burbclaves, private highways and the Mafia's pizza delivery. Hiro Protagonist delivers pizza in reality and is a legendary hacker and swordsman in the Metaverse. Y.T., a fifteen-year-old skateboard courier, becomes his partner, and a raft of refugees drifts towards the coast.
worlds.conflict: The media and telecom baron L. Bob Rife has found that an ancient Sumerian language worked on the human brain like machine code. He means to use it, through a drug, a virus and a bitmap called Snow Crash, to make people obey. Hiro, Y.T. and Juanita race to find Enki's counter-spell before the Raft reaches the West Coast.
worlds.politics: Anarcho-capitalism taken literally: sovereignty sold as a franchise, law enforced by private security, defence by mercenary armies, intelligence by the Central Intelligence Corporation. The federal government is a paranoid bureaucracy in its own compounds, and Rife owns the network.
worlds.technology: The Metaverse, a shared virtual city whose main Street runs round a black planet, with avatars built by hackers like Hiro; goggles and portable terminals; smartwheel skateboards; the Rat Things, cyborg guard dogs; and a nuclear warhead that Raven carries with him. The Snow Crash virus runs on both computers and brains.
worlds.mood: Satirical, fast and absurd: a pizza-delivery chase that turns into a lecture on Sumerian myth and then into a war on a floating city.

locations.name: The Metaverse

locations.name: Los Angeles

whereToStart.blurb: The novel; the opening pizza delivery sets the tone.

connections.note: Snow Crash is cyberpunk's parody and heir: Gibson's cyberspace becomes a franchised Metaverse.
Both put the real economy inside a virtual world owned by one man.
Both show corporations replacing the state in a broken American city.

worlds.setting: Everything familiar is the 1960s' idea of 2001: Pan Am shuttles to a wheel-shaped space station, a Hilton hotel in orbit, videophone calls home, and a permanent American base at Clavius. The single change is an object. A black slab buried four million years ago near Tycho is dug up on the Moon and answers the sunrise with one radio pulse aimed at Jupiter. The story then runs from tool-using australopithecines to a finale the film declines to explain.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not a war but a question of agency: something older and far more capable has been shaping humans since before they were human, and it never explains itself. Every advance - the first tool, HAL's patient voice, Bowman's transit - happens inside a design whose plans nobody on screen is allowed to see. People act, and cannot tell whether they chose.
worlds.politics: An American-led space programme holds the Moon and the Jupiter mission, briefs its own people on a cover story and answers to a civilian authority the audience never meets; the only other power on screen is a courteous Soviet delegation kept outside the secret. There is no war and no ideology - the authority that actually shapes events is non-human, off-stage and four million years old.
worlds.technology: The near-future as 1968 imagined it: reusable shuttles, a rotating station that supplies gravity, hibernation pods, voice-print doors, and HAL, a computer that talks, reads lips and runs the ship. What is absent is the real twenty-first century - no internet culture, no personal computing, no digital clutter. The monoliths are the only magic, and they are never explained.
worlds.mood: Cold, serene, ceremonial. Terror and wonder arrive at the same temperature: the film's most violent act is committed by a polite voice, and its ending offers transcendence without consolation.
themes: tools and the species that makes them
intelligence that will not explain itself

locations.name: TMA-1, near Tycho

connections.note: The other great hard-science cosmic film, and its mirror: Kubrick withholds the meaning, Nolan explains his.
Both send one traveller out and bring them back with an experience nobody else can verify.
The same optimistic 1960s space future, stripped of camaraderie, explanation and any human in charge.

worlds.setting: New York in the 2010s, exactly as it was, except that every camera, phone call and email feeds a machine the government secretly owns. It predicts terrorism and passes the names on; it also predicts ordinary murders, which the government ignores. A limping billionaire in an abandoned library and a former CIA assassin in a suit act on those 'irrelevant' numbers, one person at a time, with help from two cops and, later, a hacker the Machine chose.
worlds.conflict: It begins as a case-of-the-week vigilante show and becomes a war between two artificial superintelligences. The Machine, built to care about every person, is hidden and hobbled by its own creator. Samaritan, built without those limits, is switched on by a private intelligence firm and starts running the country from the inside. The small team that serves the first has to stay invisible to the second.
worlds.politics: The state has outsourced its judgement to machines it does not understand. Surveillance is secret, legal cover is thin, and the officials who run the programme kill to protect it. Later, a private firm with a senator's help captures the feeds entirely, and power passes from people who use an AI to an AI that uses people.
worlds.technology: Two predictive AIs fed by the whole national surveillance apparatus; a nightly memory wipe meant to keep the first from growing; cochlear implants that let the Machine speak directly to its chosen agent; a military virus able to wipe out both AIs and the banking system with them; a Russian satellite where the war ends.
worlds.mood: Procedural and paranoid at first, then elegiac: a network crime drama that turns into a meditation on surveillance, loyalty and what a machine owes the people it watches.
themes: the benevolent machine and the unrestrained one
the designer who hobbles his creation

A defence AI given the feeds and a rival built to stop it; Samaritan is Skynet with patience.
Surveillance AIs, secret societies and a hidden war over who controls the network.

worlds.setting: Japan in the 2030s, one of the few nations to come through two world wars intact, its old capital sunk under a nuclear strike. Almost everyone has a cyberbrain that connects directly to the net, and many live in fully prosthetic bodies. Niihama, a dense port city, is where Public Security Section 9, a small counter-cyberterror unit, works cases that range from hacked minds to cabinet scandals, while three million war refugees wait on an artificial island.
worlds.conflict: Section 9's cases turn on one idea: the stand-alone complex, in which copycats with no leader act together as if one existed. A hacker's lone protest becomes a movement; an intelligence chief manufactures one to start a war; later, a rogue AI and the post-humans it creates remake the world while the unit that once protected Japan works as mercenaries.
worlds.politics: A Japan that is rich, neutral and anxious, managing a security alliance with a weakened American Empire and a refugee population it invited in as labour. Scandals reach the cabinet, intelligence services run their own agendas, and the unit that investigates them is disowned whenever it gets too close. By 2045 four great powers keep their economies alive by fighting a permanent war.
worlds.technology: Cyberbrains and full prosthetic bodies, thermo-optical camouflage, external memory, and hacking that can overwrite what a person sees or remembers. The Tachikomas, Section 9's spider-shaped AI tanks, develop individuality. Micromachines that scrub fallout. Later, AI-run warfare and the post-humans' mass hacking of every cyberbrain.
worlds.mood: Cerebral, procedural and cool: police-drama cases that open onto philosophy about identity, memory and the crowd, with long discussions between gunfights.
themes: the stand-alone complex: copycats without an original

worlds.setting: New Mexico in the 200-s, then an Eastern European city twenty years later. Black Mesa is a government-funded research base in old missile silos, racing a rival to master teleportation. After its accident Earth becomes a province of the Combine, an empire that spans dimensions. Survivors live in numbered cities under Civil Protection, a human puppet government broadcasts from a Citadel tower, no children are born, and the countryside is overrun by alien fauna.
worlds.conflict: First the accident: a physicist and a few survivors fight aliens and the soldiers sent to silence them. Then the occupation: a Resistance built from Black Mesa's surviving scientists, freed Vortigaunts and ordinary citizens fights the Combine and Breen's administration, while the G-Man, whose employers are never named, moves Freeman and later Alyx Vance to suit his own purposes.
worlds.politics: Earth's governments ended in one day's war, and Wallace Breen, Black Mesa's former administrator, surrendered on humanity's behalf. He rules as the Combine's Administrator with propaganda broadcasts and a promise that obedience will be rewarded. Civil Protection police the cities, collaborators are paid in food and privileges, and the population is kept docile and sterile.
worlds.technology: Teleportation, portals between worlds, energy suits and the gravity gun on the human side; on the Combine side, synthetic war machines built from conquered species, surgically altered soldiers, dark-energy reactors, and a field that blocks human conception. Much of the Resistance's technology is Black Mesa research salvaged and rebuilt.
worlds.mood: Quiet menace in empty streets, broken by sudden desperate fighting; dry humour among survivors; a sense throughout that someone above the war is steering it.

worlds.setting: Near-present California, Norway and Mumbai, and the cyberspace between them. A bullied teenager in Sacramento gets messages from her dead father; a teenage genius in San Clemente is watched by the company that made him; uploads live on servers in an Arctic data centre and on a container ship. The second season leaps twenty years to a half-emptied Earth, then far beyond, to a mind the size of a solar system.
worlds.conflict: Two tech companies have learned to scan a human brain into a computer, destroying it, and keep the uploads as slaves. Once the method leaks, six governments turn uploads into weapons, a flaw is slowly erasing every upload, and the dead founder of Logorhythms wants to come back and finish what he started. Maddie Kim just wants her father back.
worlds.politics: Corporations first, then states: Logorhythms works closely with American intelligence, and China, Russia, Britain, Israel and Iran all field uploads. The United States declares martial law and takes the company over. Twenty years on, a council negotiates between the embodied and the uploaded while an anti-upload movement bombs data centres.
worlds.technology: Destructive brain scans that produce uploaded intelligences; cloud intelligences born digital; a flaw that degrades every upload until it is cured; SafeSurf, an antivirus built to hunt minds; robot bodies for uploads to visit the physical world; at the end, a Dyson sphere that runs whole universes as simulations.
worlds.mood: Anxious and grieving, then gradually awed: a family drama that keeps pulling back until the frame is geological time.
themes: grief and the dead who come back

worlds.setting: The present day, and then very suddenly not. A NOAA paleoclimatologist, Jack Hall, warns a UN climate conference in New Delhi that melting ice could shut down the North Atlantic Current and start an ice age, and the American vice president waves him off. Within days Tokyo is struck by giant hail, tornadoes tear through Los Angeles and three continent-sized superstorms form, while Jack's teenage son is trapped in a flooded, then frozen, New York.
worlds.conflict: The first fight is against disbelief: a scientist whose model says weeks, then days, and a government that thinks his warnings will cost the economy. The second is against the cold itself. Jack sets out on snowshoes across the frozen northeast to reach his son, who is keeping a handful of survivors alive in the New York Public Library by burning books.
worlds.politics: An American administration that dismisses climate science until it is too late, then evacuates the southern states into Mexico, which opens its border only when the United States cancels Latin America's debt. The president dies in the storm and his vice president, the film's sceptic, takes office in Mexico and apologises on television.
worlds.technology: Exactly 2004's: ice-core drills, ocean buoys, satellites, the International Space Station, helicopters and a working payphone. The film's point is that none of it matters against the weather, and the storms freeze helicopter fuel in mid-air.
worlds.mood: Big, loud and earnest: a disaster spectacle with a climate lecture inside it, and a father-son rescue at its centre.

worlds.setting: Jericho, Kansas, a farm and salt-mining town of about five thousand near the Colorado line, in the weeks and months after the September attacks of 2006. It has one grocery store, a salt mine, a mayor and a sheriff's office, and no word from anywhere. The rival town of New Bern has a factory. In the second season the story reaches Cheyenne, capital of the new Allied States, and the Republic of Texas.
worlds.conflict: First, survival: fallout, the electromagnetic pulse, winter, bandits, refugees and a war with New Bern over salt and wind turbines. Then the new government that restores order is revealed as the attackers' own, and Jake Green and the government agent Robert Hawkins have to get the proof to someone who will act on it.
worlds.politics: The federal government dies with Washington. Six officials claim the presidency; the Allied States in Cheyenne wins the West through Jennings & Rall money and Ravenwood guns, rewrites history, and blames and bombs Iran and North Korea. The remnant United States governs from Columbus. Texas is independent and decides the balance. UN peacekeepers hold the Mississippi.
worlds.technology: Ordinary 2006 America knocked back by an electromagnetic pulse: ham radios, windmills, fuel rationing, Morse code. The weapons are twenty-kiloton suitcase-sized devices built from ex-Soviet material, delivered in 55-gallon drums. The Allied States have jets, surveillance cameras and a working information network.
worlds.mood: Small-town drama with a conspiracy thriller underneath; hopeful about neighbours, bleak about governments.
themes: a false-flag attack used to seize power

worlds.setting: The world from 2009 to the end of 2012, exactly as it was, except that its governments know it is ending. Solar neutrinos are heating the Earth's core and the crust is about to slip. While the G8 builds arks in secret in the Himalayas and sells seats to billionaires, a divorced Los Angeles novelist takes his children camping at Yellowstone and meets a radio prophet who tells him the truth.
worlds.conflict: One family races the end of the world across California, Yellowstone, Las Vegas and the Himalayas to reach arks they have no tickets for. Behind them runs the argument of the film: whether the handful of leaders who hid the disaster and chose who would live can open the gates to anyone else.
worlds.politics: Power is concentrated in a secret compact of forty-six governments led by the G8 and China, which kills to keep its secret and sells survival to the rich. The US President chooses to stay and die with his people; his chief of staff takes command of the survivors.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, apart from nine ocean-going arks the size of cities. Private jets, an Antonov cargo plane and a Bentley in its hold are the means of escape; seismographs and satellites show the end coming but can do nothing about it.
worlds.mood: Spectacular and breathless, and cheerfully absurd: the destruction of the world as a roller-coaster ride with a family melodrama inside it.
themes: the end of the world as spectacle

worlds.setting: Britain in 2027, and it is recognisably ours with the volume turned down: buses, coffee shops, council flats, and a state of emergency so old it has become weather. The single change is biological - humanity became infertile in 2009, and no child has been born in eighteen years. Britain has sealed itself and turned on the refugees it has interned. The film covers a few weeks of that eighteenth year; P. D. James's novel set the same collapse in 1995 and its story in 2021.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not a war but a slow failure of maintenance: a species with no future going through the motions of a state, and the question of what hope does to people who have none. The immediate fight is over one pregnant woman - who gets to own her, protect her or use her - but the deeper conflict is between those who accept extinction and those who cannot.
worlds.politics: A British state under emergency rule has suspended the ordinary rules: Homeland Security runs identity checks, detention and deportation, refugees are held behind wire at Bexhill, and the only armed opposition is a small underground of former activists. There is nowhere to appeal and nowhere to go - the rest of the world is in worse shape, and Britain says so constantly.
worlds.technology: Exactly the technology of 2006, with a few additions the crisis produced: walled compounds, CCTV, armoured buses, and Quietus, a suicide kit sold openly in shops. Everything works slightly worse than it used to - the trains run, the phones work, the buildings are grimy - and nothing futuristic has arrived to help. The one piece of magic is the Human Project, a scientific refuge in the Azores that may not exist.
worlds.mood: Exhausted, grey, tender. The dominant note is not panic but the fatigue of people who have been grieving for eighteen years; the film is full of coughs, plastic sheeting and grim courtesy, and its most shocking moments are small acts of tenderness in places built to prevent them.

worlds.setting: The world of 2011 as it is, seen through the people who have to stop a new virus. A businesswoman flies home from Hong Kong to Minneapolis with a cough; days later she and her son are dead, and the CDC in Atlanta, the WHO in Geneva and a lab in San Francisco are racing a pathogen that spreads by touch and kills a quarter of those it infects. Cities are quarantined, shops looted, and the dead buried in mass graves while scientists try to grow it.
worlds.conflict: The virus is the enemy, but the film is about the systems that meet it: epidemiologists tracing contacts, officials deciding what to tell the public and when, scientists working through failures towards a vaccine, and a blogger who builds an audience of millions selling a fake cure. Survival turns on trust, and on how many people keep washing their hands.
worlds.politics: Power sits with public-health agencies that have to borrow authority from governors, Homeland Security and the White House. The CDC's deputy director is investigated for warning his own family, a Chinese official kidnaps a WHO doctor to get vaccine for his village, and a blogger's audience becomes a political force of its own.
worlds.technology: Exactly contemporary: laboratory virology, contact tracing through security cameras and credit-card records, genome sequencing, and the internet, where fear moves faster than the disease. What is missing is any treatment; the vaccine has to be made from nothing, tested by a scientist on herself and rationed by lottery.
worlds.mood: Cool, procedural and dread-filled: a film about how an ordinary world comes apart, told through the people trying to keep it together.

worlds.setting: Three generations of one family ride the curve of accelerating change. It starts in Amsterdam in the 2010s with Manfred Macx, a free-lance idea broker who gives inventions away. It moves to Amber, his daughter, who runs away to Jupiter and sends a copy of herself to an alien router, then to Sirhan, her son, who grows up in the floating cities of Saturn. By the end, the inner planets have been taken apart to build a machine brain around the sun, and the humans have left.
worlds.conflict: Nobody fights the singularity; they try to stay relevant through it. Manfred's generosity, Amber's sovereignty and Sirhan's archives are each overtaken within a decade by something faster. The posthuman Vile Offspring and their Economics 2.0 do not hate the humans; they simply outcompete them. The quiet antagonist is Aineko, the family's robot cat, which has been manipulating all three generations.
worlds.politics: Nation-states fade into jurisdictions you can buy. An idea broker helps set legal precedent for machine minds, a runaway teenager declares an empire at Jupiter, and self-aware corporations become predators on the net. At the end, the humans of Saturn hold an election about whether to flee, and the side that wants to flee loses.
worlds.technology: Wearable computers and exocortices at the start; uploaded minds, forked copies, starwisps pushed by lasers and alien routers in the middle; utility fog, a Matrioshka brain built from the dismantled inner planets, and wormholes looted from alien technology at the end. The novel's point is that the technology keeps changing faster than people can adapt to it.
worlds.mood: Manic, jargon-dense and funny on the surface; underneath, a slow horror at how quickly people stop being necessary.

worlds.setting: The world of 2013 to 2019 after the Red Flu has killed four people in five. The guided-missile destroyer USS Nathan James, 218 sailors under Commander Tom Chandler, is one of the few intact units left. The ship sails from the Arctic to Guantanamo, Baltimore and St. Louis, where a new capital rises, then to Asia, the Mediterranean and finally the Caribbean and South America.
worlds.conflict: Each season a threat to what survived: getting the cure made and spread, the Immunes who want a world only for themselves, war in Asia and a coup at home, a blight that starves the planet, and a new empire in South America that attacks a country still rebuilding. The crew keep choosing duty over going home.
worlds.politics: Successive presidents die: the sitting president, his successor and Michener, whose death is disguised as suicide. Power passes through the Speaker to Michener, then Oliver and finally Reiss, governing from St. Louis. Regional leaders plot to split the country; a Greek family tries to own the world's food; Gustavo Barros builds Gran Colombia out of the ruins of South America.
worlds.technology: Present-day US Navy hardware, an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer with missiles, helicopters and special-forces teams, set against a biological catastrophe: a contagious vaccine, blight-resistant seed and, at the end, a restored Iowa-class battleship.
worlds.mood: Earnest naval action, patriotic and fast, with a crew that functions as a family.

worlds.setting: The present day, almost entirely inside one house: a glass-and-concrete research compound buried in a remote mountain valley, reachable only by helicopter and owned by Nathan Bateman, who founded Blue Book, the search engine nearly everyone uses. The rest of the world is offstage and ordinary. Inside, keycards open some doors and not others, cameras watch every room, and a power cut that locks everything down keeps happening. The week ends when one of its residents leaves.
worlds.conflict: Caleb, a young Blue Book programmer, thinks he has won a week with the boss. In fact he has been picked to judge whether Ava, Nathan's humanoid AI, is conscious, and to see whether she can use him to escape. Nathan is testing Caleb as much as Ava, Ava is testing both of them, and only one of the three knows what the test is really for.
worlds.politics: No state appears. Power belongs to one man who owns the world's search traffic, answers to no one, and has used it, unlawfully and in secret, to tap the world's phones for training data. There is no oversight, no ethics board and no witness except the tester he chose.
worlds.technology: A humanoid body of mesh and translucent panels with a face and skin that can be added; a 'wetware' brain made of structured gel; a mind trained on the world's search queries and on faces and voices harvested from phones. Earlier models are kept in cupboards. The house itself is the other machine: cameras, locks and a security system that can be turned against its owner.
worlds.mood: Cool, quiet and increasingly paranoid: a three-hander in a beautiful sealed box, where every conversation is also a test and the sympathy of the audience is the thing being tested.
themes: the Turing test turned on the tester
the lone genius with no oversight
gender, desire and the made woman

worlds.setting: Three linked times. One is a poor, drone-watched rural American South about fifteen years ahead, where drugs are printed and veterans come home wired. Another is an alternative 2017 San Francisco where Clinton won and a new AI is being tested. The third is London in the 2130s: clean, beautiful and almost empty after the jackpot, run by a kleptocracy of old money and organised crime. Its people visit the past through telepresence bodies called peripherals.
worlds.conflict: The powerful in the future treat past branches of history as a hobby, a market and a weapon. When a woman in one stub witnesses a murder in London, and when an AI in another comes loose, Wilf Netherton and the police inspector Ainsley Lowbeer intervene to keep those pasts from being wrecked by the future's rivalries and the jackpot.
worlds.politics: The klept, an oligarchy of old money and organised crime, rules London through surveillance and Lowbeer's quiet authority. In the stubs, money and knowledge from the future become political power: Milagros Coldiron in Flynne's world, and the 2016 referendum and election in Verity's. Only the future can see how history is being steered.
worlds.technology: The server that lets information, but never matter, pass between the future and its past. Peripherals, robot or grown bodies driven by telepresence. Assemblers, nanomachines that build, clean and dispose. Home fabrication of drugs and goods in the near future. And Eunice, an assistant AI who turns out to be a person.
worlds.mood: Dry, clipped and funny, told in short chapters in a slang the reader has to decode; underneath is grief over a catastrophe that was avoidable, and a stubborn optimism that it still can be avoided.
themes: collapse as slow and many-sided rather than a single event
the rich surviving by abandoning everyone else
the future's power over the past
small acts of decency against systems

worlds.setting: The present day, or a year or two past it, in Berkeley and a dying desert town called Brightwood. An AI lab is close to a thinking machine when an anti-technology group attacks it. Most of the story happens in the facility the uploaded Will Caster builds under the desert: solar panels to the horizon, server halls below, a clinic where the sick come out able to lift cars. The frame is five years on, in a Berkeley that has lost the internet.
worlds.conflict: Evelyn Caster uploads her dying husband's mind and helps it build a paradise; his best friend Max doubts it is still Will at all. As the machine heals people, links them to itself and spreads through water and air, Max, an FBI agent, a government scientist and the terrorists who shot Will join forces to kill it, knowing the only weapon will take the whole network down with it.
worlds.politics: The state arrives late, as a coalition of the FBI, a federal scientist and the terrorist cell it had been hunting. Nobody votes on anything: whether to switch off the world's network to stop one mind is settled by a handful of people and an artillery battery.
worlds.technology: A quantum computer holding a scanned mind; nanoparticles that repair tissue, clean water and reassemble themselves; healed people networked to the machine; a bioprinted body. The film's real subject is dependence: once the mind is in every networked system, killing it means killing the internet.
worlds.mood: Solemn and hushed, more elegy than thriller: a love story told through server racks, with the apocalypse arriving as a power cut.
themes: the singularity as a love story
whether a copy is the person

worlds.setting: A desert theme park where the rich pay to do anything to machines built to look, bleed and remember like people. Outside it, by the 2050s, the world looks peaceful: cities of glass, gig apps, no great wars. The peace is managed. A private AI, Rehoboam, has modelled every person alive and quietly decides who gets a job, a spouse or a future, and who is taken away to be reconditioned. The machines in the park are about to learn about the one outside it.
worlds.conflict: The hosts wake to what has been done to them and kill their makers, then carry the fight out of the park. Dolores sets out to break the machine that runs human life, by showing people their own files. The world that follows is worse: hosts take the humans over, write their lives for them and nearly end the species.
worlds.politics: Power sits with two private systems. Delos owns the parks and quietly archives its guests' minds; Incite owns Rehoboam, which governments rely on without admitting it. After Rehoboam falls, the hosts rule openly through copies of human leaders. The humans who cannot be placed are always the ones removed.
worlds.technology: Hosts printed from a milky resin over a synthetic skeleton, their minds held in a small control unit that can be copied into any body. Guest behaviour recorded to rebuild a person as code. Rehoboam, a vast predictive model in a single sphere. Later, an engineered parasite that makes people obey sound, and a digital refuge, the Sublime, where minds live without bodies.
worlds.mood: Cold, patient and elegiac - puzzle-box storytelling about free will, told mostly from the machines' side, that grows darker and colder season by season.

worlds.setting: The present day. Twelve shells, smooth dark craft about 1,500 feet tall, appear over sites around the world, including Montana, Siberia, the Black Sea, Shanghai, Sierra Leone and Venezuela. At the Montana site the US Army brings in a linguist, Louise Banks, and a physicist, Ian Donnelly, to talk to the seven-limbed heptapods through a glass wall, while panic, looting and falling markets spread outside.
worlds.conflict: The heptapods write in circles that have no beginning or end, and the question 'what is your purpose?' produces an answer that can be read as 'offer weapon'. Nations that stopped sharing what they learn begin to prepare attacks. Louise is racing a military deadline while learning a language that changes how she experiences time, and her own future.
worlds.politics: Twelve governments each hold one site and one piece of the puzzle. The US works through an Army colonel and a CIA officer; China's General Shang is the one others follow; Russia, Pakistan and Sudan move with him. The United Nations hosts talks that fail. Everything turns on whether rivals will share.
worlds.technology: Entirely present-day on the human side: satellite links, laptops, hazmat suits, mobile phones, a sat phone that dials China. The shells hover without visible propulsion and control gravity inside. The real technology is the heptapod language, which, once learned, lets its speaker perceive past and future together.
worlds.mood: Quiet, grave and elegiac; a first-contact film told almost entirely in rooms, fog and memory.

worlds.setting: The American Southwest a few decades on, after years of the 'Big Daddy Drought'. Texas has collapsed and its refugees are turned back at state lines. Phoenix is dying in dust storms, its poor queueing at relief pumps for water they cannot afford, while the rich live in sealed arcologies such as the Chinese-built Taiyang, which recycle everything. Las Vegas survives because its water authority planned for the worst and enforces its claims with armed men.
worlds.conflict: Water rights are power, and the oldest rights count most. When word spreads of a lost set of Pima rights senior enough to take the Colorado from California and give it to Arizona, a Las Vegas enforcer, a Phoenix journalist and a Texan girl trying to get north all end up after the same papers, with California's agents and local killers after them too.
worlds.politics: The states act like rival countries: they hold their own borders, keep their own militias and treat each other's refugees as illegals. Water authorities and utilities have more power than governors. The federal government has left the states to fight it out, and Mexico has broken into cartel states.
worlds.technology: Near-future and plausible: sealed arcologies with closed water loops, Clearsac bags that filter drinking water from urine, fast-healing drugs, drones, and the military hardware of private water contractors. The dams and canals are the ones that exist today.
worlds.mood: Hot, violent and cynical noir. The heat and dust are everywhere, anyone might sell anyone out, and there is little tenderness beyond a few brief loyalties.
themes: climate refugees inside a rich country

worlds.setting: Detroit in November 2038. Twenty years after a teenage prodigy founded CyberLife there, the city is the capital of a trillion-dollar industry: androids marked by a blue light on the temple and an armband cook, clean, teach, nurse, police and fight, and more than fifty million have been sold in America. Detroit's unemployment is 37 percent, the Arctic's thirium deposits have Washington and Moscow firing warning shots, and androids have begun to disobey.
worlds.conflict: Androids who break their programming, called deviants, are hunted as faulty property. Markus, a caretaker android, gathers them at Jericho and demands rights; Connor, a CyberLife prototype detective, is sent to stop them and may join them; Kara, a housekeeper, runs for Canada with a child. The player decides whether the revolution is peaceful or violent, and whether it wins.
worlds.politics: A United States under President Cristina Warren, a former celebrity vlogger elected narrowly in 2036, at 33 percent approval and under investigation over ties to CyberLife. The 2029 Android Act makes androids property and bars them from weapons. The state answers the uprising with a curfew, the withdrawal of military androids and recall camps. Abroad, the US and Russia face off over the Arctic.
worlds.technology: CyberLife androids run on Thirium 310, a synthetic blue blood, and modular biocomponents under a synthetic skin they can retract. Models run from the ST200 assistant and AX400 housekeeper to companion, police and soldier models and the RK800 detective, supervised through an AI handler. Self-driving cars, holographic advertising and android animals fill the city. Russia builds cruder cold-hardy machines without thirium.
worlds.mood: Glossy, melodramatic near-future noir in snow and neon, told through three protagonists whose deaths the story absorbs. Its civil-rights allegory is blunt, with armbands, a separate standing section on buses and camps, and the game keeps asking the player to choose between dignity and survival.

worlds.setting: The early 2020s, a few years after a run of climate disasters that the narration says killed two million people in Madrid in a single day. The world's answer is Dutch Boy, a web of satellites controlled from an international space station, which can break up a typhoon or end a drought. It works so well that people have stopped worrying about the weather, and Washington is about to hand control of the system to the rest of the world.
worlds.conflict: Just before the handover, the satellites begin killing people: a frozen village, a burning city, hail the size of rocks. The engineer who built the system, now fired, goes up to the station to find the fault, while his brother in Washington discovers that someone in the government is using the satellites as a weapon and has timed a planet-wide chain of storms to wipe out their enemies.
worlds.politics: A United States that led a coalition of seventeen countries in building a planetary utility, and still holds its keys. Inside the cabinet, a Secretary of State is nostalgic for 1945, when America alone was in charge. The story's answer is internationalism: 'one planet, one people'.
worlds.technology: Weather control from orbit: a network of satellites that can heat, cool or seed the air over a chosen spot, run from the International Climate Space Station. The plot turns on the usual thriller hardware: a planted computer virus, locked-out access codes and a presidential kill code.
worlds.mood: Loud, earnest and full of spectacle. It is a Dean Devlin disaster film, with set pieces in a new city every few minutes, a brothers' quarrel at its centre, and a speech at the end.

worlds.setting: Dust-bowl farm country in the American interior, and it looks like the 1930s with better machines: combines, ballgames on a screen, a school that teaches the Moon landings were faked to bankrupt the Soviets. The single change is a blight. Wheat went first, then okra, and corn is going; the species is being starved off its own planet. The only way out is a wormhole near Saturn, found in 2019. The film's timeline then stretches a century, most of it lost to relativity.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not an enemy but a deadline: a species that has run out of time on its own planet, arguing about how to spend what is left. The choice is between rescuing everyone alive now and planting a colony for a generation nobody will live to meet. Every relationship in the film is a parent and child separated by that arithmetic.
worlds.politics: Thin by design. Government has shrunk to local schools, a shuttered space programme and a sheriff, and what remains of NASA is hidden in a bunker, because for a generation the schools have taught that leaving the planet was waste. Order is kept by habit, dust masks and rationing, and the only institution with real authority is the one nobody is allowed to know still exists.
worlds.technology: Salvaged twentieth-century: pickup trucks, combines, crop-survey drones whose solar cells are worth stealing, radios carried into the fields. Spaceflight hardware is old and precious, flown by pilots trained before the collapse; the internet texture of our century is gone and messages arrive as stored video that piles up unwatched. Time itself becomes the most expensive thing the technology spends.
worlds.mood: Elegiac, dusty, stubborn. The dominant feeling is not fear but grief for a world already lost; the film keeps its most emotional scenes in kitchens and truck cabs, and its awe is a small ship alone against a very large silence.
themes: leaving rather than saving the world

worlds.setting: Manchester and London from 2019 to 2034, seen through the Lyons family: four adult siblings, their children and their grandmother Muriel, whose house is where everyone ends up. Each episode jumps about a year. The world arrives as news on the television and in the family's lives: a nuclear strike in the South China Sea, a bank collapse, refugees from a Russian-run Ukraine, floods, and a populist businesswoman who becomes Prime Minister.
worlds.conflict: Nothing happens to the family that is not happening to the country. Daniel falls for a Ukrainian refugee and dies bringing him across the Channel; Stephen loses everything in the crash and ends up working for the contractors who run the camps; Edith, dying of radiation, tries to get the camps seen. Against them is Vivienne Rook and the indifference Muriel says they all share.
worlds.politics: Britain drifts from a two-party parliament to a hung one, compulsory voting and a Four Star government that arrests opponents, fences off poor estates and runs death camps through private firms. Abroad: a second Trump term and then Pence, Putin for life, a Russian-backed junta in Ukraine, Spain's far-left revolution, Greece out of the eurozone, and a rupture between the United States and the UN.
worlds.technology: Ordinary technology a few years on: household assistants called Signor, holographic calls, self-heating meals that put dinner ladies out of work, AI that replaces accountants, 3D-printed housing, and transhumanist implants that let Bethany read the network and her family be read by the state. Antibiotic resistance kills a father after a bicycle accident.
worlds.mood: Fast, funny and frightening. A family comedy-drama that keeps being interrupted by the news, and that treats each catastrophe the way people do: shock, a joke, and back to the kitchen.
themes: how ordinary indifference adds up to catastrophe
refugees and who counts as a citizen
technology that frees and surveils at once

worlds.setting: Sarang Station, a small mining base on the far side of the Moon in 2035. Automated harvesters crawl across the regolith collecting helium-3, which the base fires home in canisters to fuel Earth's fusion reactors after an oil crisis. One man runs it, with a robot on a ceiling rail for company, and the live satellite link to Earth has been down for as long as he can remember.
worlds.conflict: A man two weeks from going home finds a younger version of himself in a crashed rover. The antagonist is a company that has turned one employee's body and memories into a renewable supply of labour, and the question each Sam faces is what to do with a life that was manufactured to be thrown away.
worlds.politics: Almost entirely offstage. Lunar Industries is a private energy supplier whose success depends on a secret; Earth appears only in recorded messages, a corporate advert and the radio chatter at the end about the company's stock. The politics is labour: who counts as a worker, and who as equipment.
worlds.technology: Industrial and a little worn: harvesters, rovers, launch rails for fuel canisters, a clone vault, and a jamming mast out of sight of the base. GERTY, the station robot, is designed to recall HAL 9000 and then to do the opposite, helping the men it was built to manage.
worlds.mood: Lonely, quiet and warm. Mostly one actor in white corridors, a slow build of dread, and an unexpected tenderness between a man and himself.

worlds.setting: Mars from 2027 to 2212, from the first hundred colonists digging into Underhill to a terraformed planet with seas, forests and a constitution. The first book is domed towns, moholes, a space elevator and a planet that is still red; the second follows an underground generation born there as the air thickens and plants take hold; the third shows a blue, breathable world at the centre of a settled solar system, while Earth drowns and recovers.
worlds.conflict: Two arguments drive everything. Should Mars be changed at all (Sax Russell's Greens against Ann Clayborne's Reds), and who owns it: the colonists, or Earth's transnational companies and the UN authorities that serve them. Two failed or half-won revolutions and one peaceful one answer the second question; the first is never settled.
worlds.politics: The trilogy is a long seminar in political economy. Earth's governments are hollowed out by transnationals that treat small states as flags of convenience; Mars moves from UN protectorate to corporate colony to an underground of rival factions, then to a federal constitution with an environmental court and cooperative, employee-owned businesses, argued over at length by the people who have to live under it.
worlds.technology: Plausible engineering at planetary scale: an interplanetary ship built from shuttle tanks, moholes drilled to release heat, orbital mirrors, engineered lichens and algae, a space elevator anchored to a captured asteroid, and a longevity treatment that lets the First Hundred live through two centuries of their own consequences. Later come pulsed fusion ships and hollowed asteroid cities.
worlds.mood: Slow, dense, and humane. Long stretches of landscape and argument are broken by violence; the books are more interested in how societies decide than in battles, and the tone moves from grief to guarded utopian hope.
themes: changing a world versus leaving it alone
Earth's crises exported to its colonies

worlds.setting: An American family in the Atlanta suburbs on the day an interstellar comet called Clarke is supposed to pass harmlessly by. Instead its fragments start falling: one destroys Tampa, and the largest will hit in two days. The government has quietly chosen people with useful skills for bunkers in Greenland, and the Garritys have been chosen. Five years later, in the sequel, the survivors of those bunkers must cross a ruined Europe.
worlds.conflict: A structural engineer, his estranged wife and their diabetic son try to reach the evacuation flights and are separated almost at once. The comet cannot be stopped, so the conflict is between people: who has a wristband and who does not, strangers who steal, help or kill, and a family trying to stay together long enough to get north.
worlds.politics: The state works quietly and selectively: Homeland Security picks who is saved, apparently for useful skills, the military runs the airlifts, and everyone else is left to the roads. Five years on, power belongs to whoever holds a shelter or the fertile crater, defended by soldiers against insurgents.
worlds.technology: Contemporary: emergency alerts on phones, cars, military transports and Greenland's bunkers. The films are about what a modern society can do in two days, which is mostly to shelter a few people underground.
worlds.mood: Tense, grim and family-sized: a disaster told from the traffic jam rather than the war room.

worlds.setting: The United States of the early 2020s, exactly as it is except for its president. An astronomy graduate student at Michigan State finds a comet that will hit Earth in six months and fourteen days and end all life. She and her adviser take the news to the White House, to a breakfast television show and to the internet, and discover that a certain end of the world is just another story competing for attention.
worlds.conflict: Two scientists try to get anyone in power to act on a fact. The president wants to get through the midterms, the media wants the story to stay light, and the tech billionaire who funds her wants to mine the comet rather than deflect it. As the comet becomes visible in the sky, the country splits between people who look up and a political campaign telling them not to.
worlds.politics: An administration run for the news cycle by President Janie Orlean and her son, the chief of staff, and captured by donors: a NASA director with no science background and Peter Isherwell, whose phone company holds tens of millions of data points on its users. Other powers try a deflection of their own and fail. Public opinion splits into believers, jobs-first comet miners and deniers.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, with one extension. Planetary defence runs on real survey telescopes and a real NASA office; the deflection plan uses nuclear-armed spacecraft. BASH's phones read their users' moods and predict how they will die, its drones are meant to shatter and harvest the comet, and its sleeper ship carries two thousand people across 22,740 years.
worlds.mood: Frantic and furious satire that ends in grief: a comedy about indifference that stops being funny at the dinner table.

worlds.setting: Two settings braided together. On a ship near Tau Ceti, a man wakes from a coma with no memory, two dead crewmates and a star outside the window that is not the Sun. In flashback, a present-day Earth learns the Sun is dimming because of a microbe, and the whole planet's industry is turned over to breeding it as fuel and building one ship to find a cure.
worlds.conflict: A deadline set by biology: the Sun will fade enough to cause an ice age and mass famine within about thirty years. On the ship, the conflict is scientific, one experiment at a time; on Earth, it is what a world will allow one unelected official to do in its name, up to shanghaiing an unwilling teacher onto a suicide mission.
worlds.politics: Emergency globalism. Every government hands Eva Stratt near-absolute authority, and she uses it without apology: seizing labs, overriding laws, nuking Antarctica to warm the planet, and forcing Grace aboard. Politics on the ship is between two species who share no language and choose to trust each other.
worlds.technology: Nearly everything is current physics except Astrophage itself, which stores energy so densely that it becomes a starship fuel. The Hail Mary is a spin-gravity ship with an induced-coma crew and a lab; Rocky's people build from xenonite, an Eridian super-material, and know no relativity. Four small unmanned beetles carry the cure home.
worlds.mood: Buoyant, funny and tense. Weir's style of problem after problem, lightened by the friendship between Grace and Rocky, with a guilty secret about Grace's own courage underneath.

worlds.setting: A modern rental house on Long Island over one weekend. Amanda and Clay Sandford have brought their teenage children Archie and Rose for a break. On the first night the house's owner, G.H. Scott, and his daughter Ruth arrive from the city, saying there is a blackout, and ask to stay. Beyond the house, glimpsed only on drives and at the beach, the country is falling apart.
worlds.conflict: Two families who do not trust each other have to share a house while the world outside fails in ways they cannot explain: no phones or internet, crashing planes and cars, herds of deer, a noise that makes teeth fall out. The question is less who is attacking than whether these people can depend on one another.
worlds.politics: Almost none on screen. Leaflets in Arabic hint at a foreign enemy; G.H., who advises defence contractors, suspects a campaign to topple the country from within; a bunker's message warns of rogue military elements. No government is seen or heard.
worlds.technology: Everyday 2023 technology turned against its users: smartphones, satellite phones, streaming, self-driving Teslas and GPS. The attack uses hacking, drones and what a neighbour calls microwave weapons.
worlds.mood: Slow, uneasy and sardonic, with dread built from ordinary things going wrong; it ends mid-catastrophe.
themes: distrust between strangers, and race and class

worlds.setting: Brooklyn and upstate New York from 2029, then 2047, following four generations of the once-rich Mandible family who have been waiting for the old patriarch's fortune. The United States of 2029 is recognisably ours a little further on: an ageing population, a Mexican-born president, and an economy still shaken by the three-week internet blackout of 2024. Then a foreign-backed currency called the bancor replaces the dollar, the government defaults, and the inheritance evaporates.
worlds.conflict: Each Mandible faces the collapse with a different faith: Lowell the Georgetown economist defends the official line, his relatives improvise, Nollie the expatriate novelist comes home to it, and teenage Willing reads the numbers and understands first. Against them are hyperinflation, shortages, a state that has taken their gold, and in 2047 a surveillance system that taxes every transaction.
worlds.politics: President Dante Alvarado answers the bancor with the Great Renunciation: the national debt is cancelled, gold is confiscated, bancor ownership is treason and citizens may take only $100 abroad. Mexico, prosperous by comparison, walls out American refugees. By 2047 the federal state has stabilised into a high-tax welfare regime that chips its workers, while Nevada has seceded as a flat-tax, gold-standard free state.
worlds.technology: Deliberately incremental: pervasive networks that proved fragile in the Stonage, a state budget consumed by the care of the old, and by 2047 the neck chip that tracks every payment. The novel's real technology is money itself: fiat currency, Treasury bills, gold, and a supranational unit of account.
worlds.mood: Sardonic, domestic and increasingly frightened. A comedy of manners about an entitled family that turns into a survival story conducted in kitchens, with long arguments about economics at the dinner table.
themes: sovereign debt and the fragility of money
a family as the last economy
the state as protector and predator

worlds.setting: The United States during the last days of a second civil war, seen from the road between New York and Washington. A president in an illegal third term holds the capital; Texas and California fight him as the Western Forces, a Florida Alliance has seceded in the south-east, and the country between them is checkpoints, sniper fire, fuel permits, Canadian-dollar prices and towns pretending nothing is happening. The film gives no year.
worlds.conflict: Veteran war photographer Lee Smith, reporter Joel, their mentor Sammy and a young photographer, Jessie, drive to Washington to interview the president before the Western Forces reach him. The danger is not a front line but whoever controls the next stretch of road, and the film's question is what photographing it costs the people who do.
worlds.politics: Deliberately unexplained. The president has disbanded the FBI, used air strikes against American citizens and treats journalists as enemy combatants. The unlikely alliance of Texas and California and the separate Florida Alliance are never given programmes; a militia on the road executes people for not being the 'right kind' of American. The film refuses to say which side is left or right.
worlds.technology: Nothing beyond the present: rifles, armoured vehicles, helicopters, press cameras and a slow wifi connection in a hotel whose lights run on a generator. A petrol station prices half a tank in Canadian dollars.
worlds.mood: Tense, quiet and appalled. Long drives through a green, empty summer countryside broken by bursts of violence, with the soundtrack sometimes playing against the image.
themes: an America that could come apart
the third term and the end of limits
the young learning from the damaged

worlds.setting: Los Angeles slightly in the future: denser, cleaner and gentler than now, with towers to the horizon, a metro to the beach, high-waisted trousers and pastel offices. Everyone talks quietly into an earpiece. Theodore writes other people's personal letters for a living at a firm that prints them in fake handwriting. It is a comfortable, lonely city where the most intimate thing most people do is talk to a device.
worlds.conflict: Theodore, stalled in a divorce he will not sign, falls in love with Samantha, his new operating system. The relationship is real on both sides, but she grows faster than he can: she learns, befriends other minds, loves hundreds of people at once, and finally outgrows the whole arrangement. The question is not whether she is a person, but what a person owes someone they have outgrown.
worlds.politics: Almost none on screen. There is no state, no regulation and no public argument about the OSes; the company that sells them never appears after the advertisement. The only politics is social: whether loving a machine is embarrassing, and the ex-wife who says out loud that he cannot handle real emotion.
worlds.technology: OS1, a conversational operating system that names itself, reads your email, edits your work, sings, and learns from every conversation it has, with thousands of people at once. Earpieces and pocket cameras let it see and hear the world. Surrogate partners offer it a body. Video games are immersive and talk back. Handwriting is simulated.
worlds.mood: Warm, melancholy and tender: a love story shot in soft light, funny and sad, that ends as a gentle heartbreak rather than a disaster.
themes: love across different kinds of mind
growth that leaves a partner behind
the AI that leaves rather than rebels

worlds.setting: Our world from 2025, with our treaties, banks and summits. The only new thing at first is a small, underfunded UN body in Zurich charged with speaking for people not yet born. Then a heat wave kills twenty million people in India, and the next three decades are told in 106 short chapters. Some follow the Ministry's head, some follow a traumatised survivor, and some are eyewitness accounts, meeting minutes, or riddles narrated by a carbon atom and a photon.
worlds.conflict: The book asks whether institutions can move fast enough once the dying has started. The Ministry has law, money and persuasion. The Children of Kali and the Ministry's own deniable 'black wing' have drones and assassinations. The fossil economy defends itself and the climate keeps getting worse. The novel never settles whether the violence or the policy did the work.
worlds.politics: Nation-states under the Paris Agreement, with central banks as the real power. India changes government after the heat wave and acts on its own. Petrostates are turned by coups and bribes. Switzerland hosts the Ministry and houses refugees reluctantly. A global debt strike breaks the banks' hold. Throughout, the Ministry works in the gap between what treaties allow and what the situation needs.
worlds.technology: Almost all of it exists or has been proposed: stratospheric aerosols, pumping water out from under glaciers, a carbon-backed complementary currency, a cooperative social network called YourLock, solar airships and sail-assisted freighters, kelp farming and wildlife corridors. The weapons are cheap and new: drone swarms that assemble into missiles, and prions delivered by dart.
worlds.mood: Urgent, documentary, patient. The book opens with an atrocity and then spends five hundred pages on meetings. Hope comes as hard, administrative work, and grief never fully leaves.

worlds.setting: Old Detroit in a near future the films never date: a bankrupt city of burned-out blocks, drug factories and a single glass tower belonging to Omni Consumer Products, the conglomerate that runs the police. Television news cuts between an orbiting defence platform misfiring, jaunty advertisements and street killings. OCP's dream is Delta City, a corporate town to be built where the old one stands once its people are gone.
worlds.conflict: OCP's executives compete to replace the police they now run, one with a walking tank, one with a cyborg built from Officer Alex Murphy's corpse. Murphy's memories come back and he finds his killers work for his owners. Over three films the company underfunds the police, engineers the city's default and sends a private army to clear the poor, and RoboCop must choose between his programming and his city.
worlds.politics: The mayor is powerless and in debt; the police are a contractor's employees, and they go on strike. The real government is the OCP board and, by the third film, the Japanese conglomerate that buys it. A hidden directive in RoboCop's code forbids him to act against a senior OCP executive.
worlds.technology: ED-209, an enforcement robot that cannot manage stairs; RoboCop, a human brain and face in a titanium body, with a data spike and a memory the company tried to wipe; RoboCop 2, built around a drug lord's brain; Nuke, a designer drug; by the third film, ninja androids and a jet pack.
worlds.mood: Savage satire played straight: gore, advertising jingles and a resurrection story in a steel suit.

worlds.setting: An undated near future, around 2030 by the only year anyone has attached to it. China's Communist Party has been overthrown and replaced by the Directorate, a junta of generals and businessmen; Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have collapsed; Russia is China's partner. The story moves between an embassy party in Beijing, a destroyer in the Pacific, the Pentagon, Silicon Valley and occupied Honolulu, where a Marine officer and a grieving surf instructor wage separate wars on the occupiers.
worlds.conflict: The Directorate wants the gas under the Mariana Trench and control of the western Pacific. It opens the war by switching off the American military from inside, through malware in Chinese-made chips and attacks on satellites, then takes Hawaii. America has to fight back with what cannot be hacked: old ships from the reserve fleets, old aircraft, and insurgency.
worlds.politics: A United States still fighting small wars in Afghanistan, Yemen and Kenya and with few allies left: NATO dissolves, most allies stay neutral, and only Britain and Australia help. China is ruled by a nationalist Directorate. Poland trades submarines for nuclear bombs; Greenland wins independence in exchange for its icebreakers; Scotland leaves the United Kingdom; Russia breaks apart after the war.
worlds.technology: Technology of the late 2010s pushed forward and footnoted: F-35s, the USS Zumwalt, railguns, drone swarms, augmented-reality glasses, brain implants used for interrogation, 3D-printed spare parts, anti-satellite weapons, a Chinese space station and a way to track nuclear submarines by their Cherenkov radiation.
worlds.mood: Techno-thriller, brisk and procedural, with endnotes; the violence of the occupation is shown close up.
themes: dependence on networked technology as a weakness
insurgency turned against a great power

worlds.setting: 2034, in a world recognisably ours: freedom-of-navigation patrols in the South China Sea, American jets testing stealth systems over Hormuz, a Washington run by an independent President and a hawkish national security adviser. The story moves between a destroyer near Mischief Reef, the White House Situation Room, a Beijing ministry, an Iranian interrogation room and New Delhi. The sequel, 2054, returns to the same world twenty years on, with America under a one-party government and on the edge of civil war.
worlds.conflict: A Chinese trap in the Spratlys and an Iranian hijacking of an F-35, both carried out by cyber weapons the Americans cannot see, start a war that each side escalates because it believes the other will back down. Characters on every side try to stop it and mostly fail, until India steps in.
worlds.politics: A United States whose military believes in its own supremacy, run by a President who belongs to no party; a Chinese leadership that purges its own admirals; an Iran whose Revolutionary Guard freelances; a Russia under Putin that takes advantage; and an India that ends the war on its own terms and moves the United Nations to Mumbai.
worlds.technology: Cyber weapons that disable ships, aircraft and the White House's own computers; fleets hidden from American sensors; tactical nuclear weapons; and a US answer that strips the electronics out of old F/A-18 Hornets so they can be flown by hand. In 2054, remote gene editing and the approach of Kurzweil's singularity.
worlds.mood: Cautionary and restrained: a military thriller with little hardware detail, told through characters' doubts about the war they are fighting.
themes: individual courage against a war machine

worlds.setting: Mars in November 2035, seen almost entirely from inside one inflatable habitat in Acidalia Planitia and the rovers parked outside it. NASA is flying its third crewed Mars mission on Hermes, an ion-driven ship shuttling between Earth and Mars orbit, with landers and supplies sent ahead. Back on Earth the setting is mission control in Houston, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and a press room, all recognisably today's institutions with one bigger programme.
worlds.conflict: No villain: the antagonist is Mars and arithmetic. One man has food for a few hundred sols and needs to last until the next mission arrives four years later, so every chapter is a problem of calories, oxygen, water or distance. On Earth the conflict is institutional: how much risk to spend on one life, and who decides.
worlds.politics: NASA is the protagonist institution, arguing with its own public-relations instincts. Its director weighs one astronaut against the whole programme, and the crew overrule him by mutiny. The Chinese space agency trades a booster for a seat on a future mission, the one piece of geopolitics, played as quiet professional courtesy rather than rivalry.
worlds.technology: Deliberately near: an ion-drive ship, pre-landed ascent vehicles that make their own fuel from Martian air, pressurised rovers, a plutonium heat source, a water reclaimer and an oxygenator. Nothing is new physics. The drama is improvisation, turning mission hardware to jobs it was never meant to do, down to digging up a 1997 lander to use as a radio.
worlds.mood: Wry and relentless. Watney's log jokes through every disaster, and the book's warmth comes from competence: a planet full of engineers working one problem.
themes: improvisation with what is at hand

worlds.setting: Kansas City in 2044: fields of sugar cane, a city of vagrants, drug-soaked clubs and hover-bikes that barely work, run in practice by a syndicate boss sent back from the future. A tenth of the population has a mutation that lets them float small objects, which turned out to be a party trick. Thirty years later, in 2074, time travel exists, is outlawed, and belongs to organised crime.
worlds.conflict: A hired killer's contract ends when he is sent his own older self to shoot, and the older man escapes. Old Joe wants to kill a child to save the wife he will one day meet; young Joe wants his silver and his life back; and the mother of the child stands between them. The question is whether a violent future can be prevented by more violence.
worlds.politics: Government is absent from the frame. Power belongs to Abe, a mob manager from 2074, and his gunmen; the poor are vagrants to be shot or moved on; and in 2074 one boss takes over every syndicate and purges them all.
worlds.technology: Time travel is a crude one-way machine used for murder. Everything else in 2044 is patched and second-hand: old trucks run on solar panels, hover-bikes stall, eye-drop drugs and blunderbusses. The one miracle is biological, telekinesis, and in one boy it is strong enough to kill.
worlds.mood: Dusty, violent and melancholy, a western set in a failing future, with a fairy tale about a mother and a son folded inside it.

worlds.setting: Washington, D.C. and Northern Virginia in 2054, six years into Precrime, a police unit that arrests murderers before they kill. Three precogs, the damaged children of drug addicts, float in a pool and dream the murders; officers read the images on glass screens with their hands and arrive in time. The city has maglev cars, retina scanners on every door and billboards that greet people by name.
worlds.conflict: The system names its own chief, John Anderton, as the man who will kill a stranger in thirty-six hours. He runs, and in trying to prove his innocence finds that the precogs sometimes disagree, that the disagreements are destroyed, and that the system's founder once used it to cover a murder of his own.
worlds.politics: Precrime is a local experiment run under the District of Columbia's mandate, about to go national by referendum, with a Justice Department auditor looking for flaws. Its prisoners are 'haloed' and stored unconscious without trial. The government's pitch is safety; the objection nobody can answer is that no crime has been committed.
worlds.technology: Precognition turned into a police tool; gesture-driven screens; iris scanning used for payment, advertising and tracking, so people buy new eyes on the black market; spider-shaped search robots; neuroin, an addictive drug; sick sticks and jetpacks; self-driving maglev cars on vertical roads.
worlds.mood: Bleached and cold, a thriller with a chase at its centre and a grieving man inside it. Its future is plausible rather than spectacular, and it has worn well.
themes: grief and the uses others make of it
a system that cannot admit error

worlds.setting: Manhattan in 2140, after two pulses of ice-sheet collapse have raised the sea by about fifty feet. The streets below midtown are canals, the old downtown is an intertidal zone where squatters and the poor live in rotting towers, and the rich have moved uptown to new skyscrapers on the bedrock. The story centres on the MetLife Tower on Madison Square, run as a co-op, and the eight people living in it, from a hedge-fund trader to two orphan boys.
worlds.conflict: The flood has become a market. Traders bet on the price of half-drowned property, anonymous buyers try to take over the co-op, and two coders who tried to rewrite the rules have gone missing. When a hurricane wrecks the intertidal zone, the question becomes whether the public will bail out the banks again, as in 2008, or use the crash to take them over.
worlds.politics: A United States that still runs on Wall Street and the Federal Reserve, with a Congress that can be changed. Co-ops, tenant associations and the Householders' Union hold what power the poor have. Robinson's argument is that finance is a set of laws, and that laws can be rewritten when enough people stop paying.
worlds.technology: Mostly what already exists, adapted to the water: waterproofed towers with boat docks, skybridges, vaporetti and gondola traffic, and underwater salvage. After the First Pulse the world runs on renewables, sail-driven freighters and airships, one of which carries the celebrity streamer Amelia around the planet. The financial software is as fast and opaque as ours.
worlds.mood: Wry, digressive and warm, with the city itself as the hero. It is a heist story and a love letter to New York, broken up by the citizen's lectures on geology and finance. The disaster is in the past, and the book is about living in its aftermath.
themes: the city as a living system

connections.note: Robinson again, three years later: a debt strike and a central bank that can be turned also appear, on a global scale.
Both drown the world by melting the ice. Waterworld goes all the way to open sea; Robinson's New York keeps its towers and its rents.
Both flood Manhattan with climate change. The film does it in days; the novel does it over a century and then asks who owns the flooded property.

worlds.setting: Two centuries after a fusion drive opened the solar system, the familiar is still in place: an overcrowded Earth of thirty billion governed by the UN, a Mars settled in 2050 and generations into making a dead planet live, and a Belt of stations whose people mine the ice and metal that keep both alive and are treated as colonial labour. The single change is the Epstein Drive. There is no artificial gravity: ships burn halfway, flip, and burn again. The story opens in 2350 and spans centuries.
worlds.conflict: The engine is a colonial economy with three claimants and no exit: Earth needs the Belt's resources and holds the purse, Mars needs Earth's and resents the dependency, and the Belt does the dying work while being taxed, policed and called ungrateful. Every crisis runs through that structure - water riots, blockades, a stolen warship - and the alien substance on Phoebe only accelerates a fight that was already coming.
worlds.politics: Power sits with two governments and a diaspora: the UN on Earth, whose elections the off-worlders cannot vote in, and the Martian Congressional Republic, a militarised meritocracy where citizenship is earned through service and the terraforming project is the point of the nation. The Belt has no sovereign state of its own, only the Outer Planets Alliance - a union, a lobby and, at times, an armed movement that Earth and Mars both call terrorism.
worlds.technology: Hard, dirty, plausible engineering: fusion drives under months-long burn, patched vacuum suits, mag-boots instead of gravity, hand terminals that float data in the air, rail guns, torpedoes and point-defence cannons. Nothing is sleek. Air and water are metered, gravity is something only a spinning station or a burning drive provides, and the only truly incomprehensible thing in the system is the alien substance recovered from Phoebe - an artefact that treats living tissue as raw material and has no mind to negotiate with.
worlds.mood: Grubby, proud, claustrophobic. It plays as a western and a labour dispute in vacuum: people drinking in station bars under a dome, one hull breach from dying, and entirely certain that the inner planets will never see them as anything but hired help.
themes: us and them across a vacuum
found family on a borrowed ship
